en: The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Kapilavastu within the Nyagrodha Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that moment, all the Śākyas of this city gathered together in one place and said to one another:
"If someone were to come and ask us:..."
"Regarding the Śākya clan, who was its first ancestor?
From what did it arise?
What noble lineage of descendants does it possess?"
"If someone were to ask this question, how should I answer?
However, I do not yet know this sequence; it would be fitting for us to go together to the Blessed One and inquire about this matter, so that we may uphold it exactly as the Buddha explains."

Having deliberated thus, the Śākya sons went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and sat to one side. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they related the aforementioned matter in detail, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
If someone were to ask me:
"From what was the Śākya clan born?
Who was the very first?"
"Who is noble? What is their lineage?
How should one answer this?
“It is for such a matter that I have come to inquire.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will, out of compassion, explain it for me; as taught by the Buddha, I shall uphold it.
When the World-Honored One heard these words, he remained silent and reflected.
"If I were to speak of myself as being of noble descent within the Śākya clan, I fear the non-Buddhists would slander me, saying:
'The śramaṇa Gautama praises his own Śākya lineage as being of high and noble standing.'"
Again, he had this thought:
"Among my disciples, who is able to speak of this Śākya clan?
Knowing that Mahāmaudgalyāyana was skilled in speaking of this matter, he addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"I shall now enter meditative absorption; you are to explain the causal conditions for the Śākya clan.
Maudgalyāyana silently accepted the Buddha’s instruction.

At that time, the World-Honored One took his saṃghāṭī robe, folded it four times, and used it as a pillow. He lay on his right side with one foot upon the other, maintaining the perception of light and the perception of rising from meditation, thus attending to his mind.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"I shall now enter such a meditative absorption as to contemplate and observe so as to know the Śākya clan."
He immediately ascended the high seat before the assembly and sat cross-legged, addressing the Śākyas:
"Listen attentively, sirs!
When this world was first formed, the great earth was a single ocean of water; stirred by the wind, it became a uniform mass, like boiled milk."

Once it had cooled, solidification began to form; the surface of that ocean was likewise transformed, and upon it appeared the "savor of the earth" (pṛthivī-rasa), fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor.

When this world-system was forming, a class of sentient beings whose merit and lifespan were both exhausted passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn here. Their faculties were complete, their bodies possessed radiance, they traveled back and forth through the air, took joy as their food, and dwelt for a long time.
At that time, in this world, there were no sun, moon, stars, days, nights, or seasons; nor could one distinguish between male and female, or noble and lowly.
They merely called out to one another, saying: "Sattva!"
"Sattva! At that time, there was a sentient being among the assembly whose nature was to crave sensory pleasures; he suddenly tasted that "earth-flavor" with the tip of his finger.

As soon as he tasted it, a sense of attachment arose within him, and because of that attachment, solid food became his sustenance; it was at that moment that one may say he first partook of solid food.
When other sentient beings saw this eating, they immediately imitated them.
Once they had tasted the food, their bodies gradually became solid and heavy, and their radiance vanished, leaving all in total darkness.
Because their consumption was thus unregulated, their physical appearance and radiance diminished.
Due to this loss of physical luster, they said to one another:
"My form is radiant and pleasing, while yours has deteriorated."

Those who were radiant, relying on their physical form and complexion, gave rise to arrogance and produced unwholesome roots; because of these unwholesome conditions, the flavor of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) was extinguished.
Once the flavor of the earth had vanished, those sentient beings gathered together and, giving rise to mutual resentment, lamentation, weeping, and distress, spoke thus:
"How extraordinary is this delicious taste!"
"How wonderful is this delicious flavor!
Just as people of the present day, having once eaten fine food, often recall its former fragrance and taste, saying:
"How wonderful is this delicious flavor!"
"How wonderful is this delicious flavor!
Although they spoke these words, they still did not understand the meaning of its excellence or its faults. For what reason was it said that the *pṛthivī-rasa* (earth-flavor) vanished?

It was due to the karma of sentient beings that the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-cake) appeared, possessing color, fragrance, and delicious flavor in their entirety—like a golden flower or freshly ripened honey. They ate this earth-cake and lived for a long time.
Those who ate little possessed radiance on their bodies; because they were subsequently slighted and insulted, as described at length above, even the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-cakes) vanished.
Then all those sentient beings gathered in one place, looking at one another with sorrow and distress, and spoke these words:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"Alas! In the past, I once encountered such a calamity.
When the earth-cakes of these sentient beings disappear, it is likewise so; yet they do not know what this expression signifies.
"O virtuous ones, you should know!

Once the earth-cakes had vanished, by the power of their merit, forest creepers appeared to all sentient beings, endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor—like the *uṃbara* flower or fresh, ripened honey. They lived for a long time subsisting on these forest creepers."
Those who ate little possessed a radiance of the body; because they looked down upon one another, it unfolded extensively as previously described.
Eventually, when the forest creepers vanished, all sentient beings gathered in one place, looking at each other with sorrow and speaking these words:
"Depart from my presence!"
"Depart from my presence!
Just as when people harbor extreme resentment toward one another and refuse to allow each other to stand before them—as described at length above—so it was.

Once the forest creepers had vanished, sentient beings possessed a wondrous fragrant rice that grew spontaneously without being sown; it was free of husks and chaff, stood four finger-widths high, and would regrow immediately after being harvested in the morning or evening, the grain ripening by the evening or morning.
Although they took it repeatedly, there was no change in its appearance; by using this as food, they lived for a long time.

At that time, because those sentient beings had solid food, impurities accumulated within their bodies. To eliminate these, two passages were formed, from which the male and female organs subsequently arose, leading them to become mutually attached through passion.
Because they gave rise to defiled attachment, they subsequently drew near to one another and thereby committed unrighteous acts.
When other sentient beings saw this, they vied with one another to pelt them with refuse, shards, and stones, saying:
"You are detestable sentient beings who commit such unrighteous deeds!"
"Alas! For what reason do you now defile and insult sentient beings?

From the first night until the seventh night, they shall not dwell together with him and shall be cast out from the assembly—just as today, when a marriage is first celebrated, people scatter fragrant flowers and various objects while exclaiming their vows:
"May you always attain peace and happiness! You should know this:

that which was not Dharma in the past is now Dharma; that which was not Vinaya in the past is now Vinaya; that which was despised and held in contempt in the past is now considered excellent and sublime."

Because those people had driven him out at that time, those who delighted in practicing evil subsequently gathered together, constructed dwellings to shelter their bodies, and committed unrighteous acts; this was the first establishment of a household, and thus the institution of family life arose.
"Virtuous ones, you should know!
In the past, because of lustful desire, people constructed houses; they acted according to what was not the Dharma, treating that which is contrary to the Dharma as the Dharma."
Those sentient beings, whether at the time of sunset or at the time of sunrise, would gather rice daily according to their hunger so that no remainder was left.
Then, one sentient being, out of laziness, rose in the morning and gathered the rice for both the morning and the evening together.
When evening arrived, a companion called out to him to go together and gather rice.
The man replied, "You take it yourself; I came this morning and already gathered enough rice for two meals."
"You should go yourself; I shall not trouble myself to go.
When his companion heard these words, he praised him in his heart, saying:
"This is also very good; when I fetch [the rice] now, I shall take enough for two days' worth of grain as well."
At that time, another companion, having heard these words, spoke again:
"I shall bring three days' worth of rice.
Yet another companion, having heard these words, spoke again:
"I have gathered seven days' worth of rice," he said,
and he returned home with that seven days' worth of rice.
There was another companion who came to call him to gather rice together, and the man replied:
"I have already taken seven days' worth of rice; there is no need for you to trouble yourself by going again.
Upon hearing this, the man was again filled with joy and exclaimed, "This is a great convenience!
I shall go today to fetch fifteen days' or even a month's worth of rice."
In this manner, the number gradually doubled from its former measure; because this greedy mind increased day by day, husks and impurities consequently grew within the rice.
At first, what was harvested in the morning would grow back by evening, and what was harvested in the evening would grow back by morning, and the grain remained excellent.

However, due to greed and attachment, once it had been harvested, it would no longer grow back; even when it did grow, the grain gradually became smaller and inferior. Thereupon, people vied with one another to harvest and gather it, so that whatever remained became increasingly small and poor in quality.
Then those sentient beings gathered once more in one place and lamented to one another, saying:
"In former times, our bodies were radiant and joyful, we could fly about with ease, we were endowed with perfect beauty, and we took delight as our food."

Later, we took the essence of the earth as our food, which was still fragrant and excellent; however, because we consumed much of this essence of the earth, our bodies became solid and heavy, our radiance was consequently extinguished, and our supernormal powers (ṛddhi) then faded away.
Due to encountering various calamities that caused darkness and ruin, all people wept with grief, which gave rise to the sun, moon, and stars, as described in detail above.
Those who ate much became dark in complexion, while those who ate little remained radiant and joyful.
Due to these two types of food, they consequently came to have two distinct physical appearances.
Because of these two distinct appearances, they began to disparage one another, saying:
"I am handsome, while you are ugly."
Because these people thus disparaged one another and successively gave rise to unwholesome thoughts, the *pṛthivī-rasa* (earth-essence) was completely extinguished.
The people lamented in sorrow, after which *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-cakes) appeared, fully endowed with color, fragrance, and delicious flavor.
We ate it and lived for a long time; however, those who ate much saw their bodily radiance grow dim, while those who ate little remained radiant and pleasant in appearance.
Due to these two types of physical conditions, two classes—superior and inferior—eventually emerged, leading eventually to mutual disparagement and contempt.
Due to their mutual contempt and because they each gave rise to unwholesome thoughts, the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-cake) was completely destroyed, leaving us in a state of grief and distress.
For this reason, the *vanalatā* (forest-vines) arose once more, possessing all qualities of color, fragrance, and delicious flavor.
We have lived in this world for a long time,
yet those who eat much have their bodily radiance diminished and darkened, while those who eat little remain radiant and joyful.

Eventually, when the forest creepers perished, rice grains arose again; they grew spontaneously without being sown, were free from husks and chaff, and were four finger-widths in size, endowed with perfect fragrance and flavor.
We ate them and our bodies became full and robust; those who ate this rice lived for a long time and remained in the world for a long duration.

Because they gathered it with a mind of greed, that rice became small, poor, and increasingly covered in husks and chaff; the rice lost its vitality, ceased to grow after harvest, and sometimes there were leftovers.
Having seen this, the people said to one another,
"Let us divide the territory among ourselves.
At that time, they measured out the plots of land and demarcated their boundaries, dividing them respectively.
"This is your land; this is my land.
For this reason, the cultivation of fields began in the world, and boundaries were subsequently established.
Furthermore, although one sentient being had his own field, he privately stole another's grain. When another sentient being saw this, he said to him:
"Why have you now taken another's rice?
This is a single instance of theft; do not do it again.
However, that sentient being’s intent to steal did not cease, and he took it away again on the second day and the third day as well.
When the people saw him, they spoke to him again, saying:
"You have committed private theft three times previously.
They exhorted him repeatedly without ceasing, and some sentient beings then proceeded to seize him and bring him before the assembly to recount the matter in detail.
The crowd spoke together, saying:
"You have your own fields; why did you steal the grain from another's field three times?
Having exhorted him with these words, they immediately released him.
The one who had stolen the rice said to the great assembly:
"These sentient beings, for the sake of a small amount of rice, have now destroyed me; before this great assembly, they have brought me disgrace."
The great assembly spoke again:
"Why, for the sake of a small amount of rice, did you seize a sentient being, destroy him, and humiliate him before the public?
You must not act thus in the future."
"Because of this theft, they insulted one another in turn. For this reason, the great assembly gathered together and addressed one another, saying:
'You all have witnessed this matter; because of stealing the grain of others, they insulted each other before the assembly. We do not know which of these two is guilty.'"

"We intend to select one sentient being from among this assembly—one who is handsome in appearance, possessed of a complete physical form, and endowed with penetrating wisdom—and establish him as the lord of the earth."
Those who have transgressions shall be punished; those who are without transgression shall be nurtured.
Regarding the fields cultivated by us, the multitude, each shall, according to the law, grant one-sixth share to you.
At that time, from among the assembly, they selected a person endowed with the aforementioned virtues and immediately established him as the lord of the land.
Then the people addressed the lord of the land, saying:
"If there is anyone among the multitude who commits an offense, we request that you punish them according to the law."
If there is one who does not commit offenses, they should be supported and nurtured.
Regarding the fields cultivated by our community, each person shall, according to the law, give one-sixth of the harvest to him.
For this reason, he was established as the Lord of the Earth.
At that time, the Lord of the Earth, seeing those people, would punish those who had transgressions according to the law, and nurture those who were without offense according to the law.
At that time, the fields cultivated by the multitude were each given one-sixth share according to the law.
Because the multitude had agreed to establish him as their lord of the land, he received the name "Mahāsammata" (Greatly Agreed Upon);
because he was able to protect the weak and vulnerable, he received the name "Kṣatriya."

Ruling the country according to the Dharma, he was able to bring joy to all sentient beings; because of his virtuous conduct and wisdom, he was titled the Great King of Universal Accord (*Mahā-saṃmata*).
When that king was established, people called one another "sentient being" (*sattva*).
King Mahāsaṃmata had a son named Manu, whom he immediately established as king.
At that time, sentient beings were called Upaga.
King Manu had a son named Sudatta.
Furthermore, O virtuous ones!
During the time of King Kuśaladatta, all sentient beings were called "Spots" (Śyāma).
King Kuśaladatta had a son named Varasudatta, whom he immediately established as king.
At that time, sentient beings were known as Meghasvara.
King Varasena had a son named Vimala, whom he established as king.
At that time, sentient beings were known as Tālaśamga.
Upon the crown of King Dīrghāyu’s head there was a tumor, as soft as fine cotton or a cluster of flowers; though it grew larger, it never caused him pain or distress.

Later, it gradually ripened and burst open, from which emerged a young boy with a handsome countenance, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man. Because he was born from the crown of the king's head and thus adorned his body, he was named Mūrdhaja (Crown-Born).

At that time, King Jyotiṣprabha had sixty thousand consorts. When the father-king brought Mūrdhaja into the inner palace, the sixty thousand consorts, upon seeing him, each conceived a feeling of affection and milk flowed from their breasts; they all said to the king, "I will nurse him!"
"I shall nourish you!
For this reason, he was further named "Sustainer" (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) and was established as king.
At that time, all sentient beings reflected upon their situation, consulted one another, distinguished between the good and the bad, and each practiced a specific craft.

At that time, because those sentient beings reflected deeply, they were called Unnusa—meaning "Human"—just like the six preceding kings; their lifespan was immeasurable years, and they dwelt long in the world.
At that time, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had a small ulcer on his right thigh, which was as soft as cotton or a cluster of flowers; although it grew larger, he never experienced pain or distress.
Later, as it gradually matured and split open, a single boy was born, whose appearance was upright and handsome, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man that adorned his body.

Because of his upright beauty, he was named Danyang (Upright and Majestic); he was immediately established as king, possessing great majesty and power, ruling over the four great continents and attaining great sovereignty.
At that time, on the left thigh of King Endaraṇya, a sore suddenly appeared; this sore was as soft as layers of cotton or flowers, and though it grew larger, it never caused him pain or distress.

Later, as it gradually ripened and burst open, a young boy was born, whose appearance was upright and majestic, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man upon his body. Because he was upright and majestic like the King's attendant, he was named Upacāru; he was then immediately established as king.
He also possessed great power, ruling with sovereign influence over the three great continents.

Once, a small sore suddenly appeared on the upper part of the right foot of King Upacāru; the sore was as soft as layers of cotton or flowers, and although it grew daily, it caused him no pain or distress.

Later, as it gradually ripened and split open, a young boy was born, his physical form upright and handsome, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man. Because he was born from the right foot, he was named "Born from the Upright Foot" (Dṛḍhapāda), and he was immediately established as king.
Possessing majestic power and sovereignty, he ruled over two great continents.

At that time, on the upper part of King Sundarapāda’s left foot, a sore suddenly appeared; this sore was as soft as layers of cotton or flowers, and although it grew daily, it caused him no pain or distress.

Later, as it gradually matured and split open, a single boy was born, whose appearance was upright and handsome, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man that adorned his body. Because he was born from the left foot and was exceedingly dignified, he was named Paramaśobhana (Extremely Handsome), and he was immediately established as king.
Possessing majestic power and sovereignty, he ruled over one great continent.
This King Mahāsaṃmata’s son was named Saṃpāti; Saṃpāti’s son was named Sudatta. Sudatta—
The son of King Guṇarāja was named Jayanta; the son of King Jayanta was named Viśuddha;
the son of King Viśuddha was named Poṣa; the son of King Poṣa was named Abhirūpa; the son of King Abhirūpa was named Upābhirūpa;
the son of King Upābhirūpa was named Abhirūpaka; the son of King Abhirūpaka was named Atirūpa.
The son of King Paramaśobhana was named Priya; the son of King Priya was named Supriya; the son of King Supriya was named Tyāgin;
the son of King Tyāgin was named Atityāgin; the son of King Atityāgin was named Rathakūṭa;
the son of King Rathakūṭa was named Rathaśobhana; the son of King Rathaśobhana was named Sāgara.
King Lesser Ocean had a son named King Middle Ocean; King Middle Ocean had a son named King Great Ocean;
King Great Ocean had a son named King Auspicious Bird; King Auspicious Bird’s son was named King Great Auspicious Bird;
King Great Auspicious Bird had a son named King Fragrant Herb; and King Fragrant Herb’s son was named King Near-Fragrance.
Cāru had a son named Upacāru-rāja; Upacāru-rāja had a son named Mahācāru;
Mahācāru had a son named Sudarśana; Sudarśana had a son named Mahāsudarśana;
Mahāsudarśana had a son named Atirāga; Atirāga had a son named Mahārāga; Mahārāga had a son named Citra.
The sound *Śabda* has a pause called *Suśabda*; *Suśabda* has a pause called *Prabhākara*;
*Prabhākara* has a pause called *Tejasvin*; *Tejasvin* has a pause called *Vipula*;
*Vipula* has a pause called *Mahāmeru*; *Mahāmeru* has a pause called *Merumālin*.
Mereu had a son named Vipula-mati; Vipula-mati had a son named Prabhasa;
Prabhasa had a son named Prabhāsa; and Prabhāsa had a son named Mahāprabha.

"There was a king named Mahāpaṅka; this King Mahāpaṅka had sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons who were reborn as his descendants in the city of Bhaddiya for as many as a hundred generations."
The last of these kings was named Dāmaratha; because he was able to subdue all enemies, he was called King Dāmaratha.

In the city of Ayodhyā, his descendants reigned as kings for fifty-four thousand generations, governing the world through the True Dharma within that city. The last of these kings was named Aparājita; in the city of Vārāṇasī, his descendants reigned as kings for sixty-three generations, governing the world through the True Dharma within that city. The last of these kings was named Durjaya.
In the past, in the city of Kimpila, descendants reigned as kings for eighty-four thousand generations; the last of those kings was named Brahmadatta.
"Furthermore, O people!

In the city of Hatthigāma, the descendants of King Brahmadatta reigned as kings for thirty-two thousand generations, governing the world according to the True Dharma (Saddharma). The last of these kings was named Hatthipāla."
In the city of Śailapura, the descendants of King Hastidatta reigned as kings for five thousand generations; the last of these kings was named Kālaśoka.

At that time, in the city of Viśāṃpṛṣṭha, his descendants reigned as kings for thirty-two thousand generations, governing the world through the True Dharma; the last of these kings was named Kumārabalavijit.

Furthermore, King Śaktivaipulya had descendants who reigned in the city of Anabhibhūta; for thirty-two thousand generations they ruled the world with the True Dharma, and the last of these kings was named Uttaraśakti.

Furthermore, after that supreme king, his descendants reigned as kings in the city of Sundarī, continuing for twelve thousand generations who governed the world through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Jayasena.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!

In the city of Campā, the descendants of King Jayasena reigned as kings, continuing for eighteen thousand generations while they governed the world with the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Nāgadeva.
Furthermore, sirs!

The Dragon Heavenly King’s descendants reigned as kings within the city of Māli, continuing for twenty-five thousand generations who governed the world through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Manuṣyadeva.
Furthermore, sirs!

In the city of Tāmraliptī, the sons and grandsons of that Heavenly King reigned as kings for twelve thousand generations, transforming the world through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Sāgaradeva.
Furthermore, O noble ones!

In the city of Nandipura, the sons and grandsons of the Deva-king Sāgara succeeded one another as kings for eighteen thousand generations, transforming the world through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Kalyāṇamati.
Furthermore, O virtuous ones!

In the city of Rājagṛha, the descendants of King Sudhīra reigned as kings for twenty-five thousand generations, transforming the world through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Tamonuda.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!

King Divākara’s descendants reigned in the city of Vārāṇasī, continuing for as many as one hundred generations who governed the world through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Mahāsena.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!

In the city of Kuśinagara, the descendants of King Mahāsena reigned as kings for eighty-four thousand generations, governing the world through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Sāgaradeva.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!

In the city of Potalaka, the sons and grandsons of that Sea King reigned as kings for a thousand successive generations, governing the world through the Dharma; the last of these sovereigns was named Sādhu-caryā.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!

In the city of Kuśinagara, the descendants of that King Cakravartin reigned as kings for eighty-four thousand generations, governing the world through the True Dharma (Saddharma). The last of these kings was named Viśālamukha.
Furthermore, sirs!

King Pṛthu’s descendants succeeded one another in the city of Vārāṇasī, continuing for as many as one hundred thousand generations, transforming people through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Bhūmipati.
Furthermore, sirs!

In the city of Ayodhyā, the lineage of that sovereign king was passed down from son to grandson for a thousand generations. The last of these kings was named Mahīdhara, who ruled his people in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!
King Dharaṇīdhara’s lineage, through successive generations of sons and grandsons, ruled the world with the True Dharma for eighty-four thousand reigns; the last of these kings was named Mahādeva.

"Furthermore, sirs! In the city of Mithilā, the lineage of that Great Heavenly King (Mahādeva) continued through eighty-four thousand generations, all of whom were named Mahādeva. They all attained the supernormal powers of the rishis and practiced the conduct of the precepts, transforming people through the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Nimi."
King Nimi had a son named King Sañjaya.
That king had a son named Jita, next named Khāṇu, next named Upakhāṇu,
next named Atikhāṇu, next named Sukhī, next named Sudarśana, and next named Sañjaya.
Next is named Army Hearing; next is named Realization; next is named Great Awakening; next is named Awakening Army;
next is named Free from Sorrow; next is named Departed from Sorrow; next is named Continuing the Fruit;
next is named Skillful Union; next is named Great Sound; next is named Slayer of Great Sound; next is named Bright Dawn; next is named Enclosure.
The lords are, in order: named Strife, named Arising of Fear, named Joyful Celebration,
named Mirror Gate, named Able to Produce, named Universal Production, named Most Excellent, named Food and Drink,
named Abundant Food and Drink, named Hard to Conquer, and named Extremely Hard to Conquer.
First is named *An-sthāpana* (Establishment), next is named *Su-sthāpana* (Good Establishment), next is named *Mahābala* (Great Power),

next is named *Vijayabala* (Victorious Power), next is named *Sudhī* (Good Wisdom), next is named *Vijaya-dṛḍha* (Victorious Firmness), next is named *Daśadhanus* (Ten Bows), next is named *Śatadhanus* (Hundred Bows),
next is named *Navadhanus* (New Bows), next is named *Varṇadhana* (Excellent-Colored Bow), next is named *Vijayadhanus* (Victorious Bow), and next is named *Dṛḍha* (Firm).
The bow is next called the ten-fathom, next the hundred-fathom, next the thousand-fathom,
next the beautiful-colored fathom, and next the firm fathom.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!
The kings of Lāḍya reigned in the city of Sāṃyāti, their lineage succeeding one another for seventy-seven thousand generations; the last of those kings was named Phalada-rāja.
Furthermore, O worthy ones!
The King of the Fruit-Sages had a son named Nāgapāla.
In the city of Vārāṇasī, the lineage of Nāgapāla continued through one hundred successive generations of descendants; the last king of that line was named Kṛkin.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān Kāśyapa appeared in the world.
At that time, that Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, having resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of Kāśyapa Buddha, purified his brahmacarya and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Furthermore, sirs! King Kṛkī had a son named Sujāta.
Furthermore, sirs!
King Sujāta’s descendants reigned in the city of Puṇḍravardhana for one hundred generations; the last of those kings was named Karṇaja.
Furthermore, O noble ones!
King Karṇa had two sons:
one named Gautama and the other named Pradyota.
That Gautama desired to renounce the household life, while Pradyota desired to be the king.
When Gautama saw that his father, the king, treated what was not the Dharma as the Dharma and the Dharma as not the Dharma while governing the affairs of state, he thought to himself:

"If my father, the king, passes away and I become king, I too shall treat the Dharma as not the Dharma and what is not the Dharma as the Dharma; by governing the country in such a manner, I shall fall into hell."
"Since this difficulty exists, what skillful means should I employ to leave the household life and escape from this suffering?
Having formed this thought, he went to his father the king, prostrated himself, joined his palms, and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know!"
"I wish to renounce the household life and go forth into homelessness.
The king said to his son:

"For the sake of profit and benefit, many people give away their wealth and possessions, making offerings to celestial deities and performing fire-worship and ascetic penances, seeking the rank of a king."
"You have now attained this; after I have passed away, you shall succeed to the throne.
For what reason do you now abandon this and depart? Gautama replied:
"I have seen that the king treats what is unrighteous as righteous and what is righteous as unrighteous; due to this sinful karma, I shall fall into hell.
Now, filled with fear, I pray to leave the household life."
"Great King, have compassion!
Grant this wish of mine.
At that time, the king, knowing that his son’s heart was entirely set on leaving the household life, immediately spoke to him:
"I now release you; go as you please.
When the prince heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy.
Not far from there lived a rishi named Kṛṣṇa.

At that time, the prince prostrated before his father the king and his retinue, took his leave, and departed for the abode of the sage Kṛṣṇa. Arriving there, he knelt according to the ritual and bowed his head at the sage's feet, saying to him:
"I wish to renounce the household life; I pray that the sage, out of compassion, will grant me ordination."
The seer then granted his permission.
Once the prince had gone forth, he sought fruits, tree bark, and roots for his sustenance; thus, the world came to call him the Seer Gautama.
At that time, the father-king passed away, and the second prince, Pradyota, was immediately established as king.
At that time, the seer Gautama, because he habitually ate fruits and various tree leaves, subsequently fell ill. He said to his preceptor:
"I now wish to enter a village to beg for food and drink."
The Black Seer replied: "The Seers have a teaching:
namely, guarding the six sense faculties and remaining detached from the six objects of the senses; whether one stays in mountain valleys or enters a village, one has nothing to fear."
"If you can maintain such a rishi’s dharma, you may go as you please.
You may build a grass hut near the city of Potala and dwell there.
At that time, Gautama prostrated before his teacher, took his leave, and departed. He went to the city of Potala, built a grass hut in a secluded grove, and sustained himself by begging for alms.
"At that time, in the city of Puṇḍravardhana, there was a courtesan named Kāśisundarī, whose physical appearance was so upright and beautiful that she was beloved by all.
At that moment, there was a wicked man named Mithilā who, driven by lustful desire, sent various necklaces and exquisite garments to her, intending to take her as his wife."
At that time, the woman, adorned with various necklaces and fine garments, was about to go out.
Then, by the side of the gate, she saw a man who gave her five hundred silver coins and spoke these words: "Come here!"
"Come here! Let us play together.
The girl thought to herself:
"I have now obtained five hundred silver coins; why should I not take them?
It would be unreasonable for me not to take them.
Having thus taken the money, he dallied with her.
At that time, the courtesan sent a female attendant to Mṛṇāla and said to him:
"I have not yet finished my adornments; I will come shortly."
Having received these instructions, the female attendant went to Mṛṇāla and reported the matter in full.
At that time, the owner of the silver coins had other business and departed immediately.
At that time, the courtesan thought again:
"This man has already departed; it is not too late for me to go to my former place.
She said to her attendant girl:
She went to Mṛṇāla and spoke these words:
"I have finished my adornments; I do not yet know in which garden you would meet with me."
Then that maidservant, having received these instructions, went to Mṛṇāla and reported the matter in full.
Mṛṇāla replied: "You foolish woman! You have said:..."
“Is she not yet adorned? or “She is fully adorned.
At that time, a certain maidservant who harbored resentment toward her mistress said to her:
"My mistress is not unadorned; she intends to adorn her body with your necklace and garments so that she may go see another suitor.
When Madanika heard these words, his lustful desire subsided and a malicious intent arose within him. He then said to the maidservant:
"Inform the courtesan that once her adornments are complete, she is to come to such-and-such a grove."
Then that maidservant went to the courtesan and related the matter in detail.
Upon hearing these words, the courtesan adorned herself with necklaces and ornaments and went to that grove to see Madanika.
Mṛṇāla immediately became angry and said, "Shame on you, harlot!
Why do you take my necklaces and fine garments to see another suitor?"
The courtesan replied, “Noble son!
It is the constant failing of women; I pray you will forgive this transgression.”
At that time, Mithilā immediately gave rise to anger and resentment, drew a sharp sword, and killed that courtesan.
Then her female attendant cried out these words: "Thief!"
"Thieves!
They have killed our master!
Upon hearing this, the multitude all gathered at that place.
At that time, there was a seer named Gautama sitting in a grass hut within the grove.

When Madana saw the assembly gathered, fear arose in his heart and he had no place to hide; he then took his blood-stained sword, went to the seer’s location, placed it before the grass hut, and stood with the crowd.
At that time, the crowd, seeing the dead girl, followed her tracks until they found the bloody knife before the grass hut; they immediately seized the rishi and spoke these words:
"You have the form of a rishi; why have you committed such an evil deed?"
Then the seer replied,
"What fault have I committed?
The crowd informed him, saying:
"You have committed an unrighteous act with a woman and furthermore taken her life.
The rishi replied, "I truly did not commit such an evil deed."
The people did not believe him, so they immediately seized and bound him, bringing him before the king and saying to the Great King:
"This man committed an illicit act with that courtesan and then killed her."

Upon hearing these words, the king did not inquire further, but ordered that the seer be placed upon a sharp wooden stake and a red garland be placed upon his head. He commanded the Caṇḍālas to dress themselves in blue garments and each hold a sharp sword, surrounding him on all sides. Leading the seer through the city while beating drums to proclaim the news, he addressed the people, saying:
"You should know that this seer has committed such a crime."
He went out through the southern gate and threw the seer onto the point of a sharp stake.
At that time, the seer Kṛṣṇa came searching for him, not knowing where he was;
seeking him everywhere, he saw him thrown upon the sharp stake. He was deeply grieved and distressed, weeping as he asked:
"For what reason have you encountered such suffering?
At that time, Gautama choked with sobs and wept as he said to his upādhyāya:
"This is the result of past karma; who could possibly avoid or escape it?"
The preceptor said: "O virtuous son!
Now that you have been wounded, has your body and mind retreated from the practice of the various dharmas?"
He replied to his teacher, saying,
"Although my body is now wounded, my mind remains unharmed. His preceptor said:
"How shall I know this?
He replied to his teacher, "I utter words of truth; I have never spoken falsely."
"If my mind and conduct have truly not changed, may the venerable preceptor’s dark complexion turn to gold.
As soon as these words were spoken, the seer transformed into a golden color, and the news spread in all four directions:
"The Black Seer has turned into a Golden One."
When his teacher saw this sincere aspiration, he felt a mixture of wonder and joy, exclaiming that it was truly rare.
Then the seer Gautama spoke again to his teacher, saying:
"When I now cast off my life, what path shall I attain?"
The teacher replied:
"O virtuous son!
According to the teachings of the true Brahmins among the non-Buddhists, one who has no son shall not attain the good path."
"Do you have a son?

He replied, "In the past, while I was still a youth within the palace, I took pleasure in the path of cultivation. I then abandoned my home and family to constantly practice the holy life; how could I have obtained a son?"
The teacher said, "If it is so,
you should reflect upon past events. He replied:
"I am now so deeply wounded that my pain is extreme; every joint and limb feels as if it were being cut by a blade, and I think only of giving up my life.
How could I possibly give rise to any other thought?"
Then his preceptor, by means of supernatural power, raised a great wind and rain that bathed Gautama’s body, whereupon his suffering was finally relieved.
Recalling past acts of lust, there were then two drops of semen and blood within his body that fell from his person to the ground.
By the power of karma, they immediately became two eggs.
As stated in other sūtras, there are four kinds of inconceivable matters:
first, the inconceivability of the realm of all Buddhas;
second, the inconceivability of nāgas; [and so forth].
Third is the inconceivability of the mental states of worldly beings;
fourth is the inconceivability of the power of the karmic maturation of all sentient beings.
Due to the force of that karma, an egg is subsequently formed.
"Because those eggs were warmed by the heat of the sun's rays, they gradually matured, and from each was born a boy.

Not far from the place where they were born was a sugarcane grove; the two boys then went to play within that grove, and by the power of their merit, their countenances grew increasingly radiant day by day."
That Gautama, scorched by the sun’s rays, then passed away.

At that time, the golden-colored rishi came to visit Gautama at dawn; seeing that he had died and observing the broken eggs upon the ground, he followed the boy’s tracks to the sugarcane grove, where he found the boy.
At that time, the seer entered meditative concentration and observed: "From where have these two youths come?
Whose sons are they?
He immediately knew them to be the biological descendants of that Gautama.

Feeling affection for them, he took the two boys back to his residence and nurtured them daily until they gradually grew up. He then gave them names, calling the elder "Warmth-Born" (Uṣṇa-jāta), and because of this, they were known as the Solar Lineage (Sūryavaṃśa).
Furthermore, because he is a descendant of the Gautama lineage, he is also called Gautama.
Because he was born from the physical body [of his father], he is called "Body-born" (Kāyaja).
Moreover, because he was found within a sugarcane grove, he is also called "Sugarcane Seed" (Ikṣvāku).
Due to these four conditions, there are these four titles.
At another time, King Brahmadatta died without an heir, and the ministers deliberated together:
"The king had no son; whom shall we appoint to succeed him?"
Then a minister said:
"The king has an elder brother, Gautama, who previously entered the mountains to practice the Way; according to the order of his lineage, he is the rightful successor to the throne."
Having deliberated thus, they went to where the golden-colored seer was, and upon arrival, they prostrated with palms joined and said:
"Great Seer! Where is our king’s elder brother, the seer Gautama, now?"
The Golden Immortal replied,
"He has already been killed by you all. Thereupon,
the ministers spoke again to the Immortal, saying:
"He, Gautama, has never been seen by any of you since he first went forth into homelessness; how then could he have been killed?
The Golden Immortal replied, "I shall cause you to know for yourselves: Gautama was without fault; he was unjustly killed by you."
The multitude spoke again, asking, "How shall we kill him?
At that time, the Golden Seer recounted the aforementioned matter; having heard it, all the people said to the Seer:
"Truly, we are guilty of transgression.
Having said this, the two youths immediately went to the side of the Golden Sage (Suvarṇa-ṛṣi).
The people asked:
"Of what lineage are these two youths?
The Golden Sage replied,
"These two youths are the sons of Gautama."
The people spoke again:
"How is it that he exists? What is his name?"

At that time, the Golden Immortal recounted the aforementioned events; upon hearing this, everyone was filled with great joy. They immediately requested the elder youth from the presence of the immortal to accompany them back to their kingdom, where he was subsequently enthroned as king.
Not long after that king had been ruling the country, he passed away without leaving any heirs.
At that time, the ministers went into the mountains and invited his younger brother to succeed him to the royal throne; the assembly established his title as King Ikṣvāku.
"Furthermore, O people!

At that time, the Ikṣvāku King [reigned] in the city of Potalaka (translated in Chinese as 'Youngest Son'). His descendants succeeded one another for one hundred generations, all of whom were kings of the Ikṣvāku lineage. The last of these kings was named Senāpati."
"O people, you should know that King Ikṣvāku, also named Virūḍhaka, had four chief queens, each of whom gave birth to one son and one daughter.
These four princes were:
the first was named Ulkāmukha;"
The second was named Great-Eared;
the third, Elephant-Walk;
and the fourth, King Jewel-Bangle.
There were four consorts, all of whom had passed away; at that time, King Ikṣvāku Senāpati was dwelling within the palace, overcome with grief, sorrow, and distress.
When various people entered the palace and saw that King Senāpati was despondent and unhappy, they came forward and said to the king:
"For what reason, O King, are you now so full of grief and anxiety?"
The king replied, "My principal queen has now passed away; how could I not give rise to grief and distress?
At that time, the ministers spoke together to the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty feels sorrow on this account, the kings of neighboring lands all have fine daughters; Your Majesty should command me to appoint one as your consort.
The king replied again, "I have four sons, all of whom are grown and capable of succeeding to the throne. For this reason, who would give their daughter to me to be my queen?"
The ministers replied, "Your Majesty,
simply issue the command, and we shall search for one in all four directions on Your Majesty's behalf.
At that time, there was a certain king whose daughter was exceedingly beautiful and fit to be consecrated as a queen.
When the ministers learned of this, they immediately came to inform the king:
"Your Majesty, we have now learned that the daughter of such-and-such a king is of upright and beautiful countenance, worthy to be your queen.
The king said:
"Very well," he replied.
He immediately dispatched a royal envoy to the woman's location; upon arriving, he paid his respects to the king of that country.
The king asked the envoy:
"This country is remote and secluded; how have you come here?
At that time, the messenger said to the king:

"The commander of my army and the Great Lady of our kingdom have both passed away. Hearing that Your Majesty has a daughter worthy to be the queen of our state, I have been sent to consult you on this matter."
Having heard this, the king immediately granted permission and further addressed the messenger, saying:
"If your king wishes to form an alliance with me, he must first establish a covenant with me: that when my daughter bears a son, he shall surely succeed to the throne."
Having heard this, the messenger said to the king:
"When I return to my own country, I shall report this matter in full.
Thereupon, the messenger returned to his own country, prostrated before the king, and reported the aforementioned events in detail. The king said:
"I have an eldest son; even if he were to father a child, would you let that one succeed to the throne?
At that time, the ministers deliberated with the king, saying:
"Your Majesty should simply take her as a consort; she may give birth to a son, or perhaps a daughter, or she may be barren."
"Why does Your Majesty now first worry about this matter?
I pray that Your Majesty will soon seek me out so that we may enjoy ourselves together. The King said:

"Very well," he replied, and immediately dispatched a messenger to the kingdom of the woman to establish a prior covenant. Then, in accordance with the laws of that land, she was welcomed back to become his queen.

At that time, King Vardhana and his consort, dwelling within the inner palace, indulged in pleasure and delight; their sensual craving ran so high that they could not set it aside for even a moment. Consequently, she became pregnant, and when ten months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was so upright and handsome that all people held him dear.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka entrusted her to eight nurses to raise her.
When she was first taken as a maiden, the king and his ministers had made a solemn vow together:
"If this girl gives birth to a son, he shall be established as king and named Priya."
In later times, as he gradually grew up, his complexion flourished like a lotus emerging from the water.
Then, King Vaḍiṣṭha, wishing to install his eldest son as the crown prince, did not install Priyadarśana.
When the King, the Queen’s father, heard these words, he immediately dispatched a messenger with a letter to King Virūḍhaka, saying:
"For what reason do you now violate the vow previously established?"
"If you violate your former vow, I shall raise an army to punish your kingdom; you must prepare your troops to await me.
When King Virūḍhaka had read this letter, he assembled his ministers and informed them, saying:
"The father-king of the Queen has now sent a letter, detailing the aforementioned matters. How should we devise a plan to deal with him?"
The ministers deliberated and said, "That king possesses great power and majesty; we should establish Priyadarśana as the crown prince. King Vardhana said:
"I have an eldest son; how can I establish that younger one as the crown prince?
At that time, the ministers addressed the king again, saying:
"That king possesses a powerful fourfold army; if Your Majesty does not grant permission, he will surely invade us."
"I now request that Your Majesty enshrine that beloved son as the Crown Prince, and banish the other four sons beyond the borders of the kingdom.
Then King Vardhana said to his ministers:
"My four sons have committed no transgressions; how can I cast them out beyond the borders?"
The ministers replied, "We are the king's subjects and wish to act for his benefit.
We truly cannot summarily cast out those who are without fault; however, those who possess faults and transgressions must not be allowed to remain."
Having heard this, the king remained silent.
Then, all the ministers gathered in one place and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"O worthy ones, you should know!..."
"We shall deliberate together and devise a plan to cause the King to hate those four sons.
Thereupon, they constructed a garden, sweeping and sprinkling the ground, scattering various fragrant flowers, and hanging up banners and canopies to adorn it.
At that time, the four princes went out for recreation and, seeing the garden from afar, felt a sense of longing and affection for it; they proceeded to the garden gate.
The park superintendent, having completed his preparations for its adornment, was coming out through the gate when the four princes asked him: "To whom does this garden belong?"
The official replied, "This is the king’s garden.
Having heard this, the four sons turned back and departed immediately. The minister spoke again, saying:
"Why did you turn back and not enter the garden?
The four sons replied, "This is the father-king's garden; how would we dare to enter it?"
The ministers said, "Both the King and the Prince may enjoy their pastimes together; what fault is there in this?
Having heard this, the Prince immediately entered to play.
Having seen this, the ministers hurried to the king’s presence and addressed him, saying:
"Great King, you should know!
The garden ordered by Your Majesty to be cultivated has now been made magnificent and pure; we pray that Your Majesty will go there in person for recreation."
Then King Virūḍhaka immediately commanded, saying:
"Who has provided this music?
The ministers replied:
"The four princes are enjoying themselves therein.
Upon hearing these words, the king became greatly incensed and said: "Go there and kill them for me!"
The ministers all knelt and addressed the king, saying:
"We pray that Your Majesty, out of compassion, will not take his life; if Your Majesty finds him objectionable, let him merely be banished from the country.
Upon hearing this, the king granted their request.
At that time, having received the king’s command, the ministers immediately summoned the princes to the king’s presence and ordered them to leave the country.
Then the four sons, with their four feet planted firmly upon the ground, joined their palms and addressed the king:
“We, your four sons, beg for one favor: we wish that those among our retinues who desire to follow us may be permitted by Your Majesty’s compassionate grace to go with us.”
The king said to his sons,
"Fulfill your wishes. Thereupon,
the four princes each took their respective sister and intended to leave the country.
At that time, the people of the kingdom also wished to follow him; within seven days, the multitude of citizens who had followed were nearly exhausted.
Then the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"If you do not close these city gates, we fear the populace will be completely depleted."
The King told his ministers:
"Quickly close the city gates and do not allow them to depart all together.

"At that time, the four princes, together with the multitude of people, gradually proceeded forward until they reached the foot of the Snowy Mountains on the banks of the Gaṅgā River, near the dwelling place of the seer Kapila."

At that time, the four princes and the multitude of people each cut *māḍa* grass to construct dwellings and resided therein; meanwhile, the people together hunted and gathered provisions to sustain themselves.
At that time, the four princes went three times each day to the hermitage of the seer Kapila to attend upon and make offerings to him.
As the four princes grew older, they remained without wives and their physical forms became emaciated. The seer asked them:
"For what reason have you gradually become so haggard?"
The prince replied, "We are young men without wives or concubines; are we not withered by the sorrow and anxiety we feel day and night?
Then the seer reported:
"You should marry among yourselves as sisters.
The princes replied,
"We do not know whether this is permissible or not."
The seer replied, "Since they were not born of the same mother, this matter is permitted.
At that time, the princes each reflected to themselves:
"We brothers have already left our native land, and there is no one here with whom we may form marriage alliances. This instruction from the Rishi is most suited to our wishes.
They were immediately filled with great joy; they married one another to become husband and wife, and before long, each gave birth to sons and daughters.
At that time, the four princes felt great joy in their hearts; they brought their wives and children frequently to the seer’s abode, which consequently led to much clamor.
Seeing this, the seer could no longer maintain his meditative composure and said to the princes:
"You should remain here and dwell in peace; I shall depart from this place."
The prince asked, "For what reason are you leaving so soon? The seer replied:
"You all are clamorous and disturb my meditative concentration, like one treading upon thorns with bare feet.
The prince said, "I pray that the Rishi remain here; you may seek another favorable place for yourselves, and I shall dwell there."
The seer replied, "So be it!

At that time, the seer possessed supernormal powers; whatever he desired could be accomplished. He immediately took a golden pitcher filled with water and went to another auspicious spot, sprinkling the water to establish the boundary.
He addressed the princes, saying:
"You may establish yourselves here.

When the princes had received the instructions of the seer, they immediately constructed city walls and settled within them; the seer sprinkled water to mark the boundary, and for this reason the city was named Kapilavastu.

As the populace gradually increased, the city became increasingly cramped. At that time, a deva beheld this situation and pointed out another location where the land was vast and spacious. They immediately established a separate city at that site, and thus the city was named "Shown by the Deva" (Devadṛśya).
Then the princes gathered together and deliberated:
"Because our father the King has taken a junior wife, he has caused us, his sons and brothers, to depart from our native land.
We should all make a covenant together that from this day forward we shall each take only one wife and never take another."
At that time, King Virūḍhaka asked his ministers,
"Where are my four sons now? The ministers replied:
"Because the king's sons committed transgressions, the king banished them from the country along with their sisters.
They are now residing in the city of Devadṛśa beneath the Snowy Mountains, where they have extensively established their own capital."
King Vardhana said, "How could my sons possibly achieve such self-perfection?
The ministers replied:
"Yes," he replied.
At that time, King Vaīraṭya leaped up with great joy; sitting upright and raising his hand, he addressed his ministers, saying, "My son is truly capable!"
"My son is truly capable!
Because he was called "Greatly Capable" (*mahāsammata*) due to his great majesty and virtue, he received the name Śākya.
Later, at another time, King Bṛhadratha passed away, and Prince Priyavardhana immediately succeeded him as king.
At that time, King Priyarāma also had no son, and subsequently passed away.
Then, the ministers consulted together and went to the city of Devadarśana to install the eldest prince, named Arciṣmukha, as the sovereign; however, the prince soon died.
Dīptamukha was childless; he subsequently passed away, and they then enthroned Karṇa as the sovereign of the kingdom.
Karṇa was childless; he also subsequently passed away, and they then enthroned Gajagāmin as the sovereign of the kingdom.
When Gajagāmin died childless, they again enthroned Ratnakaṇṭha as the sovereign of the kingdom.
Ratnakaṇṭha had a son named Uparatnakaṇṭha, who later succeeded to the royal throne.
Uparatnakaṇṭha had a son named Devadvāra, who likewise succeeded to the royal throne.
"Furthermore, O worthy ones!

In the great city of Kapilavastu, the lineage of the kings of Devadaha continued for fifty-five thousand generations, ruling the kingdom according to the True Dharma. The last of these kings was named Daśaratha; Daśaratha had a son named Śataratha; Śataratha had a son named Ugraratha; Ugraratha had a son named Jayaratha; Jayaratha had a son named Dhṛtaratha; Dhṛtaratha had a son named Daśadhanus; Daśadhanus had a son named Śatadhanus; Śatadhanus had a son named Navati-dhanus; Navati-dhanus had a son named Vijayadhanus; Vijayadhanus had a son named Ugradhanus; and Ugradhanus had a son named Dhṛtadhanus."
"Furthermore, sirs! King Dṛḍhadhanus had two sons:
the first was named Siṃhahanu, and the second was named Siṃhaghoṣa."
Among all those skilled in archery throughout this Jambudvīpa, King Siṃhahanu was the foremost.
That King Siṃhahanu had four sons:
the first was named Śuddhodana, the second Śuklodana, the third Droṇodana, and the fourth Amṛtodana.
King Siṃhahanu had four daughters:
first, Viśuddhā; second, Śuklā; third, Śukṣmā; and fourth, Amṛtā.
King Śuddhodana had two sons:
The eldest crown prince was none other than our Bhagavān;
the second was the Venerable Nanda. King Śuklodana had two sons:
The first was named Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the second was named Sudatta.
King Droṇodana had two sons:
the first was named Mahānāman and the second was named Aniruddha.
King Amṛtodana had two sons:
the first was named Nanda, and the second was named Devadatta.
The maiden Viśuddhā gave birth to a son named Sudarśana.
Śuddhavarṇa had a son named Mālī. Śuddhadroṇa had a son named Balin. Amṛta had a son named Mahābala.
I, the Bhagavān, have a son named Rāhula.
From the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra down to Rāhula, the line of succession has been severed. Why is this?
"Because Rāhula has realized the fruit of non-arising and severed the seed of birth and death, I have thus terminated his lineage.
After the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had spoken thus regarding the Śākya clan to the great assembly of Śākyas, he withdrew from his seat and remained in silence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Mahāmaudgalyāyana had finished speaking of their lineage, rose from his reclining position, sat upright, and addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"For you, O Bhikṣu, speak of all the lineages of our Śākya clan from past lives until now.
Having spoken thus in accordance with the Dharma, he further addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:

"If there should be another person who extensively expounds the Śākya lineage for others, this son of good family will obtain great benefit throughout the long night and constantly experience peace and happiness."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"You should know! You ought to receive [this teaching] concerning the Śākya clan from which I have come since former lives; wherever it may be located in other regions, you should mindfully recollect it according to the Dharma and explain it extensively for others."
Why is this? Because it will bring you great benefit.
Since it possesses the meaning of profit, the meaning of the Dharma, and the meaning of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), you shall obtain all the aforementioned merits.
"Therefore, you bhikṣus, you should receive, uphold, recite, and explain this extensively for others.

At that time, the Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu, having heard this sequential account of their own lineage, were all greatly delighted; they immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and each returned to their respective abodes.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
In the past, King Siṃhahanu ruled the people with the True Dharma in the city of Kapilavastu; his realm was exceedingly prosperous and abundant, free from fear, and the populace lived in joy."

That King Susambhava ruled the city of Devadarśana with the True Dharma, transforming his people so that the land was peaceful and secure, households were well-provided for, harvests were bountiful, and there was no decline or affliction.

The Queen of King Susambhava was named Viśeṣavatī; she was of upright and beautiful countenance, a sight all delighted to behold, and all sentient beings constantly attained peace and happiness under her care.

In the city of Devadṛśa, there was an elder named Śrī who possessed vast wealth and treasures that filled his storehouses; he owned numerous gardens, groves, fields, and residences, and had many kinsmen and attendants. His precious possessions were no different from those of Vaiśravaṇa himself.

At that time, that elder possessed a fragrant garden, abounding with various flowers and fruits, flowing springs, and bathing pools; there, birds of every kind uttered harmonious and elegant songs, making it a place of peerless excellence in the world.
The king, his princes, and their consorts frequently went there to play.
At that time, the king’s consort, seeing this grove, conceived a sense of craving and attachment for it and said to the king, "This garden is most excellent; please grant it to me."
The King immediately replied:
"This garden now belongs to the elder; how could I now take it and give it to you at will?
If you must have it, I shall personally construct another within the city that surpasses this garden, for you to enjoy."

At that time, for the sake of his consort, the king immediately had a garden constructed within the royal city that was twice as magnificent as the former one; because this grove was built for the sake of Queen Miāoshèng, it was named the Garden of Miāoshèng.
King Siṃhahanu constantly thought to himself:
"I always pray for one wish: that a Golden-Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) may arise within my lineage; this would most perfectly suit my wish."
King Suvicita also requested a single boon:
"May I quickly become a kinsman to King Siṃhahanu; this would be most agreeable to my wish.
At that time, the chief queen of King Suvicita became pregnant, and when ten months had passed, she gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was so upright and beautiful as to be rare in the world.
Because this princess was so exceptionally beautiful and dignified, the king, the queen, the ladies of the inner court, and all who saw her were filled with wonder and admiration.
They discussed it among themselves, saying: "Is this princess born from a human being?"
"Was this created by the transformation of a skillful deity?
After twenty-one days had passed, they performed various celebratory rites according to the laws of the kingdom and commanded their ministers to deliberate among themselves:
"What name shall we give to this girl?"
The ministers replied,
"The people within the city of Devadṛśa all said to one another:
'It is due to the karmic retribution of her past deeds that this princess has attained such exquisite beauty.'"
They further deliberated among themselves, saying:
"This princess was not born of human origin; she was conjured by the god Viśvakarman.
They all addressed the king, saying:
"Let this girl be named Māyā. Thereupon, eight nurses were appointed to raise her together. When she gradually grew up, a physiognomist came and addressed the king, saying:

"O King, this noble daughter of yours will surely give birth to a son who possesses all the marks of excellence, has great majesty and virtue, and shall attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin)."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great joy.

Later, the chief queen of King Suvīra again became pregnant; when ten months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a daughter whose bodily radiance permeated the entire city, and whose countenance and marks of excellence were beyond compare in the world.

When the twenty-first day had arrived and the celebratory rites were completed, he immediately assembled his ministers to deliberate upon her name; because this little girl surpassed all magical transformations, they accordingly established her name as Mahāmāyā (Great Illusion).
Furthermore, for this girl, eight nurses were appointed to raise her together. When she gradually reached adulthood, a diviner came and addressed the king, saying:
"The princess of the king will surely give birth to a son who possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man; he shall be majestic and honored, destined for the rank of a Wheel-Turning King."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with redoubled joy.
King Suvicintita immediately dispatched a messenger bearing a letter to King Siṃhahanu, reporting to him:

"My chief queen has given birth to two daughters; the eldest, on the day of her birth, possessed a countenance so upright and beautiful as to be rare in this world. A physiognomist divined that she shall later give birth to a son who will attain the rank of a Cakravartin."

"The younger daughter’s bodily radiance is twice as superior; the physiognomists have prophesied that she will surely give birth to a son who shall attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin).
Having heard that Your Majesty has an eldest son named Śuddhodana, I wish for one of these two daughters to become Śuddhodana’s consort, and therefore I have sent this messenger to inform you."
Upon arriving there, he related the matter in full. When the king heard these words, he was greatly delighted and sent a messenger back to his own country to inform King Suddhodana:
"Your two daughters both possess the marks of excellence; I shall now take them both as consorts for King Śuddhodana."

"However, my late father had a solemn vow not to take two queens; therefore, let us now take the younger daughter who shall give birth to the Wheel-turning King, but do not allow the elder daughter to marry yet, while I assemble all my ministers and kinsmen to deliberate upon this matter."

When King Suprabuddha heard these words, he immediately adorned his younger daughter according to the laws of his kingdom and, having her surrounded and attended by five hundred court ladies, sent her to that country to become the consort of King Śuddhodana.
"At that time, King Siṃhahanu had a neighboring vassal state situated within the mountain valleys named Pañcāla, which suddenly rebelled and plundered and oppressed the surrounding kingdoms."
At that time, the Śākyas living in neighboring territories were oppressed and harassed by them; they fled to one another in haste and informed Siṃhahanu:
"Our villages are all being ravaged day and night by certain bandits; we pray that Your Majesty will raise an army and go in person to subdue them."
King Siṃhahanu said, "I am now old and no longer capable of engaging in battle. Those people said:
"Please request Prince Śuddhodana to go there and capture him.
The King then replied,
"O you people, if you grant the Prince one wish, I shall then dispatch him."
The assembly replied to the king, "So be it;
we shall follow your command.
Thereupon, King Siṃhahanu beat the drums and issued a proclamation within the city, strictly ordering the fourfold army to follow the prince and go there to punish him.
At that time, Prince Śuddhodana, obeying his father’s command, led the fourfold army to the location of those bandits to engage them in battle.
By the power of his majesty, the bandit host was either slain or bound by the Prince’s troops, with not a single one remaining.
Once the rebels had been eliminated, Prince Śuddhodana led his army back to his own country.
When the Śākya clansmen learned that the Prince had successfully quelled the rebellion, they were all filled with great joy and said to the King:
"Prince Śuddhodana has rid us of our enemies and harms."
We ministers and all the people were overcome with joy and celebration, saying:
"The King previously stated:
'The Prince has a vow.'"
"Please speak for us, O King. Then King Siṃhahanu said to the Śākyas:
"O Śākyas of my lineage, you previously made a solemn vow not to take two wives."
The Śākyas said, "Does Your Majesty now wish to break your former vow?
The King replied:
"Not so! You must tie it more firmly.
However, my intention is that you take only two consorts for Prince Śuddhodana; you should not take any others."
The Śākyas said, "This may be so.
Then King Siṃhahanu immediately dispatched a messenger to King Suprabuddha, saying to him:
"I have now consulted with the Śākya clan and all have agreed that I should take the King’s eldest daughter as a consort for Prince Śuddhodana; may Your Majesty grant her to me."

Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great joy; he immediately provided five hundred court ladies as her attendants, adorned her body with various precious garments, and sent her off to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

When King Siṃhahanu received his daughter's arrival, he immediately followed the laws of the kingdom, assembled his ministers, and performed music and entertainment as he took her in marriage to be the Crown Prince’s consort.
Not long thereafter, Siṃhahanu passed away, and as the heir to his father’s throne, Śuddhodana succeeded him.
He transformed people through the True Dharma; the land was peaceful and happy, the five grains were abundant, and there was no decline or affliction. The populace of that kingdom filled every place.

At another time, he ascended the various pavilions together with Queen Mahāmāyā, surrounded and attended by the ladies of the inner court, while the music of female performers played as they indulged in pleasure and sport.
"When a Bodhisattva resides in the Tuṣita Heaven, he constantly observes the world through five dharmas. What are these five?
First, observing the place of birth; second, observing the land; third, observing the season; fourth, observing the lineage; and fifth, observing the parents from whom one will be born."
For what reason does a Bodhisattva observe the place of birth?
While in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he constantly reflects:
"In what place did past Bodhisattvas take birth?"

He then immediately perceived that [the child] was either born into a family of pure-conduct brahmins, or born into a noble kṣatriya lineage, or was to become a teacher of brahmins, or a teacher of kṣatriyas.
"At this present time, the kṣatriyas are the most honored; I shall go to be born into such a kṣatriya family. Why is this?
If I were to be born into a poor or lowly family, there might be sentient beings in future lives who would slander me."
For this reason, by the power of his sovereign merit, a bodhisattva is able to be born in whatever place he intends.
For this very purpose, when a bodhisattva undergoes rebirth, he must first examine the place where he will be born.
For what reason does a bodhisattva observe the lands? While dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven, the bodhisattva constantly reflects:
"In what kind of land were past bodhisattvas born?"

He then saw that in that land there were sugarcane, non-glutinous rice, barley, and wheat, as well as yellow cattle and water buffaloes, all of which filled every household; alms were easy to obtain, the ten unwholesome deeds were absent, and the ten wholesome deeds were extensively practiced.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"Because such things as these are all fully present in the land of Central India, I shall now be born in that land of Central India. Why is this?"
"If one is born in a borderland region, it is because sentient beings there may at times slander me.
Therefore, by the power of his merit, a bodhisattva is able to be born in those places according to his intention; as the Buddha has said, there is no falsehood in this.
For what reason does he observe the seasons?
While the Bodhisattva resides in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he constantly reflects:
"At what season did past Bodhisattvas descend to be born in the human world?"

If he sees that the beings in that land have a maximum lifespan of eighty thousand years and a minimum lifespan of even one hundred years, the Bodhisattva will then take birth in that land. Why is this?

If human lifespans exceed eighty thousand years, sentient beings at that time will be free from sorrow, suffering, ignorance, dullness, and arrogance; yet, being attached to pleasure, they are not vessels for the True Dharma and are difficult to transform.
If human lifespans fall below one hundred years, sentient beings at that time will be heavily obscured by the five turbidities.

What are the five? First, the defilement of lifespan; second, the defilement of afflictions; third, the defilement of sentient beings; fourth, the defilement of views; and fifth, the defilement of the eon.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"If I were to appear in the world during an evil age, many heterodox teachers would revile my mind-king, and the five turbidities would increase such that beings would not be vessels for the true Dharma; it would be just as when all Bodhisattvas of the past did not appear in the world during times of turbid evil."
Why is this? Because the True Dharma taught by the appearance of all Buddhas never passes away in vain.
For this reason, one observes the proper timing.
Furthermore, for what reason does he observe the lineage?
While the Bodhisattva resides in the Tuṣita Heaven, he constantly reflects: "In which lineage may I take birth?"
"If he sees someone whose inner and outer kinsmen have been incapable of slandering them since past lives, he will be reborn among them.
Having performed this contemplation, the Bodhisattva then saw that the pure and noble lineage of the Śākya Cakravartin kings was worthy of his manifestation.
Why is this? If a Bodhisattva were born into a lowly family in this world, sentient beings might give rise to slander.

Having attained the power of mastery over immeasurable eons, whatever desires the Bodhisattva conceives are fulfilled according to his will, and all the teachings he proclaims have never been in vain.
For these reasons, the Bodhisattva examines the family into which he will be born.
Furthermore, for what reason does he examine the mother who will give birth?
While the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he reflected as follows:
"Just as other bodhisattvas, in what kind of mother do they receive the conception?

He observes that the woman’s lineage for seven generations is entirely pure and free from sexual impurity; her appearance is dignified and she has well-cultivated the precepts, such that she is capable of bearing the bodhisattva in her womb for ten full months.
Furthermore, in all her worldly activities—whether coming and going or standing and sitting—she encounters no obstacles whatsoever."
Furthermore, the Great Lady Mahāmāyā had once made a supreme vow before the Buddhas of the past:
"May the son born to me in a future life attain the state of a fully awakened Buddha."
For this reason, these bodhisattvas feared that sentient beings might utter such slanderous words:
"Why has the Bodhisattva appeared in the world from the womb of that signless woman?"
Therefore, the Bodhisattva has fully accomplished all the roots of goodness planted since beginningless time.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva observes the mother who shall give birth to him.
"At that time, having performed these five kinds of universal observations, the Bodhisattva earnestly proclaimed three times to the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm, saying:

'I shall now descend from this Tuṣita Heaven to be born among humans; within the womb of the principal consort of King Śuddhodana, I shall become his crown prince, and after my birth, I shall realize the fruit of eternal abiding.'"
"You gods, if you wish to follow me and realize this fruit, you may be born there together with me in the human realm.
He spoke these words three times among the assembly of devas.
At that time, having heard these words, all the devas replied with one voice:
"Excellent! Does the Bodhisattva not know?"

That Jambudvīpa is stubborn, difficult to transform, and filled with many turbidities and disturbances; it is everywhere crowded with the six heterodox teachers, the six śrāvakas who follow those heterodox teachers, and various types of practitioners of the six meditative concentrations—all of whom are deeply attached to false views and are difficult to rescue.
Who are the six teachers? First is Pūraṇa;
second is Makkhali Gosāla; third is Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra; fourth is Ajita Keśakambala; fifth is Kakuda Kātyāyana; and sixth is Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
What are the six śrāvakas who followed the non-Buddhist teachers?
First is the brahmin Gautama; second is Sunakṣatra; third is Cāmpeya; fourth is Brahmāyus; fifth is Puṣkarasārin; and sixth is Aśvajit.
