What are the six non-Buddhist practitioners of meditative concentration?

First is Udraka Rāmaputra; second is Rāḍha Kāśyapa; third is Subrahmanya; fourth is Jyotiṣka Māṇava; fifth is Kṛṣṇa Ṛṣi; and sixth is Uruvilvākāśyapa Jaṭila (translated in Chinese as Duōmáo, meaning "having much hair").
Such are the heterodox and false teachings of these outsiders who convert those sentient beings; they are so deeply attached to their wrong views that they are difficult to deliver.
How can a Bodhisattva now wish to go there?
"Now, in my Tuṣita palace, each of the seats upon which the various devas listen to the Dharma is twelve yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly equal in dimension.
While I am here preaching the Dharma, we, having heard it, will develop deep faith and acceptance, which will bring us peace, happiness, and benefit throughout the long night."
When the devas had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva then addressed them, saying:
"O devas, you should each perform various musical performances according to your own pleasure."
Then the hosts of devas all simultaneously played various musical instruments, their sounds clamoring and tumultuous.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva blew his great conch shell, and the resonance of all the music was completely silenced.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again asked the devas:
"Among all musical sounds, which is the greatest?
The devas replied:
"The sound of the conch is the greatest.
"O sons of good family! You should know this:"

Just as the sound of a great conch shell can cause all other musical sounds to be silenced and extinguished, so too am I: when I descend into Jambudvīpa to preach the Dharma, I am able to utterly subdue and destroy the six heretical teachers, the six types of śrāvaka-followers of those teachers, and the six types of practitioners of meditative absorption; I enable all sentient beings to obtain the Dharma of ambrosia and bring them all to full satisfaction.
I blow the conch of impermanence to utterly subdue and destroy the heretics' false calculations of permanence;
I blow the conch of great emptiness to likewise utterly subdue and destroy the heretics' views that cling to existence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
“The lion can subdue all fierce beasts; The vajra excels at crushing all that is hard;
Śakra can subdue the asuras; Among all lights, the sunlight is supreme.”
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva addressed the devas, saying:
"If you wish to be purified and satiated by the Dharma of ambrosia, you may be born within the six great cities of Central India."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra was seated among the assembly and thought to himself:

"I know that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni will surely take conception within the womb of Lady Māyā; I shall employ my supernormal powers to purify her body, ensuring she is free from impurity and possesses robust physical strength to await the Bodhisattva."
Having formed this thought, he immediately used his supernormal powers to purify the womb of Lady Māyā.

At that time, the Bodhisattva made five observations from the Tuṣita Heaven palace; having earnestly proclaimed his message three times to the devas, he descended to India during the night in the form of a six-tusked white elephant and entered the pure womb of Lady Māyā.
"At that time, Lady Māyā saw four kinds of dreams during that very night:

first, she saw a six-tusked white elephant entering her womb; second, she saw herself soaring through the void; third, she saw herself ascending a high mountain; and fourth, she saw a great multitude of people prostrating and surrounding her."
Having had this dream, he related the aforementioned matters to King Śuddhodana.
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately summoned the physiognomists and recounted the dream. The physiognomists replied:
"According to our methods of physiognomy, the Great Queen shall surely give birth to a son who will be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, adorning his body."
If he succeeds to the royal throne, he shall mount the golden wheel and subdue the four quarters of the world;
if he leaves the household life to cultivate the Way, he will realize the rank of Dharma King, his fame reaching the ten directions as he acts as a father to all sentient beings.
The internal summary verse says:
When I was born, the four heavenly kings protected me; like a bright moon-jewel, I was wrapped in various substances.
It is also like a precious thread; the wise one clearly understands it, personally upholding the five precepts and being free from all sensual desires.
"It is the constant law for all Bodhisattvas to descend from Tuṣita Heaven and enter their mother’s womb."

At that time, the great earth throughout the ten directions shook everywhere, and a magnificent radiance pervaded all places; even those realms of sentient beings in the six destinies who were subject to their karma, and those regions where the majestic light of the sun and moon could not reach, were all universally and completely illuminated.
The sentient beings therein said to one another:
"This radiance is unprecedented; could it be that we are about to undergo rebirth elsewhere?
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb, Śakra-devānām-indra dispatched the deities of the Four Great Kings to guard and protect her; these four deities were:
One held a sharp sword, one held a lasso, one held a halberd, and one held a bow and arrows. Why was this?
It was because they feared that the various evil Māras might find an opportunity against their mother.
When the Bodhisattvas descend into birth, all impurities such as blood within their mothers' wombs are entirely removed and do not defile them;
they are like the moon-jewel, which, though enveloped by various objects, remains unstained.
It is likewise when a Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb.

It is the constant law of all Bodhisattvas that their mothers always see the Bodhisattva within the womb, just as one might see a pure jewel wrapped in cotton of blue, yellow, red, or white; just as those with the eye of wisdom can clearly discern and understand both the jewel and the cotton, so too does the mother see the Bodhisattva within her womb.
It is the constant law of all Bodhisattvas that while they are in their mother’s womb, they cause their mother’s body to be harmonious and joyful, free from any fatigue.
While the Bodhisattva is in his mother’s womb, his mother naturally and constantly observes the five precepts.
Not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, and not drinking intoxicants.
It is the constant law for all Bodhisattvas:
while they are in their mother’s womb, their mother naturally becomes free from lustful desire.
Furthermore, Queen Māyā suddenly thought to herself,
"I wish to drink up all the waters of the four great oceans until they are exhausted.
She then expressed this aspiration to King Śuddhodana.

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner in the city of Kapilavastu named Red-Eye (Raktākṣa), who was skilled in various magical arts. The King sent a messenger to summon Red-Eye and convey the aforementioned intent.
Red-Eye replied,
"I wish to ascend the high tower with the lady.
Once they had ascended the tower, he immediately employed his illusory powers to create the waters of the four great oceans, and took those ocean waters to give to the lady to drink.
Having drunk the water, the Queen’s distress was immediately assuaged.
Then, Queen Māyā again thought to herself:
"May all sentient beings who are bound and imprisoned be completely set free."
Having thought this, she immediately spoke it to the king.
Upon hearing these words, the king issued an edict to the prison officials, ordering that all those imprisoned be released; at that time, the queen’s anxiety was immediately stilled.
Queen Māyā again thought to herself,
"I wish to give away wealth and goods.
Having formed this thought, she immediately spoke it to the King.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately bestowed various kinds of wealth and goods as alms, whereupon the queen’s anxiety was stilled.
She then reflected further:
"I wish to go to the pleasure groves to stroll and look about."
He then reported this to the king.
Upon hearing it, the king immediately took his consort to various gardens and groves to look about, and her obsessive thoughts ceased.
However, the thought arose in her mind once again:
"I wish to dwell within the garden park of my father, the King.
She then informed the King, who, upon hearing these words, immediately dispatched a messenger to King Suprabuddha with the report:
"Now Queen Māyā wishes to reside within the Lumbinī Garden of her father, the King."

Upon hearing these words, the king immediately dispatched men to prepare the grounds by sweeping and sprinkling water, and ordered Queen Māyā, along with her attendants and court ladies, to go to the Lumbinī Garden for recreation.
Then he saw an Ashoka tree with its flowers and leaves in full bloom; as the lady was about to give birth to the Prince, she reached out her hand and grasped a branch of that tree.

At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that the Bodhisattva’s mother felt shame and would not be able to give birth to her son immediately amidst such a great crowd, employed a skillful means to raise a great wind and rain, causing the multitude to disperse in all directions.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, manifested as an old nurse and stood before the lady, and the lady immediately gave birth.
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, took her up in a celestial robe; she had previously felt much distress within her womb and said to Śakra:
"Place me on the ground."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, withdrew to stand at a slight distance.
When the Bodhisattva was born, the great earth shook, and a radiance shone throughout heaven and earth, such that even places not reached by the sun and moon were made completely bright and clear.
The sentient beings therein were all able to see one another, and each said to the others:
"It is not only my own body that has been born in this place; there are other people here with me as well."
All Bodhisattvas follow a constant law:
when they emerge from the womb, there is no mucus, blood, or other impurities.
When the Bodhisattva’s mother is about to give birth, she neither sits nor lies down, but stands leaning against a tree, free from the subsequent sufferings of childbirth.

It is the constant law of Bodhisattvas that, immediately upon birth, while still on the ground and without anyone supporting them, they walk seven steps and observe the four quarters, making this declaration:
"This is the eastern direction; I am the most supreme among all sentient beings."
"This is the southern direction; I am worthy of the offerings of sentient beings.
This is the western direction; I have now resolved not to undergo further rebirth.
This is the northern direction; I have now emerged from the great ocean of birth and death."
At that time, the devas held white parasols and white whisks in their hands, and gathered precious ornaments to cover the Bodhisattva.
The dragon kings each held two kinds of pure perfumed water—namely, those of balanced temperature, both warm and cool—to bathe the Bodhisattva.
It is the constant law for all Bodhisattvas:
at the place of their birth, a great pool of water appears before their mother, so that whatever she desires for bathing is entirely provided in abundance.
It is the constant law for all Bodhisattvas:

at the time of their birth, hosts of celestial devas in the void scatter upon the Bodhisattva various kinds of exquisite celestial blended incenses, powdered incense, unguents, sandalwood, and aloeswood.
Various kinds of celestial music spontaneously resounded in the void.
At that time, the seer Asita was within a stone cave on Mount Kṣemaka; that seer constantly knew the signs of the rise and fall of all worlds.
That seer had a nephew named Nārada, who would come from time to time to pay his respects and make offerings.
At that time, the seer, teaching him according to the circumstances, said to Nārada:
"Upon hearing the seer’s prophecy, he believed it deeply and found it not false; joy overflowed from his body and mind, and he requested permission to leave the household life to become a disciple."
When the Bodhisattva was first born, the heavens and earth were filled with light. Nārada, beholding this auspicious omen, immediately addressed the Seer, saying:
"O Preceptor! Is it possible that in this degenerate age two suns have appeared simultaneously?"
"If there are not two suns, why is there such radiance in this cave?
At that time, the seer Asita spoke these verses:
"The light of the sun is extremely hot and lacks clarity; this radiance is pure and cool."
Its streaming radiance shines brilliantly within the mountain cave; I know with certainty that this is the light of the Muni.
Through the great majestic power of the Bodhisattva’s supernormal faculties, he has manifested this light upon emerging from his mother’s womb;
pure, luminous, and of true golden hue, it pervades all the lands of the world.
Narada replied: "Venerable Teacher!
I now wish to follow my teacher in order to see the Bodhisattva."
Then the seer said: "Do you not know now?
That Bodhisattva possesses great majesty and virtue, and is surrounded by the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas; we cannot go there and see him."
"Only after that Bodhisattva has entered the city of Kapilavastu three times shall I go to see him.
When the Bodhisattva was born, five hundred palace attendants each gave birth to a son, with Candaka being the foremost among them.
The five hundred palace ladies each gave birth to a daughter, with Cāṇakī as the foremost;
the five hundred ministers each gave birth to a son, with Udāyin as the foremost.
There were five hundred elephants, each giving birth to a single offspring, with the son of Sātāgira as their leader.
There were five hundred horses, each giving birth to a single offspring, with the horse Mārāha as their leader.

Five hundred treasuries spontaneously opened and appeared; the kings of all the kingdoms in the four directions were entirely subdued, constantly presenting various kinds of miscellaneous goods and coming to serve him.
At that time, having witnessed these signs, the minister came and informed the Great King.
Upon hearing this, the King reflected deeply:
"Now this son of mine has accomplished all manner of virtuous deeds."
"For this reason, the Great King named this prince 'Accomplisher of All Deeds' (Sarvārthasiddha); thus did the Bodhisattva first receive this name.

At that time, there was a yakṣa in the city of Kapilavastu named Śākyavardhana; whenever any member of the Śākya clan within the city gave birth to a son or daughter, they would first bring the child before that yakṣa to pay him homage."
Then that great king issued a command to his ministers and officials, directing them to take the crown prince to the abode of the yakṣa Vardhana-śākya and have him pay obeisance.
Having received the king’s instruction, the ministers placed the crown prince upon a palanquin adorned with the seven precious gems and proceeded to the yakṣa’s dwelling.

The Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu were by nature fierce and violent, with minds that were savage and prone to conceiving a strong sense of self and others, as well as being stubborn, evil, and brutal.
Yet, upon seeing the Bodhisattva, they all became completely tranquil and remained in silence.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:

"These Śākyas who dwell in the city of Kapilavastu are by nature fierce and violent in disposition; they harbor much of the 'self' and 'other,' and possess stubborn, harsh, and evil natures. Yet, upon seeing the Prince enter the city, they all remain silent like sages."
"For this reason, the Prince may be named Śākyamuni.

Then, when the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni arrived at the yakṣa temple, the yakṣa Śākyavardhana saw the Bodhisattva approaching the temple from afar; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and paid homage to the Bodhisattva.
When the multitude saw this, they were greatly astonished and marveled; they immediately went to King Śuddhodana and said, "Great King!
Just now, a yakṣa deity saw the Prince from afar, emerged from the temple, and prostrated at his two feet."
When the king heard this, he was filled with great joy and spoke these words:
"Since the celestial deities prostrate before the Prince, I know him to be the God among Gods."
"For this reason, he is called the God among Gods.
At that time, the great king immediately took the prince back to his own palace and ordered the palace nurses to nourish him according to the proper schedule.
The nurses and attendants were filled with great joy; they immediately received the prince from his father, the king, with both hands and diligently nurtured him within the palace chambers.
The nurses and attendants bathed him daily with fragrant water, anointed him with exquisite perfumes, and adorned him with various ornaments; every day they brought him to the King’s presence.
The King then took the Prince in his arms, placed him upon his knee, and beholding his features, was filled with great joy.
It is the established law of the kingdom that whenever a son is born in the royal palace, a brahmin physiognomist is immediately summoned to examine his features.
The king then called the physiognomist to divine the prince’s fortune; having completed the examination, he replied to the king:
"This crown prince truly possesses the fulfillment of the thirty-two marks.
If he remains in the household life, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) who rules over the four continents through the transformation of the Dharma.

He will possess the seven treasures: first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the elephant treasure; third, the horse treasure; fourth, the mani-jewel treasure; fifth, the woman treasure; sixth, the minister-treasurer treasure; and seventh, the military commander treasure. He will have a full thousand sons, all valiant, upright, and majestic, who subdue the armies of others."
May all people within this great earth who do not commit offenses against one another practice only the most excellent and sublime wholesome dharmas.
Should they leave the household life, may they attain the rank of Dharma King as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose fame is universally renowned and who is endowed with the thirty-two marks.
The king then asked:
"What are these thirty-two marks of a great man?
"First, he possesses the mark of the feet of a great man being well-placed and treading evenly upon the ground."
Second, on the soles of his two feet appear the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel;
third, he possesses the long, slender fingers of a great man;
fourth, his heels are full and elongated.
Fifth, his hands and feet are delicate and soft;
sixth, his fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane;
seventh, he has the mark of reaching down with his hanging hands to touch his knees.
Eighth, his calves are like those of the eneya antelope;
ninth, his body is not hunched;
tenth, his male organ is concealed within a sheath.
Eleventh, his bodily marks are perfectly complete like those of the nyagrodha tree;
twelfth, he possesses a constant radiance extending one fathom;
thirteenth, the hairs of his body all point upward.
Fourteenth, from each and every pore of his body a single hair grows, which is deep blue-black in color and curls to the right like a spiral;
fifteenth, his skin is golden in color;
sixteenth, his skin is so fine and smooth that dust and grime do not adhere to it.
Seventeenth, his body is perfectly rounded in seven places: the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck;
eighteenth, the upper half of his body is like that of a lion king;
nineteenth, his shoulders are well-rounded and full.
Twentieth, the space between his shoulders is well-filled;
twenty-first, his body is large, robust, and straight;
twenty-second, he possesses forty teeth, all of which are perfectly even.
Twenty-third, his teeth have no gaps;
twenty-fourth, his teeth are brilliant white;
twenty-fifth, his jaw is like that of a lion.
Twenty-sixth, his tongue is broad and thin; when extended from his mouth, it covers his entire face up to the hairline at his ears.
Twenty-seventh, among all tastes, he obtains the supreme flavor.

Twenty-eighth, he possesses the great Brahma-voice, with speech that is harmonious and elegant, capable of gladdening the minds of the multitude; his voice is like that of the kalaviṅka bird, and its resonance thunders like a celestial drum.
Twenty-ninth, his eyes are deep blue;
thirtieth, his eyelashes are like those of a bull king;
thirty-first, the *uṣṇīṣa* is manifested upon the crown of his head.
The thirty-second is the mark of the tuft of hair between the eyebrows, which is brilliant white in color and curls to the right like a conch shell.
If he does not leave the household life, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King and rule over the four great continents.
"The constant law for Bodhisattvas is this:
once a Bodhisattva’s mother has given birth to the Bodhisattva, she passes away after seven days and is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
This is the constant law for Bodhisattvas."

Once born, his body was upright and magnificent, surpassing all in the world; it was beloved by all, and those who beheld him never grew weary of the sight. He was like various forms fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold by a skilled artisan, draped with celestial robes that emitted great radiance, shining brilliantly in every direction.
The body of that bodhisattva is likewise so; just as that lotus is beloved by all people, so too is the bodhisattva.
It is the constant nature of bodhisattvas:
their eyes never blink, just like those of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

By virtue of the karma of his fruit, he constantly sees for one yojana in each of the four cardinal directions, above, and below, day and night; his Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching, as clear and exquisite as the song of a bird on the Snowy Mountains.

Once the Bodhisattva was born, he naturally possessed vast wisdom; he was well-versed in all the righteous governance of the world and understood every law of his father the king’s kingdom without exception.
At that time, the seer Nārada came and said to his teacher:

"The Bodhisattva has now entered the city of Kapilavastu; King Śuddhodana, his father, has already established three names for him. I pray that you, Master, will come with me to pay homage and behold him."
The teacher said to him, "I shall now follow your wish.

The two sages accompanied one another, intending to pay their respects; however, due to the power of the Bodhisattva, they lost their supernatural faculties and were unable to travel through the air as usual, so they proceeded on foot toward the city of Kapilavastu.
Having entered the city and arrived outside the king’s gate, he said to the gatekeeper:
"You should go and inform the Great King on my behalf that the seer Asita has now come to the gate and wishes to see the Great King."
Thereupon, the gatekeeper went to the king’s presence and reported the matter in detail.
Having heard this, the king immediately took fragrant flowers and went out to welcome the two sages, escorting them into the palace to be settled there.
Having settled him, he greeted him with kind words:
"Great Sage, for what reason have you come from so far away?
What is it that you seek?"
The two seers replied,
"We have come specifically wishing to see the Bodhisattva.
The king answered the seers:
"My eldest son is currently sleeping peacefully; wait but a moment, and you shall have him appear before you.
At that time, the two sages again addressed the king, saying, "Although he has not yet awakened, we wish to behold him for a brief moment."
At that time, the Great King led the two seers to the Bodhisattva’s location. Upon seeing the Bodhisattva, they observed that although he was asleep, his eyes remained open.
When the seer Asita witnessed this, he spoke in verse:
“Like a true flying dragon horse, Though briefly sleeping, it awakens again.”
"Just as a skillful manager is not overcome by the hindrance of sleep.

Then the nursemaid stepped forward, took up the Prince in her arms, and presented him to the two sages. At that time, Asita received him with both hands while kneeling, examined his entire body, and said to the Great King:
"Great King, have you already had the various Brahmins, diviners, and physiognomists examine the Prince?"
The father-king replied,
"I have already had him examined.
The seer Asita spoke again to the king, saying:
"What signs do these people predict for this crown prince?
The father-king replied,
"If he succeeds to the throne and governs with the precious wheel-treasure, his fame shall be heard throughout all lands in the ten directions."
Then Asita spoke in verse: "Great King, you should now know! Even those who read physiognomy cannot fathom this;
in this final age there shall be no Wheel-Turning King, for he will surely realize the path to Bodhi."
"The marks of all the Cakravartin kings are not yet so radiant;
observing the Prince now, he shall surely take the throne of the Dharma King.
*Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu (The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins): The Account of the Schism in the Saṃgha*, Fascicle Two.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, the seer Asita, having known that the prince would certainly attain perfect enlightenment, immediately observed the length of his own life-span, thinking:
"In this present life of mine, shall I be able to see the Bodhisattva realize bodhi?"
Having observed this closely, he saw that the Bodhisattva had left home at nineteen and attained the fruit of the Deathless after six years of ascetic practice.

Furthermore, he realized that his own life would end before that time, such that he would not encounter the Bodhisattva as he delivered the Dharma to liberate sentient beings; thereupon, he was overcome with grief, weeping and lamenting in distress.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having seen this, was greatly astonished and asked in verse:
"When men and women alike, upon seeing him, all leap for joy;
why now, O Great Sage, do you alone weep in sorrow before him?"
"Could it be that my prince possesses some inauspicious signs?
How excellent, O Great Seer!
I pray you, tell me this quickly."
Then the seer Asita replied in verse:
"Even if a rain of vajras were suddenly to fall from the midst of the void,
it could not harm a single hair upon this Prince’s body."
Fierce winds and blazing fires, as well as various sharp swords and blades,
poisonous vapors and venomous serpents— none of these can cause him harm.
For all those who are terrified, the Prince provides protection.
How can there be one who brings grief or harm to a Lord of Compassion?
All the sovereign Brahmā deities have come to serve as his guardians;
how can such a most supreme and victorious being feel anxiety or fear?
I now regret my old age; the time of my death is not far off.
Because I have not seen the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, I weep for myself with sorrow.
Those people of future generations who encounter this Bodhisattva—
"He shall surely hear the sublime Dharma and realize that fruit of tranquility.
When the seer Asita had spoken these verses, he felt distressed and resentment, thinking to himself:
"By the power of this prince’s majesty and virtue, I have been made to lose my supernatural powers; I can no longer fly through the air to come and go."
"If I were now to walk out of this city gate, the people would surely look upon me with contempt.
Having thought this, he said to his father the king:
"Your Majesty once made a vow, wishing that the seer Asita might enter and exit the city."
"I have now come on foot to repay the King's long-held intention; I shall likewise depart on foot.
Your Majesty should have the city roads repaired for my sake.
Thereupon, the father-king immediately ordered his great ministers to command the multitudes to adorn the streets and hang up banners and canopies, and he addressed the people of the kingdom, saying:
"The Seer Asita is now walking out of the city; you all may observe him as you please.

At that time, the seer harbored feelings of resentment within his heart. Accompanied by King Śuddhodana, the king’s ministers and officials, elders, householders, and brahmins, who surrounded him before and behind, he went outside the city gate. The seer addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, you may return to the palace; I shall now take my leave."
Having thus parted, the seer Asita proceeded by stages until he reached Mount Ṛṣivadana; thereupon he ascended that mountain, selected a superior site, and took up residence there.
At that time, the seer, exhausted from traveling a long distance, sat down to rest and entered a state of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Because he had entered this absorption, he regained his original supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); however, at a later time, he subsequently fell ill.
The assembly of the rishi’s disciples treated him with various medicinal decoctions, yet his illness did not improve. The assembly addressed the master, saying:
"Master, this present illness of yours has not been cured by medicine; the impermanence of the world cannot be denied."
"All my disciples seek tranquility; since you, our Teacher, have already attained eternal bliss, how could you not leave behind some final instructions?
We pray that you will grant us your teaching, so that we may attain realization and entry into its truth."
The teacher replied:
"Although I have left the household life in my quest for the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), I have not yet realized it and thus have nothing to transmit.
Now, this child born into the Śākya clan will surely attain the unsurpassed, sublime fruit and be able to nourish and benefit sentient beings with the nectar of immortality."
"You, my disciples! You may go forth into homelessness there.
Once you have gone forth, do not rely on the pride of your noble lineage as young brahmins; instead, exert yourselves with diligence and constantly cultivate the holy life."
"For the sake of attaining the Dharma, you must apply yourself with single-minded diligence; if this practice is perfected, you shall obtain the Deathless.
Having spoken these words, he recited this verse:
"From here, toward the east, you should go and seek it there."
"The Buddhas are truly difficult to encounter; having seen them, one should practice with diligence.
He spoke these verses on the dharma of impermanence:
"All accumulations must disperse; all that is lofty will surely fall."
"Meetings end in parting; all who have life must return to death.
Having spoken these verses, the seer Asita immediately passed away.
At that time, the disciple Nārada, having performed the funeral rites with various offerings in accordance with the Dharma according to the season, went to the city of Vārāṇasī and resided there.
Together with five hundred Māṇavakas, he instructed them in the Vedic mantras of the Brahmins.
As for Nārada, his clan name was Kātyāyana; therefore, he was called Kātyāyana.

When the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni attains perfect enlightenment, Kātyāyana will go to the Buddha’s presence. That Buddha will then call him Mahākātyāyana and instruct him with the Dharma, enabling him to cross the great ocean of suffering of birth and death and abide in the supreme tranquility of ultimate *nirvāṇa*. He shall thus be named Mahākātyāyana, and later he will receive the name Amṛta (Nectar).
"At that time, the Bodhisattva sat upon the lap of his nurse and ate fragrant rice from a golden platter in great quantities without ceasing.

When the nurse saw he was eating so much, she attempted to take away the food vessel; however, the Bodhisattva grasped the golden platter with his hand, and the nurse was unable to remove it. Even when eight nurses together attempted to take the vessel, they were likewise unable to do so."
The wet nurses and others went together to inform the king, recounting the matter in detail.
The king, along with the palace attendants, all attempted to seize this vessel together, yet they were likewise unable to do so.
The king again addressed his ministers, commanding them to seize this vessel together.
Those ministers used ropes and hooks to pull and drag at the food vessel, yet they were likewise unable to move it.
Because the ministers were unable to seize it by force, they took five hundred great elephants and used ropes to drag this vessel.
At that time, seeing the people employing such earnest and various means to pull the vessel, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"These people wish to test my strength."
The Bodhisattva then hooked the vessel with his finger; the elephants' pulling force was no longer sufficient, and they all retreated once more.
When King Śuddhodana saw this, he thought to himself:
"If this Bodhisattva can hook back the vessel with a single finger so that five hundred great elephants all retreat, then if he were to use both hands, he would surely oppose a thousand."
"For this reason, he was given the name 'Power of a Thousand Elephants'; this is the fourth title of the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva was born, there was a constant custom: if he wished to enter school, he was accompanied by five hundred attendant youths."
When the Bodhisattva was studying the arts of writing, there was a master named Citrāṅgada who was proficient in five hundred types of scripts.
At that time, King Śuddhodana took the Bodhisattva and the other youths to Citrāṅgada’s residence and ordered them to receive instruction from him.
At that time, the scholar Citrāṅgada composed a particular script and showed it to the Bodhisattva, instructing him to learn it.
The Bodhisattva replied,
"I have already mastered this script."
Next, he presented a second type of script to the Bodhisattva, showing it to him and instructing him to learn it.
The Bodhisattva replied, "I have already mastered this type of script."
Next, he gave him a third type of script and sent him to study it, but the Bodhisattva replied,
"This type of script I have already mastered.
Even when the Master Prabhāsa showed him as many as five hundred types of scripts, it was likewise the case that he had already mastered them all.
The Bodhisattva asked the teacher,
"Are there other books that you can teach me?
The teacher replied:
"These five hundred types of scripts are those currently in use in the world; I understand only these and am ignorant of all others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva himself composed a type of script and presented it to the master.
He asked the Master, saying:
"What character is this? And what is its name?"
The teacher replied,
"I do not know the name of such characters as these.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"If there are two kinds of appearances in the world—
first, the appearance of a Bodhisattva, and second, the appearance of a Golden-Wheel-Turning King— letters of this kind emerge spontaneously according to the world."
At that time, the Great Brahmā King from the midst of the sky spoke these words:
"The two kinds of manifestations and the characters spoken of by the Bodhisattva must indeed be so."
Upon hearing these words, King Śuddhodana and his ministers were filled with great joy.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva opened various new types of books for the elder and spoke extensively upon them.
When the Great King Brahmā beheld this marvel, he took it as proof that the matter must indeed be so; because of this marvel, this script was named the Brahmā Script.
"After the Bodhisattva had mastered various scripts himself, his maternal uncle, named Maṇicāra, came to take the Bodhisattva and others to teach them the art of riding horses."
Furthermore, in the city of Kapilavastu, there was a master named Sārathi, who was proficient in the arts of archery and warfare; he came to instruct the Bodhisattva as well as other Śākya youths.
Māṇava addressed the Teacher, saying:
"This Bodhisattva possesses a heart of great compassion; I wish for him to be taught all the sublime Dharmas, and the other youths as well are fit to be taught."
"Only Devadatta is inherently evil-natured and devoid of compassion; I pray that you, Master, will not teach him the methods of exquisite killing.
For what reason?"
"This man is of an evil nature.
If you teach him, he will surely kill all sentient beings without ceasing; therefore, do not teach him.
Having received these words, the teacher immediately taught the Bodhisattva-dharmas until they were completely exhausted.
As for that wondrous dharma, he did not teach it to Devadatta.
On that day, the Bodhisattva mastered five types of archery techniques:
first, shooting at distant objects; [and so forth].
Second, there are sounds in that place which the Bodhisattva does not see, yet he can shoot and hit them all exactly according to his thoughts;
third, wherever he wishes to shoot, there is no target he does not hit;
fourth, he knows the vital points upon the bodies of others, and according to his intent—whether they should die or not—he shoots those points, all exactly as he desires.
Fifth, regardless of distance, his archery was always perfectly accurate.
The Bodhisattva mastered these five kinds of arts, which were transmitted throughout the four quarters; thus, the Śākya Prince possessed such skills as described above.
"At that time, the people of the city of Vaiśālī obtained a magnificent elephant, complete in its physical characteristics.
The people gathered together and deliberated among themselves, saying:
'King Śuddhodana has a crown prince; according to the prognostications of celestial astrology and physiognomy, he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) in the future.'"
"By his majestic power, this precious elephant has appeared.
He then commanded several men to present this precious elephant to the Śākya Prince.
Those men immediately adorned the elephant and led it toward the city of Kapilavastu; traveling by stages, they arrived at the gate of King Śuddhodana’s palace.

At that time, Prince Devadatta of evil disposition came out from within and, seeing that precious elephant adorned with various ornaments, felt a greedy attachment in his heart. He immediately asked the messenger, "To whom does this elephant belong?"
The messenger replied:

"The Prince of the Śākyas, according to the calculations and signs of the celestial bodies, is destined to become a Golden-Wheel King (Cakravartin). For this reason, the people of the city of Vaiśālī have presented this precious elephant to the Prince."
Upon hearing these words, Devadatta became exceedingly enraged and immediately spoke thus:
"The crown prince of my kingdom has not yet become a Golden Wheel-turning King!"
"Why have you all brought this precious elephant here in advance to present it to the Prince?
Having spoken these words, he gradually approached the elephant; with a heart full of rage, he struck the elephant once, causing it to fall to the ground and die instantly.
Having struck this elephant, he immediately departed.
At that time, Prince Nanda came out from within next; seeing this dead elephant, he asked the people:
"To whom does this elephant belong?"
"Who struck it dead?
The people replied, "This elephant was presented as an offering; Devadatta struck it dead."
He then spoke these words:
"Devadatta is utterly unwholesome.
Nanda reflected deeply once more, saying:
"Could it be that Devadatta is testing his own strength?
At that time, Nanda seized the elephant's tail and dragged it back more than twenty-one paces; having cleared the main road, he then let it pass by.
At that time, the Great Son of the Śākyas came out from within and, seeing this dead elephant, asked the multitude:
"To whom does this elephant belong?
The people spoke as they had done before.
The Bodhisattva asked again,
"By whom was this elephant killed? The people replied:
"Prince Devadatta struck this great elephant once, and it died immediately.
The Bodhisattva asked again,
"Where exactly did he strike the elephant to cause its death?"
The people replied, "This elephant died on the road.
The Bodhisattva asked again:
"Who was it that dragged this elephant from the middle of the road and brought it here? The people replied,
"Prince Nanda seized the tail with one hand and dragged the great elephant, placing it in this spot."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"To kill a person is most unwholesome; to drag them along the road is exceedingly good.
He reflected on this once more:
"Is it not that these two men are privately testing their own strength?
I shall test them as well.
At that time, the Bodhisattva seized the elephant's trunk and flung it far beyond the city walls; it fell to the ground seven *li* away, and the earth immediately sank in.
The people of that time called it "the place where the elephant was trapped," and the faithful elder brahmin subsequently erected a great stūpa at this spot.
Then all the bhikṣus came to pay homage and spoke these verses:
"Devadatta struck down the great king of elephants; Nanda dragged him for twenty-one paces."
"The Bodhisattva hurls [objects] outside the city moats, as if tossing tiles and stones in mid-air.
At that time, the Śākya youths said to one another:
"Let us go outside and enjoy the sport of whirling swords to cut down trees."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went out into the forest.
Hearing that the youths had gone to the forest to play, the Bodhisattva led five hundred youths, with them surrounding him before and behind, and arrived at that grove.
The young Śākya princes vied with one another in hurling discus-swords, causing all the trees to fall prostrate.
At that time, the Bodhisattva also hurled a discus-sword; the forest was completely severed, yet no tree fell, because the edge of the blade was flat.

At that time, when the youths saw that the tree did not fall, they said to one another, "We have heard that the Bodhisattva is majestic and sovereign, such that there is no among the five arts in which he is not proficient; why then, when cutting the tree with his wheel-blade, could he not even topple it?"
"If even this minor art of felling trees is such as this, how much more so must his other skills be!

At that time, the deva, seeing that the youths had given rise to such slanderous opinions, wishing to dispel their doubts, immediately released a fierce wind that blew the forest trees until they all fell down with a roar.
When the young Śākyas saw this, they were all greatly astonished and finally acknowledged his marvelous skill.

Then the youths again competed with the Bodhisattva in archery, using seven layers of iron tala trees and seven iron drums, with an iron boar placed between each layer, as the targets for their shooting.
While none of the other youths could shoot beyond a single *tāla* tree, the youth Devadatta shot past one *tāla* tree, one drum, and one pig, and his arrow then came to rest.
The youth Nanda shot past two *tāla* trees, two drums, and two pigs, and his arrow then came to a halt.
At that time, the Bodhisattva released a single arrow; it pierced straight through seven trees, seven drums, and seven pigs, passing beyond the earth-wheel and entering the depths of the water.

At that time, the Dragon King immediately extracted the arrow; from the wound where the arrow had entered, water gushed forth—fragrant, light, and delicious—and all who drank of it marveled at its rarity.
At that time, faithful brahmins, householders, and others built a stupa by the waterside to make offerings.
Having finished these games, the Bodhisattva then mounted a carriage with his horse and returned to the city together with the other youths.
Beside the city gate were various physiognomists who, seeing from afar the Bodhisattva’s exceptionally sublime majesty and radiance, said to one another in competition:
"If this prince does not renounce the world within twelve years from now, he will surely ascend to the rank of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin)."
When King Śuddhodana heard these words from the physiognomist, he was filled with great joy and leaped for delight. He immediately assembled his ministers and addressed them, saying:
"I have heard the physiognomist’s assessment of my crown prince: if he does not leave the home life within twelve years, he shall attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King."
"You all should provide diligent protection so that for twelve full years he does not leave the household life, thereby enabling him to ascend the throne of a Golden Wheel-Turning King.

You all should provide diligent protection so that for twelve full years he does not leave the household life, thereby enabling him to ascend the throne of a Golden Wheel-Turning King; then, surrounded by you all, he shall soar through the void and survey the four continents."
"You all should quickly construct palaces and select beautiful women to provide him with entertainment.
At that time, the ministers came forward and said to the king:
"As we observe the Prince, he finds no pleasure in the worldly desires of sound, fragrance, or sensual love."
"How can one be detained by beautiful women?
The King said to his ministers:

"Even if my crown prince does not love all those sensual desires, it must be because he has not yet seen an exceptionally exquisite woman. From this day forward, you gentlemen must diligently select superior young maidens and bring double the number for the prince to see; among them, he will surely find one who inspires his affection."
The ministers deliberated, saying:

"Although this prince is currently free from worldly attachments, we should prepare various articles for adorning the body and have each of us send a young girl of beautiful countenance to personally present these fragrant ornaments to the prince."
Furthermore, he ordered that each of the princesses be bestowed with exquisite and precious ornaments; those whom the Prince favored were then made to remain and enjoy his company in play.

Having deliberated thus, he immediately had a palace constructed for the Prince, adorned with a hundred jewels and furnished with lion thrones. He seated the Prince upon one of these thrones and piled various treasures and diverse necklaces before him until they formed a great heap.

He issued a general command to all his ministers and other attendants, ordering them to assemble every young girl available; these girls were to adorn themselves according to their own wishes at any time, wearing various necklaces and ornaments as they entered the palace.
By nature, the Bodhisattva was fond of giving and bestowing; he universally presented necklaces to all the young maidens.
At that time, there was a young maiden among the Śākya clan named Yaśodharā, whose beauty and countenance were upright and rare in the world.

The Śākya youth Daṇḍapāṇi immediately returned home and said to his daughter, "The Prince is currently bestowing upon all the young maidens various jewels, rare treasures, and exquisite ornaments; you should go and receive them."
The girl replied, "Does my own home not have this? Why should I use anything from elsewhere?"
The father said to his daughter,
"Even though that prince bestows precious jewels, he might still take you as his consort out of love and desire.
The daughter said:
"If she becomes my consort at this time, even if I take other women as wives, I shall certainly become their Great Consort.
The father replied, "It shall surely be so."
"You may depart at once.
Thereupon Yaśodharā immediately adorned her body with various precious ornaments, and accompanied by her handmaidens, likewise beautifully arrayed, she departed together with them.
All the people by the roadside gazed upon Yaśodharā with shared affection and admiration, paying no heed to anyone else.
When Yaśodharā entered the Prince’s palace, she advanced with elegant and composed steps, her body upright, without looking to her left or right, as she stood before the Crown Prince.
At that time, the prince had already exhausted his precious jewels in giving them to the women, leaving nothing remaining behind.
He had only a single golden ring; seeing Yaśodharā, he immediately raised his finger.

However, Yaśodharā had been bound to the Bodhisattva by causes and conditions from time immemorial, and they had always cherished one another with love; she then ascended the lion throne and took the ring from the Prince’s finger.
The ministers and various officials said to one another:
"This Yaśodharā is of noble lineage and possesses perfect beauty; she is the most distinguished among all women and is fit to serve as an attendant in the Prince’s inner quarters."
After the ministers and all the people had deliberated thus together, they reported this matter in detail to King Śuddhodana.
The King immediately dispatched twenty thousand court ladies to surround Yaśodharā and enter the Prince’s inner palace.

"Furthermore, it is the constant law of Bodhisattvas that upon their appearance in a world, a tree must necessarily arise called 'Excellent Firmness' (Sudṛḍha). When it first sprouts, within a single night it reaches a height of one hundred cubits."
On the night of its initial birth, before it has seen the light of the sun, its substance is so soft that it can be cut with one's fingernails;
once it has seen the sunlight, it immediately becomes hard and rigid, such that even the application of knives, axes, or fierce fires cannot destroy it.

After the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni had appeared in the world, there was a great river named Rohiṇī between the two cities of Kapilavastu and Devadṛśa. This tree grew upon its bank; as the river water swelled and its vast waves surged and crashed, the shifting sands breached the shore and the earth and stones were scattered away, leaving the tree’s excellent and firm roots and fibers fully exposed.
Later, due to a violent wind, it was toppled and lay across the Lohita River, acting like a great dam that blocked the flow of water.
Consequently, the city of Kapilavastu was gradually submerged, while the city of Devadṛśa became parched and dry.
When King Devadaha saw this occurrence, he immediately dispatched a messenger to inform King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Now this great tree lies横跨 across the water, causing distress to both sides."
"In the king's realm there are many youths who are all brave and strong; I pray that Your Majesty will command them to remove this tree.
Then King Śuddhodana replied to the messenger, "How can I possibly issue orders regarding this matter now?"
In the kingdom of Kapilavastu, there was a high minister named Chandaka who came forward and said to the king:
"I pray that Your Majesty allow me to oversee this matter; I possess a skillful means by which the princes may remove these trees themselves, without needing Your Majesty's command."
The King said, "So be it.
The minister Chandaka immediately cleared and swept a grove by the riverbank until it was pure and fit for recreation, and invited the princes to go to the forest to play.
Each of the princes mounted a precious chariot and was surrounded by a retinue of youths; having arrived at the grove, they each spread out their seats and indulged in unrestrained merriment.
At that time, a wild goose was flying across the sky; Devadatta immediately drew his bow and shot at it, causing the goose to fall, landing right in front of the Bodhisattva’s seat.
At that time, the Bodhisattva picked up the goose and extracted the arrow from it; he treated it with medicine, and it was restored to health immediately.
Devadatta then sent a messenger to tell the Bodhisattva:
"This goose was originally shot by me; you must return it to me."
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the messenger:
"I have long since resolved upon bodhicitta; all sentient beings were previously mine. How then can this goose be yours?"
Devadatta had harbored enmity toward the Bodhisattva for a very long time; upon hearing these words, he immediately conceived malice.
However, the Bodhisattva’s karmic bonds of enmity with all sentient beings were already exhausted, with the sole exception of Devadatta, who still possessed residual habitual tendencies;
now, because of this goose, this would be his final body, and it would mark the beginning of his first conflict with Devadatta.
When King Devadaha, having failed to have King Śuddhodana remove the tree despite his request, ordered the people of his own kingdom to pull it down together,
the multitude exerted their strength and labor, and the clamor of their shouts rose up like a boiling torrent. Having heard this, the Bodhisattva asked those around him, "What is that sound?"
The minister Canda fully explained his intention regarding the tree that was damming the water.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva immediately addressed the multitude:
"I shall go there myself to remove this tree."
Then that bodhisattva, together with the youths and others, proceeded toward that place. From a hole by the side of the road, a venomous snake emerged.
Seeing this venomous snake, Udāyin, fearing it would harm the bodhisattva, immediately drew a sharp sword and cut it into two pieces.
A snake spat venom onto Udāyin’s body, turning it black; for this reason, he was named Black Udāyin.
At that time, the young boys vied with one another to display their strength as they pulled at the Sāla tree.
Devadatta summoned his courage and stepped forward, pulling with all his might, yet it moved only slightly;
the youth Nanda lifted it and held it a short distance above the ground;
but the Bodhisattva, seizing it with his hand, hurled it into the air, whereupon the tree was split in two, each half falling on opposite banks.
At that time, the Bodhisattva addressed the people, saying:
"This tree of excellent solidity is a cooling medicine capable of removing febrile diseases; you all should cut it into small pieces and divide it among yourselves."
"If there is any demonic affliction, carbuncles, or swellings, applying this [ointment] will cause them all to be cured.
At that time, the youths all mounted their carriages and returned toward the city of Kapilavastu. Upon reaching the city gate, they encountered a diviner who spoke these words:
"If the Bodhisattva does not renounce the household life during this day, he will surely ascend to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King."
At that time, there was a daughter of the Śākyas named Gopikā, who lived in the village of Kumbhakāra and was looking out from a high pavilion.
When the Bodhisattva entered the city and saw her from afar, he pressed down on her carriage with his toes, and the carriage stopped moving.

The girl saw from afar that the Bodhisattva was reflecting within his mind; in the Bodhisattva’s hand there was already an iron pestle, which he rubbed between his fingers until it crumbled into fine dust.
Gopikā watched the Bodhisattva and pressed down on the pavilion with her toes, whereupon the structure collapsed into a hole.
Upon seeing this, the people thought to themselves:
"This Śākyan maiden will surely be able to win the heart of the Bodhisattva.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he immediately welcomed the maiden Gopikā, along with twenty thousand court ladies as attendants, into the palace.
"It is the constant custom of Bodhisattvas:
when they wish to go out to tour the gardens and groves, they immediately command their charioteer, 'Prepare my favorite vehicle at once; I wish to ride it to tour the gardens and groves.'"
The charioteer, having received these instructions, prepared the supreme vehicle and went before the Bodhisattva, saying to him:
"I have prepared the supreme vehicle; I pray only that you know it is time."

As the Bodhisattva ascended his carriage to go on an excursion, he encountered an old man whose vital strength was feeble and whose body was emaciated; his waist and back were bent, he walked leaning on a staff, his body trembled, and his beard and hair had changed color, unlike those of other men.
Having seen him, the Bodhisattva said to the charioteer:
"Who is that man? His back is hunched, his body is emaciated, and he is so withered and worn."
The charioteer replied, "This is called an 'old man'; this person will soon surely die.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Will I also become like this at a later time?
The charioteer replied,
"The body of the Prince shall likewise become like this."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva was filled with sorrow and distress;
he immediately told the charioteer, "Return to the palace at once, so that I may go within the palace and contemplate this matter."
"How shall I escape from this suffering?
Following these instructions, the charioteer immediately returned to the palace.
Once he had arrived at the palace, the Bodhisattva sat upright in meditation and reflected, thinking thus:
"Such is the law of old age; before long it will come upon me as well. How can I avoid it?
He then spoke in verse:
"When one suddenly encounters such a person in decay, Their body withered and emaciated, walking while leaning on a staff;..."
"My own body is likewise bound by old age; how can I escape this suffering?
At that time, King Śuddhodana, seeing the Bodhisattva return to the palace, asked the charioteer:
"Did the Prince find joy while going out of the city to visit the groves and springs?"
The charioteer replied,
"I see that the Prince has no joy. The King said:
"Why are you not joyful?

The charioteer replied, "Accompanying the Prince out of the city, I saw an old man outside the gate; his body was frail and weak, his countenance withered and haggard, leaning on a staff as he walked forward, his whole frame trembling."
Upon seeing me, the Crown Prince immediately asked,
"Who is that person who has come here? I then replied:
"This one is called an 'old man. He then asked me:
"Will I become like this at a later time?"
I immediately replied,
"It must surely be so.
Upon hearing this, the Prince commanded me to return and contemplate this matter.
"Now, while in the palace, I am contemplating this matter.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he thought to himself:
"When the Prince was born, the physiognomists all said he would leave the household life to practice the Way."
"If it is now thus, this must be the reason.
I shall provide double the requisites for the five sensual pleasures to entertain him.
Having formed this thought, he immediately ordered that the requisites for the five sensual pleasures be doubled to amuse the Prince.
The verse says:
"When the King, his father, heard the words of the charioteer, he immediately reflected upon the words of the physiognomist;
providing him with fivefold sensual pleasures even greater than before, he wished to prevent the Bodhisattva from leaving home."
"It is the constant custom of Bodhisattvas:
when they wish to go out of the city for an excursion, they first instruct their charioteer, 'Quickly prepare my carriage for me; I shall go out of the city for an excursion.'"
The charioteer, having received his command, immediately prepared a magnificent and exquisite carriage. Once it was ready, he informed the Bodhisattva that he might now go out for an excursion.
As they were about to leave the city, they encountered a sick man whose entire body was wan and yellow, emaciated and exhausted; the people along the roadside all passed by without looking at him.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva asked his charioteer:
"Who is this person? His body is emaciated, weak, wan, and gravely ill, yet no one at all takes notice of him."
The charioteer replied, "This is called a sick person; because of this illness, he will soon die.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Is it the case that I have transcended this nature of illness?
The charioteer replied,
"You too have not yet transcended this nature of illness."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva was filled with sorrow and distress; he immediately ordered his charioteer to return to the palace so that he might contemplate this matter.
When the charioteer had delivered him to the inner palace, the Bodhisattva sat upright and contemplated the suffering of such illness.
Then King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"Did the Prince enjoy himself as he went out of the city for sightseeing?
The charioteer replied:
"The Prince is not happy.
He asked again, "Why is he unhappy?"
At that time, the charioteer related the aforementioned matters in detail.
Having heard this, the king redoubled his efforts to provide the prince with the pleasures of the five senses.
A verse says:
"Exquisite forms, sounds, and fragrances, And the most supreme tastes and textures— You shall enjoy these five sensual pleasures; Do not abandon me to go forth into homelessness."
"It is the constant custom of the Bodhisattva:
when he is about to go out of the city for an excursion, he first commands his charioteer to prepare and adorn the carriage.
Once it has been prepared, he goes out of the city for an excursion and encounters a dead man being carried on a multicolored vehicle."

Furthermore, there was another person holding a brazier who walked ahead; behind the multicolored chariot, many men and women with disheveled hair wailed in grief, causing those who saw them to feel profound sorrow.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva asked his charioteer:
"Who is this person? Why is their carriage adorned with various colors and ornaments, yet they are being carried away while men and women wail and all who see them are filled with grief?"
The charioteer replied,
"This is called a dead man. The Prince asked:
"What is meant by 'a dead person'?
The charioteer replied,
"When this person's vital breath has completely ceased, they can no longer meet again with their parents, brothers, wife, children, or kinsmen."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Am I also like this? He replied:
"It is so. Having heard this, the Bodhisattva was filled with sorrow and displeasure, and immediately ordered his return to the palace.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer:
"Did the Prince enjoy himself when he went out of the city for his excursion?
The charioteer replied,
"I saw that the Prince was sorrowful and not at all joyful."
The king asked,
"For what reason? He replied:
"Today on the road I encountered a dead man, whose parents, wife, and children were wailing and escorting him;
the Prince asked, 'Shall I also become like this?
To which I immediately replied:"
"All must be thus," he thought,
and so while in the palace he contemplated this matter.
Then King Śuddhodana further provided the five sensory pleasures, entertaining the Bodhisattva with various exquisite music, performances, jewels, and court ladies.
The verse says:
"This most excellent city is most magnificently adorned; A Son of Heaven among gods may dwell here for long.
He shall enjoy himself with the five desires redoubled, Just like the Thousand-Eyed One in the Nandana Grove."
At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens all contemplated together:
"The Bodhisattva already possesses the power of great, substantial causes; we shall act as the great conditions for the Bodhisattva."
"Why is this? Because if there is a great cause, it must await great conditions.
He then immediately manifested as a great śramaṇa, holding a mendicant’s staff and carrying an alms bowl, proceeding in order to beg for food.
It is the constant custom of Bodhisattvas:

when setting out from the city for an excursion, they first order their carriage to be prepared; once the carriage is ready, they ascend it and proceed forward. Along the road, they encounter a śramaṇa who has shaved off his hair and beard and wears the *kaṣāya* robe, holding an alms-bowl and walking slowly to beg for food.
Having seen him, the Bodhisattva asked the charioteer, "Who is this man?
The charioteer replied:
"He is called a renunciant.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"What is meant by 'renunciation'?"
He replied: "This person cultivates wholesome deeds with a virtuous mind and dwells in a state of goodness; his actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely pure.

Because of his faith, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons the robes of the Tathāgata, leaves the household life behind, and ascends the path to Nirvāṇa; therefore, he is called one who has 'left the home' (pravrajita)."
The Bodhisattva then said to the charioteer,
"You may drive the carriage near that śramaṇa.
Following his command, the charioteer immediately led the carriage to where the śramaṇa was.
At that time, the Bodhisattva asked the śramaṇa:
"Who are you? For what reason have you shaved off your hair and beard and donned robes of a distinct color, holding an alms-bowl and staff to sustain yourself by begging?"
The śramaṇa replied, "I am a renunciant.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"What is meant by one who is called a renunciant?

The śramaṇa replied, "One who constantly maintains a virtuous mind and perpetually cultivates wholesome conduct, ensuring that the actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely pure; who leaves behind the secular household and ascends the path to nirvāṇa—for these reasons, one is called a renunciant."
The Bodhisattva exclaimed:
"Excellent is this matter! Excellent is this matter!"
He then thought to himself,
"If this is so, I too shall go forth into homelessness.
He immediately commanded his charioteer:
"You should return to the palace at once; I shall go into the palace and deliberate upon this matter.
The charioteer received the command and, taking up the reins, returned to the palace.
Having arrived at the palace, he sat in silence and reflected deeply.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer,
"Did the Prince enjoy himself as he went out of the city today for an excursion? He replied:
"I have observed that the Prince is sorrowful and finds no joy.
The King then asked,
"For what reason is he not joyful?"
The charioteer replied:

"When the Prince went out of the city, he encountered a śramaṇa who had shaved off his hair and beard and donned the *kaṣāya* robe; holding an alms bowl and a mendicant’s staff, he walked slowly while begging for food."
The Crown Prince asked me,
"Who is that person? I immediately replied:
"You are called a renunciant," he said, and then asked me,
"In what sense is one called a renunciant?"
I then replied: "One abandons the secular home and ascends the path to nirvana; therefore, it is called 'leaving home' (pravrajyā).
Having heard this, the Prince ordered me to drive the carriage near the śramaṇa and asked him:
"Who are you? Having shaved off your hair and beard and donned robes of a different color, you carry a water jar and alms bowl in your hands and go about begging for food yourself.
The śramaṇa replied:
"I am a renunciant. The Prince asked, "What is meant by being a renunciant?"
He replied, "Having abandoned the household life, I have ascended the path to Nirvana.
Upon hearing this, the Prince immediately exclaimed:
“Excellent is this matter! Excellent is this matter!
If it is thus, I too shall go forth into homelessness.”
"He immediately commanded me to return to the palace quickly; he is now within the palace contemplating this matter.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he was despondent and unhappy, thinking to himself:
"When the Prince was born, the physiognomists prophesied:"
"The Prince will not ascend the throne; he will certainly renounce the household life.
Observing his current physical signs, the time for his renunciation has arrived.

I shall employ a skillful means: I will now send the Prince to the fields to see the multitude of people coming and going engaged in their labors, so that his heart may find joy and forget the matter of leaving home."
Having had this thought, he immediately went into the palace and told the prince:
"I have excellent fields that I wish to have cultivated; you may go and supervise them."

While the Prince was in the palace, as he contemplated those who were old, sick, and dead, he immediately conceived a sense of sorrow and fear; yet, as he thought of those śramaṇas, a feeling of joyful longing arose once more, and his mind remained bound to them, never for a moment letting go.

Hearing his father’s words, he realized they could not be disobeyed; he immediately followed his father’s instructions and ordered his charioteer to mount the carriage and set out. Although his body was traveling toward the fields, his mind remained constantly fixed on the thought of renouncing the household life.
As he proceeded forward, he suddenly encountered five hundred treasuries along the way, all of which had their doors opened; from within them, a voice spoke, saying:
"Excellent, O Prince!"
"These treasures of ours are the storehouse of your past kinsmen; you may take them all and use them as you please.
The prince replied, "These are the foolish requisites of past kinsmen, accumulated over time without ever knowing how to relinquish them."
"What use am I to you now? Depart quickly!
At that time, the treasure-trove again uttered a voice, saying:
"If you do not take me, I shall now enter the sea.
The Bodhisattva replied, "Go as you please."
Then Ratnagarbha and the others entered the great ocean.

At that time, the Bodhisattva continued his gradual journey forward until he reached a village of plowmen. He saw those farmers with their bodies covered in dust and sweat flowing over their entire frames; they held ox-goads in their hands, all of which were dripping with blood.

Furthermore, he saw those oxen, their hides and backs pierced and festering, tormented by hunger and thirst, emaciated and suffering with incessant panting; they were being bitten by gadflies and flies on their pus and blood, while small insects filled their sores and fed upon them, or had their legs wounded and sliced by the blades of the plow.
As the Bodhisattva traveled through the places where fields were plowed and sown, he witnessed all such instances of suffering and affliction.
Having cultivated deep compassion over immeasurable kalpas, upon encountering these karmic sufferings, he felt profound pity and immediately called out to the farmers, asking them:
"To whom do you belong?"
The people replied, "We all belong to the Prince.
The Bodhisattva said:
"I now release you all to live as you please; you need no longer be bound to me.
As for the oxen used for plowing, they too shall be set free to follow water and grass to sustain their lives."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, reflecting upon these matters of suffering, descended from his chariot and entered the first *anāsrava-sadṛśa-samādhi* (similarity samādhi free from outflows) amidst the Jambu trees. His attendants on both sides surrounded the Bodhisattva, each sitting beneath a tree to wait upon him.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"The hour for the meal is approaching; why has the Prince not yet returned to the palace?

Desiring to go in person to see his son, he ordered a carriage, mounted it, and set out. Upon reaching the fields where the plowing was taking place, he searched through all the surrounding areas for the Prince, until he saw him beneath a Jambu tree, having entered into samādhi.

At that time, the sun had already tilted toward the west, and the shadows of all the trees followed its movement; yet the tree beneath which the Prince sat continued to shade him, its shadow remaining unmoved.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having witnessed this event, thought to himself:
"Now my great son possesses immense majesty and virtue.
The sun has already tilted toward the west, and the shadows of all the trees follow the sun's movement; yet the tree beneath which my great son sits still shades him, its shadow not shifting."

Filled with joy and exultation, they gave rise to a heart of reverence; bowing their bodies and lowering their heads, they prostrated before the Prince and requested that he arise from his meditative absorption to ascend the precious chariot together with them, returning gradually to the palace.

Upon reaching the charnel ground, he saw various corpses, some yellowish, some mottled, foul-smelling and in utter disarray; having seen this, the Prince’s sorrow deepened further, and sitting cross-legged within his precious carriage, he focused his mind in contemplation.
Gradually arriving at the city of Kapilavastu, the astrologers immediately divined:
"If the Prince does not renounce the household life within seven days, he will surely ascend to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King."
Having divined this matter, he immediately presented these verses to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"If the Prince does not go forth into homelessness, within seven days— at the time of sunrise—
he will surely ascend to the rank of a Golden Wheel-turning Monarch."
The Prince shall be like the Sovereign King of the Seven Jewels;
within the seas there will be no forced labor, and enemies shall be naturally pacified.
If the Prince renounces the world, he will sit fearlessly amidst the forest groves.
"Having realized that all-knowledge, may you deliver and liberate all sentient beings.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva had entered the city, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Anatikrama. He had a daughter named Mṛgajā, who, seeing the Bodhisattva from afar through the lattice window of her tower, praised him with this verse:
"Born of a mother who brings peace and joy, Nourished by a father who brings peace and joy; He who has abandoned all worldly desires, May he attain the supreme, unsurpassed awakening."
"She is most peaceful and happy; she shall be your wife.
When the Bodhisattva heard this, his mind entered the meaning of the sound of "nirvāṇa" in profound stillness, and he heard only these words:
"O you, supreme among men, you should contemplate the tranquility of nirvāṇa."

Upon hearing this sound of Nirvana, the Bodhisattva felt affection and joy; because he heard this wondrous sound, he immediately removed a pearl necklace from around his neck and cast it into the air.
By the power of his majesty, it then fell upon the neck of the Deer King’s daughter.
When the people saw this, they were all greatly delighted and reported the matter in detail to King Śuddhodana.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately ordered twenty thousand court ladies to go and welcome the daughter of the Deer King, bringing her into the prince’s palace.
At that time, the Bodhisattva had three wives:
the first was named Mṛgajā, the second Gopikā, and the third Yaśodharā.
Among them, Yaśodharā was the foremost; each of the three queens had twenty thousand court ladies surrounding them before and behind within the palace.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard the verses of the astrologer, immediately summoned his four brothers, including Amṛtodana, to assemble in one place and deliberate together upon those verses of the astrologer:

"If he does not leave home within seven days, he shall ascend the throne as a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). Therefore, we ought to guard the Prince for these seven days, and furthermore, station our troops to provide diligent defense at the four city gates."

Having deliberated thus, they immediately constructed sevenfold city walls and moats around the city of Kapilavastu; all were fitted with iron gates, and upon each gate hung a series of ringing bells.
Whenever the gates were opened or closed, the sound of the bells could be heard spreading in all four directions for forty *li* each.

Above the pavilions where the Bodhisattva resided, female musicians performed various musical pieces, singing and dancing in his encircling attendance. Great ministers and valiant generals led the fourfold army, maintaining strict watch and guarding the city from without.

The various gates within the Bodhisattva’s palace were always closed; even if there were messengers who needed to come and go, a staircase was specially installed on the city watchtower so that five hundred men could carry it up and down.
Whenever the gates of the inner palace were opened or closed, they all produced extraordinary sounds so that King Śuddhodana could hear them.

Upon hearing the sound of the gates, all the palace women took up weapons and blades, while the hundreds of officials and men outside the city of Kapilavastu likewise redoubled their efforts to guard one another.

At that time, King Śuddhodana personally led the fourfold army to guard the eastern gate of the city; King Droṇodana personally led the fourfold army to guard the southern gate; King Śuklodana again led the fourfold army to guard the western gate; and King Amṛtodana likewise led the fourfold army to guard the northern gate.
The Greatly Renowned Śākyan, leading his valiant warriors, made a circuit through the city and arrived at the eastern gate of the city, where he asked the gatekeeper:
"Who guards this gate?
King Śuddhodana replied:
"This is my watch," said Mahānāman.
The General replied, "It is good for one to keep watch; it is evil to sleep."
He then spoke in verse:
"The one who sleeps is like a dead man; such a person belongs to the King of Māra.
The wise are always awakened; therefore, they diligently maintain their guard."
After the Śākya Mahānāma had spoken this verse, he went to the southern gate and asked the gatekeeper,
"Who guards this? King Droṇodana replied:
"This is my watch," said Mahānāman. "Diligence is good; sleep is evil."
Then he spoke in verse:
"The one who sleeps is like a dead man; This person belongs to King Māra.
The wise are always awakened; Therefore, they diligently maintain their guard."
After Mahānāma Śākya had spoken this verse, he went again to the western gate and asked the gatekeeper:
"Who is guarding this? King Śuklodana replied:
"This is my watch," said Mahānāman. "He who exerts himself is good; he who sleeps is evil."
He further spoke in verse:
“The one who sleeps is like a dead man; Such a person belongs to King Māra.
The wise are always awakened; Therefore, they diligently maintain watch.”
Having spoken this verse, he proceeded again to the northern gate and asked the gatekeeper,
"Who guards this place? King Amṛtodana replied:
"This is my watch," said Mahānāman.
The General replied, "It is good for those who are diligent; it is not good for those who sleep."
Then he spoke in verse:
“The one who sleeps is like a dead man; such a person belongs to the King of Māra.
The wise are ever awakened; therefore, they guard themselves with diligence.”
Having spoken these verses, he returned to the central camp and asked the guard:
"Who is on watch? The guard replied:
"This is so-and-so keeping watch.
"It is good for those who are diligent; it is not good for those who sleep.
He then spoke this verse:
"Exert yourself and do not transgress the Dharma; speak truth and do not speak falsehoods.
False speech leads to darkness; therefore, exert yourself to guard against it."
After the Great Sage Śākya had completed such a circuit, dawn broke, and he addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Of the seven days, one night has already passed; only six days remain."
The king then replied:
"Since six days remain, guard him with diligent care.
If these six days pass, my crown prince shall ascend to the rank of a Golden Wheel-turning King."
"We shall all follow you, soaring through the void to observe the four continents.
Thus they kept watch for six days, with only one night remaining.
