It is the constant custom of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, that when he surveys the lower realms, he utters this verse:
“The Prince of the land of Śākyamuni Has fully perfected the practice of the six pāramitās;
Delighting in renunciation, he dwells in the mountain forests To seek the unsurpassed path of True Suchness.”
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Three;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command:
"At that time, while the Bodhisattva was in the pleasure gardens within the palace, he thought to himself:
'I now have three principal wives and sixty thousand court ladies; if I do not provide them with worldly pleasures, I fear that outsiders will say:'"
"I am not her husband; I shall now enjoy myself with Yaśodharā.
Consequently, Yaśodharā became pregnant. Once she was pregnant, she gave rise to this thought:
"I shall inform the Bodhisattva at dawn.
At that time, during that night, the Bodhisattva, reflecting on the conditions of birth, spoke these verses:
"Sleeping together with this woman, this is the very last time we shall sleep together; Thus ends the translation.
"From this day forth, I shall never again do so; I shall forever leave behind sleeping and lodging with women.

On that very night, the palace ladies, court singers, and entertainers were all exhausted and fell into a deep, heavy sleep; some had their hair disheveled, some had tears and saliva flowing from their mouths, some were muttering in their sleep, and others had half their bodies exposed.
When the Bodhisattva saw this, although he was within the deep palace, it was as if he were among graves seeing various dead people. He immediately reflected upon it and spoke in verse:
"As the wind blows down the lotuses of the pond, Lying sprawled with limbs and hands in disarray;
Hair disheveled and the body exposed, All affectionate attachments have been utterly abandoned."
Now that I see these women sleeping, their bodies transformed like those of the dead;
why did I not realize sooner that I was here in this state of sentient existence, devoid of wisdom?
Desire is like that mud, the arrow, the poison, and the fire; it is like a dream or drinking salt water.
One should abandon it as the Dragon King abandoned what is difficult to abandon, for all sufferings and enmities arise because of it.
After the Bodhisattva had spoken these verses, he immediately fell asleep.
At that time, during the night, the lady Mahāprajāpatī saw four kinds of dreams:

first, she saw the moon being eclipsed; second, she saw the sun rise in the east and then immediately set; third, she saw many people prostrating themselves before her; and fourth, she saw herself either laughing or weeping.
At that time, Yaśodharā again saw eight kinds of dreams during this night: first, she saw that her maternal family and clan were all scattered and destroyed;

second, she saw that the couch on which she sat with the Bodhisattva was completely shattered; third, she saw that both her arms suddenly broke off; fourth, she saw that all her teeth fell out; fifth, she saw that all her hair and beard fell out; sixth, she saw the auspicious deity depart from outside her residence; seventh, she saw the moon being eclipsed; and eighth, she saw the sun, having just risen in the east, immediately sink back down.
During the night, the Bodhisattva saw five kinds of dreams:

first, he saw his own body lying upon the great earth, with his head resting on Mount Sumeru, his left hand entering the Eastern Sea, his right hand entering the Western Sea, and both feet entering the Southern Sea;
second, he saw auspicious grass growing from the top of his heart, rising high above the limits of space.
Third, he saw white birds with black heads that, wishing to fly into the air upon prostrating to the Bodhisattva, could not pass below the Bodhisattva’s knees;
fourth, he saw various colored birds from the four directions that, upon reaching the presence of the Bodhisattva, all became of one color;
fifth, he saw the Bodhisattva walking back and forth upon a mountain of filth and impurity.
Having seen this dream, he immediately rose from his bed and thought with joy:
"By these signs now present, before long I shall attain the unsurpassed wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, Yaśodharā immediately woke from her sleep and recounted those eight dreams to the Bodhisattva.
Fearing that Yaśodharā might give rise to sorrow and distress in her heart, the Bodhisattva used skillful means to interpret these dreams so as to bring her joy, saying:
"As for seeing the clans of your maternal family all destroyed—look, they are all present right now; how could they be destroyed?"
"As for what you saw of my bed collapsing while we sat together—how could it collapse now when it appears perfectly intact?
As for what you saw of both your arms suddenly breaking—how could they be broken now when they are entirely uninjured?"
When I saw that all your teeth had fallen out, I now see them as they were before.
When I saw that your hair and beard had also fallen out, I now see them as they were.
Regarding the sight of the auspicious deity leaving your house: the auspicious deity of women is her husband, and he is present here now.
Regarding the sight of the moon being eclipsed: you should observe it; it is now seen full.
"You see the sun rise in the east and then set; yet now, at midnight, the sun has not even risen—how could it have set?
When Yaśodharā heard this explanation, she remained silent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected upon this dream:
"According to the signs seen by Yaśodharā, it is fitting for me to go forth into homelessness this very night.
He further thought:
"I should employ skillful means to cause Yaśodharā to briefly perceive my awakening.
Having formed this thought, he said to Yaśodharā:
"I wish to renounce the household life."
Yaśodharā said, "Great King! If you wish to go, please take me with you."
The Bodhisattva thought to himself,
"When I attain Nirvana, I shall take you with me," and he said to Yaśodharā:
"I have a place to go; I shall take you with me.
When Yaśodharā heard these words, she fell asleep with joy. At that time, the Bodhisattva resolved to depart.
Mahābrahmā, Śakra, and the others, knowing the Bodhisattva’s thought, arrived at that very moment. Joining their palms in reverence, they spoke this verse:
“The mind is like an untamed horse, And also like a restless monkey;
One who can renounce the pleasures of the five desires Will swiftly realize the light of Nirvāṇa.”
"O Greatly Compassionate One, arise, arise! Renounce this earth, O Honored One;
you shall attain all-knowledge and deliver all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Śakra, Lord of Devas! Do you not see?
He then spoke in verse:
“As if a lion king were confined within an iron cage, with fierce generals guarding its side with bows and swords;
surrounded by a vast and clamorous multitude of elephants, horses, and men—how could one emerge from this city?”
The Father King was like a fierce lion; his fourfold army was fully equipped with iron armor.
The city walls, moats, towers, and galleries were filled with every kind of weapon.
Seeing those palace gates and gate-towers, even the city gates were likewise;
they were hung all around with tinkling bells, secured with such formidable bolts that they could not be passed.
Various conchs and drums surround me, their clamorous sounds never ceasing;
outside the palace are many troops of elephants and horses, guarding with diligent effort so that I may not go out.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra spoke in verse:
“Reflect now upon your former vow; The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara previously bestowed his prediction.
While sentient beings are mostly entangled in suffering and affliction, You should swiftly leave the home life to seek the True Path.”
I am now likewise able to do as such for you, as well as for that Brahmā King and the various devas;
I shall cause you to attain freedom from obstacles so that you may go into the forest and realize perfect enlightenment.
Upon hearing these verses, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with joy, and he replied to the devas, “Excellent! Then Śakra, Lord of Devas,

immediately cast the veil of darkness over the host of soldiers, King Śuddhodana, the musicians, and the court ladies, as well as all those guarding and protecting the city of Kapilavastu, causing them all to fall into sleep so that their minds remained unaware.
He commanded the Great Yakṣa General Sañjika to bring a ladder, and had the Bodhisattva descend by it to where Chandaka was.
Seeing that Chandaka was fast asleep, the Bodhisattva pushed him with his hand to awaken him; it took some time before he finally awoke.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke in verse:
“Arise, arise, you, Chandaka! Quickly saddle Kaṇṭhaka and bring him here;
To the forest of the past Victors, I shall go there to dwell in silence.”
At that time, whether Chandaka was asleep or awake, he replied in verse:
"Now is not the time for pleasure excursions; you have no enemies before you.
Since no hostile thieves have arrived, why do you seek a horse in the night?"
The Bodhisattva addressed him in verse:
“Candaka, from the past until now, you have never disobeyed my instructions;
do not, at this final hour, seek to violate my command.”
Chanda replied, "At this time of midnight, I am filled with fear and cannot take the horse.
When the Bodhisattva heard these words, he thought to himself:
"If I continue this dialogue with Chandaka without finishing, I fear that bystanders will hear it and obstruct my departure; it would be better for me to personally mount the horse-king Kanthaka."
He immediately hurried to the stable and went to where Kanthaka was.
When Kanthaka saw the Bodhisattva approaching, he became filled with a fury like a great blazing fire; he leaped and lunged about, refusing to be caught.

In the hands of the Bodhisattva there are first the marks of the hundred-jeweled wheels; when any sentient beings who are terrified see the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva immediately comforts and brings them peace with his hundred-jeweled hands.
At that time, the Bodhisattva stroked the horse’s head with his wheel-hand and spoke these verses:
“I shall now mount you for the very last time; I shall reach that destination swiftly and not linger long.
Before long, I shall realize Bodhi, And with the rain of Dharma, I shall moisten all sentient beings.”
"Furthermore, it is the constant law of all sentient beings that when there is someone to instruct them, they are able to learn and practice.
Having heard this verse, the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka immediately stood still; the Bodhisattva, filled with joy, was then led out."
Brahmā and Śakra commanded four devaputras to jointly support Kaṇṭhaka and protect the Bodhisattva.
These four devaputras were:

first, Pāra; second, Upapāra; third, Gandhaparṇa; and fourth, Gandhamādana. All possessed great power and majesty; they went to where the Bodhisattva was and stood in attendance at his left and right sides.
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Who can carry me up into the air?
The four deva kings replied:
“We are all capable of it,” they replied.
The Bodhisattva asked again,
“What supernatural powers do you possess?”
The other bank replied:
"Prince, you should know!
I can still lift up all the soil of the great earth and carry it away as well."
Jin'an replied again,
"The waters of the four great oceans and all the rivers and streams— I can now also carry them upon my back and travel with them.
Xiangye spoke once more:
"I can carry away all mountains and rocks," said Śreṇika. Śrīgandhaparṇa replied,
"I can carry away all forest trees and various thickets of grass."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva pressed down upon the earth with his foot, commanding the four celestial sons to lift it with all their might.
Thereupon, the four celestial sons exerted their full strength together, pulling and tugging at it until they were utterly exhausted, yet they could not move it even slightly.

At that time, the four deva-sons were all utterly astonished and said to the Bodhisattva, "We did not know that the Bodhisattva possessed such great power; had we known he had this strength, we would not have dared to lift him."
At that time, having heard the Bodhisattva and the four devaputras conversing with one another, Chandaka immediately hurried to where the Bodhisattva was.
The Bodhisattva then mounted Kanthaka; at that moment, the four devaputras each supported the horse’s hooves, while Chandaka grasped the crupper with one hand and held a sword in the other.
Due to the power of the Bodhisattva’s celestial majesty, he immediately ascended into the void.
Upon seeing this, the benevolent deities within the palace all wailed and wept, their tears falling like rain.
Seeing this, Chandaka said to the Bodhisattva, "Is it raining?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"This is not rain; it is the palace deities who, seeing that I am now departing, have shed tears such as these.
When Chandaka heard these words of the Bodhisattva, he choked with emotion and sobbed, remaining silent and speechless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, like an elephant turning its head to look back, gazed toward his palace and thought to himself:
"This is the last time I shall dwell in one place with these women; now I part from them all at once, and never again shall it be so."
He further reflected again:
"If I do not take my leave of the Father King at the eastern gate, I fear he will harbor resentment and reproach the soldiers for failing to provide adequate guard."
He then proceeded to the eastern gate and saw his father, the king, in a state of profound sleep.
At that time, the Bodhisattva circumambulated his father three times, knelt to prostrate at his father’s feet, and spoke these words:
"My departure now is not due to a lack of filial piety or reverence; it is because birth, old age, sickness, and death grind away and destroy all sentient beings."
"For this reason, I wish to leave the household life to realize the path to Bodhi and rescue these beings from suffering.
Having spoken these words, he immediately ascended into the air.

At that time, the great general Śakra, while patrolling and observing, arrived at the eastern gate of the city and suddenly saw the Bodhisattva soaring in the sky; he cried out in lamentation and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"What do you wish to do? What do you wish to do?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Great General, you should know!
I wish to leave the household life.
The great general said:
"This is contrary to the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva replied, "I have already,
throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, constantly practiced asceticism in pursuit of unsurpassed bodhi, uprooting all sufferings and difficulties for all sentient beings."
"How could I remain within the palace now?
I must now depart single-mindedly for the sake of the Dharma.
Upon hearing these words, Mahānāman Śākya immediately wept once more.
"Alas! Alas! Great King Śuddhodana and all the Śākya clans!"
"Alas! Alas! Though he made a great vow wishing to retain the Prince, his mere expression of affection caused this event to unfold; then, the Great General of the Śākyas spoke these verses:
“Today King Śuddhodana, for the sake of his son, is filled with grief and distress;
raising his hands, he cries out to the azure heavens, wailing in great lamentation.”
"Yaśodharā and the other great ladies of the inner court—
having now been separated from Siddhārtha, they are constantly oppressed by suffering.
After the Śākya Mahānāma had spoken this verse, weeping with grief and distress, he went quickly to Yaśodharā’s quarters, pushed her aside with his hand, and immediately spoke this verse:
“‘Since your husband Siddhārtha wishes to depart, you ought to feel a lingering attachment;
do not harbor grief later on, lest you suffer from the sorrow of remembering your husband.’”
"Now it is most difficult for us to part; this is our final meeting.
Alas! No one will hear me; wake up before you depart, lest you blame me.
Mahānāma Śākya repeatedly proclaimed this throughout the inner palace to all the people, but finding no one who would awaken, he was overcome with grief, distress, and fear.
Again, he went swiftly to King Śuddhodana’s presence and, awakening the king, spoke these verses:
“Siddhārtha now wishes to depart; Your Majesty should quickly restrain him.
Lest at a later time you remain in constant grief and distress for your son.”
"Mahānāman Śākya tried to awaken him a second and a third time, yet the King continued to sleep and did not wake for even a moment.
Then Śakra, Brahmā, and other devas, accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial retinues, came to the Bodhisattva and, upon reaching his location, immediately surrounded him."

Mahābrahmā and the various devas of the Form Realm stood solemnly and silently to the right of the Bodhisattva; Śakra-devānām-indra and the devas of the Desire Realm stood to his left. Some held banners and canopies while playing music, and others scattered various fragrant flowers from the air as an offering to the Bodhisattva—namely, *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *māndārava* flowers, and *mahāmāndārava* flowers—as well as sandalwood, aloeswood, powdered incense, and blended perfumes, scattering them over the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, they scattered various kinds of exquisite garments into the air;
then, amidst the sky, they beat drums, blew conchs, and performed various musical entertainments, reciting this verse:
"The devas in the sky All leap for great joy."
Clapping their hands and dancing before the Bodhisattva, they sang praises to the Bodhisattva.
The boundless hosts of devas mocked that army of Māra;
some played musical instruments, while others led the way.
Some opened the various gates, while others scattered flowers;
some supported the horse's hooves, gazing up as they followed along.
Some circumambulated him by turning to the left, while others remained at his left and right sides.
The learned ones, as well as Brahmā and Śakra, led the way upon the bodhisattva’s path.
Among all the majestic devas, there was not one who did not follow;
like the moon amidst the stars, he proceeded toward that forest of sages.
"At that time, after the Bodhisattva had departed from the city of Kapilavastu, the devas such as Brahmā and Śakra were all greatly rejoiced and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
'Excellent, O Benevolent One!'"
In the long night of the past, you made this aspiration, saying:
"When shall I obtain freedom from obstacles and dwell in the forest retreats?
That former vow of yours is now entirely fulfilled.
"When you have realized the unsurpassed path, please take us under your care.
The Bodhisattva said, "It shall be as you wish."
At that time, the Bodhisattva looked back toward the gods like an elephant king turning his head to the right, and spoke this verse:
"Without having realized the unsurpassed path And fully understood all Buddha-dharmas,
I shall not return again To enter this city of Kapilavastu."
At that time, during the second watch of the night, the Bodhisattva traveled twelve yojanas; he dismounted from his horse, removed his necklaces and ornaments, and said to Chandaka:
"Take the horse and my ornaments and return from here."
He then spoke in verse:
"This horse and its jeweled ornaments May be given to my kinsmen;
I now renounce craving and attachment, And from this moment forth shall don the Dharma robes."
At that time, having heard these words, Chandaka broke into a loud wail of lamentation, overcome with grief and distress; his tears fell like rain, and he spoke in verse:
“Where lions and tigers roam in packs, And where the tracks of beasts abound in thorny thickets— How can the Noble One dwell alone, Without kinsmen or attendants?”
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"The one who is born is born alone; The one who dies also dies alone.
Suffering is experienced by oneself alone; In birth and death, there is no companion."
At that time, Chandaka spoke again in verse:
"You were formerly accustomed to riding upon elephants and horses; Your hands and feet were soft and tender, never having known hardship.
This ground is covered with jagged stones like blades; How can you endure to walk or stand here?"
The Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"Even those who were cherished and nurtured from their youth, The virtuous and the various orphans,
The brave and fearless whom others revere— All such as these must return to death."
The phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, and death contend in turmoil, swiftly coming to oppress all people;
even if other vows remain, they offer no respite, for they can cause everything to be utterly extinguished in an instant.
Chanda replied: "Prince! If King Śuddhodana does not see you, he will surely suffer great anguish and will soon die."
Although the Bodhisattva heard these words, because he had long since fulfilled the provisions for awakening (bodhi-saṃbhāra), he did not give even a moment’s thought to Chandaka’s speech.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took the sword held in Chandaka’s hand; the blade was light and sharp, its deep blue radiance like the petals of a blue lotus.
Having drawn his sword, he immediately cut off his own hair and cast it into the void.
Śakra-devānām-indra, from within the void, immediately caught it in his hands and took it away to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
On each of these days, a great assembly of thirty-three thousand people gathers to circumambulate and make offerings.

At the site where his hair was shorn, faithful elders, brahmins, and others constructed a precious stūpa called the "Stūpa of the Site of Shorn Hair," which bhikṣus and laypeople should constantly honor with offerings.
After the Bodhisattva had cut off his hair, he said to Chandaka:
"Do you see me? My physical appearance has been transformed, yet my mind remains firm and resolute. How could a person such as this return once more to the human world?"
"Chanda replied, 'No. Chanda then thought to himself:"
"This crown prince is of the Kṣatriya caste and possesses a great deal of pride; though I have spoken with bitter words, he will ultimately not change his mind.

Having thought this, she prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva. The horse-king Kaṇṭhaka also prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet, then extended his tongue to lick the Bodhisattva’s feet. The Bodhisattva then stroked the horse’s back with his hand, which was marked with a wheel of a hundred jewels, and spoke these words:
"Go, Kaṇṭhaka! Once I have realized bodhi, I shall always remember your kindness."
He said to Chandaka, "You must not take my Kanthaka back into the palace. Chandaka wept with such grief that he could not overcome his sobbing;
as he returned along the road, his vision grew dim and confused, and he kept looking back toward the Bodhisattva.

By virtue of the Bodhisattva’s supernatural power, he reached that place during the second watch of the night; however, on his return path with Chandaka, it took seven days before they arrived at their own country.
Having reached the city gate, Chandaka thought to himself:
"If I enter the city together with the horse, I shall be held in reproach by the multitude, and my own life may not be spared."
At that time, Chandaka entered the grove and first sent the horse back into the city.
Once Kanthaka had entered the city, he immediately let out a mournful neigh.

At that time, the people of the city and the palace attendants, hearing the sound of this horse, were all in a state of hurried agitation; not seeing the Bodhisattva, they embraced the neck of Kaṇṭhaka, wailing in grief and distress.
However, it is the constant nature of animals that they understand all the sentiments of the world; how much more so this King of Horses.
At that time, when Candaka saw the people wailing and lamenting with such deep emotion, his breath failed and he fell unconscious, on the verge of death.
However, from ancient times, this Kanthaka has received his physical form within the womb of a Brahmin family that performs the six types of diligent service.
When the Bodhisattva attains the Unsurpassed Way, he shall say:
"You, horse of evil nature!"
He immediately regained his former mindfulness and transcended the perilous path of birth and death, ascending to the shore of ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, the Bodhisattva required a *kāṣāya* robe. In the city of Anupama, there was a householder whose wealth and treasures were vast, whose storehouses were overflowing, and who had many kinsmen, resembling the divine king Vaiśravaṇa.

At that time, the householder took a woman from among his own kindred as his wife. Having obtained her as his consort, they enjoyed each other’s company; through their worldly union, a son was born, and in this manner ten sons were eventually born, all of whom left the household life and realized the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, his mother gave these ten sons coarse garments.
Then those ten sons together said to their mother, "We shall now enter nirvana; we have no need for these things."

At that time, the ten pratyekabuddhas said to their mother, "Prince Śākyamuni of King Śuddhodana shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; we pray that you may give these garments to him, for he will surely obtain immeasurable karmic fruit."
Having spoken these words, he immediately manifested eighteen miraculous transformations within the palace, then consumed himself by fire and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
His mother, being old and suffering from a terminal illness, was on the verge of death; she took his robes and entrusted them to her daughter, recounting the preceding events in detail.
Later, when the woman fell ill and was about to die, she again took this garment and placed it in the air above the tree, addressing the tree deity:
"Guard this garment for me; on the day the son of King Śuddhodana goes forth into homelessness, you shall take it and give it to him."

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surveyed the lower realms and saw this robe hanging in the air upon the tree; he went there to take it and put it on himself, assuming the guise of an old hunter, and holding his bow and arrows, drew near to the Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva said, "These are the robes of one who has left the household life; my own robes are costly and fine, being the attire of a layperson. I wish now to exchange them with you; would this be permissible?"
The hunter replied, "I will not give it to you. Why is that?"
"If I were to take your fine garments and wander among the people, some who see me might say:
'I killed him and took these clothes of his.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"O hunter, you should know!
All people in the world know that I possess courageous wisdom and that no one is able to kill me; who could possibly bring about my death?"
"You need not fear.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knelt and offered the garment to the Bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva had received the garment, he immediately put it on; however, because the garment was narrow and his body large, it did not cover him entirely. He then thought to himself:
"This monastic robe is too small and cannot be used.
If you possess such power, I pray that it may expand by itself to cover my body.
By the power of the Bodhisattva and the celestial beings, the robe immediately became large.
At that time, the bodhisattva further thought to himself:
"Since I am now clad in these robes and possess the marks of one who has gone forth, I ought to rescue and relieve those who suffer in various afflictions."
He then took the fine and exquisite garments he was previously wearing and gave them to Śakra.
Having received them, the Lord of Devas returned to the Heaven of the Thirty-three to honor and make offerings to them with reverence.
At the place where they changed their clothes, the brahmins, householders, and elders together erected a caitya on this spot, which was named the Caitya of Receiving the Robes of Renunciation.

"At that time, having shaved his head and donned the kāṣāya robes, the Bodhisattva wandered through various places in the forest and wilderness until he reached the abode of the seer Bhagava. There he saw the seer sitting with his cheek resting upon his palm, lost in contemplation."
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Great Seer! Why do you engage in such reflection?"

The seer replied, "In my dwelling place there are tala trees which, in former times, produced golden flowers and golden fruits; suddenly, at this present time, the flowers and fruits have fallen of their own accord, and it is for this matter that I am reflecting now."
The Bodhisattva replied:

"The owner of these flowers and fruits, fearing the pressing afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, has left the household life to cultivate the Way; that is why the flowers and fruits have fallen of their own accord."
"If the owner of these flowers and fruits had not gone forth into homelessness, they would have served as a garden.

When the seer heard these words, he immediately raised his eyes and gazed intently at the Bodhisattva; seeing that the Bodhisattva’s countenance was upright and handsome, he reflected within himself and said to the Bodhisattva:
"Could you possibly be one who has gone forth?"
He replied, "It is I.

At that moment, the rishi was greatly amazed and delighted; he gazed directly at the Bodhisattva with wide-open eyes, then invited him to sit down and reverently made offerings of various flowers and fruits.
After the Bodhisattva had been seated for a short while, he asked the seer:
"How many *li* is it from this place to the city of Kapilavastu?
The seer replied:
"It is twelve yojanas [away].
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"This place is very close to the city-state; the number of the Śākya clansmen is not small, and I fear there will be great commotion. I shall cross the Gaṅgā River."
Having formed this thought, he immediately crossed the Gaṅgā River and traveled by stages until he reached the city of Rājagṛha.

"The Bodhisattva possesses skillful power and is endowed with all-knowledge; taking ten leaves of the karavīra flower, he joined them together to form a single alms-bowl, and with tranquil deportment, he entered the city to beg for food."

At that time, King Bimbisāra was looking out from his palace tower when he saw from afar the Bodhisattva walking with dignified grace, clad in a saṃghāṭī robe in accordance with the Dharma, holding a single alms bowl, and surveying his surroundings with proper decorum as he went on his systematic rounds for alms. Having witnessed this, he thought to himself:
"Among all those who have left the household life in my city of Rājagṛha, none has ever been like this."
And he spoke in verse:
“I now praise those who have gone forth, such noble and virtuous ones;
Because they contemplate birth and death, those people seek to go forth.”
Householders are oppressed by various sufferings, tormented by filth and impurity;
those who have left the home life find the flavor of meditative joy—the wise delight in renouncing the world.
Having renounced both body and mind, they abandon all evils.
His verbal karma is also pure, and he sustains himself through right livelihood.
The Sage traveled through the kingdom of Magadha and gradually reached Rājagṛha;
with his mind gathered in meditative mindfulness, he proceeded step by step to beg for food.
The lord of the land, atop his high tower, beheld this holy one from afar;
immediately giving rise to a heart of joy, he addressed his close ministers, saying:
"You all should observe him, whose sublime marks are fully perfected."
"His appearance is most dignified; he gazes at the ground as one who walks according to the Dharma.
A wise man does not look far ahead; he is not born of lowly stock.
He then ordered a messenger to observe: "Where does he reside?"
The messenger, obeying the king’s command, immediately followed that man,
observing where this renunciant would stay.
He went on his alms-round in sequence, passing from door to door until he reached the sixth house.
When the bowl was filled with food, he held it in accordance with the Dharma.
Having finished his alms-round, the Bodhisattva departed silently from the city;
he went to that Pāṇḍava forest and settled there in pure tranquility.
Once the messenger had learned of the location, he immediately dispatched one man to guard it;
another returned swiftly to the city and reported to the king:
"O Great King, that bhikṣu is now at Mount Paṇḍava."
"Sitting like a fierce tiger cub, dwelling in the mountains like a lion.
Upon hearing these words, the King immediately ascended his precious carriage;
surrounded by his ministers, he quickly proceeded to where the youth resided.
Upon reaching Mount Pāṇḍava, the king descended from his chariot;
proceeding on foot, he beheld the Bodhisattva.
With respectful greetings, the king sat down opposite him.
Seeing him dwelling in such tranquility, he spoke these words:
"You are a young bhikṣu, now in the prime of your youth;
handsome and skilled in many arts, why do you beg for your food?"
"From what clan were you born?
I shall grant you gardens and mansions,
as well as provide you with numerous court ladies, so that everything may be fully provided for."
Upon hearing these words, the Bodhisattva replied in verse:
“The Great King has a kingdom Situated beside the Snowy Mountains;
Its wealth and provisions are most abundant, And it is named Kosala.”
Ikṣvāku is called Gautama; among them dwells the Śākya.
I am of the Kṣatriya caste, and I take no pleasure in worldly desires.
Even if one were to rule the great earth, including its mountains, forests, and seacoasts—
Though possessing all manner of rare treasures, the greedy mind remains unsatisfied.
Casting fuel into a raging fire, so too is the nature of craving;
like one traveling a perilous road, the driver is ever filled with dread and anxiety.
All sufferings have desire as their root; it is able to shroud wholesome dharmas.
When I formerly left the household life, I abandoned all desires.
It is like the great Snowy Mountains, which can still be moved by the wind.
My mind relies upon liberation; no desires can drag it away.
While those driven by worldly desires perpetually turn the wheel of birth and death, I alone, O Lord of the Land, am able to liberate myself from all fears.
"I know the faults of desire; I have seen the tranquility of Nirvāṇa.
I shall now renounce it and proceed toward pure bliss.
When King Bimbisāra heard these words, he asked the Bodhisattva:
“You who have left the household life, what vow do you seek by performing such ascetic practices?
The Bodhisattva replied,
“I vow to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The king said, "If you attain the Way, you should remember me. He replied:
"According to your wish," he said, and having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva immediately went to the forest of seers on the side of Vulture Peak Mountain.

Having arrived there, he observed the conduct, standing, sitting, and reclining of that assembly of seers as they practiced their austerities; while they would stand on one foot until the first watch of the night before resting, the Bodhisattva stood on one foot until the second watch before resting.

Seeing that ascetic perform his austerities by heating his body with five fires until the first watch of the night before resting, the Bodhisattva likewise heated his body with five fires until the second watch before resting.
His austerities were thus twice as great as those of the former; when the seers saw this, they deliberated among themselves, saying, "This is a śramaṇa of great endurance."
For this reason, he is called the Great Śramaṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva asked the sages: "O great sages!..."
"What aspiration do you seek through such ascetic practices? A seer replied,
"We aspire to become Śakra, the King of Devas."
Another seer said:
"We wish to obtain the status of Great Brahmā King.
Yet another seer said:
"We wish to become the Māra kings of the desire realm.
When the Bodhisattva heard these words, he reflected to himself:
"These seers will cycle through rebirths in the heavens and the human world without end; this is a heterodox path, not the pure path."
"When the Bodhisattva saw that the seer practiced a defiled path, he immediately abandoned him and went to the hermitage of the seer Kāla.
Having arrived there, he sat facing him with palms joined in reverence and asked the seer:
'Who is your teacher?'"
"I wish to practice the holy life together with you.
That seer replied, "Venerable Gautama!"
"I have no venerable teacher; you may study as you wish without hindrance.
The Bodhisattva asked, "Great Seer, what fruit of the Dharma have you attained?"
The rishi replied, "Venerable Gautama!
I have attained the meditative absorption of non-conception."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Rāhula has faith; I too have faith.
Rāhula possesses diligence, mindfulness, virtue, and wisdom; I too possess them."
"The Ṛṣi Ārāḍa has seen and attained such a multitude of dharmas, even up to the attainment of the state of non-perception; how could I not attain such dharmas as these?

At that time, the Bodhisattva departed in silence, contemplating those dharmas, desiring to attain what he had not yet attained, to realize what he had not yet realized, and to see what he had not yet seen.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwelt alone in a secluded forest, single-mindedly contemplating this path with diligent and intense application.
Having performed these practices, before long he attained the realization and vision of this Dharma.
Having attained this Dharma, he returned to where the seer Āḷāra was and said to him:
"Now, as for this Dharma of yours, up to and including the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, have you attained it by yourself?"
The seer replied: "It is so, Gautama!
I have personally attained everything up to the state of non-percipient absorption."
The Bodhisattva replied, "Venerable one,
I too have attained these states of wisdom, up to and including the meditative absorption of non-perception.
That seer replied:
"Gautama! What you have attained, I have also attained; what I have attained, you have also attained.
Now, as for us two, we may jointly instruct this assembly of disciples, for we have attained this same Dharma and its principles."
This seer Rāla was the Bodhisattva’s first *ācārya* who provided instruction.
Because of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, that seer Rāla dwelt with him in a state of joy, making offerings and maintaining a close and affectionate relationship.
At that time, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
"This present path and dharma is neither wisdom nor realization; it does not attain the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for it is a defiled path."
Having understood this, the Bodhisattva said to Rāma:
"May you dwell in peace; I now take my leave.

At that time, as the Bodhisattva was wandering through the mountain forests, he saw the water-otter-like sage Udraka (the old transcription "Udraka Rāmaputra" is an error). He immediately approached him, paid his respects with reverence, and addressed the sage, saying:
"Who is your teacher? I wish to study and practice together with you. The seer replied:
"I have no venerable teacher; you may practice and study as you wish, without hindrance.
The Bodhisattva asked, "What path have you attained?"
The seer replied, "Venerable Gautama!
I have attained even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"This otter-seer possesses faith, and I possess it as well.
He possesses diligence, mindfulness, virtue, and wisdom, and I possess them as well."
‘If he has attained such dharmas, even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, why should I not attain them?

Thinking thus, he departed in silence, reflecting upon those dharmas, desiring to attain what had not yet been attained, to see what had not yet been seen, and to realize what had not yet been realized.

He immediately went to a secluded grove to cultivate this path with focused diligence. Before long, through his arduous application, he attained the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Having attained this concentration, he returned to the presence of the seer Māṭaṅga and said to him:
"Is this dharma of yours something you have realized by yourself?"
He replied, “It is so. The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"O Great Sage!
I too have attained this wisdom, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The otter replied:
“Since you have attained this, I too have attained it; since I have attained this, you too have attained it.
Now the two of us may dwell together and instruct disciples.”
"Why is this? Because the Dharma attained is identical.
At that time, the Bodhisattva formed this thought:
"Such a path as this is neither wisdom nor right view; it does not attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for it is a defiled path."
He addressed that seer, saying:
"May you dwell here well; I take my leave and depart.
This was the Bodhisattva’s second ācārya.

"At that time, while the Bodhisattva was wandering through the mountain forests, King Śuddhodana, longing for the Bodhisattva, dispatched messengers to search for him along the roads; they came to know the locations of all the mountain forests where he might be."

Having heard that the Prince had dismissed the otter and was traveling alone through the mountains and forests without an attendant, the king immediately dispatched three hundred youths to serve the Prince;
when King Tiṣya of the city of Devadṛśa heard of this matter, he in turn dispatched two hundred youths to serve the Prince.
Thus, surrounded by these five hundred youths, the Bodhisattva wandered at will through the mountain forests.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I now wish to dwell in quietude within the woods; it is not fitting for me to seek the nectar of immortality while surrounded by such a great multitude."
"However, I ought to retain five attendants and release the rest.

At that time, the Bodhisattva retained two from his mother’s kin and three from his father’s kin; these five served the Bodhisattva, while he ordered the others to return to their respective countries.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva, surrounded by these five men, went south of Gayā City to the village of Uruvilvā Senāyanī."

Wandering along the four directions by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, he saw a superior site where the forest was lush and beautiful, the water clear and cool, with pure sand on the bottom, level banks, and the water full, making it easy to draw.
The green grass covered the ground, the banks were broad and the embankments high, and there were trees with various flowers.
Growing luxuriantly upon the shore, they were exceptionally magnificent.
Seeing this extraordinary place, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"In this place, the trees are lush and the water is clear and cool; its bottom consists of pure sand, and the banks are level with the water full, making it easy to draw. Green grass covers the ground, and the broad banks and high embankments are lined with various flowering trees."
Situated upon the shore, it is lush and exceptionally magnificent.
If there are those who delight in cultivating meditative concentration and wisdom, they may dwell in this place.
I now wish to contemplate various states of tranquil absorption here, severing all afflictions within these forest groves.

Having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva sat upright at the foot of the tree. He pressed his tongue against the palate, joined his two rows of teeth, skillfully regulated his breath, and restrained his mind. He subdued, suppressed, and chastised the mind until sweat flowed from every pore, just as when a fierce warrior seizes a weak man, twisting, folding, pressing, and crushing him; the man’s entire body immediately breaks out in perspiration.
The Bodhisattva’s subduing of body and mind is likewise thus.

Consequently, he increases his diligence even further, never relinquishing it for even a moment; he attains a body of pliancy and achieves non-obstruction, while straightening his mind so that it is free from doubt.

The Bodhisattva thus experienced the suffering of extreme pain and the suffering of what is unpleasant; although he endured these manifold sufferings, his mind still could not settle itself in right concentration.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again thought:
"It would be better for me now to close off my sense faculties so as not to allow them to become dissolute, and to remain silent and motionless."
Thereupon, he first restrained his breath so that it neither entered nor exited.
Because the breath did not exit, it surged upward toward the crown of his head.
Consequently, the Bodhisattva suffered a pain in his crown, as if a powerful man were using iron-tipped tongs to crush the crown of another's head.
At that time, the bodhisattva further increases his diligence and does not give rise to a mind of retreat.
By means of this, he attains physical pliancy; his mind remains focused and concentrated in accordance with what he practices, free from all doubt.

Thus, through various forms of self-exertion and self-reproach, he endured extreme suffering and unpleasant suffering, never for a moment relinquishing them from his mind; yet, he still could not enter into right concentration.
Why is this? Because it has been perfumed by [the tendencies] accumulated over many lifetimes.
The Bodhisattva further reflects thus:
"I should now apply myself with even greater diligence and firmness, closing off the sense faculties so that the vital energy is confined within and enters into meditative concentration.

Having formed this thought, he then closed his breath and ceased all respiration. That vital energy then surged downward from the crown of his head and struck the faculty of hearing; the air filled his ears until there was no space left, like a bag full of compressed air with its mouth tied shut.
They undergo such various sufferings that they are unable to enter into right concentration.
Why is this? It is because of the habitual tendencies cultivated over a vast period of time.
The Bodhisattva further thought to himself:
"I shall redouble my diligence, withdrawing my breath within until it fills me completely, and then enter meditative concentration.
He closed his mouth and nose so that the flow of breath was entirely cut off.
When the breath no longer issues forth, it descends back into the abdomen until all five viscera are filled; the belly then swells like a full leather bag.
Further applying effort to bring lightness and ease to the body, one’s mind follows what is being cultivated with single-minded concentration, free from doubt.
Although the Bodhisattva thus undergoes various painful sensations, his mind still does not enter right concentration because of the long-standing perfuming of defilements.
The Bodhisattva then reflects:
"I shall now further intensify my entry into the concentration of distension."

Having entered this meditative absorption, he confined his vital energy (*prāṇa*). That energy surged upward and struck the crown of his head, causing a knot-like pain at the top of his head, just as if a strong man were binding a weak person with ropes until the entire head was distended and full.
After the Bodhisattva has undergone such extreme sufferings as these, he is still unable to attain right concentration.
Why is this? Because of the long-term habituation [to those afflictions].
The Bodhisattva further thought to himself:
"I should now apply redoubled effort to enter the concentration of inflation.
Having entered that concentration, his vital energy became fully distended; his abdomen was constricted with pain, as if a butcher were piercing a cow's belly with a sharp blade.
When a bodhisattva undergoes such painful sensations, they are unable to attain right concentration.
Why is this? It is because of the long-term perfuming of defilements.
The Bodhisattva further thought:
"I should now apply myself with redoubled diligence and enter the Samādhi of Distension.

Having entered this meditative absorption, he closed his mouth and nose; his vital energy expanded until it pervaded his entire body, and his body became intensely hot, like two strong men seizing a weak person and casting him into a fierce fire.
The Bodhisattva thus underwent various painful sensations, yet he was still unable to enter right concentration.
The Bodhisattva then thought to himself:
"It would be better for me now to cut off all food and drink."
At that time, the devas, observing that the Bodhisattva had ceased all eating and drinking, went to where he was and said to him: "Great Being!
Since you now find human food distasteful, we wish to enter the pores of your body with nectar; you should accept it."
The Bodhisattva then thought to himself:
"All people already know that I have renounced human food; if I were now to accept this ambrosia, it would constitute a falsehood."

If, because of false speech and wrong views, all sentient beings who hold such wrong views should, after the dissolution of their bodies at death, fall into the miserable realms and be born in hell, I must now ensure that this does not happen to me.
"However, I should now partake slightly of human food; perhaps I shall take small beans, large beans, and *kalāya* seeds, boil them to extract the broth, and drink it in small quantities daily.
Having formed this thought, he did not accept the celestial speech, but instead took small beans, large beans, and *kalāya* seeds, boiled them into a broth, and drank it sparingly.

Thereupon, the limbs and joints of the Bodhisattva’s body became entirely withered and emaciated, devoid of flesh; like the shriveled and parched limbs of an eighty-year-old woman, the Bodhisattva’s leanness was just the same.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva ate so little, his head became parched and withered, further swelling and aching; it was like an unripe gourd whose stalk has been severed, withering and shriveling in the sun—the Bodhisattva’s head was just like this.

Thereupon, the bodhisattva redoubled his diligence and attained physical pliancy; yet, as he cultivated practice according to his reflections, he experienced various painful sensations until his mind was unable to enter right concentration.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva had eaten so little, his eyeballs sank inward as if they had been gouged out by someone; like stars seen from the bottom of a well, such was the appearance of the Bodhisattva’s eyes.
The bodhisattva then redoubled his diligence and underwent various painful sensations, yet he still failed to enter right concentration.
Why was this? It was because of the habitual tendencies cultivated over a long period of time.

Because the Bodhisattva ate so little, the skin and bones on both sides of his ribs became withered and hollow, rising and falling like a thatched hut three hundred years old; the two sides of the Bodhisattva’s ribs were just like this.

At that time, the bodhisattva redoubled his diligent mindfulness and endured various painful sensations; yet, because of the long-term conditioning he had undergone, his mind was unable to attain entry into right concentration.
Because the Bodhisattva ate so little, his backbone became emaciated and bent,

such that when he wished to rise he would fall forward, when he wished to sit he would lean back, and when he wished to stand upright with his waist straight, his upper and lower body could not move in unison.
The Bodhisattva became so exhausted that when he rubbed his body with his hand, the hairs fell away one by one.
The Bodhisattva then thought to himself:
"What I am currently practicing is neither right knowledge nor right view; it cannot lead to unsurpassed enlightenment."
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Four;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree:
"At that time, three celestial beings approached the Bodhisattva and, upon seeing his body, deliberated among themselves. One of them said:
'This Gautama is a black śramaṇa.'"
The second deva said:
"This Gautama is a dark-complexioned śramaṇa.
The third deva said:
"Neither black nor dark, this is a sage of a greenish-blue hue.
Because of this celestial deliberation, the Bodhisattva subsequently acquired three names.
All the radiant colors upon the Bodhisattva’s body completely vanished.
At that time, although the bodhisattva had never heard of them before, three kinds of analogies for eloquence spontaneously arose in his mind. As for these three:

first, suppose there is damp wood, moist and having emerged from water, and the fire-drill is likewise damp. A person comes from afar seeking fire and uses the damp fire-drill to bore into that damp wood, wishing to produce fire; yet there is no way for the fire to emerge.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, though their bodies are detached from desire, still have minds stained by passion; who are addicted to and crave desire, who cling to desire, dwell in desire, delight in desire, and associate with desire—such states as these constantly abide within their hearts.

Although those people may afflict their bodies and undergo various extreme sufferings, enduring such agonizing pains and receiving such sensations, because they lack right knowledge and right view, they cannot attain the unsurpassed true path.

Second, there is damp wood, moist with water from the riverbank; if someone comes from afar seeking fire and uses a dry fire-drill to bore that moist wood, although he desires to obtain fire, the fire will not ignite according to the natural law.

In this way, although these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have physically distanced themselves from desire, their minds remain stained by passion; amidst all desires, they are steeped in desire, love desire, attached to desire, dwell upon desire, delight in desire, and associate with desire.

With such faults constantly present in body and mind, even if one subjects the body to suffering and endures extreme pain and all manner of acrid poisons, receiving such sensations as these, it is neither right knowledge nor right view; thus, one cannot reach the unsurpassed true path.
Third, there is rotten wood, devoid of moisture, situated on a damp bank; if someone seeks fire and drills it with a fire-drill, by its very nature, the fire will not ignite.

Thus, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, though their bodies are free from desire, their minds remain stained by attachment; they experience painful feelings, lack right knowledge and right view, and are unable to attain the unsurpassed right path.
At that time, having realized this parable, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I should now eat only one sesame seed per day.
Although he ate only one sesame seed, he was constantly tormented by the fire of hunger, and his limbs and joints became increasingly emaciated.
Because the fire of hunger did not cease, he further ate one grain of non-glutinous rice per day;
yet the fire of hunger still did not cease, so he further ate one *kula* per day, and remained emaciated and thin;
he then ate one *bimba* bean per day, and still remained withered and haggard.
Furthermore, though he ate only one sweet bean a day, he remained emaciated;
though he ate only one large bean a day, he was still haggard and exhausted.

At that time, upon hearing of these ascetic practices, King Śuddhodana wept in distress, as did the palace ladies and maidservants; they removed their jeweled ornaments, spread grass on the ground, and sat there, likewise eating only one sesame seed, one grain of rice, and one bean a day.
At that time, because Yaśodharā had eaten so little, her pregnancy gradually deteriorated.
When the King heard this, he thought to himself:

"If the Bodhisattva does not cease his ascetic practices and Yaśodharā hears these words, she will surely be overcome with great distress and anxiety, causing her fetus to miscarry and leading her to death."
"I shall now employ skillful means so that Yaśodharā does not know of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices.
Then King Śuddhodana told his palace attendants:
"Do not let Yaśodharā know of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices."
He also commanded the messengers coming and going:
"Do not let anyone else know of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices.
Although King Śuddhodana heard of the Bodhisattva’s asceticism from the messengers, he used various skillful means to inform the palace women:
"The Bodhisattva has now finished eating.
At that time, having consumed only a single grain of sesame and a single grain of rice, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Practicing this dharma is neither right knowledge nor right view; it cannot lead to the attainment of the Unsurpassed Way."
"I shall practice asceticism separately and consume various kinds of foul food. He further thought:
"What foul food shall I eat?"
"One should take the excrement and urine of a newborn calf that has not yet eaten grass.
Having thought this, he took it and ate it;
although he consumed this substance, he still caused its nutritional power to be entirely digested away.

Thereafter he ate again; having finished his meal, he lay down beneath the śmaśāna, using a corpse and various dry bones as a pillow. He rested on his right side with one foot covering the other, internally contemplating the sign of light (*prabhā-nimitta*), maintaining this mindfulness without ever relinquishing it for even a moment while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.

If a Bodhisattva was sitting, and there were men and women from the villages and wilds who saw him sitting in silent meditative concentration, they would take blades of grass in their hands and pierce the Bodhisattva’s ear canals, passing them through from one side to the other; thus playing and laughing as they came and went, pulling and tugging, they would speak into the Bodhisattva’s ear, saying:
"Look at this dust-devil!"
Again he spoke once more, saying,
"Dust-devouring ghost!
and he further hurled clods of earth, tiles, and stones at the Bodhisattva’s body.

Although these beings thus mocked the Bodhisattva’s body, at that time the Bodhisattva did not give rise to a mind of anger nor utter any harsh or evil words; the Bodhisattva was able to endure such things that are otherwise difficult to bear.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having aroused diligent exertion without ceasing, maintained physical pliancy without ever resting or abandoning it; he cultivated continuous right mindfulness with a mind free from doubt, focusing his attention one-pointedly in meditative concentration, abiding in *samādhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again had this thought:
"All those who wish to abandon suffering diligently practice various disciplines.
Yet the suffering I undergo is unsurpassed by anyone; this is not the right path, not right knowledge, not right view, and it cannot lead to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."
The Bodhisattva further thought:
"What are the right path, right knowledge, and right view that lead to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
He then thought again:

"I recall that while staying within my father Śuddhodana’s palace, overseeing the fields, I sat beneath a jambu tree and, having abandoned all unwholesome states and being free from evil dharmas of desire, with initial and sustained application of thought, gave rise to inner tranquility, attaining joy and bliss, thereby realizing the first dhyāna."
"This must be the path, the practice of a stream-enterer; it is right knowledge, right view, and perfect awakening. Yet, I am currently unable to cultivate and accomplish it well. Why is this?"
"Since I am thus weak and frail, I ought to breathe as I please and consume various foods such as rice, beans, and ghee; I should rub my body with oil and bathe in warm water."

At that time, having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva then relaxed his faculties and breathed according to his natural inclination; he partook of various flavors of food and drink without restraint, and he applied ointments, bathed, and acted as he pleased.
At that time, the five attendants said to one another:
"This śramaṇa Gautama is indolent and lazy, harboring many concerns; he indulges without moderation and is confused in his efforts to sever delusions.

Now that he has eaten and drunk extensively, and has smeared himself with bean paste, ghee, and oil, and bathed, he will certainly not attain even a small measure of realization, and will surely gain nothing at all."
Thereupon, they abandoned the Bodhisattva and proceeded by stages until they reached the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in Vārāṇasī, where they made this vow together:
"If there be any Arhats in the world, we shall follow them into the homeless life."
Because these five people lived and practiced together, they were called the "Group of Five.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gradually increased his intake of food and drink until his physical strength was robust; he then proceeded to the village of Senāyanī (translated into Chinese as Huìjūn, or "Assembly Army").
In that place there was a village headman named Senāpati.
He had two daughters:
the first was named Nandā, and the second was named Nandabalā.

At that time, these two daughters had previously heard that not far from the dwelling of the seer Kapila, on the banks of the Gaṅgā River to the south of the Snowy Mountains, a crown prince had been born into the Śākya clan in the city of Kapilavastu; he was handsome, endowed with all marks, and perfect in every way, bringing joy to all beings who beheld him.
The physiognomist prophesied:
"If this boy succeeds to the royal throne, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
Upon hearing this, the girl remained constantly chaste for twelve years.
It is the constant law of the world that if a woman can maintain her chastity for twelve full years, she is fit to become the consort of a Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin).
Therefore, those two women did not commit any of the ten unwholesome deeds during the twelve-year period. When the twelve years were complete, they thought to themselves:
"I have now finished performing pure conduct for twelve years; I ought to offer sixteen-fold churned milk-rice porridge as an offering to the ascetic seer."
Regarding what is called the "sixteen-fold transformation": one takes the milk of a thousand cows and feeds it to a thousand cows;
then takes that [milk] and feeds it to five hundred; then takes that [milk] and feeds it to five hundred; then takes that [milk] and feeds it to two hundred and fifty;
then takes that [milk] and feeds it to two hundred and fifty; and again takes that [milk] and feeds it to two hundred and fifty.
He drank one hundred and twenty-five; then he drank another one hundred and twenty-five for each of those one hundred and twenty-five;
then he drank another one hundred and twenty-five for sixty-four; then he drank another sixty-four for sixty-four;
then he drank another sixty-four for thirty-two; then he drank another thirty-two for thirty-two.
12. Again, he drinks sixteen with thirty-two; again, he drinks sixteen with sixteen;
again, he drinks eight with sixteen; again, he drinks eight with eight; again, he drinks four with eight.
Having formed this thought, he immediately took this milk and boiled it into gruel within a crystal vessel.
While it was being cooked, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens perceived that once the Bodhisattva had eaten this gruel, he would immediately attain the path of Bodhi;
they thought, "We ought to assist his majestic power."
He then took the superior medicine that grants swift efficacy, placed it in a milk vessel, and protected it; at that moment, the porridge manifested various kinds of wheel-signs (*cakra*).
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Upaga who came and, seeing these various signs in the porridge, thought to himself:
"Whoever eats this porridge will surely realize unsurpassed wisdom; I should beg for some and eat it."
Having thought this, he departed.
When the gruel was finished cooking, that non-Buddhist practitioner returned and said to the two daughters:
"I have come from afar and am extremely hungry and exhausted; you may now share some of this milk-gruel with me."
The two women replied,
"We will not give them to you," and departed in silence.

Then the two women poured the milk porridge from crystal vessels into precious bowls; Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came and stood before the two women, while Brahmā, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and others stood at a distance.
When the two daughters saw Śakra standing before them, they immediately took up their milk bowls and offered them to Śakra.
Śakra replied, "Give these to one who is superior to me."
The two women asked,
"Who now has surpassed you? He replied:
"O Brahmā Devānām-Indra.
At that time, the two daughters again took their milk and offered it to Brahmā Devānām-Indra.
Brahmā Devānām-Indra replied:
"I shall give to one who excels me. He asked, "Who excels you?"
He replied, "The Śuddhāvāsa devas.
Then the woman offered the milk-bowl to the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas responded:
"I shall give to one who is superior to me.
He asked again: "Who is superior to you?"
He replied, "That bodhisattva is currently bathing in the Nairañjanā River; because he lacks strength, he cannot emerge. He is superior to me; you should give it to him."
Then the two women took the milk porridge and went to the Nairañjanā River to offer it to the Bodhisattva.

At that time, there was a female tree spirit on the riverbank who saw that the Bodhisattva was so emaciated and weak he could not reach the shore; she immediately emerged halfway from the tree and extended her hand, wishing to receive him.
The Bodhisattva asked,
"What kind of body are you?
The tree spirit replied:
"I am a woman," she said. The Bodhisattva replied, "I cannot touch you;
please bend down a branch for me, for I wish to climb out by grasping it."
Then that tree spirit immediately lowered a branch, and the Bodhisattva climbed it and emerged; he then put on his robes and sat beneath a tree by the riverbank.
Then the two women brought the congee and, bowing with reverence, offered it to the Bodhisattva; for the sake of benefiting both himself and others, the Bodhisattva accepted the congee.
He then asked again,
"Can you give away these precious vessels as well?
The two daughters replied:
"Noble One! I now offer this all to you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately ate the gruel, washed the precious bowl, and cast it into the Nairañjanā River; the Dragon King then took up the bowl and entered his dragon palace.

Śakra Devānām Indra, having seen this, transformed himself into a garuḍa and flew into the dragon palace; there, he intimidated the dragon king, seized the bowl, and departed, establishing a stūpa for the bowl in the Heaven of the Thirty-three and making offerings to it at the proper times.
The Bodhisattva asked the two women,
"Now that you have given these to me, what wish do you desire?
The two women replied:

"Noble One! To the south of the Snowy Mountains, on the banks of the Gaṅgā River, in the city of Kapilavastu, a prince has been born among the Śākya clan. His countenance is exceptionally beautiful and pleasing to all who behold him; physiognomists have prophesied that he shall become a Wheel-Turning King."
"By this merit of mine, I vow to become his consort.
The Bodhisattva replied, "That prince does not delight in worldly desires; he has already left the household life."
The two women replied,
"If you have already left the household life and do not crave worldly desires, by this merit we shall cause that person’s wishes to be fulfilled.
They then spoke in verse:
“‘This Prince Siddhārtha is the most supreme person in the world;
if he wishes to fulfill his aspiration, it shall be swiftly accomplished.’”
At that time, having seen these two women speak this verse of aspiration, the Bodhisattva said to them:
"It shall be according to your wish.
When the two women heard these words of the Bodhisattva, they prostrated at his feet and withdrew.

Having consumed the milk gruel, the Bodhisattva’s physical strength was fully restored and his six sense faculties were completely satisfied; he then wandered along the banks of the Nairañjanā River, observing his surroundings to seek a pure place where he might establish his residence.
Seeing a solitary rock mountain adorned and surrounded by various flowers and fruits, the Bodhisattva, having seen it, immediately ascended the mountain and sat cross-legged upon the leveled stone.
At that time, this mountain suddenly split and crumbled of its own accord. The Bodhisattva rose and stood up, forming this thought of doubt:
"Is it because my evil karma is not yet exhausted that the mountain has been shattered?"
The devas in the sky, perceiving the Bodhisattva’s doubt regarding this matter, immediately addressed him from mid-air:
“World-Honored One!

You have no evil karma in the past; this is the constant law for a Bodhisattva attaining the Way. The merit of your roots of goodness fills your body and mind, such that the strength of all the earths cannot support you.”
This current location is not the place where a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment; the power of the entire earth cannot support two kinds of people:
first, those with the greatest amount of goodness, and second, those with the greatest amount of evil.
The meritorious karma of the Bodhisattva was so immense that this mountain spontaneously shattered.

Now, beyond the eastern bank of the Nairañjanā River, there is a diamond ground (*vajra-bhūmi*). Therein, all Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future have attained, are attaining, and shall attain the most supreme wisdom.

Having heard this, the Bodhisattva set out for that land; with every step he took, lotus flowers sprang up beneath his feet, and the waters of the four great oceans became lotus ponds to welcome him. As his feet trod upon the ground, the earth shook everywhere like the striking of bronze vessels, while *caṭaka* birds and auspicious deer came to circle around the Bodhisattva.
The deity presiding over wind regulates its cool breezes to blow away dust and impurities;
the deity presiding over rain sprinkles a fine, sweet moisture so that the swirling dust does not fly.
When the Bodhisattva saw these signs, he thought to himself:
"Beholding these signs now, I shall surely attain perfect enlightenment this very day.

There was a dragon named Kalinga dwelling in the Nairañjanā River due to the conditions of his past karma; both his eyes were blind. "If a Buddha appears in the world, his eyes will immediately regain their sight;

if after a Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his eyes will return to blindness. Hearing the sound of the earth quaking, he suspected that a Buddha had appeared in the world. He emerged from his palace to look and suddenly beheld the Bodhisattva, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, with a halo extending one fathom, radiant like a thousand suns and as magnificent as a great mountain of jewels.
Having seen this, the Dragon King spoke in verse as a praise:
“I have seen many bodhisattvas Attaining Buddhahood and endowed with majestic power;
What I saw in the past and what I see now— Between these two visions, there is no difference.”
I observed his first steps, and again beheld his left and right attendants;
capable of receiving the offerings of the world, he will undoubtedly now attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, I gazed upon him as he donned his robes and entered the Nairañjanā River.
The river waters have turned pure and clear; there is no doubt that you will now attain Buddhahood.
Greatly firm and courageous, your gait is like that of a bull king;
like a king among men, there is no doubt that you will now attain Buddhahood.
Above flies the *cāṣa* bird; below are auspicious deer.
His physical marks are most upright and handsome; there is no doubt he shall now attain Buddhahood.
A gentle breeze blows most harmoniously, and a fine rain falls from the sky.
The birds praise him as the tree lowers its branches; there is no doubt that he has now attained Buddhahood.
His pure light adorns his features like Jāmbūnada gold;
his face is as perfect as the full moon—there is no doubt that he has now attained Buddhahood.
After the Dragon King had thus praised the Bodhisattva, he entered the dragon palace.
At that time, having heard the praise from the Kalinga Dragon King, the Bodhisattva went to the Diamond Ground (vajrabhūmi) and thought to himself:
"I must have some grass."

At that time, Śakra, knowing the Bodhisattva’s thought, went immediately to Gandhamādana Mountain to fetch those soft, auspicious, and wondrous grasses; he then transformed himself into a hired laborer and brought the auspicious grasses before the Bodhisattva.
Upon seeing this, the Bodhisattva immediately requested it; Śakra prostrated himself before him and offered the grass to the Bodhisattva.
Having obtained the grass, he went at once to the foot of the Bodhi tree, intending to spread it for his seat, whereupon the grass spontaneously turned to the right.
Having seen these signs, the Bodhisattva further thought to himself:
"Today I shall realize awakening without doubt.
He then ascended the Vajrāsana and sat cross-legged like a nāga king; majestic and sublime, his mind was single-pointed and concentrated, as he spoke these words:
"I shall not rise from this seat until I have exhausted all outflows (āsrava) here and now.
Now, it is the constant law of Māra that he possesses two kinds of banners:
first, the banner of joy, and second, the banner of sorrow.
Suddenly, his Banner of Sorrow shook, and the Māra-king immediately thought:
"Now that the Banner of Sorrow has suddenly shaken, there will certainly be some calamity.
He then observed closely and saw the Bodhisattva seated upon the Vajra-seat.
He further thought:
"While this son of Śuddhodana sits upon the Vajrāsana, until he has encroached upon my domain, I shall first create various obstacles for him."

Having formed this thought, he bared his brows and glared with fury; donning the śāṇa robes, he transformed himself into the form of a minor messenger and approached the Bodhisattva in a state of hurried agitation, addressing him thus:
"Why do you sit here so complacently?"
The city of Kapilavastu has already fallen under the control of Devadatta; the palace women and maidens have all been defiled, and the Śākyas have already been slaughtered.
At that time, three kinds of unwholesome thoughts of sin arose in the Bodhisattva:
first, thoughts of sensual desire; second, thoughts of killing; and third, thoughts of destruction. He gave rise to thoughts of sensual desire toward Yaśodharā, Gopikā, Miṅkā, and Cañcā;
and he gave rise to thoughts of killing toward Devadatta.
Regarding those Śākyas who followed Devadatta, he gave rise to thoughts of disparagement.
Having given rise to these thoughts, he immediately became aware of them and said:
"Why have I now given rise to these three kinds of sinful, unwholesome thoughts?"
He then further observed:
"I know that this is the Māra King who has come here to disturb me and cause me distraction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately gave rise to three kinds of wholesome thoughts:
First, the thought of renunciation; second, the thought of non-violence; third, the thought of non-destruction.
Then the celestial Māra spoke again, saying:
"For what reason do you now sit beneath the Bodhi tree?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect wisdom.
The Māra spoke again:
"How can one realize unsurpassed, perfect wisdom?
The Bodhisattva replied, "O sinner!"
"You have merely performed a single sacrificial assembly;
yet by this very cause, you have attained sovereign accomplishment among the devas of the desire realm.

How much more so for me, who throughout countless eons have performed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sacrificial assemblies? For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I have given away my head, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, wife, children, sons, daughters, gold, silver, and all manner of treasures, in order to realize unsurpassed wisdom."
"For this reason, why should I not realize unsurpassed perfect wisdom?
I shall now certainly realize this unsurpassed perfect wisdom.
After the Bodhisattva had spoken these words, Māra replied:
"However, you yourself have witnessed that by performing a single sacrificial assembly, I attained the sovereignty of the Lord of the Desire Realm;

yet, throughout three incalculable eons, you have performed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sacrificial assemblies for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, giving away your head, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, wife, children, gold, silver, and all manner of treasures in pursuit of unsurpassed, perfect wisdom—who will bear witness to your deeds?"

At that time, the World-Honored One raised his hand, which possessed the wheel-mark with webbed fingers, born of immeasurable merit and capable of consoling all who are terrified. Pointing his finger at the great earth, he said:

"Let this bear witness for me! If, throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have performed immeasurable koṭi-nayuta hundreds of thousands of sacrificial assemblies; and if, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I have truly not lied when I gave away my head, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, wife, children, gold, silver, and all manner of treasures—then let it bear witness for me!"
At that time, the Earth Deity emerged from the earth, joined her palms, and cried out:
"O sinner! It is so, it is so!"
"Indeed, what the World-Honored One has spoken is true and not false.
Having said these words, the wicked Māra remained silent, inwardly filled with shame; his countenance grew haggard and he lost his majestic splendor. Bitter with vexation, he thought to himself:
"Though I have employed such expedients, I have been unable to cause even the slightest harm to the son of Śuddhodana. I must now devise another stratagem to create an obstacle for him."
Having thought this, he departed.
At that time, the Māra King had three daughters whose beauty was seductive and peerlessly exquisite:
the first was named Greed, the second was named Desire, and the third was named Attachment.
Adorned with various celestial garments upon their bodies, they went to where the Bodhisattva was and stood before him, employing all manner of flattery and artifice in an attempt to cause confusion.
When the Bodhisattva saw them, he transformed these three women so that they all became old matriarchs, whereupon they immediately departed.
Seeing this, the Māra King’s distress increased all the more; resting his cheek upon his hand, he contemplated the matter deeply:
"How else might I create obstacles for this son of Śuddhodana?"

He immediately dispatched thirty-six *koṭis* of demonic troops with heads like those of elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, deer, oxen, pigs, dogs, foxes, weasels, monkeys, wild foxes, lions, tigers, and other such strange and various-headed soldiers.
