Some held spears and halberds, some held bows and arrows, some held battle-axes, some held discus-swords, some held nooses, and some held hoes; bearing these various weapons, they advanced toward the Bodhisattva. King Māra himself took up bow and arrow, intending to shoot the Bodhisattva.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva reflected:
"In all instances of contention, one seeks companions; as I now contend with the king of this desire realm, shall I not seek an ally?"
He further reflected:
"I must now seek a skillful means to eliminate these obstacles.

At that moment, the hosts of Māra’s soldiers unleashed various blades to strike the Bodhisattva simultaneously. However, as the Bodhisattva then entered the *samādhi* of Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī-samādhi*), all the weapons of the Māra soldiers were transformed into lotus flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and various other colors, falling to the left, right, front, and back of the Bodhisattva.

At that time, the Māra King again ascended into the air and rained down various dusts and earth; however, these dusts and earth were transformed into agallochum, sandalwood, powdered incense, and various flowers, which fell upon the Bodhisattva.

The Māra King again released various venomous bees from the air and rained down vajra-stones; the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens transformed them into a leaf-hut to cover the Bodhisattva, so that neither the venomous bees nor the rain of stones could cause him harm.
Having seen this, the Māra King again thought to himself:
"How long can I continue to surround and harass him?
All sounds have the power to shatter samādhi; I should now transform the leaves of the Bodhi tree into crystal."
"Furthermore, let the wind blow so that they strike against one another and produce sound; if he hears that sound, his mind will not be able to attain concentration.
Having formed this thought, he immediately acted accordingly.
At that time, the leaves of the Bodhi tree struck against one another and produced a sound; having heard it, the Bodhisattva was unable to remain focused in concentration.
At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven saw this from afar and thought:
"I must now assist the Bodhisattva.
Thereupon, all the gods came to the Bodhi tree, each grasping a leaf so as not to let it move.
At that time, the demonic armies still refused to disperse, and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens again thought to themselves:
"This sinful army of Māra has long tormented the Bodhisattva and yet does not withdraw."
He then used his supernormal power to hurl the hosts of Māra onto Mount Cakravāḍa.

At that time, the Bodhisattva was staying in the village of Uruvilvā; seated beneath the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, he remained there constantly practicing and cultivating the preparatory applications for the factors of sublime awakening without interruption.
During the first watch of the night, he accomplished the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhividhi-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).

That is to say: he transformed one into many and many into one; he became invisible or visible at will; passing through walls and mountains without obstruction as if through open space; emerging from and sinking into the great earth as if walking upon water, while the characteristics of the earth remained unchanged; sitting cross-legged in the sky as if on the ground; or soaring through the air like a bird in flight; even reaching up with his hand to touch the sun and moon despite their great majesty and power; and even traveling to and fro within the Brahma heavens with complete mastery over his body.
At that time, Māra the King again thought to himself:
"Among all meditative concentrations, only sound can act as an obstacle; I should produce a sound.
He then, together with thirty-six thousand *koṭis* of demons, ghosts, and spirits, let out a great roar from afar.
For the sake of this sound, the Bodhisattva created a grove of twelve *yojana* of *khaṇḍava* trees; because of this grove, he did not hear that sound.
The Bodhisattva then thought:
"I should cultivate the supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear-knowledge, so that I may hear all sounds of both gods and humans."
The Bodhisattva, transcending the human ear with his purified divine ear, understands without exception all sounds of humans and non-humans, whether near or far.
The Bodhisattva then reflects:
"Among the thirty-six thousand koṭis of Māra’s retinue, which of them conceives an evil mind toward me? How may I come to know this?"
The Bodhisattva further thought, "How shall I realize the knowledge of others' minds?

Thereupon, during the night, he attained realization: he understood, as they truly are, the discursive thoughts and investigations arising in sentient beings, as well as their minds and mental factors—whether their minds were desirous or desireless, hateful or non-hateful, deluded or non-deluded, expansive or not expansive, withdrawn or collected, arrogant or non-arrogant, tranquil or untranquil, concentrated or unconcentrated, and distracted or undistracted. He knew them all exactly as they are.
Having understood this, he further reflected:
"Within these demonic armies, who has been my father since time immemorial?
Who has been my mother?"
Who is the enemy? Who is the friend?
How can this be known?
He further thought to himself: "I must now cultivate the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) in order to attain full realization.

During the middle of the night, he applied himself with diligence and mindfulness to cultivate the knowledge of past lives. He then came to clearly understand all manner of events from times long past: namely, one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, a hundred, a thousand, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of births; births over one *kalpa*, two *kalpas*, during the period of formation (*vivartakalpa*), or the period of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*), and even births throughout countless *kalpas*. He understood them as soon as he brought them to mind: the name and clan of such-and-such a person, the family lineage and caste into which he was born, and all matters such as his food, suffering, and pleasure—all of these he fully realized.

Thus he knows their long lives and their long durations; he fully knows the length of their lifespans, from their passing away there to their birth here, as well as all their physical characteristics, locations, and various immeasurable categories of beings, without exception.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"In considering this army of Māras, who will fall into the evil destinies?
Who will fall into the good destinies?"
"How can this be known? He further thought:
"Only through the supernormal power of the knowledge of birth and cessation can this matter be understood."
During the middle watch of the night, the Bodhisattva cultivated the supernormal power of the knowledge of arising and ceasing, whereby he attained the pure divine eye that transcends that of humans.
With this divine eye, he clearly and definitively beheld all sentient beings:

those dying and those being born; those who were handsome and those who were ugly; those who were wealthy and noble and those who were lowly and base; those going to the good realms and those going to the evil realms; and those performing wholesome deeds and those performing unwholesome deeds.

Furthermore, he clearly understands that for each and every sentient being, the physical, verbal, and mental actions performed as various evil deeds—such as slandering the noble ones, being deeply attached to false views, or committing acts based on false views—cause them, by virtue of such karma, to pass away from this life and fall into the miserable realms;

or he sees sentient beings performing various wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, honoring the worthy and noble and practicing right view, whereby, by virtue of such karma, they pass away from this life and are born into the happy realms—all of which he knows with complete clarity.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:
"How may all sentient beings be liberated from the ocean of suffering caused by their outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)?"
He further reflected:
"Only the realization of untainted supernormal knowledge (*anāsrava-abhijñā*) can sever this matter.

For this purpose, at that time, beneath the Bodhi tree during the night, the Bodhisattva constantly cultivated and brought to maturity through appropriate practice, dwelling with single-minded focus upon the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). Resolving to realize untainted supernormal knowledge, he understood the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as it truly is; he did likewise for the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path (*samudaya-nirodha-mārga-satya*).
Having realized this path, his mind attained liberation from the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Having attained liberation, he realized the knowledge of the exhaustion of all outflows:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence. Thus he realized enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Within that state, he perceived the factors of enlightenment; having accomplished what was to be done, the World-Honored One entered the fire-element samādhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, using compassion as his weapon, subdued thirty-six koṭis of māra armies and realized unsurpassed wisdom.
At that time, the sinful Māra’s bow fell from his hand, his banner collapsed to the ground, and his palace shook in every direction.
The Māra, along with his retinue of thirty-six koṭis, felt deep distress and harbored regret; he then vanished on the spot and went to the city of Kapilavastu, where he told the people:
"The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, having practiced various austerities, ascended the Vajrāsana and has now given up his life upon the spread of grass."

When King Śuddhodana, the ladies of the palace, and the various ministers and officials heard these words, their hearts were filled with great anguish as if scorched by fire. The people of the city, as well as the three chief queens, including Gopikā, remembered the virtues of the Bodhisattva; they fainted and fell to the ground, and though water was sprinkled on their faces, they only regained consciousness after a long time, weeping and sobbing uncontrollably.
The attendants on his left and right exhorted and restrained him, and in this manner they offered countless such reproaches and censures.

At that time, the deva Pure Faith, seeing Māra’s deceitful falsehood and further knowing that the Tathāgata had already perfected wondrous wisdom, felt great joy in his heart and proclaimed everywhere:
"All you people, you should know!"
"Śākyamuni will not relinquish his life now; he shall witness unsurpassed, perfect wisdom.
Upon hearing these words, King Śuddhodana, his retinue, and the people of Kapilavastu were overcome with boundless joy.
At that time, when Yaśodharā heard that the World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva, had realized unsurpassed wisdom, she gave birth to a son with joyful delight and said,
"I have given birth to a son. King Droṇodana also gave birth to a son.

At that time, during a lunar eclipse, King Śuddhodana beheld this magnificent event; filled with immense joy and overflowing with delight, he immediately issued an edict to clear away all debris within the city. He had the ground everywhere sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water and placed incense burners at the crossroads, where various famous incenses were lit. Colorful banners and canopies were suspended, filling the streets, while fresh and pure flowers were strewn across the ground. Furthermore, almsgiving stations were established at the four city gates and along the thoroughfares.

At that time, at the almsgiving assembly held at the eastern city gate, he bestowed gifts upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, tīrthikas, brahmacārins, the poor, the solitary, the stingy, and beggars; all such classes were given to in full. It was likewise so at the southern, western, and northern gates, as well as throughout the streets and alleys within the city.
He assembled his ministers and conferred a name upon the son born to Yaśodharā.
A maidservant from the inner palace came forward and addressed the King, saying:
"When this child was born, Rāhu obstructed the moon; therefore, he should be named Rāhula."
At that time, King Droṇodana, for the sake of his son, performed extensive acts of charity as described above. He also gathered his kinsmen to confer a name upon the child and asked the people:
"What name should be given to this son?"
The relatives replied, "On the day this son was born, the people of the city of Kapilavastu were filled with joy; therefore, this son should be named Ānanda."
At that time, King Śuddhodana looked at Rāhula and said, "This is not the son born of my Śākyamuni.
When Yaśodharā heard these words from the king, she was filled with deep fear; she immediately took Rāhula and went to the edge of the pond where the Bodhisattva had bathed.
There was a large rock that had previously been used for the Bodhisattva’s playful exercises; he placed Rāhula upon this rock, joined his palms, and made this vow:
"If this child is truly the biological son of the Bodhisattva, then when thrown into the pool, he shall not sink."
"If this were not the biological son of a Bodhisattva, he would sink as soon as he entered the water.
Having made this vow, he immediately took up the stone along with Rāhula and cast them into the pool; the stone then floated upon the water.
At that time, Rāhula fell into the water and sat upon a rock; like a tuft of light cotton drifting with the waves, he did not sink at all.

Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana was filled with wonder. Accompanied by a retinue of ministers who surrounded and guarded him, he went to the edge of the pond and beheld Rāhula sitting on the floating rock within the pool, and he rejoiced with great joy and exultation.
At that time, King Śuddhodana entered the pool himself and took Rāhula into his arms; the stone then sank, and he returned to the palace, where he cherished and nurtured him with redoubled affection.
"Previously, when the Bodhisattva, using the weapon of loving-kindness, had subdued thirty-six *koṭis* of Māra’s hosts, he realized unsurpassed, perfect wisdom."

At that time, the great earth shook, and the entire world was pervaded by light; even those dark places upon the earth where the majestic radiance of the sun and moon could not dispel the gloom, were all rendered clear and transparent through this light of the Buddha.
Thereupon, the sentient beings suddenly see one another and say to each other:
"It is not only we who have been born in this place; there are other sentient beings as well who have been born here."
The summary verse says:
The four kinds of bathing pools; the father and son in harmony;
Śākyamuni’s renunciation; and the river-goddess’s prostration.
"At that time, there were two devaputras in the Brahma realm who, seeing the World-Honored One seated beneath the Bodhi tree, deliberated together, saying:

'Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwelling at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, having first attained perfect enlightenment, has entered the fire-element samādhi; seven days have passed, and he still remains in this meditative absorption.'"
"We should go together to the place where the Tathāgata is and offer incense and flowers as worship; each of us shall speak two verses in praise of the Buddha.

Having made this deliberation, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, they arrived at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Prostrating themselves before the World-Honored One’s feet, one of the devaputras spoke a verse to request his awakening:
"Arise, arise, O Great Compassionate One! The enemies and thieves have now retreated and dispersed;
The sinless Great Caravan Leader should wander through the world,
preaching the sublime Dharma with skillful mastery and bestowing the vast wealth of true meaning;
immeasurable sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma, shall all receive and uphold it.
The second devaputra again spoke in verse, requesting:
"Arise, arise, O Great Compassionate One! The enemy thieves have now retreated and dispersed;
All defilements have been removed— You should now wander through the world."
"Since body and mind are already pure, like that full moon;
immeasurable sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma, shall all receive and uphold it.
When the two deva-sons had spoken these verses, they prostrated to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and spoke in verse:
“The various pleasures of the desire realm, The various pleasures of the form realm—
When craving and afflictions are exhausted, This is the most supreme bliss.”
I have now laid down the heavy burden; forever free from the weight of carrying.
To bear the burden is to suffer much; to lay it down brings peace and joy.
All desires have been relinquished; all conditioned practices are complete.
"All phenomena have been fully known; this person shall not be born again.

While the World-Honored One remained in samādhi for seven days, having severed all afflictions and experienced the bliss of liberation, no one made offerings to him; he neither drank nor ate, yet he had no thought of hunger or thirst.
At that time, there were two caravan leaders:
one named Karkaṭaka and the other named Grāmika. Each had a hundred wagons and a large retinue, and as they were traveling together on business, their route passed by where the Buddha was staying.
At that time, there were two merchant leaders who had previously known a person who had passed away and been reborn in heaven. This being looked upon the merchants and thought to himself:

"Now the Buddha is beneath the Bodhi tree, having entered meditative absorption for seven days; having severed all afflictions, he experiences the bliss of liberation, yet no one is making offerings to him."
I should now cause these two merchant leaders to be the first to make an offering, so that they may enjoy various merits throughout many lifetimes.
It is fitting that I now exhort them to do this for the sake of their spiritual kinship.

Having formed this thought, during the middle of the night, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated five hundred chariots; manifesting his half-body in the midst of space, he addressed the two merchants, saying:
"You should now know!"

The World-Honored One Śākyamuni, having first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree on the broad banks of the Nairañjanā River, remained for seven days liberated from all afflictions and experiencing that bliss, neither drinking nor eating, as no one had yet offered him sustenance.
"You two, perform this offering with haste; as the very first offering, you shall obtain great benefit.
Having spoken these words, the deity then vanished.
When the two merchant leaders heard these words, they consulted with one another, saying: "We should know this!
The World-Honored One’s majestic virtue is most extraordinary; today Heaven has come to inform us of him so that we may make offerings."

Having deliberated thus, they conceived a heart of profound reverence for the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Taking various offerings—curd-milk, parched grain flour, and honey—they went to where the World-Honored One was. Upon arrival, they prostrated at his feet and stood to one side, addressing the World-Honored One:
"We two have brought much curd-milk, parched grain flour, and honey to offer to the World-Honored One; we pray that you will look upon us with compassionate grace and accept our humble offering."
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"I must not now receive food with my hands as the various non-Buddhists do.
He then reflected upon how the Buddhas of the past had received it for the benefit of sentient beings.
At that time, the Pure Deva announced from the sky:
"World-Honored One, you should know!
Past Tathāgatas held their alms bowls and ate for the sake of sentient beings; the World-Honored One likewise knows this matter to be so."
At that time, as the World-Honored One previously had no almsbowl, he made this aspiration:
"If I obtain a bowl, only then shall I accept food.
Then the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing the World-Honored One’s heart's wish, each brought a stone bowl and came to offer it to the Buddha.
However, these stone alms bowls were pure, light, and exquisite, with a fine, seamless texture; their form and color were dignified and majestic, not the work of humans.
When the Four Heavenly Kings had each brought their bowls to the World-Honored One, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"We each come from our respective stone mountains bearing these stone bowls to offer to the World-Honored One; we only pray that, out of compassion, you will deign to accept them.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Now these four kings each bring a stone bowl to give to me. If I were to accept only one, the other devas would feel resentment; the same would apply if I were to accept two or three."
"I should now accept them all; by means of my supernormal powers, I shall combine them into a single bowl to fulfill the wishes of the multitude.
Having formed this thought, he accepted the four bowls and, through the Buddha's supernatural power, nested them one within another so that they became a single bowl.
He then took this bowl and, for the benefit of sentient beings, accepted the offering of the merchant leader.
Having accepted the offering, he immediately spoke these verses of benediction for the merchant leader, saying:
"Whoever practices giving Will surely obtain its benefit; Whoever practices giving Will surely attain its purpose."
If one gives for the sake of happiness, one will certainly attain peace and joy later on.
Merit can summon pleasant fruits, and all that is wished for shall be accomplished;
one will swiftly reach the state of parinirvāṇa and realize the bliss of nirvana.
For those who diligently cultivate merit and virtue, no calamities or misfortunes,
nor even the hosts of celestial Māras, can cause them harm or affliction.
Those who rouse courageous vigor and possess noble wisdom are able to practice giving.
"When one reaches the far shore of the ocean of suffering, one will surely attain the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
At that time, having heard these verses, the Four Heavenly Kings and the two merchant leaders were filled with great joy; they prostrated at his feet and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One took this stone bowl to the banks of the Nairañjanā River, where he partook of a meal upon a mud altar according to the Dharma. Having finished eating, he returned beneath the Bodhi tree, set away his bowl, and washed his feet.
Because parched grain, curdled milk, gruel, and honey are cold by nature, at that time the World-Honored One suffered from a wind-disorder.
Seeing that the Buddha was afflicted by this cold wind-disorder, the Māra King came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The time for parinirvāṇa has arrived; what is the use of remaining in the world for long?
You should enter parinirvāṇa soon.
Knowing that he was being tormented by the Māra King, the World-Honored One said:
"You are a sinful Māra!
I have not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
For what reason? "

I have not yet had śrāvaka disciples who are intelligent and wise, capable of answering questions posed by others in accordance with the Dharma, skillfully refuting heterodox arguments, and extensively establishing the True Dharma;

nor have they been endowed with the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—who, from the heavens above to the realms below and throughout the ten directions, would widely understand my teachings, practice the various holy lives, and fully comprehend them all.
"If this is not so, I shall not enter parinirvāṇa.
When Māra the King heard these words of the Buddha, his heart was filled with distress; he vanished from sight and departed.

Seeing that the World-Honored Buddha was afflicted by a wind ailment, Śakra Devendra immediately went to the foot of the Jambū tree. Nearby was a grove of harītakī trees; from within that grove, he took a harītakī fruit endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor. He quickly proceeded to the Buddha’s location, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Seeing that the World-Honored One’s body was afflicted by wind-disorder, I took this harītakī fruit and now offer it to you.
If you eat this fruit, the wind-disorder will be immediately removed; I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept this medicine from me."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted and consumed it, and his ailment was immediately cured.

When the World-Honored One’s illness had been healed, he rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and went to the edge of the pond of the Nāga King Mucilinda, where he sat beneath a tree and entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

At that time, it rained continuously for seven days upon this pond. Knowing that the rain would not cease for seven days, the Naga King Mucilinda emerged from the pond and coiled his body around the Buddha seven times.
He drew his head over the Buddha’s head.
Why? He feared that the World-Honored One might suffer from an imbalance of cold and heat, or that bees, flies, and other insects might disturb the World-Honored One.

Then, after seven days had passed and having seen that the rain had ceased, this dragon king finally released his transformed body and manifested in the form of a deva. He prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"During these seven days, have you been at ease?
My body is coarse and unrefined, so there should be no cause for disturbance or distress; I hope you will look upon me with joy.
Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Contentment brings the fruit of peace; the learned know the Dharma.
By not harming sentient beings, one possesses great compassion among humans.”
"Able to eliminate worldly desires and pleasures, And having distanced oneself from all evils;
With the complete subduing of pride— Such a person is most at peace.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, the Dragon King prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and returned to his own abode.

At that time, the World-Honored One again departed from the side of the pond and returned to the foot of the Bodhi tree. Upon a spread of grass, he sat upright in the full lotus posture according to the Dharma, contemplating the cyclical progression of the twelve links of dependent origination:

namely, "because this exists, that arises": ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

With the cessation of this, that ceases: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had entered samādhi for seven days, he arose and spoke these verses:
"If this Dharma can be produced, the Buddha remains constantly in meditative concentration;
if one can know the Dharma of causes, its meaning extinguishes all [suffering]."
If this Dharma can be brought forth, the Buddha is always in meditative concentration;
if one can understand suffering through its causes, that meaning extinguishes all [afflictions].
If this Dharma can be brought forth, the Buddha is always in meditative concentration.
If one can extinguish the exhaustion of feeling, that principle extinguishes all.
If this dharma can arise, the Buddha is always in meditative concentration;
if one can extinguish the exhaustion of conditions, that principle extinguishes all.
If this Dharma can be brought forth, the Buddha is always in meditative concentration;
if one can extinguish all outflows, that meaning extinguishes everything.
If this Dharma can be brought forth, the Buddha is always in meditative concentration.
Universally illuminating the world, like the sun in the sky;
if this Dharma can be brought forth, the Buddha is always in meditative concentration;
having subdued the armies of Māra, the Buddha is able to sever the fetters.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having had this thought:

"I have attained a most profound Dharma, difficult to see yet capable of being seen, difficult to know yet capable of being known; it is beyond ordinary thought and difficult to conceive; its meaning is subtle and exquisite, and only those who possess wisdom can understand this Dharma."
"If I were to explain this to others, they would not understand it.
My Dharma would be given in vain, and I would only weary myself, increasing my sorrow and distress.
I should now dwell alone in a quiet place, contemplating the state of peace and bliss that I have realized."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having reflected as above, stilled his mind and remained therein, no longer intending to preach the Dharma.
Then Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, knowing the Buddha’s thought, reflected to himself:
"These sentient beings of this world, ruined and decaying, are unable to achieve liberation from those realms of suffering."
At this time, the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in the world is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower.
Although the Buddha has now appeared in the world, he delights in his own tranquility and does not think of preaching the Dharma.
"I should now go and invite the Buddha.

Having formed this thought, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from the Brahma Heaven and appeared before the World-Honored One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and spoke these verses:
"How wonderful is this Magadha today, Where the unprecedented, pure, and sublime Dharma has appeared!"
"Among all dharmas, you have attained awakening; we only pray that you shall open the gate of the nectar of immortality.
The World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"The Dharma I have attained is extremely difficult to encounter; it can cause the ocean of existence to be entirely emptied without remainder."
"Those of little wisdom and foolish minds always go against the current, For they are perpetually swept away and submerged by the entanglements of desire.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Scroll Five.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda on the Schism of the Saṃgha*.
Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In this world there are sentient beings who are either born or aging; yet their faculties differ as superior, middling, or inferior, and as sharp or dull. Some have upright and majestic forms, and their natures and conduct are harmonious and compliant, with few afflictions and few varieties of afflictions.
Nevertheless, because they do not hear the True Dharma, their understanding remains narrow and inferior.”
“World-Honored One!
It is like the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, which are all born and mature within the water; yet the nature of their roots is of three grades—superior, middling, and inferior:
one floats above the water, one is level with the water, and one remains beneath the water.”

Sentient beings are likewise: within this world, they are born or grow old; yet their faculties vary as superior, middling, or inferior, and as sharp or dull; some possess handsome physical forms and well-disciplined natures and conducts, having few afflictions and few varieties of afflictions.
Nevertheless, because they do not listen to the True Dharma, their understanding remains narrow and inferior.
"For the sake of these people, I shall preach the True Dharma; when they hear this Jewel of the Dharma, they will all attain awakening and understanding.
At that time, having heard this request, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Shall I observe with my Buddha-eye the distinctions in the natures of those sentient beings?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately beheld sentient beings with his Buddha-eye—some born, some aging; yet their faculties were of superior, middling, or inferior capacity, differing in sharpness or dullness. Some possessed upright and dignified forms and were harmonious in character and conduct, having few afflictions and few varieties of afflictions;
nevertheless, because they did not listen to the True Dharma, their understanding was narrow and inferior.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to great compassion for sentient beings and spoke in verse:
“If there are those who deeply delight in hearing the Dharma, I shall then open the gate of the nectar of immortality;
But as for those who revile, are arrogant, and disparage themselves, O Great Brahmā, I shall never speak it for them.”
At that time, having heard these verses, the Great Brahmā King thought to himself:
"The Buddha now wishes to proclaim the True Dharma.
His heart was filled with joy and exultation; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and suddenly vanished.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, again had this thought: "To whom should I first preach now?
He further reflected, saying:
"There is Kāla, who in the past, while still in the causal stage, was once my teacher and provided me with various kinds of offerings; I shall preach the True Dharma to him first."
At that time, the devas in the sky addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"World-Honored One!
It has been seven days since Kālakasūtra passed away."
The World-Honored One likewise observed with his Buddha-eye that [Kāla] would pass away after seven days had elapsed.
He further reflected:
"If Kāla does not hear my Dharma, he will lose a great benefit; were he to hear the Dharma, his benefit would be boundless."
Again, he thought to himself:
"I shall now preach the Dharma for Udraka Rāmaputra; since he was my second teacher during my time as a seeker, and provided me with various kinds of offerings, I shall preach it for him."
The devas in the sky also addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This son of Udraka passed away last night.
The Buddha likewise perceived through his own knowledge that he had died last night, and further reflected thus:
"He has not heard my Dharma and thus misses out on great benefit; had he heard the Dharma, his benefit would have been boundless.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Whom should I teach the Dharma first?"
Again, he thought: "I should first preach the Dharma for those five men. Why is this?"
"In the past, when I was practicing austerities, those five men served and made offerings to me with faith and respect.
He then thought further: "Where are those five men now?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his superhuman divine eye, saw five persons in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī.
Having seen this, he rose from his seat beneath the Bodhi tree and proceeded toward the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi; on the way, he encountered an outsider named Upaka.
Seeing that the Blessed One’s form was dignified and majestic, his complexion pure and his features excellent, he asked: "Venerable Gautama!
Your faculties are so well-proportioned, your countenance so pure, and your skin so delicate and smooth—under which teacher have you gone forth?"
"Whose Dharma teachings have you received?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I now receive no instruction from a teacher, Nor is there anyone equal to me."
Of all that ought to be awakened within the world, I alone am well able to understand.
Having attained universal penetration and transcended the world, I am unattached to any phenomena;
having relinquished everything, I have realized liberation, awakening spontaneously without relying on a teacher.
Since no one exists who is equal to me, I have naturally awakened to all things;
as the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher of devas and humans, I have already realized the possession of all-encompassing wisdom-power.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he proceeded to the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, to the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the five men were in that forest; seeing the World-Honored One from afar, they said to one another:
"Let us establish a rule among ourselves: this śramaṇa Gautama is by nature dilatory, always lives by wrong livelihood, and repeatedly falls back despite having severed his delusions."
"He now eats rich foods in abundance—namely ghee, honey, curd, and so forth—and anoints his body with ghee-oil and bathes in fragrant water.
When that Gautama comes to our place, we should not rise to greet him or prostrate before him, nor should we invite him to sit; even if he sits, let him sit at a distance."
As soon as this agreement was concluded, the Tathāgata gradually approached the five men.

At that time, those five could not withstand the majesty and dignity of the Tathāgata; they rose from their seats, and one man prepared a seat for the Tathāgata, another fetched water for the Tathāgata, another set out a vessel for washing his feet, and two received his three robes as he arrived, saying: "Welcome, Gautama!"
"You may sit on this seat.
The World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This foolish person!"
"Having established rules together, you have now violated them yourself.
Having thought this, he took his seat.

The five men made offerings, yet not knowing that the World-Honored One had attained perfect enlightenment, they felt contempt in their hearts; all the names they used to address the Tathāgata were his secular appellations—some calling him Gautama, some calling him "Venerable One," and others calling him by his clan name.
At that time, having seen them thus disparaging him, the World-Honored One addressed the five men, saying:
"In the presence of the Tathāgata, do not address me by my secular name, nor as 'Gautama,' nor as 'Venerable,' nor by the names of our clans."
If one reviles the Tathāgata in such a manner, one will lose great benefit and shall suffer affliction throughout the long night of existence in every birth. Why is this?

Furthermore, if there are those who repeatedly call upon the Tathāgata by his secular name or other such titles, those ignorant persons will lose great benefit in every place of their rebirth and shall constantly experience suffering and affliction.
"You should know this!
From this day forward, do not address the Tathāgata by his secular surname.
The five men replied:

“Venerable Gautama! Previously, through your ascetic practices, you did not attain the Dharma of perfectly awakened wisdom, nor did you perceive any state of sublime peace and happiness; therefore, you shall not attain it now.”
What is meant by breaking the precepts and abandoning ascetic practices today?

The mind cannot achieve concentration; being deluded and deranged with a distracted mind, one partakes extensively in fine foods such as ghee, milk, and curd, and anoints the body with clarified butter while bathing in perfumed water.
"First, there was no ascetic practice; how then can you say that he attained perfect enlightenment?
The World-Honored One replied:
"You foolish person!"
"We do not perceive any difference in the Tathāgata’s physical appearance or faculties before and after.
The five men replied, "Venerable Gautama!"
"Such are the characteristics by which I perceive their distinctions.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five men, saying:
"A person who has left the household life must not draw near two kinds of false teachers."

What are these two? First, delighting in and being attached to the inferior, mundane dharmas of ordinary worldlings, as well as indulging in sensual pleasures; second, inflicting suffering upon one's own body and committing various transgressions.
These are not the dharmas practiced by the noble ones.
These two wrong dharmas must be avoided by those who have gone forth.
I possess a middle way, and for those who practice it, they shall attain the pure eye and great wisdom, and achieve perfect enlightenment and the peace of nirvāṇa.
What is the Dharma of the Middle Way?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path. What are the eight?
"Namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught this instruction with a resolute mind to the five men.
At that time, among the five men, two attended upon the Buddha to study the Dharma, while three went out for alms in the morning and returned to their original location to provide food for all six.

Furthermore, after midday, three attended upon the Buddha to study the Dharma, while two entered the village to beg for food; they returned to their original location where the five ate together, with the sole exception of the World-Honored One, the Buddha, who did not eat at improper times.
"At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five men, saying:
'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, a Dharma which I had never heard before;
through the power of diligent application of proper mental attention, there arose in me the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.'"
"This noble truth of the origin of suffering, a dharma that I had never heard before;
through the power of diligent application of appropriate attention, there arose in me the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."
Regarding this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, which I had never heard before:
through the power of diligent application of appropriate attention, there arose in me the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.
Regarding this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, which I had never heard before:
through the power of diligent application of appropriate attention, there arose in me the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.
He further addressed the five men:
"This noble truth of suffering is a dharma that I had not previously known; now it must be known!
Through the power of diligence and appropriate mental attention, the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening have arisen."
"This noble truth of the origin of suffering has not yet been abandoned by me; it must now be abandoned!
Through the power of right attention and diligence, the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening arise."
"This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is a dharma not yet realized by me; now it must be realized!
Through the power of right attention and diligence, the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening arise."
"This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has not yet been cultivated by me; now it must be cultivated!
Through the power of appropriate attention and diligence, there arose in him the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.

"This noble truth of suffering has been fully known by me; there is nothing further to be known. Because of the power of my diligent application of appropriate attention, the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening have arisen—things never heard before."

"This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been permanently abandoned by me; it need not be abandoned again. Because of the power of my diligent application of attention in accordance with reality, having never heard this before, there arose in me the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."

"This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized by me; there is nothing further to be realized. Because of the power of my diligent application of appropriate attention, which was previously unattained, the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening have arisen."

"This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated by me; though it was not previously cultivated, through the power of right attention and diligence, the pure eye of wisdom, knowledge, clarity, and awakening have arisen."
"You five, you should know!

As long as I had not yet attained these Four Noble Truths in their three turnings and twelve aspects, and as long as the pure eye, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening had not arisen within me, I was unable to transcend the world of humans and devas, nor even the Brahma realm, nor all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, nor any of the gods, humans, and asuras in the entire world; I had not realized liberation or deliverance, nor was I free from inversion. I did not realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."
"You should know this!

Having personally cultivated these Four Noble Truths through their three turnings and twelve aspects, and having realized them, I have given birth to the pure eye, knowledge, and wisdom, and have attained full awakening."

At that time, I transcended the realms of humans, devas, Māras, and Brahmās, as well as the world of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; I was liberated from gods, humans, and asuras, having emerged from the inversions of the mind.
"I have attained supreme, perfect enlightenment through right knowledge.

When the Blessed One spoke these words, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya realized the stainless, dustless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, and eighty thousand deities likewise realized the Dharma-eye regarding the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kauṇḍinya,
"Have you realized the Dharma? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have realized it.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Kauṇḍinya! Have you realized the Dharma? He replied:
“Sugata, it has been realized.
The Buddha said:
"Since the Venerable Kauṇḍinya has fully realized the Dharma, for this reason he is named Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
At that time, the host of yakṣas who travel the earth heard the words of the Blessed One and cried out with one voice:
"Virtuous ones, you should know!"

This Buddha, the World-Honored One, at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī, has turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects—a wheel that no śramaṇa, brahmin, human, deva, Māra, or Brahmā is able to turn—for the sake of the peace and happiness of many, for the benefit of many, and out of compassion for sentient beings.
"For this reason, the hosts of devas will increase and the asuras will diminish.

At that time, having heard the voices of the earth-dwelling yakṣas, the sky-dwelling yakṣas likewise raised their voices; and so it continued until the Cāturmahārājika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, as well as all the Brahmās, simultaneously, at the same kṣaṇa, at the same lava, and at the same muhūrta, raised their voices.
Having heard these words, the gods of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven also spoke in unison:
"Virtuous ones, you should know!

This Buddha, the World-Honored One, has turned the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects in three revolutions at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī—a wheel that no śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, human, māra, or Brahmā is able to turn."

For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to many people, for the sake of bringing benefit to many people, and out of compassion for sentient beings, the hosts of devas increase while the asuras diminish.

Because the World-Honored One turned the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects in three revolutions at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī, this Dharma-sūtra and this site are therefore named the "Sūtra on the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the four men, saying:
"There are four noble truths.
What are the four? They are as follows:"

These are the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering?

It refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and even the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
In this way, one should understand the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
What is called the noble truth of the origin?

It refers to craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight and attachment here and there; for the sake of abandoning this, one should cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path.
What is the noble truth of cessation?

It is the craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight in this and that; for the sake of its destruction, its stilling, its utter disappearance, its fading away, and its realization, one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path.
"What is the Noble Truth of the Path?
It is the Eightfold Noble Path, which should be cultivated.

When the World-Honored One taught this Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, Ājñātakauṇḍinya realized the exhaustion of all outflows and his mind attained liberation; the other four persons, within this Dharma, were freed from all dust and defilement and realized the pure eye.
At that time, there were two Arhats in the world:
one was the World-Honored One, and the other was Kauṇḍinya.
Then the World-Honored One again addressed the four men, saying:
"You should know this! Form is non-self.
If form were self, it would not give rise to various ailments and sufferings, and one would be able to dictate within form: 'Let my form be thus' or 'let my form not be thus.'"
Therefore, you should know that because form is non-self, it gives rise to various ailments and sufferings, and one cannot command it to "be thus" or "not be thus.
You should know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the four men, saying:
"What do you think? Is form permanent?"
"Is it impermanent? He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"Form is impermanent.
He asked, "If form is impermanent, is it suffering?"
"Is it not suffering? He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"This is suffering. He said:
"If form is impermanent and suffering, it is subject to change and decay."
"If a learned disciple were to grasp that 'form is the self,' or 'I possess form,' or 'form belongs to me,' or 'I am within form'—
would he do so? He replied, "No."
The World-Honored One said:
“In this way, are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
He replied, "Venerable sir,
it is impermanent."
He said: "As for consciousness and the other aggregates being impermanent, are they suffering or not suffering?"
He replied, “It is suffering, Great Virtue!
He [the Buddha] said:
"That consciousness and the other aggregates are impermanent and suffering means they are subject to change and decay.

If a learned disciple were to grasp that form, up to and including consciousness, is the self; or that 'I have consciousness,' or that 'consciousness belongs to me,' or that 'I am within consciousness'—would this be so?"
He replied: "No, Venerable Sir!"
He said: "Therefore, you should know this!

Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—all such forms are not self, do not belong to a self, are not contained within a self, and a self does not exist within form. By knowing them thoroughly and as they truly are, one should see them in this way."
Even so should you view feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
You, my disciples, śrāvakas, being endowed with great learning, contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as being devoid of "I" and "mine."
Having observed thus, he knows that in all the worlds there is truly nothing to be grasped.
Because there is nothing to be grasped, fear does not arise; because there is no fear, he personally realizes parinirvāṇa:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
“At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, those four persons, having heard this Dharma, attained liberation of mind and realized the fruit of arhatship.”
At that time, there were six arhats in the world, with the Buddha being the first.

At that time, the Buddha was staying by the Vārāṇasī River in the city of Vārāṇasī. In that city, there was the son of an elder named Yaśas, who every day entertained himself with female musicians and enjoyed the five sensual pleasures; becoming weary in body and mind, he would fall asleep while the various female musicians surrounded him as they slept.

At that time, during the middle of the night, Yaśas suddenly awoke and saw the female musicians: various impurities were flowing from their nine orifices; their hair was disheveled and their clothes were filthy; their hands and feet were restless, and their delirious chatter was loud and confused.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"Am I in a cemetery tonight? His heart was filled with terror;
he rose and stepped into his jeweled sandals, which were worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, and hastened to the door, crying out at the top of his voice:
"O people, you should know! Suffering comes to oppress me!
O people, you should know! Suffering comes to oppress me!
Thus he wept, his tears falling like rain.
At that time, there was a non-human being who concealed Yaśas’s voice so as not to awaken others, and immediately opened the door for him.
Then Yaśas went out to the main gate and let out a loud cry; sobbing with choked sobs, he spoke these words:
"May all people know: suffering has come to oppress me!"
Then that non-human being concealed Yaśas’s voice so as not to awaken anyone, and opened the door for him.
At that time, Yaśas went out to the city gate and called out as before; then that non-human being likewise opened the gate for him.

At that time, having exited the city gate, Yaśas arrived at the banks of the Bārakā River. At that moment, the World-Honored One was walking up and down along the riverbank. Seeing the water as before, Yaśas cried out; the Buddha heard his voice and said: "Young man!"
"This place is free from fear; you may cross over and come.
Thereupon, Yaśas removed his jeweled sandals, crossed over to the Buddha’s location, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
"At that time, the World-Honored One led Yaśas to his dwelling and took his place upon the original seat.
Then Yaśas, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat down before the Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately expounded the sublime Dharma for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
first to preach this teaching, namely, the causes for giving, observing precepts, and rebirth in the heavens.
Furthermore, he spoke of all the faults and afflictions inherent in the five desires;
he praised leaving the household life to dwell alone in mountain forests, contemplating and observing in order to sever all defilements;
and he expounded the vast and subtle Dharma, revealing it so that others might understand.
All those who heard this Dharma teaching felt joy, were purified, and became free from doubt.
Having perceived this, the Buddha further taught them the supramundane Dharma:
namely, the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as when washing clothes, one first removes the dirt and impurities so that once they are clean, the dye takes easily; so it was with Yaśas.

Upon first hearing the Buddha’s teaching, his mental vessel became pure, and he was able to comprehend the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. He realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), seeing the Dharma, attaining the Dharma, and thoroughly penetrating the Dharma. Having reached the ultimate firmness of the Dharma, he transcended all longing and crossed over all doubt. No longer dependent on others, he could not be led astray by any other teacher’s instruction, and he attained fearlessness regarding all phenomena.

At that time, having attained this Dharma, Yaśas was filled with great joy; he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have now entered this subtle and wondrous Dharma and attained great benefit. From this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) bound by the five precepts:
I shall not kill, I shall not steal, I shall not engage in sexual misconduct, I shall not speak falsely, and I shall not drink intoxicants.
Having spoken these words, he withdrew and sat to one side.
After Yaśas had departed the city, his wife woke from her sleep and, not seeing Yaśas, searched everywhere for him but could not find where he was. She said to her father, the elder:
"Elder, you should know this!"
"Now, your son Yaśas is nowhere to be found.
Upon hearing this, the elder thought to himself:
"Could it be that my son has been taken outside the city by wicked bandits or enemies to do him harm?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately dispatched horsemen in the four directions and personally carried a torch along with his men to search everywhere. They eventually emerged from the city gate and gradually reached the riverbank, where they saw a pair of precious sandals worth hundreds of thousands. Thereupon, he thought:
"My son has certainly not been taken away by wicked bandits; since the precious sandals have been left behind, it is clear he has crossed the river."
The elder then crossed the river and proceeded gradually toward the Buddha’s location.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw the elder approaching from afar and, employing his supernatural powers, caused the elder not to see his son even though he had entered the midst of the assembly.
Then that elder, having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
"World-Honored One!
Have you seen my Yaśas?"
The Buddha said, "Householder!
You should sit for a moment; let us meet with your son here."
When the householder had heard the Buddha’s words, he was filled with joy and attained a state of unprecedented wonder; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas:

whenever they deliver a discourse, they first explain the causes for rebirth in the heavens through generosity and ethical discipline, then describe the faults and afflictions inherent in the five sensual desires, and praise the renunciation of worldly life to dwell alone in mountain forests, until they lead that householder to attain the fruit of stream-entry.
His son, Yaśas, while still wearing various precious ornaments and finery from his time as a layman, attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that moment, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal power and spoke these verses:
"Subdued and tranquil, upholding the pure precepts, He is ever adorned with the sublime Dharma."
"To have a mind free from harm toward all sentient beings—this is called the practice of a śramaṇa bhikṣu.
At that time, there were seven arhats in the world, with the Buddha as the foremost.
At that time, the elder suddenly saw his son sitting before the Buddha; having seen him, he said:
"Child, come here; let us return home together."
"Your mother remembers you and weeps in sorrowful lamentation.
Then the World-Honored One said to the elder,
"What do you think?"
"Is there anyone who, having already attained the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) and having witnessed the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths,
would return home to eat what has been vomited up? The householder replied, "No, Venerable Sir!"
The Buddha said, "Householder!
Have you now attained the knowledge of one in training and realized the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths?"
He replied, "I have. The Buddha said to the householder:
"This youth Yaśas has attained the knowledge and vision of one beyond training and realized the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

The householder said, "My son Yaśas has obtained the great fruit and benefit; he has attained the knowledge and vision of one beyond training and realized the principles of the Four Noble Truths—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."
At that time, the elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will come to my residence with your son Yaśas tomorrow at the appointed hour to accept my offerings."
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted his invitation; knowing that the Buddha had granted permission, the elder prostrated at his feet and departed.
Then, when the time came, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went with the youth Yaśas to the elder’s residence.
Yaśas’s mother and wife were by the middle gate, waiting for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and Yaśas.
Upon seeing the Buddha approaching, they personally decorated the bedding and prepared the seats with their own hands, then invited the World-Honored One to sit.
At that time, the World-Honored One took his seat. Then Yaśas’s mother and wife prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for them, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them; he first expounded upon generosity and ethical discipline as the causes for rebirth among humans and devas, and subsequently taught the cultivation of practice to sever all afflictions, leading up to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
At that time, having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, his mother and wife rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
Having attained this sublime Dharma today, we shall, for the rest of our lives, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, forever uphold the five precepts, and become upāsikās.”
"I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will accept my offering at the time of this meal.
The World-Honored One consented by remaining silent.

When Yaśas’s mother saw that the Buddha had granted his permission, she immediately prepared various pure and exquisite foods within her home. She then adorned a fragrant altar before the World-Honored One and presented various fragrances and flavors as an offering.
After the World-Honored One had finished eating, [the devotee] swept and cleansed the area, once again making offerings of incense and flowers all around, and sat to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for him once more and then departed.

At that time, the elders and others of the city of Vārāṇasī heard that Yaśas, the son of the foremost elder, had shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and followed the Blessed One as a disciple.

The second son of the elder was named Pūrṇa; the third son of the elder was named Vimala; the fourth son of the elder was named Gavāmpati; and the fifth son of the elder was named Citra-skandha. Upon hearing that Yaśas had renounced the household life, they all thought to themselves:

"Now this youth Yaśas, born into a noble family, possessing abundant treasures and jewels, with a body so upright and majestic, and constantly enjoying every pleasure, has abandoned what he cherished to become a disciple of the Buddha."

Knowing that the Tathāgata possesses such great majesty and virtue, and that the Dharma is likewise subtle and wondrous, we ought to shave off our hair and beards to serve and support the Tathāgata, and study and receive the supreme Dharma.

Having deliberated thus, they immediately became of one mind and went from the city of Vārāṇasī to where the World-Honored One was. Prostrating at the feet of the World-Honored One, they stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We wish to receive the sublime Dharma; we shall go forth as disciples of the Buddha and, in accordance with the Tathāgata’s teachings, uphold the holy life.
The Buddha said to the sons of the elders, "Now is the very time. Welcome, Bhikṣus!"
"You shall then go forth from the household life and cultivate the various holy practices.

As soon as these words were spoken, the hair and beards of those sons of the elder fell away of their own accord, and saffron robes appeared upon their bodies, so that they took on the appearance of bhikṣus, just like those who had been ordained for seven days; yet their realization was equal to that of bhikṣus of a hundred years' standing.
At that time, the World-Honored One again preached the Dharma for them, saying: "O Bhikṣus!

In solitary and quiet places, far removed from clamor and confusion, always guard your own minds and diligently practice asceticism. Now that you have left the household life, you should seek the holy life (brahmacarya), cross over to the other shore, realize your own right knowledge, and attain the supernormal powers of a Buddha to bring an end to birth and death. Establish the holy life, complete what is to be done, and do not undergo further existence; those who practice in this way shall attain the fruit of non-arising."
When the four bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, they immediately attained realization and realized the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, there were eleven arhats in this world, with the Buddha as the first.

In the city of Vārāṇasī, there were fifty prominent families who, upon hearing that these five sons of elders had all gone forth from home, shaved off their hair and beards, donned the dharma robes, and realized the fruit of arhatship, each said:
"The teaching of the Tathāgata is exceedingly profound and subtle, for it has caused those five sons of elders to each renounce their great wealth and go forth."
"We, too, should go to the Buddha and become his disciples.
Having made this deliberation, they all went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"We pray that you will allow us to go forth within this sublime Dharma and Vinaya to become bhikṣus and constantly cultivate the holy life.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣus!"
His hair and beard fell away naturally and the kāṣāya robe appeared upon his body, as if he had been ordained for seven days.
The Buddha said,
"Venerable one!"

Now, those who have left the household life dwell alone in mountain forests, far removed from clamor and confusion; they constantly guard their own minds and diligently practice asceticism, crossing over to the other shore and realizing their own authentic wisdom. Having attained the Buddha’s power of tranquility, they bring an end to the limits of birth and death and do not undergo further existence. Those who cultivate in this manner shall attain the fruit of non-arising.
When the fifty bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, their minds attained unimpeded liberation, and they realized the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, there were sixty-one arhats in this world, with the Buddha as the foremost.
"At that time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, surrounded by sixty bhikṣus.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
'I and you have now attained liberation from all the bonds of gods and humans.'"
Each of you may proceed as you see fit to various directions to bring great benefit to sentient beings; for now, let each of you go individually, without traveling together.
"I too shall go to the village of Uruvilvā for the sake of benefiting [beings].
At that time, Māra the Evil One thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa Gautama is staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, preaching the Dharma to his assembly of śrāvakas in this way:..."
“I have attained liberation from all the bonds of gods and humans.
You bhikṣus, too, have likewise attained liberation from all the bonds of gods and humans; you should now go among human beings to bring about extensive benefit.”
"You all should go separately; there is no need for you to travel together.
I, too, shall proceed to the village of Uruvilvā.
[Thinking this, he decided: "I must now create obstacles for him."
At that time, having formed this thought, the Evil Māra transformed himself into a young brahmin and went to where the Buddha was. Standing before the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
"You have not attained liberation, yet you harbor the notion that you are liberated;
While you remain bound within fetters, you cannot liberate me."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Now this evil Māra wishes for me to become distracted.
Having known this, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“Amidst the fetters of humans and devas, I have already attained liberation;
you who are guilty should now know: I have utterly subdued you.”
At that time, the Evil Māra thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa Gautama can know my mind.
Having had this thought, he was filled with distress; harboring remorse within, he vanished and departed.
"At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
'I have attained liberation from the bonds of gods and humans; you, too, have attained liberation.'"
"You all should go to other regions to perform various acts of benefit and compassion for the world, so that gods and humans may attain peace and happiness.
You must not travel in pairs; I shall now also go to the village of Uruvilvā."
The bhikṣus all received the Buddha’s instruction, saying, “So be it,” and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the village of Uruvilvā in the city of Vārāṇasī; having arrived there, he proceeded to the Śāṇa Forest and sat in meditative seclusion beneath a tree.
At that time, there were sixty virtuous men living outside a village who spent their days sporting with female musicians.

One woman failed to meet her appointment and departed; the sixty virtuous men then searched for her and gradually made their way to the Śāṇa forest, where they saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree, his countenance serene and majestic—anyone who beheld him would give rise to a pure mind, his faculties subdued and his mind tranquil, having attained the most supreme perfection, like a golden pillar of exquisite radiance. Having seen him, they approached the Buddha and said: "Bhadanta!..."
“Have you seen a certain woman?
The World-Honored One replied,
“What relation is that woman to you?”
The people replied, "We,
the sixty virtuous clans, have had female musicians perform various entertainments every day outside the village."
"This woman has broken our appointment and abandoned me; I have now come to search for her.
He said to them: "O people!..."
"What do you think?
Of what is it that you now stand in need: is it the female body that you seek as essential, or is it your own self that you seek as essential?"
The people replied, "Venerable Sir!
Seeking a woman's body is of no benefit; seeking one's own self is the most supreme."
The World-Honored One said:
"Young men! Come and sit; I shall now proclaim the sublime Dharma for you."
Then the sixty members of the Noble Group prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. The Buddha taught them the sublime Dharma, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them.
It is the constant practice of all Buddhas to first teach this Dharma:

namely, generosity and observance of the precepts as the causes for rebirth in the heavens; he further explained the faults and perils inherent in the five desires, and praised renouncing the world to dwell alone in the mountain forests, contemplating and investigating to sever all afflictions.
He expounds the vast and subtle Dharma, revealing it so that others may understand;
all who hear this teaching rejoice, become pure, and are free from doubt.
Having observed and understood this, the Buddha further taught them the supramundane Dharma:
namely, the principles of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
It is like washing a garment; once the coarse impurities have been removed and it has become pure, the dye takes easily.

When the sixty virtuous ones first heard the Buddha’s teaching, their mental faculties were purified, and they were immediately able to comprehend the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).

Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and thoroughly mastered the Dharma, they reached the ultimate firmness of the Dharma, transcended all worldly hopes, and crossed over all doubts. No longer dependent on others, they could not be led astray by any other teacher within the Great Master’s teaching; regarding all phenomena, they attained fearlessness.

When the sixty virtuous ones had received this Dharma, their hearts were filled with great joy; they rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with both knees upon the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

We have entered this subtle and wondrous Dharma and attained great benefit; from this day forth until the end of our lives, we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and receive the five precepts as upāsakas:
to refrain from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from false speech, and refraining from drinking intoxicants.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
At that time, when the night had turned to dawn, the World-Honored One dressed in the morning and entered the village of Bahuputra, reflecting thus:
"To whom among those in this village shall I first preach the Dharma?"
Again, he had this thought:
"At that time, the village headman had two daughters:
the first was named Nandā and the second was named Nandabalā."
In the past, when I was about to relinquish my ascetic practices, these two women first offered me milk-rice along with ghee and honey; because I consumed this, my physical strength became robust.
At that time, having formed this thought, the World-Honored One went to the home of the two women.
From afar, the two women saw the World-Honored One; they prepared a seat for the Buddha, welcomed him, prostrated at his feet, and spoke these words:
“Welcome! Welcome!”
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
We pray that the World-Honored One will please take this seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the seat, and the woman prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them; he spoke extensively until they attained fearlessness regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the two women rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with both knees upon the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have encountered the sublime Dharma and attained great benefit; from this day forth, for as long as I live, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and become an upāsikā.
Having spoken these words, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Today, out of compassion, please accept my humble offering.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had accepted, the woman immediately prepared an earthen altar before him; once the World-Honored One had washed his hands and feet, he sat down according to the Dharma.
Then those two women prepared various kinds of pure, sweet, and delicious food and drink; they served it with their own hands, repeatedly bringing it forward as an offering.

When the World-Honored One had finished eating, washed his hands, and put away his utensils, [the lay devotee] swept and sprinkled the ground, burned incense, and scattered flowers. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him with a blessing before departing.
As he was about to leave the village, he thought to himself:

"In this kingdom of Magadha, who among the most venerable non-Buddhists and brahmins, upon hearing my teaching of the Dharma, would conceive a heart of faith and reverence, thereby enabling many people to enter into my Dharma?"

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who was one hundred and twenty years old and had five hundred disciples; he resided in a forest by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, practicing asceticism.
At that time, all the people of the kingdom of Magadha will give rise to reverence, respect, and offerings, regarding him as a supreme field of merit, like an Arhat.
I shall now go there to preach the sublime Dharma, so that many people may attain great benefit.
Having formed this thought, he went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River to where Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was staying.
Upon seeing the World-Honored One from afar, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa immediately prepared and adorned a seat for him.
The Buddha sat down and spoke these words:
"Welcome! Welcome, great śramaṇa!"
"It has been a long time since we last saw a śramaṇa come here.
They then exchanged greetings, saying:
"Venerable sir!"
"Is your daily life light and at ease?
Having spoken these words, they sat facing one another.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Venerable sir, you hold this fire-hut in high regard; please seek out a corner and stay here for one night.
Kāśyapa replied, "It is not that I hold it in high regard, but there is a great venomous dragon in this stone cave, and I fear he might harm you."
