The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I have requested this dwelling; the nāga will not harm me. Kāśyapa replied:
“Great Śramaṇa! If the nāga does not harm you, sit as you please.

At that time, during the first watch of the night, the World-Honored One washed his hands and feet, entered the fire-hall, and sat cross-legged upon the grass spread as usual, unmoving and with right mindfulness.
At that time, when the venomous dragon saw the World-Honored One from afar, anger arose in his heart and he spat forth poisonous smoke;
thereupon, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, emitted smoke from his own mouth to block that poisonous smoke.
At that time, seeing the Buddha emit smoke, the venomous dragon’s wrath blazed up fiercely and fire erupted from its entire body.

Then, wishing to subdue that venomous dragon, the World-Honored One entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi), and fire issued forth from his entire body, so that a fierce and blazing fire filled the stone chamber.

At that time, during the middle watch of the night, Kāśyapa emerged from his dwelling place and observed the constellations; seeing from afar the flames blazing intensely within the stone cave, he thought to himself:
"The Great Śramaṇa Gautama is of handsome and upright countenance."
Alas! Alas! You did not heed my words, and now you have been burned to ashes by the fire of the venomous dragon.
He told his disciples:
"Each of you take water and extinguish the fire to rescue the Great Śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the intention of Kāśyapa, thought to himself:
"In order to subdue that venomous dragon, he further entered into samādhi and emitted various kinds of fiery light, which extinguished the dragon's fire without harming the dragon's body."
At that time, the venomous dragon, seeing various kinds of fire, felt terror in his heart and came to where the Buddha was; he then entered the bowl and remained there coiled up.
Knowing that the dragon had been tamed, the World-Honored One arose from meditative concentration, took the bowl, and went to where Kāśyapa was. Upon seeing him, Kāśyapa immediately asked:
"Great Śramaṇa, have you survived?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"I have attained peace. Kāśyapa asked:
"What is there in your bowl? The World-Honored One replied, "This is the poisonous dragon that you fear; I have tamed it and placed it here in this bowl."
Having seen this, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Although the śramaṇa Gautama possesses great majestic power and is well able to perform such feats, I too am an arhat."
“At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest grove near the village where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa resided.
At that time, Kāśyapa had five hundred young brahmin students (*māṇava*), each of whom maintained three sacrificial fire altars; in total, there were fifteen hundred such fire altars.”
Those five hundred young brahmins (māṇava), at the time of early morning, were about to perform a fire sacrifice at their altar; however, when they lit the fires, none of them would catch.
Those young brahmins, all finding this matter strange, went to Kāśyapa and said to him:
"We now wish to make offerings at our fire altar, yet the fires will not catch."
Having heard these words, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"It is because the Great Śramaṇa is staying near my dwelling that his majestic power prevents the fire from catching."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was and spoke these words:
"O Śramaṇa, you should know!
I have five hundred young brahmins who wished to perform a fire sacrifice; yet when they lit the fires, none would catch. Because of this matter, they have all come together to inform me."
"I thought to myself:
'It must be because of the power of the Great Śramaṇa dwelling near my hermitage that the fire will not ignite.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Do you wish for the fire to be kindled now? Kāśyapa replied,
"I wish for the fire to be kindled."
Having spoken these words, the fire altars he served all rose up simultaneously and became completely ablaze.
Upon seeing this, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Although the śramaṇa Gautama possesses such majestic power that he can perform wonders like this, I too am an arhat."

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the grove where Uruvilvā Kāśyapa practiced his ascetic path. After that young brahmin had finished his fire sacrifice, he wished to extinguish the fire but was unable to do so.
Then the young brahmin went to Kāśyapa and said to him: "Upādhyāya,
you should know that after we have performed our fire sacrifice,
we wish to extinguish the flames, yet we are unable to do so."
At that time, Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"The Great Śramaṇa Gautama dwells near my residence; could it not be by his power that the fire will not be extinguished?"
Having formed this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Great Śramaṇa, please know that these young brahmins of mine, having completed their fire sacrifice, wished to extinguish the flames but were unable to do so."
"Therefore, I thought: 'The Great Śramaṇa dwells near me; could it be that by his power this has come to pass?
Having said this, the World-Honored One replied:"
"Do you wish to extinguish that fire?
Kāśyapa replied, "Great Śramaṇa!"
"I truly wish for them to be extinguished.
At that moment, by the Buddha's majestic power, they were all completely extinguished. Then, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
“Rare indeed is this majestic power!
Although the Great Virtuous Śramaṇa is thus able, I too am a great Arhat.

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa practiced his austerities. On another occasion, Kāśyapa wished to offer oblations to the sacrificial fire but was unable to ignite it. Kāśyapa then thought to himself:
"The Great Śramaṇa resides near me; could it be that his power has brought this about?
Having had this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Great Śramaṇa, you should know!"
"I intended to offer a sacrifice to the fire here, but I was unable to ignite it.
Therefore, I thought: 'The Great Śramaṇa is dwelling near me; could it be that his power has caused this to happen?'"
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One asked:
"Do you wish now for the fire to be kindled? Kāśyapa replied:
"Great Śramaṇa! I wish to wear it.
By the Buddha's supernatural power, the fire suddenly blazed up with fierce and intense flames.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"How extraordinary is the World-Honored One! How rare is this!"
"Although my great majestic power is such as this, I too am an Arhat.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Scroll Six.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*.
Fascicle Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.

"At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest where Kāśyapa practiced his austerities. On another occasion, after Kāśyapa had completed his fire sacrifice, he wished to extinguish the flames but was unable to do so."
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"The Great Śramaṇa is now living near me; could it be that his power prevents the fire from being extinguished?
Having had this thought, he went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"Great Śramaṇa, you should know!
Having performed this fire sacrifice here, I wished to extinguish the flames but was unable to do so. Therefore, I thought:
'The Great Śramaṇa dwells near me; could it be that his power has caused this?'"
After he had spoken these words, the Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"Do you now wish to extinguish this fire? Kāśyapa replied:
“Great Śramaṇa! It is my wish that this fire be extinguished.
At that moment, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the fire was entirely extinguished.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Although this Great Śramaṇa possesses such great supernormal powers as these, I too am an Arhat."
“At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa practiced his austerities.
Later, on another occasion, the buildings of the hermitage where Kāśyapa resided suddenly blazed up on all four sides at once; he sought to extinguish the fire but was unable to do so.”
At that time, Kāśyapa and his followers, along with the great assembly, exerted themselves with one mind to extinguish the fire, yet they were unable to do so.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa is staying at my dwelling; could it be that by his power he has released these flames?"
Having had this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Great Śramaṇa!

In the house and vihāra where I reside, a sudden and fierce conflagration has broken out on all four sides. My family, my retinue, and the great assembly have united our hearts to extinguish it, yet we have been unable to do so."
"Therefore, I had this thought:
'The Great Śramaṇa dwells near me; could it be that by his power such a thing has been brought about?
Having said this, the World-Honored One replied:"
"Do you wish to extinguish that fire? Kāśyapa replied, "Great Śramaṇa!"
"I wish to extinguish this fire.
At that moment, by the Buddha's supernatural power, the blazing flames were entirely extinguished and vanished.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa then thought to himself:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
Although you possess such great supernormal powers, I too am an Arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest retreat of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa.
Then, during that night, the Four Great Kings, their bodily radiance illuminating like four mountains of fire, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, during the night, while Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was observing the stars and constellations, he saw four masses of fire before the Buddha whose radiance reached far off. He then thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa practices the fire ritual just as I do; that is why there are four masses of fire by his side."
Then, on the following day, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa went to the place where the World-Honored One was and said to him:
"Great Śramaṇa! Was it as I saw it?"
Last night, while observing the constellations, I saw a mass of fire before the Great Śramaṇa; having seen it, I thought:
"This Great Śramaṇa practices fire-worship just as I do."
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa! I do not tend the sacrificial fire.
Last night, the Four Heavenly Kings came to my place to listen to the Dharma; it is because of this that there was such radiance, and not from any other mass of fire.”
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"Although this Great Śramaṇa possesses such supernatural powers and majestic virtue, I too am an Arhat."

At that time, while the World-Honored One was staying in the forest grove where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa practiced, Śakra, King of the Devas, and Brahmā appeared in the middle of the night with bodies as brilliantly radiant as two masses of fire; they approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, during the night, while Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was observing the stars, he saw from afar two masses of fire before the Buddha whose light reached him from a distance. He then thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa practices fire-worship just as I do; therefore, there are these masses of fire by his side."
At dawn, he went to the World-Honored One and said:
"Great Śramaṇa! Is it as I have seen?"
Last night, while observing the constellations, I saw two masses of fire before the Great Śramaṇa, and I immediately thought:
"This Great Śramaṇa practices fire-worship just as I do."
The Buddha said: “Kāśyapa! I do not serve fire.
Last night, the Brahmā King Śakra came to my place to listen to the Dharma; it was because of this that there was such radiance, and not from any other mass of fire.”
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"Although this Great Śramaṇa possesses such supernatural powers and majestic virtue, I too am an Arhat."
“At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa’s hermitage.
It was a time of festival for the people of Magadha; for seven days, they all went to the place of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa to perform great offerings.”
As the time drew near, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"If the people of Magadha come here and behold such supernatural power in this śramaṇa, they will surely abandon me and follow him."
"It would be a good thing if that great śramaṇa did not remain here for seven days.
At that moment, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, withdrew his physical form so that it was no longer visible.
At that time, when the people of the country had finished making their offerings, Kāśyapa obtained great gains and sustenance.
Once the crowd had dispersed, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"I have obtained all my necessities during these seven days; if the Great Śramaṇa comes here now, I shall provide him with offerings."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, immediately manifested his body.
From afar, Kāśyapa saw him and thought to himself, saying:
"Great Śramaṇa!..."
"You too shall return.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
"I have come here as well.
Kāśyapa asked, "Great Śramaṇa!"
"It has been seven days since you left; for what reason did you go?
The Buddha replied, "Kāśyapa!"
Did you not previously think to yourself:
"If people from Magadha come to my place and see the supernatural power and majestic virtue of this śramaṇa, will they not surely abandon me and follow him?"
"It would have been a good thing if that great śramaṇa had not stayed here for seven days.
At that time, knowing your thought, I did not stay here for those seven days.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Since you knew my intention and departed, how could you have returned now?
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, you have now thought to yourself:
'I have already obtained the necessary provisions; if the Great Śramaṇa comes to this place, I shall provide for him.'"
"Furthermore, I know your thoughts, which is why I have returned. Kāśyapa said, "Great Śramaṇa!"
"I truly had this thought," he said,
and then addressed the Buddha: "Great Śramaṇa!"
"You may enjoy these various foods and drinks as you please.
At that time, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa!"
"Although he possesses such great majestic power and inconceivable [virtues], I too am a great Arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa practiced his austerities.
Then Kāśyapa came and invited the World-Honored One, saying: "Great Śramaṇa!
I pray that you will dwell here; we shall provide for your needs according to the Dharma."
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation, Kāśyapa personally prepared the utensils and cooked the food and drink. He then went to where the World-Honored One was and said, "Śramaṇa!..."
"When the food and drink are prepared, please know that it is time.
The World-Honored One replied to Kāśyapa, "You should go on ahead; I shall follow immediately after you."

At that time, after Kāśyapa had departed, the World-Honored One used his supernormal powers to go to the Jambu tree, where he gathered its fruit. Having filled his alms bowl with the fragrant, delicious, and brilliantly colored fruit, he returned to Kāśyapa’s place and sat down upon his seat.
Kāśyapa arrived later; having seen the World-Honored One, he asked:
"Great Śramaṇa! Have you already come here so early?"
He replied, "I have arrived. Kāśyapa asked again:
"Great Śramaṇa, what is this object in your bowl?
The Buddha said:

"When you previously invited me, after you had departed, I went by means of my power of concentration to the Jambu tree and brought back these fruits, which are beautiful in color, fragrant, and delicious."
"If you require food, you may take it. Kāśyapa said,
"May the Great Śramaṇa eat as he pleases."
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses such great supernormal power and majestic virtue; yet I too am an Arhat."

At that time, the World-Honored One took the fruit of the Jambū tree, as well as the āmalaka fruit, the kapittha, and the naturally grown non-glutinous rice of Kuru, all of which were described in the same manner as above.
"At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the forest retreat of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa.
When Kāśyapa had finished preparing the food with his own hands, he went at once to invite the Buddha."
The Blessed One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and sat down upon the seat.
Having seen that the Buddha was seated, Kāśyapa took the Buddha’s bowl, filled it with various exquisite foods, and offered it to the Buddha with his own hands.
Having accepted [the food], the World-Honored One went to another place to eat, and upon arriving there, he required water.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that the Buddha required water, went to where the Buddha was and struck the ground with his finger, whereupon a spring surged forth and flowed out.
Later, while Kāśyapa was walking back and forth, he saw this spring gushing forth and thought to himself:
"I have lived here for a long time without seeing this spring; how is it that such water has suddenly appeared today?"
He went to where the World-Honored One was and said to him: "Great Śramaṇa!
I have lived here for a long time without seeing this spring; why has it suddenly appeared today?"
"Who was this? The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
"Yesterday I accepted your food and drink and came here to sit and eat; I required water for use.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived my intention and quickly arrived here, striking the ground with his finger so that a spring gushed forth—this is how this spring came to be."
That spring was named "The Spring Struck by Hand.
At that time, Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"This great śramaṇa!..."
“Such is my inconceivable supernormal power, yet I am also an Arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest retreat of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, went out at the hour of late afternoon to a spring. He removed his robes and entered the spring to bathe.
As he was about to emerge from the water, there was a great tree by the bank named Aśvattha, which stood at a considerable distance from the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, intending to grasp the tree; it immediately bent down, and the Buddha climbed out by clutching its branches.
When Kāśyapa saw this event, he thought to himself:
"This great tree never bent before; who has now caused it to curve downward?"
He went to where the World-Honored One was and said to him: "Great Śramaṇa!
This great Aśvattha tree was not previously bent; who has now caused it to bend?"
The Buddha spoke as above.
This tree is called the Hastipracālaka-śiṃśapā tree.
Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses such supernormal powers, yet I too am an arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa’s practice grove.
When the Buddha obtained a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) and wished to wash it, he thought to himself, "With what shall I wash it?
At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the Buddha's thought, brought a large stone and placed it by the spring, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will accept and use this.
At that time, the Tathāgata washed the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) and then thought to himself:
"With what shall I dry it?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived the Buddha's intention; he went to another mountain, took a square stone, and placed it before the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"You may dry it here.
The World-Honored One covered the stone with his robe.
At that time, Kāśyapa came by, saw this stone, and had this thought:
"I have never seen these two stones before; why have they suddenly appeared now?
He went to ask the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!..."
I wished to wash and dry my clothes, yet I wondered what tools I should use.
At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing my thoughts, brought these two stones:
one for washing clothes and one for drying garments.
Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses such supernormal power, yet I too am an arhat.

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the forest retreat of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; he went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River to walk in meditation, when suddenly the water swelled up until it rose above the level of a person's head.
When the World-Honored One was in that water, the waves immediately subsided on all four sides, and the Tathāgata walked back and forth with ease.
Kāśyapa saw this from afar and thought to himself: "That great śramaṇa!"
"One with such marks and signs is now being swept away by the water.
He and his disciples immediately boarded a small boat and entered the river.
Seeing the World-Honored One there, at a place where the walking path was untouched by the waves, he asked:
"Is the Great Śramaṇa still alive?
The World-Honored One replied, "Kāśyapa!"
"I am now safe and well.
Kāśyapa said, "Great Śramaṇa, please board this boat."
By means of his supernormal power, the World-Honored One suddenly vanished and appeared upon the boat.
Having witnessed this, Kāśyapa thought again: "This Great Śramaṇa!"
"Although you possess such great majestic power, I too am an Arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa’s mind, spoke these words: "Kāśyapa!..."
"You have not attained the fruit of arhatship, nor are you a candidate for arhatship, nor do you know the path of an arhat.
When Kāśyapa heard these words, he thought to himself:
"The Great Śramaṇa Gautama knows the thoughts within my mind."
Having reflected thus, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:

"Great Śramaṇa! I pray that you will grant me permission to go forth within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Great Śramaṇa, to receive full ordination and become a bhikṣu, so that I may practice the holy life within the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa."
The World-Honored One said,
"If you wish to go forth, do your disciples know of this? Kāśyapa replied:
“They all do not know. The World-Honored One said:
“Your reputation is heard afar, and everyone knows that you are endowed with excellent wisdom; therefore, you ought to inform your disciples.”
"If you will listen to me, you may do as you please.
Having heard the Buddha's words, Kāśyapa immediately went to his own dwelling place and told his disciples:
"You should all know this!"
"I now wish to go forth in the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa Gautama and receive full ordination; what do you intend?
They replied, "We have studied under our upādhyāya based on his original guidance; if you depart now, we shall follow you and practice the holy life."

Kāśyapa replied, "If you are able to follow my example and train as I do, you may all cast away the deer skins, bark garments, mendicant staffs, and sacrificial vessels you wear into the Nairañjanā River, and then go as you please."
Having heard these words, the disciples cast away all their robes, sacrificial vessels, and other belongings into the Nairañjanā River.
Having discarded these items, they returned to where Kāśyapa was and said:
"We have now abandoned everything that was told to be discarded; what should we do next?"
"I only pray that you will instruct me.
Then Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his five hundred followers went to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"Great Śramaṇa!..."

"I have informed my followers and they have all granted their permission; I only pray that you will ordain me, so that I may go forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu."
"At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa had two younger brothers:

one named Nadī-Kāśyapa and the other named Gayā-Kāśyapa. Each had two hundred and fifty disciples, who were previously practicing the conduct of tranquility at the place where they diligently cultivated the holy life on the banks of the Nairañjanā River."

Nadī-Kāśyapa was dwelling downstream from the Nairañjanā River. Later, at one time, he saw deer skins, bark garments, a mendicant’s staff, sacrificial vessels, and other such items being carried away by the current in the Nairañjanā River. Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"What calamity has befallen my fellow practitioners of the holy life?"
Were such things as these swept away by a flood?
Was it destroyed by the king?
Or was it plundered by bandits?
"Was it burned by fire?
Or was it damaged by being swept away by water?
We fellow practitioners of the holy life ought to go there and inquire about the matter."

At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and the others went to the place where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was practicing his asceticism. Upon arrival, they saw him nearby, wearing a saṃghāṭī robe and having shaved off his hair and beard, sitting to one side before the Great Śramaṇa to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.
Having seen him, he spoke thus to Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa:
"Venerable one! Is this dharma of renunciation superior to your former dharma?"
He replied, "It is superior to that.
At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa had this thought:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers; he must surely have other even more excellent and sublime dharmas.

If it were not so, why would Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa—of venerable seniority and long-standing virtue, over one hundred and twenty years of age, respected and venerated by the people of Magadha, and whom the great assembly all regarded as an Arhat—now abandon his original studies to rely upon this great śramaṇa to leave the household life and practice the Way? We, too, should follow this great śramaṇa to leave the household life and study the Way."
Having thought thus, they immediately joined their palms together and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, saying:

"We only pray that you will grant us permission to go forth within the discipline and Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa, to receive full ordination and become bhikṣus, so that we may practice the holy life within the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa."
The World-Honored One asked,
"If you wish to leave the household life, do your disciples know of your intention?
Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa replied:
“They do not know this at all.
The World-Honored One said:
“Your reputations are far-reaching and you are well-known to the multitude; you are endowed with wisdom. Therefore, you ought to inform your disciples.”
"If you grant me permission, I shall do as I please.
Having heard the Buddha's words, Nadi-Kāśyapa and the others immediately went to their respective dwellings and told their disciples:
"You should know this!"
"I wish to go forth and receive full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Great Śramaṇa Gautama; what do you think?
They replied, "Our studies have always been based upon our upādhyāya. If he now departs, we, the entire assembly, wish to follow him and practice the holy life."

Kāśyapa replied, “If you can follow my example and cast away all that you wear— the deer skins, the bark garments, the staffs, and the sacrificial vessels— into the Nairañjanā River, then you may go as you please.”
When the disciples heard these words, they cast all their robes, sacrificial vessels, and other belongings into the Nairañjanā River.
Having discarded these items, they returned to the presence of their preceptor (upādhyāya) and said:
"That which was ordered to be abandoned has now all been relinquished; what should we do next?"
"We only pray that you will instruct us.
Then Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, together with five hundred disciples, went to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"Great Śramaṇa!"

"I have informed my disciples and they have all granted their permission; I only pray that you will ordain me, so that I may go forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, become a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa."
The World-Honored One said, "Nadī-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, welcome! You should practice the holy life.
As soon as these words were spoken, Nadī-Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples all attained renunciation and received full ordination, becoming bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One ordained one thousand matted-hair ascetics and granted them full ordination. Having stayed as he pleased in the region of Uruvilvā, he gradually traveled on until he reached Mount Gayā. There, at the site of a stūpa on the mountain peak, he resided together with those one thousand former matted-hair ascetics who had become bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One transformed one thousand bhikṣus by means of three kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
These three supernormal powers are: the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), the power of telepathic communication (*ādeśanā*), and the power of instruction (*anuśāsana*).

Regarding the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): the Tathāgata enters *samādhi*, and because his mind is thus concentrated, he suddenly vanishes from his original seat and appears in the eastern direction. There, in the midst of the void, he ascends, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; he enters the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), and from within his body, various lights emerge—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson.

He manifests these forms in pairs: fire issues from the lower part of his body while clear water flows from the upper, or water issues from the lower part of his body while fire blazes from the upper.
As it was in the eastern direction, so it was in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Having manifested these signs, he vanished from that space and reappeared at his original location; this is the World-Honored One’s supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi*).

Regarding the supernormal power of declaration (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*): it is when a bhikṣu observes the mind, mentation, and consciousness, thinking, "In this way one should engage in wholesome investigation and reflection, and not in unwholesome investigation and reflection; this is mental attention, and this is the realization of bodily consciousness. This is the supernormal power of declaration of the Blessed One.
The Teacher, being omniscient, addressed the bhikṣus: "All phenomena are ablaze. What is it that is ablaze?
The eye is ablaze; forms are ablaze;
eye-consciousness is ablaze; eye-contact is ablaze. The feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises internally conditioned by eye-contact is also ablaze."
By what fires does it burn?

It burns with the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, despair, and vexation likewise burn with these fires—all of which are suffering.
As it is with the eye, so it is likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; this is the teaching of the World-Honored One for attaining supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).

When the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, those thousand bhikṣus, through no further existence, attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) and all realized the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at the stūpa on the summit of Mount Gayā in the kingdom of Magadha, together with a thousand bhikṣus. These had previously been non-Buddhist ascetics with matted hair, all of whom had now realized the fruit of arhatship; they had exhausted all outflows, accomplished what was to be done, completed their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, severed the fetters of existence, and their minds were rightly liberated.

The great multitude of people in the kingdom of Magadha, while traveling about, heard that a crown prince had been born among the Śākya clan; that near the side of the Snowy Mountains, on the banks of the Gaṅgā River at the dwelling place of the seer Kapila, there was a diviner not far from there who, being well-versed in the arts of prognostication, bestowed a prophecy upon the prince:

"If he remains a householder, he shall succeed to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), able to bring the four quarters under his sway and transform the world through the Dharma. He will be endowed with the seven treasures—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure—and surrounded by a thousand sons who are handsome, brave, and strong. He shall subdue the armies of others throughout the four continents, ruling as a sovereign over all without enemies; all suffering and the use of weapons shall be entirely stilled, and he shall dwell in peace and happiness.

If he leaves the home life, he will, with right faith, abandon the household for the homeless state, shave off his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, realize unsurpassed awakening, and become an Arhat, whose praises the world shall sing and whose fame shall spread afar."
Having heard these words, that wandering mendicant went to King Bimbisāra and spoke thus:
"Great King, you should know!"

We have been wandering through this human world and have heard that a crown prince has been born into the Śākya clan. He was born near the side of the Snowy Mountains, by the banks of the Gaṅgā River, at the place where the seer Kapila practices his ascetic path; and so forth, until the praise and fame of his name resound throughout the world, as described above.
"I only pray that Your Majesty will put that crown prince to death; if he is eliminated, Your Majesty shall enjoy a long-lasting reign.
The king replied, "None of you should speak such words."
For what reason?
If that Prince Śākya should attain the rank of a Golden Wheel-turning King, I shall follow him;
if he attains perfect enlightenment, I shall serve him as his attendant and provide him with intimate offerings.
At that time, Bimbisāra, the Lord of Magadha, ascended to the upper story of his palace and made five aspirations:

"May a Great Teacher arise in my kingdom—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons, trainer of men, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Bhagavān;
and may I be one who reverently serves and gazes upon him."
They cause them to attain awakening through the essential teachings they have expounded;
having heard the Dharma, they receive and uphold the pure precepts,
and they abide in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was on Mount Gayā, he saw King Bimbisāra from afar and, having heard these words, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Bimbisāra, currently upon his palace tower, has made five kinds of vows, all as previously described."

"Furthermore, the great multitude of people in the kingdom of Magadha, while traveling about, had previously heard that a crown prince had been born into the Śākya clan; that near the side of the Snowy Mountains, on the banks of the Gaṅgā River at the dwelling place of the seer Kapila, there was a diviner not far from there who was well-versed in the arts of prognostication and who bestowed a prophecy upon the prince:..."

"If he remains a householder, he will succeed to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), able to bring the four quarters under his sway and transform the world through the Dharma. He will be fully endowed with the seven treasures—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure—and surrounded by a thousand sons who are handsome, brave, and strong. He will subdue the armies of others throughout the four continents, reigning as a sovereign over all without enemies; all suffering, distress, swords, and staves will be entirely stilled, and he will dwell in peace and happiness."

If one who has gone forth, out of right faith, abandons the home life for the homeless state, shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, realizes unsurpassed enlightenment, and becomes an Arhat whose fame is celebrated by the world and heard afar—such a person has renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to seek going forth and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Now he is seen at the site of the stūpa on the summit of Mount Gayā, surrounded by a thousand bhikṣus before and behind him—all of whom were formerly hair-tying non-Buddhists who have all realized the fruit of arhatship, exhausted all outflows, accomplished what was to be done, fulfilled their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, severed the fetters of existence, and whose minds are rightly liberated.
Having heard these words, he went to King Bimbisāra and spoke thus:
"Great King, you should know!

We were wandering through this human realm when we first heard that a crown prince had been born among the Śākya clan, and so forth, until he attained unsurpassed enlightenment. He is now at Mount Gayā, surrounded by a thousand bhikṣus before and behind him, having exhausted all fetters of existence and attained liberation of mind through perfect understanding."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will personally attend upon and make offerings to that Buddha, the World-Honored One.
If you do so, it will cause the king’s realm to be peaceful, secure, and prosperous.
Having heard these words, the king was filled with great joy; he immediately commanded a person to go to the Buddha's presence and, using my words, prostrate at his feet and say:
“World-Honored One!
Are you light and at ease in your daily life? Are you free from illness and affliction, and dwelling in peace and happiness?
Having spoken these words, he further prostrated himself and requested, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, will come to my residence in Rājagṛha to accept my lifelong offerings of the four requisites.
Having received these words from the king, the messenger went to Gayāśīrṣa to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke thus:

"The Lord of Magadha, Bimbisāra, has sent me here specifically to pay homage to the World-Honored One and inquire whether you are light and at ease, free from illness and affliction, and dwelling in peace and happiness?"
The Buddha said,
"May the King and all of you enjoy peace and happiness.
The messenger replied:

"The King requests with prostration: 'I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, will come to my residence in Rājagṛha city to accept my fourfold offerings for the duration of this life.'"
The World-Honored One immediately accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had silently accepted, the messenger prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and returned to his own place.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded before and behind by a thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were formerly matted-hair heterodox practitioners who had all realized the fruit of Arhatship, having exhausted all fetters of existence and attained liberation through right understanding of the mind. Traveling gradually through the human realm of Magadha, he arrived at the Bamboo Grove near the Sthira Stūpa and took up residence there.

When the King of Magadha heard that the Buddha had arrived here, surrounded by a thousand bhikṣus who all had already realized the fruit of arhatship, exhausted all outflows (āsravas), accomplished what was to be done, completed their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, severed the fetters of existence, and whose minds were rightly liberated.

Having heard this, the king prepared his excellent carriage and, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of attendants, set out for the Buddha’s dwelling to pay homage and make offerings; however, the wheels and hubs of the king's excellent carriage sank into the earth, and he was unable to proceed.
The king thought to himself:
"What fault is it of mine that causes this wheel to no longer move forward?"
Suddenly, he heard a voice from the sky saying:

"The King has committed no transgression; however, there are immeasurable multitudes of people within the King's prison who previously cultivated wholesome karma together with the Great King. If you release them now, you shall find the way forward."

Upon hearing these words, the king pardoned those who were imprisoned and released them all. As the king wished to proceed on his way, his crown tilted sideways as he passed through the palace gate, whereupon he thought to himself:
"What karma have I created in the past that has resulted in such a sign?"
Immediately, he heard a voice from the sky saying:

"Great King, you are innocent; however, there are immeasurable sentient beings who previously practiced sublime deeds together with the Great King, and they are now all scattered and living in remote villages and hamlets. You should summon them so that they may together behold the Buddha."
The king then issued a proclamation to assemble them.

Once they had assembled, he prepared twelve thousand chariots and a host of soldiers and cavalry numbering one hundred and eighty thousand, as well as fifteen thousand elephant troops. Accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Māgadha brahmins and householders, who surrounded him in front and behind, he departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he descended from his carriage and removed five superior articles—
namely, the parasol, the crown, the jeweled sword, the jeweled fan, and the jeweled sandals. Having set these objects aside,
he approached the Buddha, joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I am King Bimbisāra, the ruler of the kingdom of Magadha.
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"So it is, so it is! You are indeed King Bimbisāra, the lord of the kingdom of Magadha."
Thus he replied three times. "You may sit now.
Having heard the Buddha's words, King Bimbisāra prostrated at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
The brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha, some of whom prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side, while others joined their palms in greeting, said:
“Great Śramaṇa!...”
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your physical strength at ease?
One group sat to one side; another group sat to one side with palms joined, yet did not offer a greeting; still another group stayed at a distance, sitting in silence.
At that time, among the great assembly, the brahmins and householders of Magadha saw Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa there and conceived this doubt:
"Is the śramaṇa Gautama practicing under Kāśyapa?"
"Could it be that Kāśyapa has gone toward the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama to learn what he has not yet heard?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the assembly, questioned Kāśyapa with a sublime verse:
"Kāśyapa, what benefit did you see in the past?"
"Having renounced worldly life to leave home and serve the fire,
and the benefits obtained by upholding this dharma— explain these meanings to me now.
At that time, Kāśyapa also replied to the Buddha in verse:
"One might say that there are those who claim to have gained benefit— beauties of exquisite form and various wonderful flavors—
and seeing such advantages within that dharma, they thereby renounce the secular world to serve the sacrificial fire."
The World-Honored One again questioned Kāśyapa with these verses:
“If beautiful women and all manner of exquisite flavors Could be obtained through the practice of fire-worship,
And likewise the pleasures of the world of humans and devas— Why have you abandoned them all without a second thought?”
Kāśyapa also replied to the Buddha in verse:
"Because I have beheld the supreme tranquility beyond all words, I do not even dwell in the sphere of nothingness;
There is no dharma more sublime than this, And so my mind now abandons that state without a second thought."
Due to my former state of deluded mind, I maintained the fire-ascetic precepts in hope of liberation;
yet regarding the sublime Dharma, I was instead perverse, wandering blindly through the cycle of birth and death.
Contemplate with clarity the supreme state of the unconditioned; the Tamer of Elephants can eloquently explain it.
The Muni’s teaching truly benefits the world; Gautama guides others without weariness.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa with these verses:
“Welcome, Kāśyapa! You have no thought for evil states;
Into this most excellent and vast Dharma, You have now been able to enter.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa,
"Arise and manifest your supernormal powers for the great assembly.
Having heard the Buddha's words, Kāśyapa immediately entered samādhi.

Because this mind was concentrated, he suddenly vanished from his original location and, in the eastern direction, ascended into the void where he walked, stood, sat, and lay down. Entering the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), he emitted various kinds of light from within his body—namely blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson.
He manifested these signs in pairs: fire issued from the lower part of his body while clear water flowed from the upper; water issued from the lower part of his body while fire blazed from the upper.
As it was in the eastern direction, so it was likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions.

Having manifested these signs, they vanished from the sky and returned to their original places on the ground, where they stood. Then, approaching the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and spoke thus:
"World-Honored One, you are our teacher; we are the World-Honored One’s śrāvaka disciples."
The World-Honored One said:
"So it is, so it is! Kāśyapa!"
"I am your teacher; you are my disciple, a śrāvaka.
Kāśyapa, arise and take your original seat.
Then, at that time, Uruvilvākāśyapa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the brahmins and householders of Magadha, having witnessed this event, thought to themselves:
"It is not the case that the śramaṇa Gautama has studied under Kāśyapa; rather, it is Kāśyapa who has learned what he must do from the Blessed One."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Bimbisāra, the Lord of Magadha, saying:
"O Great King, form is subject to arising and ceasing."
One must thoroughly understand the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Great King!

If one can thoroughly understand the difference between the arising and ceasing of form, one will then be able to understand the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
"Great King!

If a son of good family, having understood the nature of form (*rūpa*), does not become attached to it, does not appropriate it, and does not maintain it, he will be able to resolve that there is neither self nor what belongs to self (*ātman* or *ātmīya*) therein; and it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

If a son of good family thoroughly understands the nature of this form (*rūpa*), does not crave it, does not cling to it, and does not grasp it, and definitively knows that it is without self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), I say that this person attains the liberation of *nirvāṇa*. It is the same for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*).
When the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, the brahmins and householders of Magadha thought to themselves:
"If form is not-self, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also not-self, then what dharma is this 'self'?"
Who is the sentient being?

And who is the life-principle, the creature, the nourisher, the person, the individual subject to repeated rebirth, the mind-born, the manava, the agent, the actor, and the one who performs contact, sensation, action, and abiding?

Since all these various phenomena are entirely devoid of self, what further entity could there be that is neither born nor extinguished, does not exist within the three periods of time, yet is capable of acting and experiencing?

If there were no one who experiences the karmic results of actions—whether those that ought to be done or those that ought not to be done, whether virtuous or non-virtuous—who would undergo them such that they cast off these aggregates and take up those other aggregates?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that these brahmins and householders were thinking such thoughts, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Because people lacking wisdom have not heard much of the Dharma, they give rise to such thoughts and cling to 'I' and 'mine,' not understanding non-self and what belongs to self."
Why is this? Bhikṣus!
Suffering arises from accumulation; by realizing cessation, one abandons suffering.
From the arising of formations through accumulation, one realizes the cessation of formations through cessation; when those causes and conditions cease, that [cessation] occurs.

By virtue of those causes and conditions, sentient beings are able to arise and undergo successive transmigration; thus, regarding the arising and ceasing of sentient beings through such causes and conditions, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands them to be ultimately without self.
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I have attained the pure divine eye, surpassing that of humans, by which I perceive sentient beings transmigrating through birth and death—those who are superior and those who are inferior;
those of beautiful form and those of ugly form."
I know, as it truly is, all the karmic actions performed by those who go to the good or evil realms.
Thus I see a certain sentient being who has committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind; who reviles the noble ones, clings to false views, and practices wicked conduct;
and by reason of these causes and conditions, upon passing away from this life, falls into hell.
Furthermore, he sees sentient beings who have performed the three types of wholesome karma, who do not slander the noble ones, who abide in right faith and practice right livelihood;
by reason of these causes and conditions, they pass away from here and are reborn in the heavens.
I fully know and see all such matters as these, yet I have never spoken of them:

that sentient beings are the self, the life-force, the nourisher, the person, the one who repeatedly takes up existence, the mind-born, the manava, the agent, the object of action, or the creator of contact, sensation, volition, abiding, and so forth.

If a person, regarding the fruits of all actions—whether wholesome or unwholesome, and whether performed or not performed—were to abandon these aggregates and receive those aggregates, none of these would be called "self. Rather, they are dependent conditions, namely: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;

with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, grasping arises; with grasping as condition, becoming arises; with becoming as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise. In this way, there is this great accumulation of the five aggregates.

That is to say: because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this ceases, that ceases. Namely: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;

with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this great mass of the five aggregates ceases.
"O Bhikṣus! Thus all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are suffering, and Nirvāṇa is bliss.

Through the arising of causes, suffering arises; through the cessation of causes, suffering ceases. By means of this, the continuous flow of transmigration is severed and extinguished; this is the exhaustion of suffering."

What is nirvāṇa? It is nirvāṇa because suffering has been exhausted, just as one attains coolness when a fire is extinguished. Therefore, I say that this phrase is able to relinquish the aggregates; through the exhaustion of craving and suffering, one attains parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra, the Lord of Magadha, saying:
"What do you think? Is form permanent?"
"Is it impermanent? He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"Form is impermanent.
He asked again:
"If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?"
He replied, "It is suffering.
He asked again:
"If form is impermanent and suffering, it is subject to change and decay.
Would a learned disciple grasp at form as 'this is my self,' or 'I possess these forms,' or 'form belongs to me,' or 'I am within form'?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent,
or are they impermanent? He replied:
"This is impermanent. He asked again:
"As for these things, from form up to consciousness, which are impermanent, are they suffering or not suffering?"
He replied, "It is suffering.
He asked again:
"Consciousness and so forth, being impermanent and suffering, are subject to transformation and decay.
If a learned disciple were to grasp that 'consciousness is my self,' or 'I possess consciousness,' or 'consciousness belongs to me,' or 'I am within consciousness'—would this be so?"
He replied, “No. [The Buddha said:

“Therefore, you should know that whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—all such forms are neither self nor belong to a self.”

"I have various forms; they do not belong to me, nor am I within form. One should see this by knowing it thoroughly and as it truly is. This applies likewise to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Great King!
There is a disciple of the Śrāvaka who, being endowed with great learning, contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as being devoid of 'I' and 'mine.

Having contemplated them thus, he knows that in all the worlds there is truly nothing to be grasped; because there is nothing to be grasped, fear does not arise; and because there is no fear, he personally realizes parinirvāṇa within himself."
“Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence.

When the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, King Bimbisāra, lord of Magadha, along with eighty thousand devaputras and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of brāhmaṇas and householders of Magadha, all became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. They likewise saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, thoroughly penetrated the Dharma, reached the ultimate firmness of the Dharma, transcended all hope, and crossed beyond all doubt. No longer relying on others, they could not be led astray by any other teacher; regarding all dharmas, they attained fearlessness.

At that time, the great king and the householders, having received this Dharma, were filled with great joy. They rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and placing their right knees upon the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:

“We have now entered this subtle and wondrous Dharma and attained great benefit. From this day forward until the end of our lives, we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, becoming upāsakas who observe the five precepts: we shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not speak falsely, and not drink intoxicants.”
Having spoken these words, he immediately invited the Buddha and the bhikṣus, saying:
"I pray that you will come to dwell in my city of Rājagṛha, so that I may provide for you with the four requisites throughout my life."
The World-Honored One then accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had silently accepted the invitation, the King of Magadha and the assembly prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to their respective abodes.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
You possess all-encompassing wisdom and are able to sever all doubts. We do not understand what causes and karmic actions the Great King and his retinue have performed.”
"By the power of this karma, he has obtained the pure eye.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen well, all of you, to the karma performed by King Bimbisāra!"
I shall explain this for you:

when the karma one has performed reaches fruition, the convergence of causes and conditions is like a torrential flood; the karma one has created must certainly be experienced by oneself, and no one can take its place.

"O bhikṣus, the karma you yourselves have created does not ripen in external elements such as earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, you shall experience its retribution within your own bodies. Once good or evil karma has matured, it is certain and will never be in vain."
And he spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When the causes and conditions meet, One must receive the retribution oneself."

“O bhikṣus! In the past, there was a Buddha named Arana-vi, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Men, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān, who appeared in the world.”
When his buddha-work was complete, he entered nirvana without remainder, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
After the fire had been extinguished, the people of that land collected the Buddha’s relics and erected a great stūpa in a pure location, making offerings to them.

At that time, there was a Golden Wheel-turning King named Kṛkī, who, surrounded by eighteen koṭis of military generals, passed through the air, intending to go to the human realm to reach the site of the stūpa.

At that time, there were devas who were devotees of the Buddha; each, by means of their supernatural power, seized the King’s precious wheel in mid-air, causing it to remain there and unable to proceed.
When King Kṛkī saw that his golden wheel could no longer turn, he immediately thought to himself:
"My merit is exhausted, for this precious wheel no longer moves forward."
The various devas, from the midst of the sky, said to the king:
"It is not that your merit has been exhausted; rather, because there is beneath you a stūpa containing the relics of a Buddha, it prevents your precious wheel-treasure from proceeding further."
When King Kṛkī heard these words, he descended surrounded by eighteen koṭis of military generals; he saw that the Buddha’s stūpa was still not yet completed.

Those various assemblies exhorted one another, collectively adorning themselves with rare treasures; they further offered various kinds of incense, flowers, and music as an act of worship. Kneeling on their right knees with palms joined, the great multitude raised their voices in unison to make this vow:
"By these roots of goodness we have planted, may we hear the Dharma from the Buddhas of the future and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye."
Having spoken these words, he prostrated at the Buddha’s stūpa.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts: the Universal Monarch Kṛkī and his attendants at that time were none other than King Bimbisāra and his retinue."

At that time, after the king and his retinue had made offerings to the stūpa of the World-Honored One Araṇābhi, by virtue of the conditions of this wholesome karma, they were born among gods and humans for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss.
"By the power of their vows, the king and his retinue have now attained the pure eye from me.
Monks, you should know this:
black karma has purely black maturation; white karma yields purely white maturation; and mixed black-and-white karma yields mixed maturation."
"Therefore, you bhikṣus!
Abandoning black-black karma and that mixed karma, you should diligently cultivate white-white karma.
*Vinaya-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Scroll Seven.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
You possess all-encompassing wisdom and are able to sever all doubts."
"We do not understand why Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was subdued through five hundred miraculous transformations,
while Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa were subdued spontaneously."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen well, O monks, to the karmic accumulation of provisions gathered by that Kāśyapa; I shall explain it for you.
This continued until he spoke in verse as previously stated.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, who was fully endowed with the ten titles. He resided at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī."

At that time, when that Blessed One had completed his Buddha-activities and entered parinirvāṇa, there was a king named Kṛkin who gathered various kinds of fragrant wood to cremate him. He then extinguished the fire by sprinkling it with fragrant milk. He enshrined the relics in four precious jars and erected a stūpa at a prominent location, measuring one yojana in length and breadth and half a yojana in height.
At that time, there was an elder in the city of Vārāṇasī whose family was immensely wealthy; his treasures were abundant and his enjoyments manifold, like those of the god Vaiśravaṇa.
That householder married a woman from a family of similar status, and after enjoying each other's company, they fathered three sons.
Later, the householder suddenly fell ill; though various medicines and treatments were applied, he could not be cured and soon passed away.
Then his sons adorned the bier with various silks and fabrics, escorted it to the cold forest (śītavana) to cremate him by fire, and having finished the funeral rites, they wailed and wept in grief.
Then the eldest brother said,
"I now wish to divide all our wealth and property.
At that time, his two younger brothers did not comply.
The elder brother repeatedly spoke of his desire to divide the property, to which the two younger brothers replied,
"If that is the case, we shall first cultivate meritorious deeds and only then allow the division.
The elder brother said:
"What kind of deed did you perform?
The younger brother replied,
"I made offerings at the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha."
At that time, the elder brother did not believe and raised many objections for a long while before finally granting his permission.
The two younger brothers, having made various offerings of rare and precious items at the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha, then made this aspiration:
"By virtue of these roots of goodness, may we receive the highest prediction of future enlightenment from the one who is like Kāśyapa Buddha—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

“Māṇava! In a future age when the human lifespan is one hundred years, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; within that Buddha’s Dharma, you shall go forth and attain a most excellent fruit.”
When the elder brother heard his younger brothers make this vow, he prostrated at their feet and immediately made a virtuous aspiration.

"Though I am of a wicked nature and do not believe in the True Dharma, by virtue of this root of goodness from my sympathetic joy, may Śākyamuni Buddha likewise manifest five hundred miraculous transformations for me, subduing me so that I may leave the household life; having left the household life, may I then attain the supreme fruit."
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts: that eldest brother of yours who was of a quick-tempered nature and lacked faith in the True Dharma was Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa;
those two younger brothers were Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa."
It was by the power of his vows that he was able to subdue them through five hundred miraculous transformations; thus, Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa were easily subdued.
When King Bimbisāra was still a crown prince, there was an elder in the city of Rājagṛha who possessed a garden with flourishing flowers and fruits, which he cherished with constant affection.
At that time, Prince Bimbisāra went outside and saw that garden park; having seen it, he immediately conceived a sense of affection and delight for it and said to the elder:
"You may give this garden park to me."
The elder felt a sense of stinginess in his heart and ultimately did not give it to him.
After three such attempts, he still refused to comply, so the prince spoke again, saying:
"Give me the wealth and property; the garden shall belong to me."
He replied to the Prince, saying:
"I might as well leave the country as give this to you.
The Prince spoke again to the elder:
"You should keep my words in mind:
'If you obtain the royal throne, you must certainly take it.
The householder replied:
"When you attain the royal throne, I shall certainly come forth.
The prince said, "You must remember this: I am Prince Bimbisāra."
Having spoken these words, he immediately turned the chariot back.
Later, when King Mahāpadma had grown old and reached the end of his life, the crown prince succeeded him as king.
Once he had obtained the royal throne, he used force to seize that park from him.
The elder was immediately overcome with burning distress and developed a heart ailment, dying of resentment.
Dwelling within this garden, he transformed himself into a venomous serpent; this snake constantly sought an opportunity near the king.

Later, during the month of spring, the king went to the garden with his palace ladies and various court maids. Having dismissed his attendants, he enjoyed himself in joy and pleasure with his retinue, and then fell asleep.
All the women, out of love for the flowers, abandoned the king and departed; only one woman remained, holding a sword to guard him.
At that moment, seeing that the assembly of women had all dispersed, the serpent emerged swiftly from its hole, intending to bite the king.

By the power of the king’s merit, the kalaviṅka birds surrounded the snake and raised their voices in unison. Hearing the cries of the birds and seeing the venomous snake approaching the king, the woman holding the sword immediately severed the snake’s life with her sharp blade.
Out of fear, the woman let out a great cry; the king, startled from his sleep, woke up and rose, asking the woman, "What is this?
The woman replied to the king:
"A venomous snake was about to come and bite the King, but a flock of *kalaviṅka* birds surrounded the snake with their cries, and I have already finished dispatching it.

When the King heard this, he issued an edict to the crown prince and his ministers to assemble all the people of Rājagṛha; the park was filled from near to far, and they heard the sound of the commotion erupting.
The king governed his realm both within and without with great excellence; when the people heard this, they all wept with profound sorrow. The king addressed them, saying:
"If a person saves the life of a consecrated Kṣatriya king, what boon should that person be granted in recompense?"
The ministers addressed the king, saying,
"It is fitting to bestow upon that man a reward equal to half the kingdom.
The king said:
"The Kalantaka bird has saved my life.
If this is so, it is fitting that it be granted the reward of half the kingdom.
The minister spoke again to the king, saying:
"The Kalavinka birds are not human beings; even if they were to receive the King's reward, what use would it be to them?
Therefore, let this park be given to the Kalavinka birds, and let food and drink be provided for them for as long as they live."
The King said, "It shall be as you have said.
Thereupon, the various ministers had bamboo planted throughout the royal park; for this reason, it was called the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling among the people of Magadha outside the city of Rājagṛha and stayed at a certain spot beneath a tree.

When King Bimbisāra heard that the Buddha had arrived outside the city of Rājagṛha and was staying beneath a tree, he departed from the city with his retinue and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the sublime Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, he remained silent.
Then King Bimbisāra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus will accept my humble offering tomorrow morning."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

King Bimbisāra, knowing that the Buddha had accepted, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his palace. He commanded his attendants to prepare various kinds of exquisite food and drink, to arrange seats, and to place jeweled vases filled with water before those seats within the assembly hall.
Once the preparations were complete, he commanded a messenger to go to the World-Honored One and announce:
"The time has come.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, entered the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to the royal palace. Having washed his hands and feet, he spread out his seat and sat down.

At that time, seeing the Buddha and the bhikṣus sitting in silent composure, King Bimbisāra personally served various kinds of fine foods as an offering, providing them continuously and without interruption until all were fully satisfied.
When the meal was finished, the king personally offered water for washing.
After the Buddha and the bhikṣus had completed their ablutions and rinsing, the king took a precious vase and poured water over the World-Honored One’s palm, saying to the Buddha:
"I offer this Veṇuvana Garden to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will graciously accept it."
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke these verses of benediction:
"Whoever practices giving shall surely obtain its benefit;
Giving for the sake of profit and joy, one will later attain peace and happiness."
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he went together with the bhikṣus to the Kalandaka Garden and took up residence there.

For this reason, the Venerable [Mahākāśyapa] compiled and declared in the Sūtras: "The Buddha was staying here in the Kalandaka Grove, until Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went forth and attained the path of Arhatship."
"At that time, there was an elder in the city of Rājagṛha who invited the Blessed One and the community of bhikṣus to his home for a meal offering.
At that moment, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, having some other business, arrived at this elder’s house in Rājagṛha and stayed there overnight."
During the first watch of the night, the elder rose and called out to his family members: "Worthy ones!
You holy ones should rise, gather firewood and kindle the fires, filter water and prepare various foods and drinks, sweep and sprinkle the ground, and arrange excellent and superior seats."
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍika heard these words, he thought to himself:
"In this householder's family, is it that they are giving away a daughter in marriage,
or are they taking a wife?"
Is it that you have invited distinguished guests?
Or have you requested certain individuals?
Or perhaps you have invited the royal family to partake of a meal at your home?
Having formed this thought, he again asked the elder about the matter he had been reflecting upon. The elder replied:
"It is not for the purpose of marrying off a daughter, taking a wife, entertaining guests, nor even for the sake of kings and such."
"Having made these preparations, tomorrow I shall invite the Buddha, the World-Honored One, along with the community of bhikṣus, and provide them with food according to the Dharma.

When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada first heard the name "Buddha," the hairs on his entire body stood on end and his heart was filled with joy; he asked the host householder, "What is this that is called 'Buddha'?"
The host replied:

"There is a śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who, out of right faith, has gone forth from the Śākya clan, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and left the household life for the homeless state; he has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and is called a Buddha."
He asked again: "What is meant by 'saṃgha'?
The host replied once more:

"There is a son of good family from the kṣatriya caste who, out of right faith, goes forth from home into homelessness, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the dharma robes; he has taken refuge in the Buddha and is called the Saṃgha."

Furthermore, there are sons of good family who, from among the Brahmin caste, the Vaiśya caste, or the Śūdra caste, out of faith shave off their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, go forth from the home to the homeless life, and practice the Way; they are called the Saṃgha.
"I have invited that Buddha and the community of monks to receive a meal offering at my home tomorrow.
He then asked the elder,
"Where is that Buddha now?"
He replied, "I am currently staying at the vihāra in the Śītavana cemetery where corpses are abandoned.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked again:
"May I see that Buddha? The elder replied, "You may see him; however, wait here for now."
"If the World-Honored One arrives tomorrow, you will certainly be able to see him.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada focused his mind on the Buddha and immediately fell into a state of drowsiness; he suddenly woke up before dawn, yet perceiving it to be light, he set out for the gate of the city of Śrāvastī.

The established custom of that kingdom was to keep the gates unbarred during the first watch of the night so as not to obstruct visiting envoys from outside, and likewise to keep the city gates open during the final watch of the night so as not to obstruct envoys from within.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw the gate open and the light, he followed the light and went out; once he had passed through the city gate, the light immediately vanished.
At that time, the sky was dark, and fear arose in his heart so that the hair on his body stood on end.
"I fear that humans or non-humans may cause me harm here," he thought,
and was about to turn back. At that moment,
the deity dwelling at this city gate emitted a brilliant light, such that from outside the gate all the way to the Śītavana cemetery, everything in between became brilliantly illuminated.
The deity replied again to the elder, saying:
"You may proceed further; there will be great benefit, so do not harbor thoughts of turning back. Why is this?"
And he spoke in verse:
"A hundred fine horses, A hundred pounds of purple-polished gold;
Two chariots drawn by mares, Each numbering a hundred."
To load various kinds of goods upon it and use them to practice the giving of alms is not equal to taking even a single step toward the Buddha;
when measured against such merit, the former is but one-sixteenth part of the latter.
Even if one were to give as an act of charity a hundred elephants,
all adorned with golden trappings and carrying exquisite jeweled canopies,
it would not equal the merit of taking even a single step toward the Buddha.
One part in sixteen among the most excellent of ladies;
with a wondrous string of pearls draped around her neck and many precious bracelets jingling on her arms— such as these she practiced the giving of alms.
"It is not equal to even one-sixteenth part of the merit of taking a single step toward the Buddha.
The deva spoke again, saying:
"You should proceed forward; there will be great benefit, so do not harbor thoughts of turning back.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to the deity: "O noble one!..."
"Who are you? The deva replied, "In the past, I was your good friend named Mātṛśoṇa.

Because I possessed great faith in Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana and paid them deep respect and veneration, after my life ended, I was reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings. To protect sentient beings, I now dwell here at the gate of this city of Good Sovereignty."
"This was your former friend; that is why I have come to inform you now.
You should proceed forward, for there will be great benefit; do not give rise to thoughts of retreat.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself:

"The Buddha transcends ordinary beings and differs from other noble ones; the Dharma he teaches is profoundly worthy of reverence. For this reason, the devas experience great joy upon seeing the Buddha."
Having thought this, he mounted the celestial radiance and proceeded immediately to the Śītavana forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was coming, had already stepped out of the monastery gate and was walking up and down in meditation.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the Buddha and, according to the custom of a lay devotee, inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being:
"Are you at ease in your sleep and your meals?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Having abandoned all defilements, The mind is unstained by any desires;
Attaining untainted liberation, One always sleeps in peace."
"Having severed all fetters and bonds, With the mind’s feverish afflictions stilled, One who has attained tranquility May sleep in peace and happiness.
