When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he returned with the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to the monastery. He spread out his seat and sat down, while the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him.

According to the Buddha’s constant practice, he first spoke of the merit of giving, the merit of observing the precepts, and the merit of receiving the fruits of rebirth in heaven; he spoke of the faults and afflictions inherent in the pleasures of desire, and praised the supreme merit of the pure observation of the life of renunciation, extensively expounding upon these fundamental teachings.

The World-Honored One, knowing that the heart of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was leaping with joy and gladness, and that his mind was free from hindrances, capable of receiving the sublime Dharma, and well able to understand it,
then taught him the sublime Dharma— namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— and extensively expounded these Four Noble Truths.

Just as a stainless, pure cloth readily takes on a fresh and beautiful dye, so too was it with the householder Anāthapiṇḍada; without leaving his original seat, he realized the Four Noble Truths—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and penetrated deeply into the Dharma, cut off all doubts and hesitations; no longer relying on the teachings of others, he was able to understand for himself without being led by another, and his mind felt no fear regarding the Teacher’s instruction.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, and with palms joined in reverence before the Buddha, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have entered the Dharma; with single-minded devotion, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus."
"I only pray that you will grant me the upāsaka precepts; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall forever renounce taking life, with a pure heart taking refuge [in the Triple Gem].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, saying: "What is your name?"
The householder replied, "My name is Sudatta;
however, because I provide food for those who are alone and destitute, people call me 'Givaka' (the Provider for the Lonely)."
The Buddha asked the householder, "Where are you from?
The householder replied:
"In this northern land of Kośala, outside the city of Śrāvastī, there is a town where I reside.

I pray that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation to go to the city of Śrāvastī and receive from me, for as long as life lasts, the fourfold requisites of offering, along with the Bhikṣu Saṃgha."
The Buddha asked the householder,
"Is there a monastery in the city of Śrāvastī?
The householder replied:
"There is no monastery in that city.
The World-Honored One said:
"If there were a monastery there, the Saṃgha would come and go."
"Since he has no monastery, where shall he be accommodated?

The householder replied, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation to go toward the city of Śrāvastī; I shall construct a monastery there so that the community of bhikṣus may come and go, take up residence, and dwell in meditative reflection."
The World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
At that time, the elder, knowing that the Buddha had consented, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to his own place.

At that time, having completed his business in the city of Rājagṛha, the householder returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I pray only that the World-Honored One will dispatch a bhikṣu to accompany me as I go to Śrāvastī to construct a dwelling for the World-Honored One and to provide a place for the assembly of bhikṣus to reside.”
The Buddha had this thought:
"Who among the community of bhikṣus is capable of subduing the people of Śrāvastī and the kinsmen of the elder?
Knowing that Śāriputra was capable of such subduing, the World-Honored One, having reflected, addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"You should observe the kinsmen of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the people of Śrāvastī; you should go and instruct them to construct a vihāra.
Having silently accepted the Buddha’s command, Śāriputra prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and set out together with the householder.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, when the night had ended and it was the clear dawn, took up his robe and bowl and entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in succession. Having returned to his own place and finished his meal, he gathered his robe, bowl, and all his bedding, folded them together in one spot, entrusted them to another bhikṣu, and departed for the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepared provisions for the journey and gradually reached the outskirts of Śrāvastī. There he wandered through various gardens and groves, seeking a site with excellent natural features—forests, springs, and scenic beauty—that would be pleasing and suitable for constructing a monastery.

"Not far from and not near the city of Śrāvastī, it was secluded and free from distracting noises; there was neither strong wind nor excessive heat, and no mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, or scorpions."
"There is this excellent site; let me build a monastery for my World-Honored One.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went wandering until he reached Prince Jeta’s grove.

That garden was neither too far from nor too near the city; it was tranquil by day and night, even to the point that there were no venomous insects or other such creatures, making it suitable for a monastery.
Having seen this garden, he did not return to his own residence in Śrāvastī, but went instead to the palace of Prince Jeta and said to him:
"Please give me that garden, and I shall build a monastery for the World-Honored One."
The Prince replied,
"That is not a garden, but rather a grove.
The elder spoke again, saying:
"Please grant me this grove, free from all questions.
Thus he requested three times, and the Prince replied:
"I truly ought not to relinquish this grove; even if you were to cover the ground with gold, I would ultimately never give it up."
The elder spoke again, saying:
"Since you have set the price, you may take the payment; the grove belongs to me.
The Prince replied:
"Who set the price?
The householder replied,
"You yourself set the price."
Because they could not reach an agreement through their dispute, they went together to a legal arbiter.
At that time, having heard of this matter, the Four Great Kings thought to themselves:
"Now that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is building a monastery for the World-Honored One, we shall provide assistance."
Having formed this thought, they immediately each transformed themselves into judges and took their seats in the court of law.
At that time, Prince Jeta and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada went together to that place; the Elder and the Prince each presented their respective circumstances.
The judges deliberated and said:
"Prince! You yourself set the price; the garden belongs to the elder, and you, Prince, take the gold."
Having seen that [the ground] had been cut away, the Prince departed in silence.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada returned home and commanded his servants to load carts, elephants, oxen, and donkeys with baskets and crates to transport the gold. Upon arriving at the Jetavana Grove, they spread it over the ground until there was a small portion that remained uncovered.
At that time, the elder thought to himself:
"If I take from the great treasury, there will be too much; yet if I open the small treasury, I fear it will not suffice.
He then had this further thought:
"Among all the treasuries, which one is neither too much nor too little, but sufficient?
At that time, seeing the elder standing in silence and deep reflection, the Prince immediately thought to himself:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍada must be losing heart; for the sake of a single grove, how could he possibly give up this vast accumulation of gold?"
Having had this thought, he said to the householder, "Your mind should now recede;
you ought to take back the gold, and I shall return the park to you.
The householder replied:
“‘O Prince! My mind does not waver; however, what I am contemplating is this: which treasury should I open so that it may provide sufficiency, neither too much nor too little?
Having heard these words, the Prince then thought to himself:”

“The majestic power and virtue of the World-Honored One are inconceivable, and his Dharma is likewise inconceivable; therefore, this elder has been able to relinquish his accumulated immeasurable gold and treasures.”
Having formed this thought, he said to the elder:
"The portions of ground where the gold has not yet covered them should be reclaimed; I shall use them to construct a temple gate for the World-Honored One."
The householder replied, "As you wish, you may construct a gate for the monastery of the World-Honored One.

At that time, as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was first desiring to build a monastery for the World-Honored One, the various groups of non-Buddhists gave rise to extreme resentment and harbored burning affliction; they gathered together in one place and went to the householder's location.
Having arrived, he spoke these words: "Householder!
You ought not to construct a monastery for the śramaṇa Gautama."

Why is this? We have already divided the territories previously: the city of Rājagṛha may be the dwelling place of Gautama, while we shall reside here in the city of Śrāvastī; therefore, you should not construct a monastery.
The elder replied:
"You may only divide your own national territories; you should not share in my garden, for the merit I have created arises entirely from my own mind."

When the various non-Buddhists saw that the elder’s resolve remained firm and unshakable, they went to the king and reported the matter in full; however, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada emerged victorious in the debate.
That non-Buddhist felt anger arise in his heart and an evil expression appeared on his face; he then spoke these words:
"I will never comply with your wishes. However, let a chief disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama debate with us; if he can defeat me, you may build the monastery as you please."
The householder replied, "So be it!
However, let me first consult Śāriputra; if he grants his permission, I shall come back to inform you."
The householder then went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
The various non-Buddhists all spoke these words:
"You wish to build a monastery; we shall restrain you.
They further said:
"The foremost disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama is present here now; if he can defeat me in debate, you may build a monastery.
Venerable sir, how do you intend to respond to this?
Having heard these words, Śāriputra immediately observed whether these non-Buddhists and the people of Śrāvastī possessed any roots of goodness;
having observed them, he knew that they did possess roots of goodness.
Furthermore, he observes:
"Who possesses the roots of goodness that can be tamed?
Looking within his own mind, he perceives: "I am able to tame them."
Furthermore, he observed:
"At what time should they assemble?
Examining their faculties, he saw that they could assemble after seven days.
Having made this observation, he said to the householder, "It shall be as you wish; seven days from now, I shall engage in debate.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada was filled with joy and exultation; he prostrated at the feet of Śāriputra and went to the place of the non-Buddhists, saying these words:
“Venerable One!
The Venerable Śāriputra has spoken thus:
‘Seven days from now, we shall engage in debate.’”
When those followers of external paths heard these words, they said to one another:
"There are two kinds of causes and conditions. What are the two?"
"First, Śāriputra must certainly flee; second, we should seek allies. For these reasons, let us extend the time for seven days.
The non-Buddhists then said to one another, "We too should seek out friends who share our own school."

They all dispersed in different directions to search for someone who had mastered their own school. Eventually, they encountered a brahmin named Red-Eye (*Raktākṣa*), who was skilled in magical illusions. Having found him, they immediately said to him:
"You and we have practiced the same path; we now wish to summon the chief disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama to engage in debate with him."
"He has now sought out companions; you may assist him together.
The brahmin asked, "When will the debate take place?"
He replied, "Seven days hence. The brahmin answered:
"Very well! When you have assembled them, you should inform me.
The various non-Buddhists, filled with fear and distress, sought out companions each day.

When the period had nearly reached its seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepared a magnificent and excellent lion throne for the Venerable Śāriputra upon the vast and superior site, and he also prepared a seat for the non-Buddhist teachers.
The various foreign non-Buddhist teachers all gathered at that assembly, as did hundreds of thousands of millions of people from the city of Śrāvastī.
Among them were some who had come merely to observe the debate, while others had their roots of virtue matured and had likewise assembled there.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, surrounded by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his retinue, came to the assembly and surveyed the great multitude to see who was capable of being tamed.
Smiling, he composed his demeanor and ascended the seat of discourse; the entire assembly, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms and gazed up at Śāriputra.
Then Śāriputra addressed the non-Buddhists:
"Shall you establish a thesis for me to refute?"
"Shall I establish a thesis for you to refute?
The non-Buddhist replied,
"I shall establish my thesis first."
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"If I were to establish a thesis first, no one could refute it—let alone the heretic Red-Eye—even excluding the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
He then thought to himself and replied to the non-Buddhist, saying:
"Let your school of thought stand as you wish; I shall refute it accordingly.
That Red-Eyed One was highly skilled in magical arts, and he immediately manifested a great *āmra* tree, which blossomed and bore fruit.

Venerable Śāriputra, a great wind and rain arose that shattered trees and uprooted them, dispersing and destroying them in an instant so that even those skilled in esoteric arts could not perceive them.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhists conjured a large lotus pond;
Venerable Śāriputra transformed himself into a young elephant that trampled the pond and broke the flowers, immediately leveling it back into plain ground.
The non-Buddhist practitioner transformed himself into a seven-headed dragon king;
Śāriputra transformed himself into a great garuḍa, swooping down from the sky to devour the dragon and depart.
The non-Buddhist practitioner then transformed himself into a vetāla (reanimated corpse), intending to harm Śāriputra.
Śāriputra cast a spell upon them, causing the spirits to turn back and harm the non-Buddhists.
Terrified, the non-Buddhists hurriedly descended from their seats, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground before Śāriputra, and spoke these words:
"We pray that you save our lives!"
"May you save my life!

At that time, Śāriputra withdrew his supernatural power of incantation, and the ghost immediately vanished. Śāriputra then preached the Dharma to the heretic Red-Eye (Lohitākṣa), who immediately conceived faith. Rising from his seat, he prostrated at [Śāriputra’s] feet and said:
"I pray that you will allow me to go forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination to become a bhikṣu, and seek to be your disciple to practice the holy life."

Having spoken these words, Śāriputra immediately had him shave his head and receive full ordination. Through diligent practice, before long he realized the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*). He was endowed with the three knowledges (*traividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

He attained the knowledge of reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence. His mind was unobstructed like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, neither love nor hatred arose. He viewed gold and earth as equal and without distinction, renouncing all fame and profit without exception. Thus, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas made offerings to him.
At that time, the great assembly, seeing this marvel, each marveled and looked up in reverence; they all conceived faith toward Śāriputra and spoke these words: "Noble Śāriputra!..."
"He has defeated the great masters of debate and subdued the non-Buddhists.
The great assembly, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms and gazed up at Śāriputra.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing the inclinations and afflictions of that assembly, understood the nature of the six elements and taught the Dharma; this was the realization of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard this, the great assembly attained immeasurable and sublime excellence: some gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka; some gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha; some gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; some gave rise to the mind of the Three Refuges and received the five precepts; some realized the fruit of srotāpanna; some attained the stage of sakṛdāgāmin; some realized the stage of anāgāmin; and some left the household life, severed all afflictions, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, the great assembly conceived a profound sense of reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

When Śāriputra had finished preaching this Dharma and returned to his original place, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, his kinsmen, and all the people were filled with great joy; they paid their respects and departed.
At that time, the various non-Buddhists felt resentment and anger in their hearts, and they said to one another:

"We have been unable to defeat Śāriputra; we must employ a stratagem to kill him. We shall first enter this monastery to work as laborers, and while waiting for an opportunity, we must take his life."
Then the various non-Buddhist practitioners went to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and said:

"You have now taken away all our gains and offerings. We have lived here for a long time and cannot bear to leave this country; we only pray that out of compassion you will allow us to work as laborers within the monastery."
The householder replied,
"Wait while I inform Śāriputra.
He then went at once to where the Venerable Śāriputra was, and having arrived, he addressed the Elder, saying:
“Venerable One! Now these non-Buddhists say this:
‘You have cut off all our gains and offerings; we only pray that you will show us compassion and allow us to perform labor within your monastery.’”
"Because we have resided here for a long time, we are unable to leave this country.
Having heard these words, Śāriputra immediately observed:
"Do these non-Buddhists possess any roots of goodness?"
Having observed and known that they possess roots of goodness,
he further observed who among them could be disciplined.
Seeing that he himself was able to discipline them, he said to the householder:
"Very well! We shall not oppose you at all.
Those non-Buddhist practitioners then began performing manual labor within the monastery.
At that time, Śāriputra manifested two staff-bearers to stand among the laborers; being of a very violent nature, they drove those men away.
Knowing that the time for their conversion had arrived, Śāriputra went not far from them and practiced walking meditation beneath a tree in the forest.
When those non-Buddhists saw him walking in meditation, they thought to themselves, "We have been waiting for this moment;
now is precisely the opportune time. Thereupon, they all came at once and surrounded him.
Having seen this, Śāriputra gave rise to an investigative thought:
"With what intention have these non-Buddhists come to me?
He then saw that they had come all at once for the purpose of harming him.
At that moment, the manifested staff-bearers arrived and drove them forward, striking them with their staves, and immediately commanded:
"You must go and perform your labor!
They then replied in unison:
“Śāriputra! We pray that you will save us!
Śāriputra then spoke to the staff-bearer:
"Go for now, and let him rest as he pleases.
Those non-Buddhists then thought to themselves and said to one another, "This Śāriputra possesses great majestic power;
although we all conceived thoughts of malice toward him, he has instead given rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward us."
Having spoken these words, they conceived faith in their hearts.

Śāriputra, observing their inclinations, latent tendencies, temperaments, and natures, and having understood them, he taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths according to their respective faculties.
By virtue of hearing the Dharma, they all shattered the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of a personal identity with the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the true truths, they all addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable One!

We pray that you will allow us to go forth into homelessness under the well-taught Dharma to undergo discipline, receive full ordination, and attain the status of bhikṣus; we shall practice the holy life under Śāriputra."

Then Śāriputra ordained those non-Buddhists and conferred upon them the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He instructed them in their duties, and through gradual, diligent practice, they perceived this fivefold wheel of birth and death as flickering and unstable, seeing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are subject to destruction, decay, and dissolution.

Having attained full understanding, he severed all afflictions and realized arhatship. Possessing the three types of clear knowledge (*traividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), he attained the wisdom of reality:

"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence. His mind was unobstructed like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with incense, neither love nor hatred arose. He viewed gold and earth as equal, without distinction, and renounced all fame and profit. Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas offered him their worship.
At that time, Śāriputra and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took a cord in their hands to measure the ground for the site of the monastery.
As soon as the Venerable Śāriputra smiled, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, seeing him smile, immediately addressed him, saying:
"Noble Śāriputra! Why do you smile?"
“The World-Honored One and his disciples do not smile without cause.
What is the reason for this present smile? Śāriputra replied:
"So it is, so it is! Householder, neither the World-Honored One nor his disciples ever smile without a cause."

Regarding what you have just laughed at: while the elder was holding the cord to measure the ground, the pure gold palace of that Śuddhāvāsa deva had already been fully accomplished. It is for this reason that I now smile.
Upon hearing this, the elder was filled with great joy and said to Śāriputra:
"If it is truly so, I shall further extend the cord and construct a larger monastery.
Thereupon, he made a grand vow.

Then Śāriputra, following the elder’s intention, drew the cord wide; at that time, the elder further expanded his vows to construct a great monastery, and the four-jeweled palace of the Śuddhāvāsa devas was already fully accomplished.
Having seen this, Śāriputra was filled with joy and further addressed the elder:
"Because of the vastness of your vow, those Śuddhāvāsa devas have surpassed your former palace, which is composed of the four precious substances."

Having heard these words, he redoubled his efforts in decoration and construction, building sixteen more monasteries in total; outside each monastery, he further constructed sixty-four separate courtyards, all of which were multi-storied pavilions.
Once it was completed, all the necessary furniture required for the monastery was fully provided.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the Venerable Śāriputra; having arrived and performed his salutations, he stood to one side and asked: "Noble One!"
"How far does the World-Honored One travel on his daily journey? Śāriputra replied,
"It is according to the manner of the travels of a Wheel-Turning King."
He asked again:
"How far does a Wheel-Turning King travel in one day? He replied:
"A Wheel-turning King travels two and a half yojanas in one day.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada established provisions for the fourfold offerings at intervals of two *krośas* and a half along the way from Śrāvastī, ensuring that both timely and untimely meals were fully provided.

He erected auspicious gates and appointed a chief official to oversee all affairs; he adorned them with banners, canopies, and precious victory standards, sprinkled the ground with sandalwood-scented water, scattered various famous flowers, and placed incense burners filled with diverse jewels along the roads. Having completed these tasks, he addressed his messenger, saying:
"You should now go to the World-Honored One’s dwelling, prostrate at his feet, and on my behalf inquire after the World-Honored One:
'Are you light and agile in your movements? Are you free from illness and affliction? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?'"

"I only pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will proceed toward the city of Śrāvastī; I shall provide them with the four types of requisites for as long as I live, hoping there may be no lack.

Having received these instructions, the messenger immediately departed for Rājagṛha. Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated at His feet and stood to one side, saying to the World-Honored One:
"That householder Anāthapiṇḍada prostrates at the feet of the World-Honored One and says to the World-Honored One:"
"I hope you are physically light and agile, with little illness or affliction, and that you are dwelling in peace and happiness?
I pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will come to Śrāvastī; for the remainder of my life, I shall provide the four requisites as offerings, hoping there will be no lack."
The World-Honored One replied,
“May Anāthapiṇḍika and you yourself always enjoy peace and happiness.
After the messenger had addressed the World-Honored One, he spoke to him again, saying:
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada spoke these words:
"I pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will come to the city of Śrāvastī; for as long as I live, I shall provide them with the four types of requisites."
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Having seen that the World-Honored One had accepted by his silence, the messenger paid homage and departed.
At that time, because the World-Honored One was himself tamed, he was surrounded by those who were tamed;
Because they themselves are tranquil, they are surrounded by tranquility;
because they themselves are liberated, they are surrounded by liberation;
because they themselves are secure, they are surrounded by security.
Because he himself is well-disciplined, he is surrounded by those who are well-disciplined;
because he himself is an Arhat, he is surrounded by Arhats;
because he himself is free from desire, he is surrounded by those who are free from desire.
Because he is himself majestic, he is surrounded by those who are majestic;
just as a bull king is surrounded by a herd of cattle,
or a lordly elephant is surrounded by young elephants.
Like a lion king surrounded by lions;
like a king of geese surrounded by geese;
like a king of garuḍas surrounded by birds.
Like a Brahmin scholar surrounded by his disciples;
like a great physician surrounded by patients;
like a great general surrounded by a host of valiant warriors.
Like a great guide surrounded by travelers;
like a merchant leader surrounded by a multitude of merchants;
like a great householder surrounded by many householders.
He was like a king surrounded by his ministers;
like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by a thousand sons;
like the bright moon surrounded by the host of stars.
He was like the orb of the sun, surrounded by a thousand rays;
like the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, surrounded by gandharvas;
like the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, surrounded by kumbhāṇḍas.
He was like the celestial king Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of nāgas;
like the celestial king Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by a host of yakṣas;
like the king of the Pure and Wondrous Realm surrounded by asuras.
Like Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
like Brahmā, King of the Gods, surrounded by the Brahmā deities;
and like the great ocean, serene and tranquil.
He was like a great cloud, hanging low and spreading wide;

like a king of elephants, having stilled his wild intoxication, with his senses subdued and his deportment serene. He was adorned with the thirty-two marks and graced his body with the eighty minor characteristics. His halo extended one fathom, its brilliance surpassing a thousand suns. He advanced with a steady, slow gait, like a moving mountain of jewels. Possessing the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness, he was fully perfected in immeasurable merits.

Surrounded by a multitude of great śrāvakas and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of people, he proceeded toward Śrāvastī. Having reached the outskirts of the city and being about to enter the city gate, as soon as he lifted one foot to step upon the threshold, the great earth immediately shook in six ways:

it moved and moved intensely, trembled and trembled intensely, quaked and quaked intensely; it surged in the east and sank in the west, surged in the west and sank in the east, surged in the south and sank in the north, surged in the north and sank in the south, surged in the center and sank at the edges, and surged at the edges and sank in the center.

Great radiance issued forth throughout the world, so that even the dark and obscure places between the Iron Ring Mountains were filled with brilliant light. Celestial drums resounded spontaneously, and various exquisite flowers fell in profusion and disarray; various exquisite fragrances descended like rain, as did celestial garments falling like rain. All narrow paths naturally became wide and spacious, and all uneven ground naturally became level.
Within the city, elephants, horses, and other animals all let out their cries.
All furniture and articles for personal use resounded spontaneously at once.

The blind were able to see, the deaf were able to hear, the mute regained their speech, the lame were able to walk, and those with impaired faculties all attained full perfection. Those intoxicated became sober of their own accord; those who had encountered poison were naturally cured; those harboring grudges released their bonds; pregnant women gave birth without anxiety; prisoners confined in dungeons were naturally liberated; and those who were impoverished were spontaneously provided with various kinds of wealth and treasures.
“At that time, the World-Honored One and the great assembly, having entered the city, witnessed these various rare and extraordinary events.
Then the World-Honored One, from within the city of Śrāvastī, together with the community of bhikṣus, proceeded to the monastery, where he spread his seat and sat down.”

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, surrounded by his retinue of attendants, went together to the place where the Buddha was. He took a golden pitcher filled with water to wash the hands of the World-Honored One, but the water would not come out.
The householder, distressed with grief, thought to himself:
"I must have some karmic obstruction from a previous life that prevents the water from coming forth.
At that moment, the World-Honored One, knowing what the householder was thinking, spoke to him:
"You have no karmic obstacles. On this temple site, you previously constructed a vihāra and offered it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

That you pour water here now is not the original place where the offering was established; therefore, the water from your jar does not flow forth for you. You should move and establish it at the site of the original donated monastery."
The householder accepted the instruction and stood at his former place, whereupon the water immediately gushed forth.
The World-Honored One then uttered five kinds of wondrous sounds, offering extensive praise. As he was about to pronounce a blessing, Prince Jeta thought to himself:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will speak my name first."
The World-Honored One, knowing this, in accordance with the intention of Śrāvastī, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, is offered to the Buddha and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus from the four quarters."

At that time, when Prince Jeta heard the World-Honored One first mention his own name, he was filled with great joy and conceived a profound faith; he then constructed a temple gate for the Buddha made of the four precious substances.
For this reason, it is stated in the compilation of the Noble Sūtras:
"The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park."
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Volume Eight;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command:

"At that time, the Great King Jayasena of Kośala heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala and had arrived at the city of Śrāvastī, where he was staying in the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma. It was said that the World-Honored One, the śramaṇa Gautama, declared:
'I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
Having heard these words, King Prasenajit went to where the World-Honored One was, stood before the Buddha, and after greeting the World-Honored One, sat to one side and said:
"I have heard that the World-Honored One has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Some people say:
'The Gautama has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.'"
"Does that person not slander the World-Honored One by falsely claiming to have realized what he has not? Is this a true attainment,
or is it a teaching of the True Dharma, or is it a teaching in accordance with the Dharma?"
If that assembly of people were to say,
"The World-Honored One has attained such an Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and yet there were someone who could challenge and refute it, would that not be a source of shame?
The World-Honored One replied:
"If anyone were to say that I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these words would not constitute proof.
I have indeed realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; should there be any debate or slander, it would be unfounded."
Why is this? Great King!
I have realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
King Prasenajit replied: “The Gautama has said:
‘I have indeed attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
"I do not believe you now. Why is that? O Gautama!"

As for those aged non-Buddhist teachers—the six masters known as Pūraṇa, Maskarin, Sañjayin, Kakuda, Ajita, and Nirgrantha—since they themselves have not realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much less could the Śramaṇa Gautama, who is young in years and has only recently left the household life, have realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; who would be willing to believe it?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"There are four kinds of small beings that should not be deceived. What are these four?"
First, a young kṣatriya; second, a small venomous snake; third, a small fire; fourth, one who has recently left home to join the monastic order.
These should not be treated with contempt or deceived.
"Why is this? Because even one who has gone forth as a novice can attain arhatship and possess great majestic power.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Kṣatriya is endowed with the marks of a great man; his parents and his reputation are both pure.
Seeing even a minor one, he honors them and does not treat them with contempt; the wise person should not thus deceive him.”
Great King, you should know that one must not despise those who are small;
for if they later succeed to the royal throne, they will surely be able to bring you down and harm you.
Fearing that they may harbor resentment and jealousy in the future, you should therefore treat them with respect.
If you wish to preserve your life and body, and seek benefit for the future, you must comply with their wishes;
you should honor them with respect and never treat them with contempt.
Whether in a village or in the wild fields, if you see even a small venomous snake, [you should act accordingly].
One must not say it is small, for the wise harbor no contempt;
that serpent, for the sake of food, searches everywhere, and later,
if it finds an opportunity, it will surely cause one harm.
If you wish to preserve your life and body, and seek future benefit, you must keep far away from them; therefore, you should not treat them with contempt.
A tiny fire can burn extensively, leaving everything behind it blackened by the flames.
One should not despise them because they are small; the wise should harbor no contempt.
Though a small fire is yet slight, when fuel is abundant the fire spreads wide;
its blazing intensity destroys all—cities and villages alike.
If you wish to preserve your life and body, and seek future benefit, you must quickly distance yourself from this; therefore, you should not treat it with contempt.
Even if that blazing fire were to burn down cities and villages, [it would still be better than the fire of desire].
Though all sprouts may be burned, they grow back again after a single night;
yet if one treats those who possess the full precepts with contempt, it will burn away one's own wholesome karma,
so that children, grandchildren, and wealth are all lost at once.
Just as a tāla tree, once its crown is severed, will not grow again,
so too one who treats a bhikṣu with contempt will soon be like that tāla tree.
If you wish to preserve your life and well-being, and to secure future benefit, [you must refrain from such conduct].
One must always keep far away from these; therefore, one should not treat them with contempt.
A Kṣatriya endowed with all auspicious marks, a venomous snake, a small fire, and a Bhikṣu who is fully possessed of the precepts—the wise should not treat any of these with contempt.
"If you wish to preserve your life and body, and seek future benefit, you must always remain far removed from such things; therefore, you should not practice deception.

At that time, King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala, and the others, having heard these verses, felt great joy in their hearts; they immediately rose from their seats, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala dispatched an envoy carrying a letter to the city of Kapilavastu, addressing it to King Śuddhodana:
"May Your Majesty rejoice! Your Crown Prince has attained perfect enlightenment and realized the Dharma of the Deathless."
"By bestowing the subtle and profound meaning universally upon all living beings, they shall all attain fulfillment and be deeply moved by joy.
When King Śuddhodana had finished reading the letter, his heart was filled with great delight; yet he rested his cheek in his palm and remained silent, his face bearing an expression of sorrow.
At that time, the king’s chief minister, named Udāyin, seeing the king distressed and dejected, looked up and addressed him, saying: "Great King!
For what reason do you rest in silence with your hand upon your cheek, your heart filled with sorrow?"
He said to Udāyin: "How could I not be filled with grief and distress now?
When Prince Sarvārthasiddha was practicing austerities, I sent a messenger to inquire after him; he carried the news back and reported upon my place of residence."
"Now that I have dispatched messengers, not a single one has returned to report any news of him.
At that time, Udāyin immediately addressed the king, saying:
"I request permission to go there to inquire after the Prince; once I have learned his news, I shall return and report it to Your Majesty."
Then King Śuddhodana replied to Udāyin, "Recently I dispatched a messenger;
once he arrived at my son's location and saw the complete teachings, he stayed there and did not return."
"You should now look and see that he is certainly staying there! Udāyin replied,
"I am certain to come."
At that time, King Śuddhodana personally composed a verse in a letter, saying:
"From the moment you were conceived, I have longed for the Bodhi tree to grow to maturity.
I myself raised and nurtured you; My heart burns with constant anxiety and distress."
"Now you have attained growth, with disciples like branches and leaves;
others obtain happiness, while I now suffer only grief and pain.
He then spoke again in verse:
"In the past, when you were but a sprout, I nurtured you from your youth;
now that you have borne fruit, you no longer requite my kindness."
When you were first born, you made extensive vows:
"May I attain supreme enlightenment and deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
Having now realized these matters, you have given rise to a heart of great compassion.
"For myself and my retinue, I pray that you will come to my city.

When King Śuddhodana had finished writing this letter, he gave it to Udāyin. Having received it, Udāyin set out for Śrāvastī; after traveling for three days, he arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, where he approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, and presented the letter to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"King Śuddhodana has sent me with this letter to present to the Blessed One.
Then, after the Blessed One had opened and read the letter, he set it aside. Udāyin rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One!"
"May I go to the city of Kapilavastu?
The World-Honored One replied, "I shall now go."
Because Udāyin had been his virtuous friend in a previous life, he spoke these words:
"If the World-Honored One will not go, I shall now forcibly take the World-Honored One to Kapilavastu."
When the World-Honored One had seen these words, he replied with a verse as found elsewhere.
Having heard this verse, Udāyin was unable to respond and spoke thus:
"World-Honored One!"
"I shall now go to King Śuddhodana and report:
'The World-Honored One wishes to come toward the city of Kapilavastu.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Udāyin! A messenger of the Tathāgata should not be like you. Udāyin replied:
"What kind of messenger is the World-Honored One's?
The Buddha told him:
"The one who has left the household life is the Tathāgata’s messenger."
Udāyin replied, "In the past,
I made a solemn promise before King Śuddhodana:
'I shall now go there and certainly bring back news.'"
The Buddha told him:
"Since you have spoken these sincere words, there is no need for you to break your word of honor; you may go forth into homelessness and then return.

Because the Tathāgata, in the past through immeasurable lifetimes while practicing the bodhisattva path, never dared to disobey the commands of his parents, teachers, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), or venerable elders, Udāyin heard the Buddha’s instruction and did not dare to go against it.
Then, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Udāyin replied:
“So be it; I accept it with faith.
I shall now go forth.”
The Buddha said, "Welcome,
Bhikṣu! You have thus become one who has gone forth, perfected the full ordination, and entered the holy life."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"You may return, but you must not enter the royal palace as before. Stay outside the gate and send someone to announce:
'Outside the gate is a Śākya bhikṣu.'"
If someone is told to enter, they may enter immediately.
Once inside, if they ask, "Are there any other Śākya bhikṣus here? [one should answer accordingly].
One may answer: "There is. If [he] asks:
"Does Prince Siddhārtha’s appearance and attire resemble yours? One may answer:
"They are no different from mine."
"If you are made to stay overnight within the palace, you must not stay.
If they ask,
'Why does Prince Siddhārtha not stay within the palace?'"
"You may answer: 'I do not remain within the palace. If they ask:"
"Where do you dwell? You may answer: "In an araṇya."
If someone asks,
"Has Siddhārtha come? you may answer:
"Come. If asked, "When shall you come?
[one should reply: "At such-and-such a time."
"You may say: 'You may come after seven days have passed.
When Udāyin heard these words, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and said:
"I shall now go. The World-Honored One said, "You may go now."
Through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, they arrived at the gate of the royal palace in the city of Kapilavastu on that very day.
At that time, Udāyin stood outside the palace gate and said to the gatekeeper:
"You may announce me to the King:"
"There is a Śākya bhikṣu outside the gate.
The king said, "Let him enter."
After the bhikṣu had entered, King Śuddhodana recognized Udāyin immediately and asked,
"Have you been able to renounce the household life? He replied:
"Great King! I have already left the household life.
The king said:
"Are there any other Śākya bhikṣus? He replied, "There are."
The King asked again,
"Does Prince Siddhārtha's appearance resemble yours? He replied:
"It is no different.
Upon hearing these words, the king fainted and fell to the ground; water was sprinkled on his face, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
He asked again:
"Udāyin! When will Prince Siddhārtha arrive? He replied:
"Let him come," the king replied. He asked again,
"By what time must he arrive?"
He replied, "He shall come after seven days have passed.
The King immediately issued an edict to his ministers and aides:
"One should repair the palace towers; Siddhārtha wishes to come. Udāyin replied, "Great King!"
“The World-Honored One does not dwell in palaces.
The king asked again,
“If he comes, where will he stay?”
Udāyin replied, "He dwells in an araṇya. The king commanded his ministers,
"Construct a park and garden such that it is in every way identical to that Jetavana Grove."
Those ministers and assistants asked Udāyin:
"How many monasteries, courtyards, and buildings are there in that Jetavana monastery? Udāyin replied:
"There are sixteen great courtyards, and all the smaller ones together number sixty-four; within each courtyard there are multi-storied pavilions.
Upon hearing this, the ministers immediately ordered skilled artisans to construct the various buildings within seven days, making them no different from those at Jetavana and other such sites.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should inform the bhikṣus:

'The World-Honored One wishes to go to the city of Kapilavastu so that father and son may meet. You should put on your robes and take up your bowls; if there are those who wish to see this, they should go together with you.'"
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
“The World-Honored One wishes to go to the city of Kapilavastu so that father and son may meet. Those among you who wish to see this should take up their robes and bowls and go together with me.”
At that time, when the World-Honored One and the great assembly arrived at the banks of the Rohitā River, King Śuddhodana heard that Prince Siddhārtha had reached the banks of the Rohitā River.
The king commanded his ministers to adorn the city walls and sprinkle the ground with scented water, scattering various kinds of flowers and burning exquisite incense.
From the Nyagrodha Garden to the Rohitā River, the entire road between them was thoroughly adorned.
Furthermore, within the garden, lion thrones were spread out, as well as seats for the various members of the assembly.

When the people within the city heard that the Prince had returned, they all assembled; among the great multitude, some had come because of prior karmic conditions, while others came specifically to see whether the Prince would first pay his respects to the Father King.
"Should the Father King first pay homage to the Prince?
Because of such causes, they all came to attend the assembly.
On the morning of the eighth day, the bhikṣus washed their hands, rinsed their mouths, bathed, and approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"If I were to enter the city of Kapilavastu on foot, the Śākyas, who are all of haughty pride, would surely mock me with scorn upon seeing me walking, saying:

'When Prince Siddhārtha went forth from home, he was surrounded by immeasurable devas and ascended into the air; after practicing austerities for a long time, he attained the taste of the Deathless and achieved Perfect Enlightenment, yet now he enters the city on foot.'"

Having formed this thought, he immediately entered *samādhi*. He vanished and reappeared in the eastern direction, ascending into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees; the bhikṣus ascended to a height of six *tāla* trees.
Traveling through the air toward Kapilavastu, the World-Honored One gradually descended to six *tāla* trees, while the bhikṣus gradually descended to five *tāla* trees;
as the Buddha gradually reached five *tāla* trees, the bhikṣus reached four *tāla* trees.
When the Buddha reached the height of four *tāla* trees, the bhikṣus reached three;
when the World-Honored One was at three *tāla* trees, the bhikṣus were at two;
when the World-Honored One was at two *tāla* trees, the bhikṣus were at one.
When the World-Honored One was one *tāla* tall, the bhikṣus were six *ratni*;
when the World-Honored One was six *ratni*, the bhikṣus were five *ratni*;
when the World-Honored One was five *ratni*, the bhikṣus were four *ratni*.
When the World-Honored One was four *tāla* high, the bhikṣus were three;
when the World-Honored One was three *tāla*, the bhikṣus were two;
when the World-Honored One was two *tāla*, the bhikṣus were one.
The World-Honored One traveled by leaping one fathom at a time, while the bhikṣus walked on foot.
When King Śuddhodana saw this miraculous manifestation, he observed that there were so many bhikṣus that he did not know which one was the World-Honored One.
Then the king summoned Udāyin and, having had drums beaten and gongs sounded, proclaimed the royal decree:
"Let every household within the city of Kapilavastu send forth one son to follow the Buddha and renounce the household life."
"At that time, King Droṇodana had two sons:
the first was named Aniruddha and the second was named Mahānāman.

Mahānāman was constantly charged with overseeing the household affairs, while Aniruddha sat perpetually within a multi-storied pavilion, surrounded by court ladies, enjoying himself in pleasure and delight."
At that time, his mother said to Mahānāman:
"Do you know what has happened?
The King has issued a decree that from among the Śākya clan, one person from each family must renounce the secular life."
Mahānāma said to his mother,
"I will not go forth into homelessness.
His mother said:

"Why is this? Mahānāman replied, "The son my mother loves sits within the multi-storied pavilion; she has not sent him forth to leave the household life, but instead has caused me to abandon the world."
The mother said, "My son!
Aniruddha has great merit while living at home; you should not now give rise to envy toward him."
Mahānāman replied:
"If my mother develops a heart of attachment toward Aniruddha and serves him with partiality, it will not bring her merit. Mother, simply do not send food and drink; shall we not test his merit?"
The mother replied,
"Very well! I shall cause you to see it with your own eyes."
His mother took a basket and filled it with empty vessels; she covered it with a cloth in front of her young son, sealed it tightly, and commanded a female attendant to deliver it to Aniruddha.
He further instructed his daughter, saying:
"If someone asks, 'What is this?
[you should answer thus]."
He should immediately reply:
"It is empty; there is not a single thing in it.
Then the messenger shall take the basket and depart.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, looked down toward the lower realms; having witnessed these events, he thought to himself:
"In the past, Aniruddha once made offerings of food and drink to the Pratyekabuddha Upāriṣṭa; how can his food be cut off so suddenly?"
"I should now provide him with food and drink.
Śakra then filled all the vessels within the basket with various kinds of food and drink.
At that time, the female attendant took the food basket, sealed it as before, and went to Amogharāja; she then questioned the woman:
"What is there in here? the girl replied to the youth,
"There is nothing in here."
Having heard these words, he thought to himself:
"My mother loves me; how could she possibly send a messenger to my place for nothing?
There must certainly be food in this basket, and its name is 'Nothing'."

He immediately opened it to look inside and saw that his dwelling was filled with various requisites; within the vessels were fragrant and delicious foods, all completely full. The scent was so rich and pervasive that he felt a sense of wonder, having never experienced such a thing before.
Amṛtodana, out of filial piety, took choice food and presented it to his mother; he then instructed his messenger to address the mother, saying:
"I only wish that you would have this 'nothing' food sent here every day."
When the mother obtained that food, she felt extreme wonder and looked at Mahānāman.
She then said to him,
"Son, do you see this food?"
Mahānāman replied, “I have now seen it.
His mother said to Mahānāman:
"I have already informed you before that Aniruddha possesses great merit; you should not now give rise to jealousy.
Mahānāman replied, "Mother, whether Aniruddha possesses merit or lacks merit, I still cannot go forth into the religious life."
When his mother saw that Mahānāma would not consent to go forth despite her various exhortations, she went to Aniruddha and spoke to him, saying:
"O eldest son, do you know this now?"
The King has issued a decree that from among the Śākya clan, one person from each household shall renounce the secular life.
As for your intention now, will you remain at home or will you go forth into homelessness?
Aniruddha replied: "Now, what faults are there in living at home?
What benefits are there?"
"If you now leave the household life, what benefit will there be?
The mother replied to her son:
"If one dwells at home in accordance with the Dharma, free from all faults, one should attain rebirth among gods or humans."
If one dwells as a householder in an unrighteous manner, they will fall into the three evil realms.
If one leaves the household life in accordance with the Dharma and relies upon the holy teachings, they will attain supreme nirvana;
if one cannot fully fulfill the requirements of leaving the household life, they will at least obtain the bodies of humans or devas.
Having heard this, Aniruddha immediately said to his mother:
"The transgressions committed by one who has left the home life are outweighed by the merit of diligence while in the home life; I pray that my mother will release me so that I may go forth myself."
The mother then replied,
"I grant you permission to leave the home life.
Aniruddha, who had long been on intimate terms with King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan, immediately went to the king's residence.

When he arrived at the entrance of the gate, the King was upon the pavilion playing the lute and performing as a musician. Suddenly, a string of the lute snapped, and the singing became discordant. Aniruddha, being skilled at the lute, stood outside the gate and knew that the sound had become wrong because a string had snapped.
The gatekeeper informed the King: "Aniruddha is standing at the entrance, wishing to see Your Majesty."
"Who has created this obstacle?
Summon him here at once.
Once they had met, the king patted him on the back and sat down, then asked Aniruddha:
"How long have you been at this gate? Aniruddha replied,
"I arrived outside the gate just as the strings of my lute snapped."
At that time, Aniruddha stroked the white cotton cloth on the king’s mat with his hand and said to the king:
"When the weaver who wove this cloth was weaving it, he suffered from a fever; why does Your Majesty now lie upon this stone?"
The king was immediately struck with wonder and, upon lifting the mat to look beneath it, saw that the lower mat was heavily stained with grease and filth.
Upon seeing this, the noble King Śākyamuni was filled with extreme astonishment and alarm.
He called the weaver over and asked him,
"When you were weaving this cotton cloth, did you suffer from a fever? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the noble King Śākyamuni said to Aniruddha: "Young man!"
"Why do you know this?
He replied, "When I touched it, I perceived heat; therefore, I know."
He was filled with extreme wonder, and the king asked again:
"For what reason have you come here? He replied:
"Great King! King Śuddhodana has issued an instruction, decreeing that each of the Śākya clans shall permit one person to go forth.
Desiring to leave home and become a renunciant, I have come to bid you farewell."
The king said, "Stay here for one night; we shall deliberate together.
Aniruddha stayed there for one night, and the king said:

"O youth! If I were to follow you into the homeless life, Devadatta would become the king of the Śākyas and would become a source of great affliction for all the Śākyas; therefore, let us together exhort Devadatta to renounce the world as well."
He immediately summoned Devadatta to that place, and the king said to him: "Devadatta!
We all now wish to leave the household life; what do you intend to do?"
Having heard this, he immediately thought to himself:
"If I reply that I will not leave the home life, the noble King Śākyamuni will likewise not leave the home life; I must employ a skillful means to deceive him."
Again, he thought to himself:

"At that time, when the World-Honored One manifested supernatural transformations through illusion within the Nyagrodha Grove, causing the entire great assembly to believe and submit, I had already devised this plan."
Having reflected thus, he said:
"Great King! Since Your Majesty has gone forth from the household life, I too shall not remain."
He then thought to himself:
"This deceiver shall now be known and heard by the entire great assembly.
At that time, the king issued an edict, proclaiming it to all the people:
"I, along with Aniruddha, Devadatta, and five hundred other members of the Śākya clan, shall all go forth together. You should all know of this and rejoice.
Upon hearing these words, Devadatta felt deep distress in his heart and thought to himself:
"If I had known for certain that the Worthy King was going forth, I should not have said that we were going forth together."
"If he does not renounce the world now, this man of false speech shall not become king; he must first renounce the world and only then become king.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:

"For the sake of all the Śākyas, I shall arrange a great offering. I will purify the roads by removing tiles and rubble, sprinkle the ground with sandalwood water, erect banners and streamers, hang various silk canopies, burn famous incenses, and scatter a variety of exquisite flowers."

At that time, the King, surrounded before and behind by hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyas and their retinues, proceeded to the lion throne and sat upon it. Then, from the various windows, the Śākya women all desired to behold these renunciant Śākyas, their noble and majestic deportment, and their offerings.
People had come from all directions and filled the streets and alleys, standing there gazing up at him.
The King again summoned various physiognomists and commanded them to examine the Śākyas:
"Who among you desires to leave the household life and dwell according to the Dharma?"
"Who is not acting according to the Dharma?

At that time, each of the Śākyas took leave of their parents and adorned their bodies with various ornaments. Each mounted a carriage, with the Worthy King leading the way. When the physiognomist saw this, he said:
"I would be happy to serve you."
The same was true for Aniruddha and the provisional combination of conditions.
Next it was Devadatta’s turn; a hawk flew down, snatched the jewel from his topknot, and carried it off. When the physiognomist saw this, he said:
"Based on such an omen, it is certain that he will bring harm upon the World-Honored One's person and shall fall into hell."

Next, when Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya (translated as "Deficient Wealth"), Kakuda Kātyāyana, Tiṣya, Samudradatta, and others were leaving the city, they heard the braying of a donkey. An interpreter of omens, having seen this, said:
"Because of their malicious speech and their harassment of the Saṃgha, these individuals shall all fall into hell."
Next, Upānanda emerged riding an elephant; as he looked back toward the four directions, his pearl necklace snapped. An interpreter of signs saw this and predicted:
"Because of excessive greed, he shall fall into hell."

"Thus, even as these five hundred Śākyas all came forth like those going to a garden, each manifesting their own noble, majestic, and magnificent splendor, they proceeded to the place where the Buddha was. Upon their arrival, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
'Regarding these five hundred Śākyas, I cannot say to them all at once:
"Welcome, come forth into the homeless life."'"
Why is this? Because among them, some have attained arhatship while others have not.
I shall now perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to ordain them as monks.
Having formed this thought, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
Regarding these five hundred Śākyas, you should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) to cause them to go forth and receive full ordination."
The bhikṣus replied, “So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, the Father King commanded Upāli:
"Go to the Nyagrodha Garden and shave the hair and beards of those five hundred people, including the Śākya nobleman Bhadrika.
At that time, Bhadrika and the others washed their heads according to the ritual and sat down in order.
At that time, when Upāli was about to shave the hair of Prince Kalyāṇa, he wept with tears of sorrow and sighed repeatedly as he performed the shaving.
When Prince Kalyāṇa saw this, he asked Upāli:
"For what reason are you weeping so repeatedly now?"
Then Upāli, kneeling with palms joined and weeping tears of sorrow, replied to the Worthy King:
"Since ancient times, I have always served the Worthy King in Jambudvīpa; now that the King has renounced the world and I am left without a protector, I would rather die than serve an evil king."
The Worthy King said to Upāli:
"I now know that you are truly sincere in heart; there is no need for sorrow.
I shall now ensure that you do not serve an evil king."
At that time, Upāli felt great joy; rising from his kneeling position, he immediately shaved the king’s head.
Once the king’s head was shaven, the king dispatched a messenger to spread out a white woolen cloth, and the Noble King stood up and addressed the five hundred Śākyas:
"Listen attentively! All of you!"
"This Upāli has served me from the past, yet he possesses no wealth.
You, members of the Śākya clan, should each remove your upper garments and ornaments, and place one such item upon this cotton cloth."
"Why is this? Since I have already left the household life, all my secular garments and various ornaments should no longer be used; I shall give them to Upāli.
When King Śuddhodana had spoken these words, the five hundred Śākya clansmen took all their clothing and various ornaments and cast them onto a white woolen cloth for Upāli.
Then Upāli shaved his hair in sequence and bathed according to the Dharma; he immediately donned the monastic robes and departed from there. At that time, Upāli reflected:

"Even these five hundred Śākya nobles, who are so illustrious, have abandoned their kingdoms, cities, wives, children, treasures, and garments to shave their heads and go forth. How much more so for me, of low birth and formerly a servant, to harbor greed and attachment toward these very garments?"
Again, resting his right hand upon his cheek, he thought to himself:
"If I were not of low birth, I too would have been fit to go forth and attain the fruit of Arhatship."
At that time, it was the Buddha’s constant practice to observe all sentient beings during the six periods of the day and night; the Arhats and others did likewise.
The Venerable Śāriputra, perceiving the mental distress of Upāli, having understood and seen this, went to where Upāli was. Upon arrival, he spoke to Upāli, saying:
"For what reason do you rest your cheek in your hand, harboring such mental distress?"
Then Upāli said to Śāriputra: "Venerable One!
How could I not feel sorrow and distress now?"

Now I see the Worthy King and the five hundred Śākyas, all of whom have renounced their royal thrones, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, as well as immeasurable and boundless treasures and garments; they have now abandoned them all to leave the household life and cultivate the Way.
"I am now so deeply attached that I will surely fall into the evil realms.
Venerable Sir!
Had I not been born into a lowly family, I would certainly have gone forth under the Vinaya taught by the Buddha, applied myself with diligent effort, and realized the fruit of Arhatship."
Then Śāriputra said to Upāli:

"Within the Buddha’s True Dharma, there is no discrimination against those of low birth or those with little learning. Anyone who, relying on the Buddha's teachings, practices the pure precepts with unimpaired dignified conduct may become a renunciant; this is the Buddha’s True Dharma."
If you wish to go forth, you may receive the full ordination within the Buddha’s True Dharma and Vinaya to become a bhikṣu.
You should accompany me to the presence of the World-Honored One; the Tathāgata will certainly grant you the going forth.
When Upāli heard these words, his heart was filled with joy; he cast away all his precious jewels and exquisite garments as if discarding snot or spittle.
Then Śāriputra, together with Upāli, went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
Then Śāriputra addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

This Upāli is fit to go forth within the Buddha’s True Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, and to become a bhikṣu; out of compassion, the World-Honored One has granted him permission to go forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Welcome! You should practice the holy life."

When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, Upāli’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord and the dharma robes were donned upon his body, as if he had already been a renunciant for seven days. Holding the appropriate utensils and possessing pure precepts, his majestic deportment was as perfect as that of a bhikṣu with a hundred years of seniority. Having thus gone forth, he stood to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One addressed him, saying, ‘Welcome! His robes transformed into a *saṃghāṭī* and his hair and beard fell away;
With his faculties tranquil, he remained at ease, Possessing majestic deportment through the power of the Buddha.”
At that time, the five hundred Śākya noble kings, following the Buddha’s True Dharma, underwent the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

Having gone forth, they returned to the Buddha’s presence to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One; in this manner, they successively paid homage to the various bhikṣus until they reached Upāli.
At that time, King Śuddhodana saw Upāli’s feet; having recognized him, he straightened his body, gazed at him, and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"This is Upāli, my attendant; is it appropriate for me to prostrate before him?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"O son of good family!
The dharma of renunciation requires that one subdue the mind of self-conceit."
"For this reason, I permit Upāli to go forth first; therefore, you all should pay him homage.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, having received the Buddha’s instruction, subdued his pride and prostrated at Upāli’s feet. Once he had prostrated, the earth shook in six ways. Following that sequence, he paid homage to the remaining four hundred and ninety-nine men.
At that time, Devadatta went to Upāli’s place but did not prostrate himself. Then the World-Honored One said to Devadatta:
"O son of good family!
You ought to subdue the mind of pride; you should indeed pay homage at the feet of Upāli."
At that time, Devadatta said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!
What benefit or harm would there be in sending me to prostrate at the feet of Upāli?"
"I ought not to pay homage.
Having spoken these words, Devadatta was the very first to give rise to the intention to destroy the Buddha.
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw King Bimbisāra and the others prostrate at the feet of Upāli and the earth shake in six ways, they were filled with doubt and said to the World-Honored One:
"Why did the earth tremble in six ways when the Worthy King prostrated at Upāli’s feet?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It was not only now that the earth trembled in six ways when the Worthy King prostrated at his feet; it was likewise so when he prostrated at them in previous lives."
Listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you.

In the past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled the world according to the Dharma; his realm was free from famine, and the population flourished in peace, security, and abundance.
At that time, there was a courtesan in that city named Bhadrāyus, who was beautiful in form and appearance and enjoyed amorous dalliances with other men.
Every time she spent a night with a man, she received five hundred gold coins.
In the city there was a young brahmin named Sundara, who went to the courtesan’s house and said to Bhadra:
“I wish to stay the night with you.
The woman replied:
"Do you have five hundred coins?
Puṇḍarīka replied, "My family is poor; I have none."
The girl replied, "You may take five hundred silver kārṣāpaṇas and bring them here.
Although Upacāru was without wealth, he cherished her deeply; at that time, he gathered various flowers and fruits to present to her.
The girl repeatedly obtained flowers and fruits, and her heart became stained with attachment.
Then, on a festival day in that city, all the women dressed themselves in exquisite garments and various necklaces, each enjoying pleasure together with her husband in their own home.
At that time, on the festival day, no one came to the courtesan to enjoy her company.
Then the courtesan thought to herself:
"On this festival day, all the women in the city are dressed in fine garments and adorned with jewelry, each enjoying various pleasures with their husbands within their own homes."
"Would it not be joyful if this young brahmin were now to come and visit us?

Having had this thought, the young brahmin suddenly arrived at her house. Upon seeing him, the courtesan recalled their past exchange of flowers and fruit; her heart filled with joy, she spoke these words:
"O handsome one!"
"Go and gather flowers; you may come tomorrow morning to enjoy our pleasures together.

Having heard these words, Upacāra was filled with great joy, like a prisoner released from captivity. He returned to his own quarters, his mind dwelling incessantly on that woman’s exquisite countenance and her graceful deportment. From the first watch of the night until the last, his thoughts never ceased. As dawn was about to break, he suddenly fell into a deep sleep and remained unconscious of anything at all.
When morning arrived, he finally woke up with a start and immediately sought out beautiful flowers.
At that time, the people had already gathered all the flowers; though he searched everywhere for them, he found none at all.
There was only one place where *nyagrodha* flowers could be found; he took these flowers to the girl's house. Upon seeing them, the girl spoke this verse:

"The dull-witted one who wears skin and craves desire, The clever and wise *pāṃśula* who loves beauty— While fine flowers are found everywhere at this time, You have now brought only a few *nyagrodha* blooms."
Having spoken this verse, he said:
"Go quickly and seek out other fine flowers.
Driven by desire, that man forgot his hardships.

At that time, during the height of the midday heat, he departed from the city for a distant aranya; there, he gathered beautiful flowers without shrinking from the toil, singing as he walked to delight himself.

At that time, King Brahmadatta returned from a hunting expedition; weary from the journey and the heat, he went to a grove to rest. Hearing that singing voice, the king proceeded forward gradually and spoke this verse:
"The blazing sun scorches my head, And the hot sands beneath my feet steam up;
Bhadraśubha, you delight in singing as you walk— How can you not fear the heat?"
Then the young brahmin replied to the king in verse:
"The sun does not terrify me; it is the thought of desire that can burn me.
The world of desires possesses the suffering of heat; the sun cannot scorch a person."
“When King Brahmadatta had heard these verses, he thought to himself:
‘One should know that because this young brahmin has spoken such cooling words, he was unaware of the heat while gathering flowers in the midst of the day.’”
The king immediately dismounted and sat beneath a tree, then commanded the young brahmin:
"Speak some cooling words; I shall listen to them.
Having heard the king's words, the young brahmin thought to himself:
"I must know that the King is currently suffering from extreme heat and requires cool conversation.
Having formed this thought, he immediately spoke of various cooling matters at that time.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s body immediately felt great coolness and his heart was filled with joy;
he addressed his ministers, saying, "If there were anyone capable of saving the life of this consecrated king, what reward should be granted to them?"
The minister replied,
"One should divide half of the kingdom and bestow it upon that man.
Then the king said to the māṇava:
"You may stay overnight with me in the palace; tomorrow morning, I shall grant you the reward of half the kingdom.

At that time, the Māṇava stayed overnight with the king. The king immediately prepared various kinds of pure food, exquisite garments, and bedding for his comfort, and had him rest. Having no other companion, he thought to himself:
"If I were to obtain half the kingdom and become a king of half the realm, the ladies of the inner court would all belong to me; I could enjoy every pleasure as I pleased."
He further thought to himself:
"A reward of half a kingdom is hardly worth mentioning; what if I were to kill the king and seize the entire throne?
He then thought again:
"Those in positions of high honor and supremacy all covet [power]; why should I now desire half a kingdom or even the full throne?
For what reason?
Because by coveting the position of king, one would seek to harm the reigning monarch."
Having had this thought, he spoke these verses:
"When wealth has not yet been obtained, craving arises; When seeking it and failing to find it, suffering and distress are born.
Even when wealth has been obtained, greed does not cease; Thus one knows that the pursuit of profit brings only disadvantage."
“Having recited this verse, he immediately fell asleep.
Waking in the middle of the night, his heart was filled with regret; he rose from his bed, took an old deer skin, spread it upon the ground, and lay down.”
Then, at the time of dawn, King Brahmadatta addressed a messenger, saying:
"Summon the young brahmin!
I shall now grant him half the kingdom."
The messenger, having received these instructions, went to the young brahmin and said: "Great King!
Having observed that man’s deportment and conduct, I find him unfit for the position of half the kingdom."
The king asked for the reason, and he replied: "Great King!
I have just personally observed that he has abandoned his exquisite bed and bedding to lie upon the ground, sleeping on a deer skin. How could such a lowly man be fit for the royal throne?"
The king said, "He is a wise man; it cannot be without cause. You must go and summon him.
The messenger went back again and reported this.
"The King summons you.
Having arrived at the King's presence, the King said to him:
"Why have you abandoned your bed and bedding to lie upon a deer skin?"
He then related the matter in full and in due order, and again addressed the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty permits, I wish to go forth; I pray that Your Majesty grant me leave."
The king said,
"First let us establish an agreement, and I shall release you. If,
after you have left the household life, you attain some realization and return to inform me, I will permit you to go."
He replied to the king, "I dare not disobey Your Majesty's command.
He then took his leave with a prostration and went to a quiet grove; without a preceptor or an instructor, he exerted himself and realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Having attained realization, he further thought:
"In the past, I made a verbal agreement with the king; I should now go and fulfill his long-held aspiration.
He returned to the king's location, ascended into the void, emitted a great mass of fire, and manifested various supernatural transformations.
The King then prostrated himself with his head at the feet of that Honored One and spoke in verse:
"Beholding this small cultivation that has realized such a great fruit, And attained this state of great distinction and excellence;
The young brahmin has now gained a sublime benefit— Having gone forth and reached this point, what more could he seek?"
“At that time, having inspired King Brahmadatta with reverent faith, the Venerable One left him and departed.
King Brahmadatta had a barber named Gaganapāla, to whom he commanded that these verses be entrusted.”
He replied, "You should recite this verse from time to time so that I may remember it.
