At that time, the barber Sindhuka was skilled at shaving hair; while he was shaving the king's head, the king fell fast asleep.
As he was about to shave his hair, he snapped his fingers to alert the king; once the king had awakened from his sleep, he was filled with great joy and said to Gopāla:
"What is it that you now seek?"
"I shall grant your request. He replied,
"I pray that Your Majesty will allow me a moment's reflection before I present my report."
When Gaṅgapāla had thus recited the verses, he would regularly proclaim them before the king.

Hearing this, the king was filled with joy; he conceived a sense of weary detachment toward the five objects of desire, no longer casting even a glance at the women present before him, nor did he deign to listen to their pure songs or beautiful chants, much less develop any attachment to them.
At that time, the palace ladies, having lost the King’s favor, felt deep distress in their hearts and said to one another:

"We have lost his affection because of this Gopāla; since he recites those verses and turns our King's mind so that he no longer feels passion or love for us, we should devise a plan together to expel him quickly."
Having formed this plan, one of the palace women went to Gandharva and said to him,
"Uncle! If the King, being pleased, asks what you require?"
"You should immediately request the King to explain the verse you have recited.
Later, on another occasion, that Devadatta again recited the aforementioned gāthā for the King.
Upon hearing it, the King was filled with joy and asked what he required.
He then addressed the king:
"I have no other desire; I only wish for you to explain this verse for me.
The king complied with his request and provided a detailed exposition. Having heard it, Gaṅgāpāla conceived a sense of weary detachment and said to the king:
"I have served Your Majesty for a long time; I pray that you will show me compassion and grant me permission to leave the household life.
The King said, "I shall now enter into a covenant with you: if, after leaving the household life, you attain some realization, you must return and inform me, and only then will I release you to go."
"If it were not so, I would not grant your request. Gaṅgāpāla replied,
"I shall not disobey the King's command."
He was then permitted to go forth.
At that time, Gaṅgāpāla went to the mountain forest to the abode of the rishis; through diligent cultivation, he eventually realized the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā). He then thought:
"Formerly, I made a verbal agreement with the king; it is now fitting that I go to fulfill his long-held aspiration."
Having reflected thus, he immediately went to the king’s location, ascended into the air, emitted great flames of fire, and manifested various supernatural transformations.
The king then prostrated himself with his head at [the monk's] feet and spoke these words:
"Venerable One!..."
“You have attained such a capacity.
The rishi replied, “Great King!”
The seer immediately prostrated and spoke in verse:
"In this Āmra grove, the followers of King Brahmadatta Laid aside their shaving tools and went forth to attain the five supernormal powers."
When King Brahmadatta heard this verse, he replied with a verse of his own:
"Do not say that Devadaha is silent because he has gone forth;
his ascetic practices are difficult to perform, and by performing such austerities, he has attained great wisdom."
Austerity can destroy all evil dharmas; austerity can transcend the world;
austerity can purify all defilements—O Mother, I pray you do not speak ill of austerity.
“At that time, the seer Gaṅgāpāla felt great joy in his heart and departed immediately.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“That King Brahmadatta was none other than the present Śākyan king, Bhadraśrī.”
That seer Gaṅgāpāla was none other than this very Upāli.
The present Śākyan King Bhadraśiras was formerly King Brahmadatta.
In days past, when he paid homage to Gaṅgāpāla, the entire earth shook.
Now that the Worthy Leader, King Śākyamuni, has paid homage to the bhikṣu Upāli, the earth has shaken in six ways.
You bhikṣus, you should know this.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins:
Matters Concerning Schism in the Sangha), Fascicle Nine. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma for King Ajātaśatru, causing rootless faith to arise within him, the king once mounted an elephant and went out for a stroll. Upon seeing the World-Honored One atop a high pavilion, he suddenly and unconsciously leaped from his elephant and fell to the ground.

On another occasion, while riding out on an elephant, he saw the Blessed One and, unable to contain himself, threw himself down before him. Having conceived deep reverence and faith toward the World-Honored One, he then addressed his armed attendants, saying:
"You must know this!..."
"From this day forward, I take complete refuge in the Bhagavat and the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas.

From now on, whenever you see the World-Honored One and his assembly of disciples—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—approaching, do not obstruct their entry at the gateways, but open the doors and let them enter."
"If you see Devadatta and his followers, you must shield yourself and not let them pass.
Later, on another occasion, Devadatta had business that required him to enter the residence of Ajātaśatru.
Then the gatekeeper said to him, "Virtuous one, you should stop;
it is not appropriate for you to proceed further. Devadatta asked:
"For what reason has someone suddenly appeared to prevent you from proceeding?
The gatekeeper replied,
"The Great King has issued a command:"
"From this day forward, we take full refuge in the Bhagavat and the Śrāvaka Saṃgha.

From now on, whenever you see the World-Honored One and his assembly of disciples—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—approaching, do not obstruct their entry at the gates, but open them and allow them to enter."
"If you see Devadatta and his followers, you must shield them from view and not allow them to come forward.
When Devadatta was thus barred, he remained outside the gate in a state of displeasure.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, having finished her alms-round within the royal palace, was departing with her bowl.
When Devadatta saw Utpalavarṇā, this thought occurred to him:
"Could it not be that because of this shaven-headed woman’s sowing of discord between Ajātaśatru, the ladies of the inner court, and the houses of the ministers, I have been subjected to this delay?"
Having thought this, he said to Utpalavarṇā,
"What fault have I committed against you,
that because of you all the houses where I go for alms have become obstructed?"
He then stepped forward and struck the nun.
As she was being beaten, the nun uttered words of bitter suffering and pleaded with him, saying:
"May you see me as pure."
"For what reason have I done such a thing?
Venerable sir!
Since you are both brothers of the World-Honored One and have gone forth from the noble Śākya lineage."
"I truly have no intention to engage in such talk; I beg you to forgive me and accept this as an expression of my loyalty.
Although she heard these words, he disregarded her speech and, baring his great fist, struck the nun until her head was split open.

Since his vital points (*marmāṇi*) had been damaged and all manner of sufferings converged upon him, he then sustained his life-force and summoned a spirit of heroic exertion, hastening to the nunnery where that bhikṣuṇī resided.
At that time, seeing her great suffering, the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs all asked her, saying:
"Alas, Āryakā! For what reason have you suddenly encountered such distress and humiliation?"
He then addressed the assembly, saying:
"O sisters! All life is impermanent; all phenomena are devoid of self."
The state of tranquility is called Nirvana.
You all should diligently apply yourselves to the practice of wholesome dharmas and remain mindful; do not be negligent.
Devadatta has already committed the third deed of immediate retribution; the time for my own entry into Nirvana has now arrived.
At that time, he manifested various extraordinary miraculous transformations before the assembly of nuns and entered the sublime realm of nirvana without remainder.
Then, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; desiring to sever their uncertainty, they requested the World-Honored One, saying: "Bhadanta!..."

Have you not seen how Devadatta, when the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā spoke to him with words of compassion and apology, did not deign to heed her speech, but instead struck her on the head with his fist until it was shattered, whereby she passed away?
The World-Honored One said:

"It is not only today that such a thing has occurred; in a past life as well, when he was in a state of grief and suffering and offered his apologies, I did not listen to his piteous words, but instead took his life and ate his flesh."
Listen now! In times past, there was a great elder living in a certain village who kept a large flock of sheep grazing in the vast pastures.

As evening fell, the herder drove the flock back; among them was an old, weak ewe who could not keep pace with her companions and lagged behind alone. Suddenly, by the side of the road, she encountered a hungry jackal.
The ewe asked the jackal: "Uncle, you often travel alone; Do you find peace and happiness?
Dwelling constantly within the forests and wilds, How do you nourish your spirit?"
The jackal replied to him:
"You have constantly trampled upon my tail and always plucked out my fur;
yet from your mouth you utter the words 'Uncle,' seeking only a place to flee for your own life."
The sheep replied again,
"Your tail is bent behind you, while I am coming from the front;
why do you wrong me?"
"Usually, I tread upon my own tail.
The jackal replied again,
"The four continents, along with the oceans and mountains, are all my tail."
"If you do not tread upon it, from where have you come?
The sheep replied, "In the presence of my kinsmen and acquaintances, I heard it said that all are kind toward the tail."
"I dare not tread upon the ground; I have come through the air!
The jackal replied again:
"Because you, ewe, fell from the air, you caused the wild deer in the forest to be startled."
"To abandon the food I have consumed this morning—would that not be a clear and logical conclusion?

At that time, although the ewe offered her lamentations and recounted her words of suffering at length, the jackal of sinful karma refused to release her; he finally severed her head and devoured her flesh.
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thought; he who was the jackal in the past is none other than Devadatta today."
The ewe of former times was none other than the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā of today.
Although she uttered words of lamentation and suffering in the past, she could not escape death.
"Even though I utter various words of lamentation today, I shall still be harmed.
At that time, Devadatta again had this thought:
"I have repeatedly committed great offenses against the World-Honored One; I have already fully performed three of the deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma)."
He hurled a large stone from afar at the World-Honored One, causing blood to flow from the Tathāgata’s body with an evil mind;
this is the first ānantarya-karma. He caused a harmonious Saṃgha to be split; this is the second ānantarya-karma.
The nun Utpalavarṇā intentionally took his life; this is the third karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).

Yet, I have not yet attained omniscience, nor have I seen the completion of my remaining tasks. According to this course of action, there is no other place for me to be born; I am certain to go to the *naraka* hells.
Having had this thought, he rested his cheek in his hand and sat to one side, brooding in sorrow.
At that time, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, having some business to attend to, happened upon him and said to him: "Devadatta!
“What is the meaning of this? Why do you now lean on your hand against your cheek, standing to one side, dwelling in sorrowful reflection?
He replied: “How could I not be filled with sorrow?

Because of my anger and affliction, I repeatedly committed grave harms against the Blessed One and have fully created three deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*). For a long time I shall dwell in the great *naraka* hell, undergoing unceasing suffering.”
Pūraṇa said: "I have always considered you to be the only one among the Śākyas who is discerning and intelligent; how could I have thought that you too have now become foolish?"
"How could there be a future life that would cause you such anxiety?
If there were a future life, and you had committed such deeds, I too would dwell in sorrow and contemplation because of them.
To console Devadatta’s mind, he then smashed his own jar right before his face and said:
"Even within the world of gods, it would be impossible to bring these back into harmony; furthermore, if there were no future life, who would go to experience [the results]?
Both the agent and the experiencer would thus become mere empty words."
However, you may go to the city of Piṭṛvaṃśastūpa and dwell there, styling yourself as a Heavenly Son and acting as king; I shall become your foremost śrāvaka.
At that time, Devadatta slandered the noble ones, and his false views subsequently arose, which caused all his roots of virtue to be severed.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know that from this point on, all the roots of virtue belonging to Devadatta shall be severed."
"O bhikṣus! If I had seen even a slight degree of wholesome dharma (śukladharma) in Devadatta, I would not have given this prediction concerning Devadatta: 'O Devadatta!'"
"Those born in the evil realms, those born in the hells, shall remain there for an entire kalpa, incapable of being healed.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!
I did not see even a hair’s breadth of white dharma in Devadatta; only then did I grant this prediction concerning Devadatta:
"Devadatta! You who are born into the evil realms and born into the hells shall remain there for an eon, beyond the possibility of cure.

It is, for example, like being some distance from a village or a city, where along the way there is a pit of excrement and filth, over a fathom deep and so foul-smelling that it is difficult to approach.
At that time, there was a person who fell into this pit, his head, hands, feet, and all submerged within it.

Later, there was another person who, throughout the long night, acted for the sake of those who cherish righteousness, those who delight in benefit, those to whom he gives joy, those to whom he grants happiness, and those to whom he bestows peace and security. This person went to the edge of that cesspool and looked around on all sides, his heart intent on rescuing him:
"If I see even a single part of that person fallen into the cesspool that is not defiled by filth, I shall employ skillful means to draw him out."
Having searched everywhere, he did not see even the slightest part of that person’s body that was not defiled by excrement, such that he could even grasp it with his hand and pull him out. O Bhikṣus!
I am also like this: if I were to see even a small amount of white dharma in Devadatta, I would not have given Devadatta this prediction: "O Devadatta!..."
"Those born into evil realms and those born into the hells shall remain there for an entire kalpa, incapable of being cured.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!
I do not see even a hair’s tip of a single white dharma in Devadatta; only then did I grant this prediction concerning Devadatta:
"Devadatta! You who are born into the evil realms, you who are born into the hells, shall remain there for an eon, incapable of being cured.
You, monks, should know this:
Devadatta has already fulfilled three conditions; as one born into the evil realms and the hells, he shall remain there for an entire kalpa, beyond the possibility of salvation.
What are these three conditions?
"O bhikṣus! Devadatta first gave rise to sinful desires, and was subsequently dragged away by those evil cravings.
Once Devadatta had given rise to these evil desires and was pulled along by them, this is called the first unwholesome quality accomplished by that Devadatta."
Devadatta, having been born into the evil realms and having fallen into hell, shall remain there for an entire kalpa, incapable of being cured.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!
Devadatta associated with evil friends, obtained unwholesome companions, and consorted with wicked people.

Since Devadatta has drawn near to evil associates, obtained unwholesome companions, and associated with wicked people, this is called the second dharma of sinful accomplishment achieved by that Devadatta.
Devadatta, having been born into the evil realms and the hells, shall remain there for an entire kalpa, beyond the possibility of cure.
Furthermore, monks!

Devadatta attained only a small portion and a low grade; at the moment of his realization, he became complacent and satisfied, and even though there were higher stages, he did not pursue further cultivation.

Having obtained only a small portion and attained only the inferior grade, Devadatta became complacent at the moment of his realization; even though there were superior stages, he made no further effort toward cultivation. This was the third sinful practice accomplished by that Devadatta.
“Devadatta, having been born into the evil realms and having been born into hell, shall remain there for an eon, incapable of being cured.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“O people of the world, do not give rise to the desire for transgression;”
From this you should recognize the calamities summoned by evil desires.
The world knows well of Devadatta; though brilliant and intelligent, he could not subdue his own mind.
Unable to maintain even a modicum of fewness of desire, he merely possessed a handsome physical form.
He then acted with arrogance and insolence, seeking to surpass the World-Honored One;
therefore, I have predicted for this person that for one kalpa he shall be born without leisure.
Born of stinginess and greed, he gave rise to evil thoughts; holding false views, he was neither reverent nor respectful.
Born from meditative concentration within a space free of gaps, with the four gates firmly sealed and blocked—
if another is without fault, yet one slanders them with evil words to create a transgression,
then in this life or the next, the fool shall receive [the retribution] themselves.
If a person were to take a vessel of poison into the great ocean, intending to spoil its waters;
though the vast seas have no known limits, there would surely be no way to corrupt them with evil.
So it is with the World-Honored One: when a wicked person gives rise to slander and abuse, [it cannot affect him].
Constantly practicing for the benefit of oneself and others, how could blame or slander ever prevail?
With right view, the mind is always tranquil, and adverse conditions have no place to arise;
one should associate with such spiritual friends, for those who draw near them become wise.
"Because of this, one does not commit evil; one should respectfully rely upon and practice [the teaching].

At that time, Devadatta slandered and reviled the holy teachings, firmly giving rise to wrong views and definitively severing his roots of goodness, asserting: "There is only this life, and there is no future world."
Having realized this, he established five distinct rules for his followers and addressed them, saying: "You should know!
Since the śramaṇa Gautama and all his followers consume milk and curd, we shall from now on no longer eat them."
For what reason does this cause that calf to constantly suffer from hunger?
Furthermore, since the śramaṇa Gautama permits the eating of fish and meat, we should not eat them from this day forward.
"For what reason? Because by means of this, we have committed the act of taking the lives of sentient beings.
Furthermore, since the śramaṇa Gautama permits the consumption of salt, we should not eat it from this day forward."
"For what reason?
Because there is much dust and soil within that salt.
Furthermore, when the Śramaṇa Gautama uses his robes, he cuts away the loose threads; from this day forward, when we use our robes, we shall leave the long threads intact."
"For what reason? Because it destroys the labor of that weaver.
Furthermore, while the śramaṇa Gautama dwells in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka), from now on we shall dwell within village houses."
"For what reason? Because it involves the abandonment of the goods bestowed by a donor.
A summary verse states:
Not consuming milk, curd, fish, meat, or salt,
and remaining in villages for long periods— these are the five practices of Devadatta.
At that time, the Blessed One was traveling through the human realm and gradually proceeded to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, Devadatta conceived this thought:
"I have repeatedly attempted to inflict harm upon the śramaṇa Gautama, yet I have ultimately been unable to injure his life."
"I should now proceed to humiliate his wife.
He then went to the city of Kapilavastu and sent a messenger to inform Yaśodharā, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned his royal duties to become a renunciant; for this reason, I have come to succeed him as your husband. You ought to be my wife."
At that time, having gained faith, he went about reporting the matter to Gopikā. Then Gopikā replied to Yaśodharā, saying:
"Your ladyship should send a messenger to tell Devadatta:
'When the Bodhisattva grasped my hand in the past, his strength was sufficient to support it.'"
"If you have the ability, you may come and see me.
At that time, Devadatta was devoid of shame; disregarding the strength of his own body, he entered the inner palace, ascended the steps, and climbed the stairs, desiring to reach that place.
At that time, Gopikā looked at the palace ladies and laughed with a derisive snort; Devadatta, unaware of what was happening, remained there with his palms joined.

Gopikā possessed the strength of a mahānagna; she then seized Devadatta with her left hand, whereupon blood gushed from his ten fingers in a startling torrent. She then hurled him into the pool where the Bodhisattva had formerly played, and having fallen into the water, he let out a great cry.
At that time, the Śākyas vied with one another to come to his aid, and they deliberated at length, saying:
"Devadatta, relying on his own strength, has rashly entered the inner palace with the intent to commit acts of arrogance and insult."
Turning again to follow the sound, they saw him within the pond and said to one another:
"This man who has brought disorder within our ranks—his life should be taken.
They then deliberated further, saying:

"Do not inflict further harm upon one who is already dead. The World-Honored One has declared that this Devadatta, having been born into the evil realms and fallen into hell, shall remain there for an entire *kalpa* in the Avīci hell, beyond all possibility of cure."
"This is already like death; why trouble yourself further by harming me?
At that time, the crowd abandoned him and ceased speaking with him.

Then Devadatta rose from the pond and fled through a drainage opening, but his garment was torn by the wooden stakes; his single piece of white cotton cloth was split into two parts, whereupon he thought to himself:
"Excellent! These garments are skillfully suited to a pure deportment; fashion them as lower robes for my śrāvakas.
On another occasion, he addressed the Śākya clan:
"You all should appoint me as king. The people replied, "The Bodhisattva already possesses an inner palace;
you may assume power and bring him into submission, and once he has taken a wife, you may then be called king."

At that time, Devadatta laid aside his suspicions regarding the Śākyas and cast off his feelings of fear; he then entered the palace, ascended a high tower, and approached Yaśodharā. Joining his palms to one side, he addressed her, saying:
"I pray you will deign to show me favor and look upon me with compassion. You are the principal queen of the kingdom, and I am the king of this city."

At that time, Yaśodharā possessed the power of a great *bhaiṣajyarāja*; she rose from her exquisite jeweled couch and approached Devadatta, seizing him by his palms pressed together and pressing down on both his knees until they broke the ground. Blood gushed from the ten fingers of Devadatta as he writhed upon the earth, unable to endure the agony.
Then Yaśodharā said to him: "You are truly a scoundrel, the very height of folly;
you could not even endure holding her hand for a moment, much less seek to arouse desire for sexual union."

"A Universal Monarch should be my husband, or perhaps a Bodhisattva in his final birth; only by being joined with one such as he would it be fitting for me, while all others are entirely unsuitable matches."
At that time, Devadatta, filled with shame, departed from the palace. Seeing his distress and suffering, the Śākyas said to him:
"You should now first go to the World-Honored One and seek his forgiveness; only when you have been granted pardon may you again be called 'Son of Heaven'."
At that time, Devadatta filled his ten fingernails with extremely virulent poison and approached the World-Honored One, thinking to himself:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama shows me forgiveness, I shall say: 'Excellent!'"
"It will certainly not allow it;
I shall approach to pay my respects and use my poisonous claws to scratch his feet until they are wounded.
Having reached the Buddha's side, he prostrated at his two feet and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that you will take pity on me and grant me your forgiveness.
At that time, the World-Honored One observed what kind of intention Devadatta harbored as he approached him;
perceiving that Devadatta’s intent was to kill him, he then used his supernormal powers to transform the area beneath both knees into crystal stone and remained there in silence.

At that time, Devadatta, seeing that [the Buddha] remained silent and spoke not a word, gave rise to a heart of anger and conceived a malicious intent; he then used his poisoned claws to scratch and claw at the World-Honored One.
At once, all ten of his fingers were crushed and shattered, and he was instead struck by their own poison, giving rise to great agony.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to him:
"Devadatta! You should take refuge in the Blessed One."
He replied to Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable One! If I were now to take refuge in the Buddha, as the Buddha has said:..."
"If one takes refuge in the Buddha, one will not be reborn in the evil realms; having cast off this human body, one shall be born in the superior heavens.
Yet the World-Honored One has prophesied that I shall be reborn in the Avīci hell within the evil realms for one entire kalpa, beyond all hope of rescue or healing.
"If I am born in heaven, those words will prove false;
if I fall into the evil realms, they are likewise a lie.

While he was thus giving rise to extreme rage, his evil karma having reached its full measure and nothing remaining to be awaited, the fires of the Avīci Hell engulfed his entire body. He then cried out in a loud voice, declaring:
"Venerable Ānanda! I am currently being burned!
I am now being scorched!"
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, seeing his extreme suffering, felt profound compassion; moreover, out of even greater affection for his kinsman, he addressed him, saying: "Devadatta!
"You should now, with utmost sincerity, take refuge in the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; do not harbor other thoughts.

At that time, Devadatta’s body was scorched by the fire of the gapless hell (*avīci*), and as the retribution of his karma manifested before him, he experienced most severe suffering. With deep and earnest resolve, he cried out:
"Today, even to my very marrow, I take refuge with a sincere heart in the Bhagavat."
Having spoken these words, his body immediately fell into the Avīci Hell, which is without interval or gap.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this:"

Devadatta’s roots of goodness have been reconnected; he shall be born in the Avīci Great Hell for one great kalpa. Once his transgressions are exhausted, he will obtain a human body, and through successive cultivation, he will ultimately realize the state of a Pratyekabuddha named Asthisaṃcayā.

At that time, having attained realization, he went on his alms-round through the houses with his bowl; having obtained food, he returned to his dwelling, set the bowl aside, washed his hands and feet, and was just about to eat when he composed his mind and contemplated his past lives:
"By what cause have I long remained in the flow of birth, wandering in delusion through saṃsāra, only now to attain awakening in this body?"

He then beheld how he had committed various acts of malice and rebellion against the World-Honored One; furthermore, he saw that in the past, when the World-Honored One was practicing the bodhisattva path, they had been enemies and adversaries life after life, all because of a slight amount of respect and gain, which led them to this state.

Having realized this matter, he did not consume even a single morsel of the food he had received; instead, he ascended into the air, emitted great radiance, and manifested various supernatural transformations, before finally attaining parinirvāṇa within the realm of the wondrous nirvana without remainder.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana would go from time to time to the hells to observe their conditions.
Then Śāriputra said to Maudgalyāyana, "Venerable one,
shall we go together with me to the Avīci Hell to visit Devadatta and offer him our greetings?"
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to the Abhayasthāna cave;
having arrived at that place, Śāriputra addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Do you know, friend?"
This is precisely the Avīci hell, where the space above, below, and on all four sides is completely permeated by a single mass of fierce flames without any intervening gaps.

Among the assembly of those of great power and great virtue, the World-Honored One has declared you to be the foremost; you ought to direct your mind toward observing the beings suffering in the gapless hells and extinguish their calamity of fire.
Having spoken these words, Maūḍgalyāyana then entered the meditative absorption of the great waters.
Once his mind was thus concentrated, he caused rain to pour down from above, with drops as large as pestles falling into the Avīci hell; yet that water entirely dispersed and vanished into the sky.
Again, heavy rain poured down, with drops as large as plowshafts or chariot axles; yet even this rain was entirely dispersed.
When Śāriputra Ullāra witnessed this occurrence, he then composed his mind and entered the meditative absorption of resolute practice (*adhimukti-caryā-samādhi*).
Once he had entered meditative absorption, the water surged forth and filled the entire hell, causing the sounds of suffering to cease and restoring them to their original state of mind.
Then, the Āyuṣmat Maugalyāyana spoke and commanded:
"If you are Devadatta, you should step forward."
Upon hearing this command, many thousands of Devadattas vied with one another to come forward.
Then the Āyuṣmat Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed that multitude, saying:
"If you are Devadatta, the biological brother of the Blessed One, you should remain here."
Then Devadatta proceeded toward the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Having arrived at that place and prostrated at the feet of the two Honored Ones, the two Honored Ones asked:
"Devadatta! Is there any variation in the suffering of the great hell that you are currently undergoing?"
Devadatta replied:
"As for the shared sufferings within the Avīci hell, there is no need to speak of them.
However, please deign to listen to the particular sufferings that I myself am undergoing."

At that time, there will be iron mountains from which heat and fire arise everywhere; a great conflagration will become a single mass of flame and come to where I am, grinding my body to pieces, just as sesame seeds are ground upon a stone.
Furthermore, there are extremely sharp double-toothed iron saws, blazing with fierce heat, that cut through my body until every limb and bone falls away piece by piece.
Moreover, iron clubs, entirely ablaze with fire, come repeatedly to smash my head.
"Furthermore, there shall be great elephants coming from the four directions that will trample my body until it is crushed like rice flour.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana said to him together: "Devadatta!"
As you have said:

"At that time, there will be an iron mountain, extremely hot and intensely burning, from which great flames rise everywhere until it becomes a single mass of fire. It will come to where I am and grind my body to pieces, just like grinding sesame seeds upon a stone."

This is because you once hurled a large stone from Vulture Peak Mountain to strike and injure the Tathāgata; it is due to that evil karma that you have brought upon yourself this bitter fruit of suffering.
Furthermore, as for what you said:

"Moreover, there are iron clubs, all ablaze with flames, that come repeatedly to smash my head," this is because you once struck the head of the Arhatī Utpalavarṇā with your fist until she died; it is due to that evil karma that you have brought upon yourself this bitter fruit of suffering.
Furthermore, as for what you said:
"There were also great elephants coming from the four directions, trampling my body until it was crushed like rice flour"—
this was because you gave rise to a malicious intent and released the elephant Dhanapāla, wishing to trample the World-Honored One.
"It is because of those evil karmas that he has brought forth this bitter fruit.
The two Honored Ones then addressed him, saying: "Devadatta!"
Although you now undergo such extreme suffering,
the World-Honored One has prophesied for you:
"When you have finished undergoing these retributions, you will ultimately realize the state of a *pratyekabuddha*, named Asthisamcaya (The One Endowed with Bones)."
When Devadatta heard these words, he addressed the two Honored Ones, saying:
"If it be so, my heart is now filled with courage; I am able to lie upon one side within the vast Avīci Hell and willingly endure its suffering."
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.

Then the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana proceeded next to the place where those six non-Buddhist teachers were undergoing their suffering; there they saw Kokālika, upon whose tongue a hundred plows were furrowing the ground on all sides.
At that time, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the lord of the Sahā world-system, also followed the two Honored Ones and went along. Upon seeing Kokālika, he addressed him, saying:
"Kokālika, you should give rise to a heart of supreme reverence toward these two great venerable bhikṣus."
"However, these two masters are steadfast in pure conduct and are foremost among the assembly in wisdom and supernormal powers.
When Kokālika saw those two venerable ones, he said to them:
"These two people of sinful and depraved desires—how have they come here?"
As soon as these evil words were uttered, a thousand plows immediately began to furrow his tongue all over.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana thought to themselves:
"The karma of this sentient being is so heavy that he is difficult to save; there is nothing that can be done."
Having abandoned them, he departed.
Next, he went to where Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was staying.
Upon his arrival, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa then approached and prostrated at the feet of the two Honored Ones, addressing them as follows:
"I pray, O two Great Virtuous Ones!

Examine me, a sinner. Because in former times I preached false doctrines and deceived the people of my era by obstructing their right faith, due to this karmic offense, five hundred plows shall at all times till my tongue."

Furthermore, when my disciples who have heard my teachings present offerings at the stūpas containing my remaining revered bones, they will be oppressed by great suffering; I pray that you will inform me of the calamities I am undergoing.
Furthermore, he informed them:
"Do not offer further worship at that stūpa.
At that time, the two Honored Ones, having consented to his words and finished their tour of the hells, both returned together to Jambudvīpa.
Then the two Honored Ones, in the presence of the Bhagavān and the great assembly, fully recounted the sufferings endured by Devadatta, Kokālika, and Putraka within the hells.
Having thus spoken at length, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and, seeking to resolve their uncertainty, they questioned the World-Honored One, the Dispeller of Doubts, saying:
"O Bhadanta World-Honored One!"
For what reason did Devadatta refuse to accept what the World-Honored One told him, falling into the Avīci hell to undergo such great and extreme suffering as this?
The World-Honored One said:

"O bhikṣus! It is not only today that you have suffered such cruel punishment for refusing to follow my words; in a past life as well, you encountered suffering and distress because you did not accept my words."
You should listen!
In the past, when I was in the stage of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, I was born among the animal realm as a great bull.
Every night he would go to that royal bean field and eat as much as he desired; once the sun had risen, he would return to the city and sleep at his ease.
At that time, a donkey came to where the ox was and spoke these words:
"Uncle! Why is it that your skin, flesh, and blood are all so full and robust?"
"I have never seen you go out for even a moment to roam and enjoy yourself. The ox said to him, "Nephew!..."
"Every night I go out to eat the king's beans, and before the morning sun has risen,
I return to my former dwelling. The donkey then said,
"Shall I follow my uncle to eat as well?"
The ox then said to him: "Nephew!
Your mouth produces many sounds that reach far; do not, because of these cries, end up being caught by a tether."
The donkey replied, "Uncle!
If I follow you away, I shall certainly not make a sound."
Thereupon, they followed one another to the field, broke down the fence, and entered together to eat the king’s seedlings.
While the donkey was not yet full, it remained silent; once its belly was sated, it spoke, saying: "Uncle!..."
"I shall sing for now.
The bull replied, "Bear with the sound for a moment; wait until I have emerged, and afterwards you may sing as you please, nephew."
Having spoken these words, he hurriedly ran out of the garden; the donkey then began to bray behind him.
At that time, the field-watchers of the royal household immediately seized the animal, drove it away, and announced to the crowd:
"The royal bean fields have been devoured by this donkey; it must be subjected to severe humiliation before it may be abandoned."
Then the field-guard cut off both ears of the donkey and hung a wooden mortar around its neck; he then drove it out with painful blows from his staff.
As the donkey wandered about in distress after being so humiliated, the bull saw it at the spot and spoke this verse:
“Excellent song! A truly fine song! It is by virtue of such singing that you have obtained this fruit.”
Seeing that you were able to sing, they cut off both your ears.
If one cannot guard one’s mouth and does not heed the words of a virtuous friend, it is not merely the ears that are cut off;
a mortar shall be suspended from the side of one’s neck.
The donkey replied with a verse:
“The gap-toothed one should speak softly; An old bull should not talk much.
You merely wander about seeking food at night; Before long, you shall be bound by the tether.”
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus! Do not harbor other thoughts."
The exceptional ox of former times was none other than myself.
The donkey of those days was Devadatta.
Because he did not heed my words in the past, he has already encountered such suffering.
"Today, having failed to listen to my words, he now undergoes such great calamity.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus, you should know this:
just as Devadatta today, by refusing to heed my words, has brought upon himself this great suffering."
"You should listen further to a past event.
O bhikṣus! Long ago, in a certain village, there lived an elder who possessed a great bull endowed with all auspicious marks."

At that time, the elder invited śramaṇas, brahmins, the destitute, the orphaned, and impoverished merchants, providing them with universal offerings. Having performed the act of giving, he then released [the bull]; the great bull, endowed with auspicious marks, wandered wherever it pleased, no longer subject to any restraint.
At that time, having been granted release, the great ox wandered at will in search of water and grass.
While traveling through a marshy wetland, he fell into deep mud from which he had no means of emerging.
At that time, as the sun was about to set, the elder heard people speaking of it and went to search for him.
Upon reaching the place where the ox was, the elder thought to himself:
"The mud is deep and the ox is large; I am alone and cannot manage this. I shall wait until tomorrow morning to come and rescue him."
The ox then said, "You may bind me by my horns with a rope and place me in front; you may come at dawn as you please.
If any monkeys or raccoons come to harass me, I shall shake my horns with the rope to frighten them away."
The man then immediately tied a long rope to the horn, coiled it up, placed it on the ground, and departed.
When night fell, a wild monkey arrived; seeing the ox from afar, it spoke these words:
"Who has stolen the lotus roots from this place?"
The ox replied, "I am submerged in mud and have no means of getting out myself; it was not with a thieving heart that I stole another's lotus root.
Upon hearing these words, the monkey spoke to him:
"My exquisite meal has suddenly come of its own accord!
he exclaimed, and approached the ox with the intent to slaughter it. The ox addressed the monkey, saying:
"You should keep your distance from me; do not seek to harm me, lest you yourself fall into the bitter suffering of the net."
Although the monkey heard these words, he paid them no heed and proceeded toward the ox, intending to seize him.
At that time, Bṛhaspati—translated as "Ox King"—seeing that his words were being disregarded, spoke this verse:
"I have not stolen the lotus roots, Nor am I a thief of the lotuses; [The one who steals the lotus stalks] Is surely that other monkey."
"If you truly intend to eat me, you should first cut me open from the back.
The monkey said, "Now is precisely the right time; you should eat me starting from the back in sequence."

He threw it onto the back of the ox and opened his mouth to eat it; however, the ox’s horns shook the rope, which became entangled around the monkey’s neck, causing him to swing in the air with his body suspended.
At that time, the great ox spoke this verse:
“You are a handsome youth, A dancer performing in the sky!”
"I perform my arts in the village fields; in the wild fields there is no patron.
At that time, the wild monkey also replied to the ox in verse:
"I am not a dancer, nor am I a handsome youth;"
"Śakra has cast down the ladder; I shall now proceed to the Brahma Heaven.
Again, the Bull King spoke in verse:
"It is not truly Śakra, Lord of Devas, who has cast down the ladder to go to the Brahma Heaven;"
"The ropes are tightened and the collar is constricted; at this moment, my life comes to its end. "O bhikṣus!
Do not harbor any other thoughts."
The one who was the Bull King in former times was none other than myself.
The wild monkey of those days was Devadatta.
Just as he suffered for disregarding my words in the past, he now undergoes such great calamity for refusing to listen to my speech.
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and, seeking to resolve them,
asked the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One,

for what reason did Devadatta give rise to such great hatred toward the World-Honored One, refuse to follow his correct words, and undergo the great suffering of having his body scorched in the Avīci hell?"
The World-Honored One said:
"It is not only today that you have disregarded my words, resulting in your bodies being beset by fierce flames with no one to save you. You bhikṣus!..."
You should listen further.
In the past, there was a royal capital where a king named Caityaka ruled and spread his influence.
By the power of that king’s merit, his realm was prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, and abundant; it was filled with many people who lacked for nothing.
Furthermore, that king possessed great and supreme merit; whenever he wished to sit, hosts of devas would support the feet of his throne, holding it suspended in mid-air.
The king had a chief minister who knew the affairs of state, who fathered two sons:
the elder was named Udayana, and the younger was named Viśākha.
At that time, whenever the eldest son saw his father instructing the multitude according to both the Dharma and non-Dharma, he would think to himself:

"As the eldest son, it is my duty to inherit the office; when my father passes away, I shall occupy the position of a high minister. I too shall instruct beings through both the Dharma and non-Dharma, and by virtue of such evil karma, I shall be reborn in hell."
"How can this compare to my practicing the life of a renunciant now?

He then went to his father's place and entreated him for permission to leave the household life; his father granted him leave, and he went forth from the world to become a monk under the World-Honored One.

Later, at another time, his father, the great minister, passed away. At that time, the second son became the state minister; he governed the people through both righteous and unrighteous means, and the citizens, resentful of his cruelty, spoke of his irrationality.
At that time, there was a man who, while traveling through villages and towns, happened by chance to encounter his elder brother practicing the life of a renunciant.
When the bhikṣu saw the guest arrive, he asked him:
"From where have you come to reach this place?"
The man replied, "I reside in such-and-such a city.
He then questioned his younger brother, and the traveler answered in full detail:
"He practices what is not the Dharma and oppresses the common people with harshness; the masses all harbor resentment and live in a state of lawlessness.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu said to that person:

"You may go now and do not give way to grief. When I have the leisure, I shall go to that city to guide them with reason and lead them to practice the True Dharma, hoping that the common people may leave suffering behind and attain peace."
Having heard this, the man returned to his home and informed his kinsmen in detail of the circumstances; as the news spread from one to another, it reached his younger brother.
The brother immediately went to see the king and said, "My eldest brother wishes to come here."
The king then said: "Excellent!
If he arrives, he shall be the prime minister."
The man replied, "I have served Your Majesty for a long time; my labor and sincerity are well-established. What is the nature of this matter?
The King then informed him:
"In our national law, the crown prince succeeds his father; this matter cannot be altered. Knowing this, what plan do you intend to employ?
The king spoke again, saying:
"If it is truly your wish, when he comes, you should say: [the rest of the speech follows]."
"I am great. Having received the King's instruction, he returned home with inward joy.
Before long, the Bhikṣu returned to his native city; when the King and the multitude saw him, they all rose to welcome him, yet only his younger brother remained seated as before.
The bhikṣu said, "You are my younger brother; why do you sit here so idly? The man replied:
"You are small and I am large.
If you do not believe me, you should take someone as a witness.
Since I have been raised in the royal palace, the King knows our relative ages; it would be appropriate to consult him together to determine who is truly older and who is false."
Then the bhikṣu approached and addressed the king, saying,
"Between these two of mine, which one is the elder son?
The king then intentionally spoke a falsehood, saying:
"This person shall be great, while you shall be small.

No sooner had these words been spoken than, following the sound, the deity descended from his seat and cast him to the ground; immediately, a foul stench issued forth from within his mouth and filled the air.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Bhikṣu, the Prince, spoke many verses, saying:
"If a person utters false speech, The devas will abandon them;
A foul odor shall issue from their mouth, And they lose the path to the heavenly realms."
The King should speak words of truth, and [the tongue] shall be restored to its former state.
If he speaks falsely, he will certainly proceed upon the lower paths;
he shall incur the retribution of being tongueless, like a fish in the water.
If a person speaks contrary to the Dharma and utters unrighteous words,
the King should speak the truth and restore things to their former state as they were.
If he utters falsehoods, he will certainly travel upon the lower paths.
One shall become neither male nor female, certainly taking on the form of a eunuch.
If a person speaks words contrary to the Dharma and utters such unrighteous discourse,
the King should speak words of truth, restoring [the situation] back to its former state.
If one utters false speech, one will certainly travel upon the lower paths;
at the proper time the heavens do not rain, and at improper times there are torrential rains.
If a person speaks contrary to the Dharma, making unrighteous declarations;
The King should speak words of truth, and [the earth] shall be restored to its former state.
If he speaks falsehoods, he will certainly proceed upon the lower paths;
he shall receive the retribution of a snake’s body, with double-tongued speech born within his mouth.
If a person speaks contrary to the Dharma and utters unrighteous words,
the King should speak the truth and restore things to their former state as they were.
If he utters falsehoods, he will certainly travel upon the lower paths.
"Just as King Ceti, having committed extremely evil karma, was destined for the Avīci hell and the retribution of the niraya. "O bhikṣus! You all..."
Do not harbor any other thoughts: that eldest son of the minister was my own self in a former life.
That King Citra is none other than Devadatta at this very time!
Even now, he gives rise to extreme malice toward me and will not accept my words.
"Due to this evil retribution, he will be born in the Avīci hell.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who still harbored doubts, so he again requested the World-Honored One, the Dispeller of Doubts, saying: "Bhadanta!..."

For what reason did Devadatta, despite the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One speaking words for his benefit, fail to believe and accept them, and instead fall into the Avīci hell to undergo such extreme suffering?
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus! It is not only today that Devadatta, having disregarded my words, has suffered such torment in hell."
Furthermore, in a past life, he also did not accept [their] words and once underwent great hardship.
You should now listen. O Bhikṣus!
In times past, there lived in a certain village a master craftsman who was highly skilled in mechanical arts; he took a woman from a family of equal status and reputation as his wife.
Bound by deep affection, they lived in joy and contentment; before long, she conceived, and after eight or nine months, she gave birth to a son.

When twenty-one days had passed since his birth, a celebratory feast was held and he was given the name Qiáoróng (Skillful Beauty). He was raised according to the proper rites until he gradually reached maturity.

Before long, his father passed away; thereafter, the son went to another village to further study the arts of mechanics under a skilled master, and subsequently traveled to other towns in search of a wife.
There was an elder who lived with his daughter; he agreed to give her in marriage and informed her, saying:
"Come to me promptly on such-and-such a day. If you do not miss this appointment, we shall proceed with the wedding; if you fail to arrive, it shall not be my fault."
Xiaorong then went back to inform her master, saying:

"A girl from a certain village has agreed to marry me; the auspicious day is approaching and we have made an appointment for her to arrive promptly. If you can attend to this occasion, our word shall not be broken."
"If it should happen that we miss the auspicious time, it shall not be my fault.
The master artisan replied, "If that must be so, I shall accompany you to meet that urgent deadline; a favorable day and a propitious hour are difficult to encounter again."
Taking the wooden peacock, they ascended it together; without traversing the long distance, they hastened to the appointed day.

At that time, the people of the village and town gathered to watch; seeing what they had never witnessed before, they marveled at its marvelous ingenuity. Having presented their gifts and taken his bride, he returned home. Then, with the three of them, they ascended the peacock; as the mechanisms were activated, they suddenly soared into the great void, returning to their native city in less than a full day.
Once they had arrived, the master artisan said to the boy’s mother:
"You may hide this mechanical elephant; if your son asks for it, you must certainly not give it to him."
"Since he has already departed and has not yet learned how to return, do not let his son encounter suffering and calamity.
Later, the son repeatedly asked his mother for the peacock, saying:
"I wish to mount the wooden elephant and go out for a brief excursion, so that many people may be brought to submit to me."
The mother then replied:

"When your teacher departed, he left a specific instruction: 'If your son asks for the elephant, you must not give it to him; rather, let him learn how to ride it away and return without having mastered the art of coming back. Do not allow him to bring upon himself suffering and calamity because of this.'"
The son replied to his mother,
"I already know all the methods for going and returning.
It is because the teacher has a stingy mind that he does not allow me to see them or give them to me."
The woman’s heart was soft, and having been repeatedly entreated by him, she finally handed the mechanical device over to her son.
Once the son had obtained the elephant, he activated the mechanism; it soared straight up toward the clouds, and the multitude marveled at its excellence.
When his teacher saw this, he sighed and said, "This boy will go away once and never return.

He further turned the mechanism so that it went forth without returning; upon reaching the great ocean, where there was much rain and little sunshine, all the mechanical ropes became completely rotted and snapped. Caught within the hail of the sea, he then met his end.
The devas, seeing this, spoke a verse:
"Those who possess compassion speak words of benefit, Yet you do not follow their instruction, but act according to your own whims;
Like a wooden elephant that attempts to ride without a teacher, In the end, at the great ocean, you shall see your body sink."
The World-Honored One told them:
"O bhikṣus! Do not harbor such thoughts."
The mechanical engineer of former times was none other than myself;
his disciple was Devadatta. Because he rejected beneficial words in the past, he has already suffered the calamity of sinking into the depths.
"Now, having abandoned beneficial words, you are currently undergoing the cruelty of having your body burned.

At that time, the Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"As for what the Venerable One said:
'The Saṃgha is split,' and further said:"
"The Saṃgha is in harmony.
I do not yet know to what extent it is called "schism," nor do I know to what degree it is called "reconciliation."
The World-Honored One said:

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, and while there is an actual separate residence, he maintains the intention of a separate residence and performs the formal ritual (karmavācanā), this is called 'breaking the Saṃgha by means of a ritual.'"
If one perceives the Dharma as the Dharma, and perceives the harmonious assembly as a harmonious assembly, and performs the formal ritual (karmavācanā), this is defined as the harmony of the Saṃgha.
What is meant by "causing a schism in the Saṃgha"?
If there is but a single bhikṣu, he likewise cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Whether there be two, three, or even up to eight, they likewise cannot cause a division within the harmonious assembly.
If it reaches nine or exceeds that number, there are two *saṃghas*, which is then called "splitting the assembly"; they perform the *karmavācanā* and also cast the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
What is meant by *karmavācanā*?
It was just as when Devadatta instructed and exhorted the bhikṣus, establishing a training rule for them:
"O bhikṣus! You must know that there are five kinds of prohibitive rules."
What are these five? Venerable ones!

If there is a bhikṣu who does not dwell in an araṇya, thinking, "This is purity; this is liberation; this is the right departure that transcends suffering and pleasure, by which one can attain the supreme state"—[this is the first].
"Thus, O Venerable One, sitting under a tree, constantly practicing alms-gathering, possessing only three robes, and wearing rag-robes—this is called a bhikṣu.
This is purity; this is liberation; this is the right departure that transcends suffering and pleasure, and is able to attain the supreme state."
"Venerable sirs!

If this assembly of bhikṣus endures these five superior rules of conduct as being purity, liberation, and renunciation, then you should distance yourselves from that śramaṇa Gautama; you should separate yourselves from him and dwell apart from him, and not associate with him. This is the motion."
The formal ritual (karmavācanā) should be performed according to the preceding announcement.
How are the voting sticks (śalākā) to be distributed?
It is as when Devadatta issued a proclamation and instruction to the bhikṣus, establishing various rules of training (śikṣāpada):
"Venerable One!

There are five superior qualities that constitute purity, that constitute liberation, that are the right departure which transcends suffering and pleasure, and by which one attains the supreme state."
What are the five? Venerable one!

If there is a bhikṣu who does not dwell in an araṇya, thinking, "This is purity; this is liberation; this is the right departure that transcends suffering and pleasure, whereby one can attain the superior state"—[this is the first].
Thus, sitting under a tree, constantly practicing alms-gathering, possessing only three robes, and wearing rag-robes— O Venerable One!
When a bhikṣu practices in this way, it is purity, it is liberation, it is the right departure that transcends suffering and pleasure, and it enables one to attain the supreme state.

If the venerable bhikṣus accept these five superior rules of conduct as being pure, liberating, and leading to deliverance, they should distance themselves from that śramaṇa Gautama, separate themselves from him and live apart from him, not associate with him, and they should take up the voting tally.
"That Devadatta, together with himself as the fifth, received the voting tally—this is called 'receiving the tally.
The internal verse says:
"It is not by one that the Saṃgha is split; it requires nine to be able to cause a schism."
They also performed formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*) and cast voting sticks while proclaiming what was contrary to the Dharma.

Furthermore, for example, suppose there is a person who has been suspended (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*), and this person is capable of performing the act of schism in the Saṃgha; as well as those who follow such a suspended person, even down to those who follow those followers, performing the act of schism in the Saṃgha.
Is it not the case that the one who performed the suspension, those who followed the suspension, and those who followed the followers do not perform the act of schism in the Saṃgha?
Is it the case that one who is subject to suspension performs the act of schism in the Saṃgha, as does one who follows such a person, and even those who follow these followers;
or is it rather that neither the one suspended, nor those following the suspended, nor those following their followers perform the act of schism?
Furthermore, is it the case that one who has been subject to suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and those who follow such a person perform the act of schism;

or is it not those who follow the followers, nor those capable of suspending, nor even those who follow those capable of suspending, nor even those who follow the followers of those, who perform the act of schism?
Is it the case that one who has been suspended, as well as those who follow and further follow such a person, performs the act of schism;

whereas one who is not subject to suspension, one who is not capable of suspending others, and those who do not follow those capable of suspending—up to and including those who do not even follow such followers—does not perform the act of schism?
"Is it by means of one who is subject to suspension (*ukkhepanīya*), or those who follow such a person, that the schism of the Saṃgha occurs?

Or is it by means of one who does not follow such a person, one who is not subject to suspension, one who does not follow a suspended person, and one who does not follow such a person, that the schism of the Saṃgha occurs?"
"Is it the case that one who is capable of being suspended, as well as those who follow and further follow such a person, constitutes the act of schism;
whereas one who is not capable of being suspended or has already been suspended, nor one who follows the one who is suspended or further follows them, does not constitute the act of schism?"
"Is it by acting in accordance with one who has been suspended (*ukkhitto*), and in accordance with those who act in accordance with him, that the schism of the Saṃgha occurs;
and not by the other four [types of persons]?"
"Is it that those who follow one who has been suspended, and those who follow those followers, constitute the act of schism;
and not the other four?
Or is it that the person who has been suspended and the person who suspended him constitute the act of schism?"
"Is it not the other four?
Furthermore, is it that one who has been subject to the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) performs the act of schism in the Saṅgha, and not the other five?
Is it that one who follows such a person subject to suspension performs the act of schism in the Saṅgha, and not the other five?"
"Is it this person who follows and conforms [to the schism] who performs the act of schism in the Saṃgha, and not the other five?
Is it this person who is capable of being set aside who performs the act of schism in the Saṃgha, and not the other five?"
"Is it that one who follows this person capable of setting aside [the matter] constitutes the schism of the Saṃgha, and not the other five?
Or is it that one who follows this compliant person constitutes the schism of the Saṃgha, and not the other five?"
The Blessed One said: "Upāli!
All these people are capable of breaking a harmonious Saṃgha, with the sole exception of that person who has been subject to the act of suspension; this one alone cannot break the Saṃgha."
Therefore, the internal verse says:
Three, two, or one can cause a schism; The others are not to be known by analogy.
Regarding the breaking of an assembly, there are three and six distinctions, Excluding only those who have been subject to the act of suspension (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*).
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta,
as the Blessed One has said:"

"Venerable Sir! If there is a person who has caused a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, that person will certainly give rise to the offense of an immediate retribution (ānantarya) and will also accomplish the karma of an immediate retribution."
"Venerable Bhikṣu, to what extent is one said to have 'broken the harmony of the Saṃgha,' thereby giving rise to an ānantarya offense and accomplishing an ānantarya karma?
As for an "ānantarya offense," it refers to that which, once one has fallen into the hells (naraka), involves no interval whatsoever during the time one undergoes the retribution.
Regarding "immediate karma" (*ānantarya-karman*): it refers to falling directly from the human realm into the hells without any interval.
Although the characters for "immediate" (*anantara*) are the same, their meanings are distinct; it signifies that there is no gap between suffering.
In Sanskrit, it is called "Avīci.
Regarding "uninterrupted falling," the Sanskrit is "Ānantarya"; if translated literally, it should be rendered as "without interval" (or "gapless").
There is no gap and no interval, such that it cannot differ from the former; moreover, both subsequent [cases] are titled with the word "uninterrupted" (*anantara*), rather than saying "without gap.

This matter concerns the demarcation of boundaries and the uninterrupted [succession] until one is born and falls into hell without gap, or else another body must first undergo [the retribution]; because there is this distinction, eighteen differences arise.
The World-Honored One said: "Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives an unlawful matter as unlawful, and while in the process of actually causing a schism he likewise perceives it as unlawful, yet instructs and exhorts the other bhikṣus to train [in that view], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Upāli! To this extent it is called "breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha"; this gives rise to a crime of immediate retribution and constitutes an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!

If a bhikṣu perceives an unlawful matter as unlawful, yet at the time of the actual schism perceives it as lawful, and instructs other bhikṣus to train accordingly, he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.

"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; it gives rise to the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), yet it does not constitute the full karmic act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives an unlawful matter as unlawful, yet at the time of the formal schism gives rise to doubt, and instructs other bhikṣus to train accordingly, he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the crime of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an uninterrupted karma (ānantarya-karma).
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives an unlawful matter as lawful, and at the time of the actual schism perceives it as unlawful, yet instructs and exhorts other bhikṣus to train accordingly, saying, "This is a schism of the Saṃgha."
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to an immediate transgression and constitutes an immediate karma.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives an illegal matter as legal, and at the time of the actual schism likewise perceives it as legal, and instructs the other bhikṣus to train accordingly, he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.

"Upāli! To this extent it is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the immediate transgression (*ānantarya-āpatti*), yet it does not constitute an immediate karma (*ānantarya-karma*).
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives an unlawful matter as lawful, and while the formal schism is actually taking place, he gives rise to doubt yet still instructs and exhorts the other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Upāli! To this extent it is called "breaking a harmonious Saṃgha"; this gives rise to the offense of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!

If a bhikṣu perceives what is Dharma as non-Dharma, and at the time of the actual schism likewise perceives it as non-Dharma, yet instructs and exhorts the other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to an immediate transgression and constitutes an immediate karma.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives what is Dharma as non-Dharma, yet at the time of the actual schism perceives it as Dharma, and instructs other bhikṣus to train accordingly, he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! To this extent it is called 'breaking a harmonious Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the crime of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives what is Dharma as non-Dharma, and while in the midst of causing a schism, he gives rise to doubt, yet instructs and exhorts the other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the crime of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives the Dharma as the Dharma, yet at the time of the formal schism perceives it as non-Dharma, and instructs and exhorts the other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! To this extent it is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to an ānantarya offense, yet it does not constitute an ānantarya karmic act.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives the Dharma as the Dharma, and at the time of the actual schism likewise perceives it as the Dharma, and instructs other bhikṣus to train therein, he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.

"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha. This gives rise only to the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya-āpatti), but it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma).
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu perceives the Dharma as the Dharma, yet at the very moment of the formal schism gives rise to doubt, and proceeds to instruct and exhort other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he certainly causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the crime of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an uninterrupted karma (ānantarya-karma).
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu harbors doubt regarding what is not the Dharma, and at the time of the actual schism perceives it as being not the Dharma, yet instructs and exhorts other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to a crime of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu conceives doubt regarding what is not the Dharma, yet at the time of the actual schism forms the perception that it is the Dharma, and instructs other bhikṣus to train accordingly, he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to an immediate transgression, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu harbors doubt regarding what is not the Dharma, and also gives rise to doubt at the very moment of the schism, yet instructs and exhorts the other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the crime of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu conceives doubt regarding the Dharma, and at the time of the formal schism forms the perception that it is not the Dharma, yet instructs and exhorts the other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the offense of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu conceives doubt regarding the Dharma, yet at the very moment of the schism gives rise to the perception that it is the Dharma, and instructs other bhikṣus to train accordingly, he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Upāli! This is what is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the crime of immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution.
Furthermore, Upāli!"

If a bhikṣu conceives doubt regarding the Dharma, and also conceives doubt at the very time of the schism, yet instructs and exhorts other bhikṣus to train [accordingly], he will certainly cause a schism in the Saṃgha.

"Upāli! To this extent it is called 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'; this gives rise to the offense of an immediate retribution, yet it does not constitute an act of immediate retribution. Upāli!"

In this context, there are eighteen statements in total; among them, six involve making false assertions while harboring the thought that one’s actions are contrary to the Dharma at the time of a formal refutation.

Although there exist both the prose and the summary verses (*uddāna*), I still feared that beginners might not yet grasp their distinctions; therefore, I have again provided headings based on the verses so that the prose may be easily understood. This is intended to prevent novices from encountering obstructions and to ensure that the eighteen sections are clearly demarcated, so that they will not harbor doubts when the text is recited later.

Furthermore, fearing that scribes might introduce errors or that the translated text might become corrupted, I have printed it in nine lines per column, hoping thus to avoid the error of "three pigs" (the famous mistake of confusing *shǐ* for *shì*).

To examine in detail the history of the Vinaya teachings as they flowed eastward over many successive generations, the masters of the four schools of translation all exerted themselves with earnest devotion; some traveled personally to the Dragon River (Nālandā), while others transmitted the texts from the Turtle River (the Luo). Yet, regarding the specific enumerations for the schism of the Sangha, these have largely remained unclarified, causing later generations to harbor doubts.

Those who study the text at the end of the year find themselves doubting the phrasing within its structural divisions; those who pursue the meaning become confused regarding the meaning across its boundaries; and the masters who compose commentaries and provide exegeses all harbor doubts concerning the original pronouncements.

Thus, we know that you have cast aside your body and risked your life to shake your mendicant’s staff at the Crane Grove (Haelin), and sacrificed yourself to save others by lifting your robes on Vulture Peak (Jiuling). You were able to discuss in detail those points of doubt and hesitation, resolving what is right and wrong; we hope this will supplement what was omitted and forever eliminate our perplexity.

these constitute the four permutations. "Venerable Sir!"

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of Ājñātakauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devaputras, bestowed the flavor of the Dharma upon them, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and questioned the World-Honored One:
"What karma did Kauṇḍinya and those devaputras previously perform to cause them to be so fully endowed with the flavor of the Dharma?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
In the past, while I was in the state of indeterminate existence, I took birth as a tortoise in the great ocean and became the king among all the tortoises."
Later, at another time, there were five hundred merchants who boarded a ship and entered the sea, reaching a place of treasures to gather various kinds of jewels.

Having acquired the jewels, they were returning to their own country when, midway along the route, they encountered a makara fish that unreasonably damaged the ship; all the merchants then wailed in grief, crying out together with one voice.
At that time, the king of turtles, hearing this cry, emerged from the water and went to where the merchants were, saying to them:
"Do not be afraid; you should mount upon my back."
"I shall now carry you so that you may emerge from the sea and your lives may be preserved.

Thereupon, the merchants all boarded the tortoise and set out for the shore. As the multitude was vast, the burden they carried was exceedingly heavy; yet, abiding in diligence with minds that did not retreat, they endured great exhaustion and suffering until they had finally crossed over. Once they reached the shore, the tortoise stretched out its head and lay down.

Not far from where the tortoise was, there were several anthills. One ant, wandering about in succession, caught the scent of the tortoise and approached its location; there he saw the tortoise lying with its neck extended, its body vast in size and utterly motionless.
The ants immediately hurried back to their original city and called out to the ant host; numbering eighty thousand, they all went there at once.
At that time, the tortoise was so deeply asleep as if dead that he had no awareness at all; the ants were eating his skin, and though he was exhausted, he did not wake.
As he gradually consumed the choice meat, he finally became aware of it; seeing that ants were devouring his entire body, he thought to himself:
"If I were to move or turn my body, I would surely harm these ants. I would rather sacrifice my own life than ever cause injury to another."
Having formed this thought, as his limbs were about to fall apart and a hole had pierced his vital parts, he made this vow:
"Just as I have now used the flesh and blood of my body to provide for these ants and satisfy them, when I realize Bodhi in a future life, may I satisfy all these ants with the flavor of the Dharma."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor any other thoughts. The turtle king of the past was none other than myself.
Those ants whom he led were none other than Kauṇḍinya."
Those eighty thousand ants who were led by Kauṇḍinya to eat my flesh and blood so that they might be satisfied are none other than these eighty thousand devas.
Just as I satisfied them with my flesh and blood in a past life, I have now attained Buddhahood and satisfy them with the flavor of the Dharma.
Bhikṣus, you should know:
as has been commonly taught, you should abandon both black and mixed karma;
you should cultivate white-white karma.
