At that time, the World-Honored One first taught the flavor of the Dharma to the five bhikṣus, satisfying them all and causing them to transcend the ocean of birth and death, as they were about to proceed toward the ultimate nirvana of the supreme cause.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and questioned the World-Honored One:
"What karma did these five bhikṣus perform in the past, such that they have come to possess the fullness of the flavor of the Dharma?"
"The Great Master, out of compassion, forcibly pulled us from the ocean of birth and death and, through skillful means, established us in ultimate nirvana.
We only pray that you will explain this for us. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This is not rare! I am now free from greed, hatred, and delusion; I am fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Having attained mastery over all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*), and the knowledge of all knowledges (*sarvajñajñāna*), I have caused these five bhikṣus—who were endowed with the flavor of the Dharma—to forcibly emerge from the ocean of birth and death and established them in ultimate nirvāṇa."

In the past, when I had not yet abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion, nor transcended birth, old age, sickness, and death, and had not yet attained liberation, I nevertheless provided these people with my own blood to satisfy them and established them in the five precepts; this is truly rare.
Listen attentively!

In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Vajrabāhu who ruled the world according to the True Dharma; his realm was peaceful and happy, the population was flourishing, and the five grains were abundant.

That king was pure in faith and naturally virtuous; he delighted in benefiting himself and others, possessed a heart of compassion, and was endowed with great majesty and virtue. He took pleasure in practicing the True Dharma, felt pity for all sentient beings, and was able to relinquish and bestow whatever wealth and possessions he had, abiding securely within that great renunciation.

That king practiced compassion to the utmost; day and night, during the six periods, he entered the meditative absorption of loving-kindness and compassion. Because he was absorbed in this concentration, none of those who came seeking anything were able to receive a gift.
The King, knowing of this matter, addressed his ministers, saying:

"Establish almshouses at each of the four gates of the city to store wealth and goods; should there be any śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, or those who have come from afar seeking alms, give to them all."

Upon hearing the command, the ministers immediately carried out the King’s decree. At each of the four gates of the city of Vārāṇasī, they established halls for almsgiving. They accumulated and stored therein wealth and provisions—including various foods and drinks, clothing, bedding, gold, silver, *maṇi* gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, agate, beryl, *kaṣa* shells, red pearls, and right-spiraling conch shells—to provide sufficient gifts for the poor.
Furthermore, at another time, the yakṣa Bahuśruta was driven out from the royal city of Alokavatī, where he began to suck the vital essence of humans.
Wandering from place to place with four other yakṣas, he arrived outside the city of Vārāṇasī, where he saw cowherds, shepherds, wood-gatherers, and various merchants in their shops.
Having seen this, he immediately asked the people:
"Are you not afraid of me? The people replied:
"Why do you fear me? The yakṣa replied again, "Why do you not fear?"
The people replied, "Our king is by nature greatly compassionate;
with the altruistic intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, he enters the meditative absorption of loving-kindness and compassion six times throughout the day and night."
At that time, the yakṣa immediately transformed his body into that of a brāhmaṇa and wandered through the four halls of almsgiving.
Having perceived this, King Golden Arm emerged from his meditative concentration, adjusted his robes, and assumed all the proper dignified deportment.
Then the five yakṣas went to the king's presence and, raising their hands in praise,
said: "May the Great King’s merit and longevity be long and far-reaching!"
He addressed him, saying: "Great King!
I am now hungry and thirsty; I only pray that you will compassionately bestow upon me food and drink."
The king commanded his attendants, "Prepare various kinds of the most excellent food and drink.
At that time, the five yakṣas addressed the king, saying, "We thirst for blood to drink and hunger for nothing but flesh; we do not eat other foods."
The King said to his attendants:
"Do not harm living beings; you should seek out the flesh and blood of those who have died naturally and give it to him to eat.
Then the five yakṣas again addressed the King, saying:
"I shall now eat only warm flesh and blood, and not that which comes from animals that have died of themselves.
Having heard this, the king further thought:
"It is not right to harm living beings to provide them for his food; I shall instead give my own body's warm blood and warm flesh for him to eat."
Having formed this thought, he immediately summoned a physician.
Once the physician had arrived, the king spoke to him at once:
"Puncture five places on my body and draw blood, so that each of the five yakṣas may drink it."
The physician then replied to the king:
"These five yakṣas are of the most inferior sort; I cannot bear to pierce Your Majesty and draw blood.

Since the king was thoroughly proficient and well-versed in medical arts, he proceeded to pierce the five locations himself with a needle, causing the blood to flow so that they would be satiated. He further preached the Dharma to them to bring them complete satisfaction and conferred upon them the five precepts.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!
That King Suvarnabāhu was none other than myself; those five yakṣas were these five bhikṣus."
In the past, I gave him my flesh and blood and taught him the Dharma by bestowing upon him the five precepts.
Now, I shall teach him the True Dharma so that he may abide in the vision of the Truth and attain ultimate Nirvana.
"O bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way.

At that time, the World-Honored One first preached the flavor of the Dharma for the five bhikṣus, satisfying them all, causing them to transcend the ocean of birth and death, and establishing them in the vision of the Truth and ultimate nirvāṇa.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having conceived doubts, spoke to the Blessed One in order to sever them:
"World-Honored One!
What are the causes and conditions for these five bhikṣus?"
“The World-Honored One has satisfied them with the flavor of the True Dharma, pulled them out from the ocean of birth and death, and established them in ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“This is not rare; for I am now free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and have completely liberated myself from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.”

Having attained mastery over all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*), and the knowledge of all-knowing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), he causes the five bhikṣus to be fully satiated with the flavor of the Dharma; he rescues them from the ocean of birth and death and establishes them in ultimate nirvana.

In the past, when I had not yet abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion, and had not yet attained liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, I still used my own body’s blood to satisfy these beings and bestowed upon them the five precepts; this was truly rare.
Listen attentively!

In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a great king named Maitrībala. He ruled the world according to the Dharma; the population was flourishing, the five grains ripened in abundance, and the realm was peaceful, secure, and prosperous.
That king was by nature endowed with great compassion and possessed of great majesty; he constantly felt pity for all sentient beings.
Later, at another time, the yakṣa Bahuśruta was driven out from the city of Alokavatī, where he would suck the vital essence of human beings.

At that time, five yakṣas were wandering from place to place until they reached the city of Vārāṇasī. Not seeing people there making offerings of food for sacrifices, they became enraged; consequently, many epidemics broke out within the kingdom, and those who died were exceedingly numerous.
At that time, the ministers informed the king of the matter, saying:
"Your Majesty, the number of deaths within the kingdom is now exceedingly great.
Thereupon, the king issued an edict to his ministers:
"You should proclaim throughout the city, making this announcement:
'The King commands you: for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I have sought diligently with single-minded devotion, day and night, without ceasing.'"
"You all should give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; by constantly cultivating this mind, all calamities will be stilled.

When the people had received the king's command, they gave rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and because the sentient beings had given rise to such a mind of loving-kindness, those five yakṣas were unable to cause harm within their country.
At that time, the five yakṣas roamed everywhere outside the city; they were unable to enter and could not cause harm.
Seeing cowherds, shepherds, wood-gatherers, and various shopkeepers and merchants outside the city, they asked them:
"Are you not afraid of us?"
That person replied, "Why should I fear you? The yakṣa answered:
"Why are you not afraid?
The people replied, "King Maitrībala constantly contemplates this, and we, too, contemplate it."
The yakṣa asked, "What was King Maitrībala contemplating? The people replied:
"Always cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and contemplate that we, too, are likewise.
When those yakṣas heard these words, they thought to themselves:
"Because these people are now practicing loving-kindness and compassion, we shall be unable to cause harm within this city."

Those yakṣas roamed outside the four gates of the city seeking an audience with King Maitrībala. Later, on another occasion, when King Maitrībala went outside the city, the yakṣas saw him and immediately transformed their bodies into the likeness of brahmins; raising their hands, they praised the king, saying, "May your merit and longevity endure for a long time."
He said: "Great King!
I am now hungry and thirsty; I only pray that you will compassionately grant me food and drink."
The king told his attendants:
"One should provide various kinds of the most excellent food and drink.
Then the five yakṣas addressed the king, saying:
"I am thirsty for blood and hungry only for flesh; I will eat no other food.
The king told his attendants:
"Do not harm living beings; you should seek out the flesh and blood of those who have died naturally and give them to him to eat."
Then the five yakṣas spoke again to the king, saying:
"What we now eat is only warm flesh and blood; we do not eat any flesh or blood that has died of its own accord.
Having heard this, the king then thought to himself:
"I must not harm living beings to provide food for them; rather, I shall offer my own warm flesh and warm blood for them to eat.
Having formed this thought, he immediately summoned a physician. When the physician arrived, the King spoke to him:
"Pierce five places on my body to draw out blood, so that each of the five yakṣas may drink from it."
The physician replied to the king, "These five yakṣas are of the most inferior class; I cannot bear to pierce the King and draw his blood.

At that time, the king was skillful and fully proficient in all expedient means; he immediately pierced those five places with needles, causing the blood to flow so that they were satiated. He then preached the Dharma to them to bring them full satisfaction and conferred upon them the five precepts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor any other thoughts; that King Maitrībala was none other than myself.
As for the five yakṣas, they were none other than the five bhikṣus, Kauṇḍinya and the others."
In the past, I gave him my flesh and blood, and for his sake I preached the Dharma and bestowed upon him the five precepts.
Today, I shall preach the True Dharma for him, enabling him to abide in the vision of the Truth and attain ultimate Nirvana.
“You bhikṣus! You should train yourselves thus.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having first practiced austerities for six years and subsequently attained unsurpassed enlightenment, went to the city of Vārāṇasī. There he delivered the group of five bhikṣus headed by Kauṇḍinya; next, he delivered the five men headed by Yaśas; and next, he delivered the sixty people of the group of the Noble Ones (Bhadrayaśas). Thus, O bhikṣus, his assembly gradually increased.
At that time, the bhikṣus conceived a doubt in their minds and again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhadanta! What karma did the World-Honored One perform in the past?"
"Now I am experiencing the maturation of six years of ascetic practice.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I myself performed the actions, and I myself receive the retribution."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there was a village named Analysis (Vibhaṅga). In that village, the population was flourishing, it was peaceful and prosperous, and the five grains ripened in abundance."
In that village there was a brahmin named Nyagrodha, who possessed many followers and was wealthy and powerful.
He served as the local chief under King Kṛkī, who bestowed this village upon Nyagrodha as a gift.

That brahmin had a disciple named Jyotiṣka (Most Victorious), whose parents were pure and whose lineage was noble and excellent; even his ancestors back through seven generations were all preeminent. He studied various heterodox treatises and mastered the four Vedas; there were no scripts or writings he did not thoroughly comprehend. His countenance was upright and handsome, such that all who beheld him found him pleasing.
At that time, Nyagrodha had five hundred disciples whom he constantly taught to recite and chant.

In that village there was also a potter named Nandipāla, who had taken refuge in the Triple Gem, possessed deep faith in the Four Noble Truths, and was free from all doubt. Having realized the principle of the Four Noble Truths and attained the fruit of Stream-entry (srotāpanna), he abandoned all tools used for crafting living things and instead fashioned various earthenware vessels using soil from a molehill, water free of insects, and wood free of insects.
He placed these vessels outside his door and announced to all people:
"Give me rice and beans; take as much as you wish from these vessels.
With the rice and beans he obtained, he supported his blind parents and occasionally offered them to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
At that time, Sujāta and Nandīpāla had been close friends since their youth.
Later, on another occasion, Nandīpāla went to the place where Kāśyapa Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.

The Buddha taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened him with various subtle and wondrous dharmas for the sake of Nandipāla; then, having heard the Dharma, Nandipāla rejoiced, prostrated himself, and departed.

At that time, the most excellent vehicle, a white horse chariot, surrounded by five hundred disciples in front and behind, emerged from the city; on the way, it encountered Nandipāla, who, upon seeing him, asked:
"O noble one!..."
"From where have you come?
Priyapālita replied, "I have come from the presence of Kāśyapa Buddha, having made offerings and paid homage to him; now we may go together to the Buddha's presence to pay homage and make offerings."
The Most Victorious One replied:
"O Worthy One! Why is it necessary to see the Buddha in order to practice making offerings?"
"Why is this? To achieve such renunciation and perfect enlightenment is difficult to attain.
Thus did Priyapālita reply.
"O Worthy One! Do not speak such words.
This Kāśyapa Buddha attained perfect enlightenment not long after leaving the household life; he possesses all-knowledge, and the True Dharma is manifest before him."
Then Nandipāla spoke thus three times:
"I shall go with you to the presence of the Buddha.
Then Saṃjaya likewise replied three times:
"Thus, it is difficult to attain the perfect enlightenment of one who has gone forth.

With this thought, Nandipāla immediately ascended the chariot, took hold of that most excellent [horse], and went together with him to the place where the Buddha was, in order to behold and pay homage to him.
At that time, having seen him take it up, he spoke these words:
"That Kāśyapa Buddha is certainly the most supreme and unsurpassed Great Teacher; all his dharmas are truly sublime."
Why is this? Because that Nandapāla was previously virtuous and good, lacking any sudden violence or abrupt ferocity; it was for the sake of that Tathāgata that he seized me.
Having formed this thought, he then said to Nandipāla,
"You must release me. Nandipāla replied:
"I will not release you; if you go with me to the World-Honored One’s presence to make offerings and pay homage, I shall release you.
Thus he spoke three times.
Then that Most Excellent One replied, "Nandipāla!
Mount this chariot; I shall go with you together to the place where the Buddha is."
Where the carriage could pass, he traveled by carriage; where the carriage could not pass, he proceeded on foot.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, Nandipāla rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:

"This Most Excellent One does not have faith in the Triple Gem; I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the sublime Dharma for him, so that this Most Excellent One may come to believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."

At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the invitation; he then preached the sublime Dharma for Jyotiṣka, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, and finally remained silent.
At that time, Jyotipāla said to Nandīpāla:
"Having heard this Dharma, why do you not go forth into the homeless life? Nandīpāla replied:
"O Most Victorious One!
Do you not know that I support my two blind parents and from time to time make offerings to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa?
Most Victorious One replied:
"If you do not go forth into homelessness, I shall certainly go forth now.
At that time, Nandipāla rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Now, Most Excellent One, I wish to go forth as a renunciant within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to go forth.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated before the Buddha and sat down.
At that time, the World-Honored One granted him permission to go forth according to the Dharma as a most excellent renunciant.

Then, departing from the village of Anupiya, the World-Honored One traveled among the people toward the city of Vārāṇasī, gradually arriving at that city at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages (Ṛṣipatana).

At that time, King Kṛkī heard that the Buddha was wandering among the people and had arrived at the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva). The king departed from the city and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.

Upon arrival, he prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha then expounded the sublime Dharma for King Kṛkī, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, until finally remaining silent.
Then King Kṛkī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One and assembly of bhikṣus, please accept my invitation for tomorrow morning; I shall provide offerings within my palace and serve a meal to the Buddha and the Saṃgha."
The World-Honored One then accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When King Kṛkī saw that the World-Honored One had accepted the invitation through his silence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rose from his seat, took leave of the Buddha, and returned home.
When the king had arrived, during that night he prepared various kinds of fragrant and delicious food and drink.
When morning came, he arranged excellent seats and prepared various scented waters. Having performed these tasks, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; we pray that you will know it is time."

In the first part of the day, Kāśyapa Buddha, taking his bhikṣus with him and surrounded by them as they held their robes and bowls before and behind him, went to the place where the king had prepared the offerings.
Having arrived, the Buddha took his place at the head of the assembly, and the other bhikṣus sat down, each spreading out their seats in order of seniority.
Then King Kṛkī personally served various kinds of food and drink to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.

Having made the offerings, the Buddha and the bhikṣus each set aside their bowls, washed their hands, and rinsed their mouths. The King, holding a golden pitcher filled with water, knelt before the World-Honored One and spoke these words:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One accept that I shall construct a great monastery for the World-Honored One, consisting of five hundred courtyards. In each and every courtyard, I shall provide various large and small beds and furnishings, as well as fragrant rice, to serve the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Kṛkī:
"Since you have now been able to give rise to this most excellent and great resolve, you shall fully receive the merit thereof."
King Kṛkī made this request three times:

"During the three months of the summer retreat, I pray that the World-honored One will accept my various offerings of the four requisites. For the World-honored One, I shall construct five hundred great monasteries; in each monastery, there shall be one large bed, one small bed, a table, a desk, carpets, rugs, and pillows, with five hundred of each provided in full. Furthermore, I shall provide exquisite non-glutinous rice and various rare treasures to make offerings to the World-honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Kṛkī: "Great King!
That you are now able to give rise to this thought is no different from having already provided for it."
Then King Kṛkī said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Although I am currently unable to provide offerings to the World-Honored One, is there anyone else who has already been able to prepare offerings with a sincerity as great as mine?”
The World-Honored One replied,
"Great King! Within your kingdom,
there are already those who have made such offerings to me."
The King then asked:
"Who is the name of this person who made the offering?
The World-Honored One replied:

"Within Your Majesty’s realm there is a village named Veṇḍu. There dwells a potter named Nandipāla who has firm faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; having taken refuge in the Triple Gem with resolute conviction, he has realized the truth of the noble truths and attained the fruit of sainthood. He has completely renounced all implements used for the business of harming living beings."
Using soil from a rat's burrow and water and wood free of insects, he fashioned various earthenware vessels. Placing these utensils outside his door, he announced to all people:
"Give me oil, sesame, rice, and beans; take as much as you wish from these vessels."
"Whatever rice, beans, and other items he obtains to support his blind parents, he shall also bring here to offer to me.
The Buddha said to the king:
"Once, while traveling through cities and towns, I arrived at the village of Micchindika for alms."
At that time, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, he went on his alms-round in due order. Upon reaching the gate of the potter Nandīpāla’s house, he gently knocked.

At that moment, the potter Nandīpāla had gone away on business, and only his blind parents remained in the house. Hearing the sound of the knocking, they came to the gate and asked, "Who is there, O noble sir?"
"Who is this person coming to knock at the door?
The Buddha said, "I am Kāśyapa Buddha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I have come here for the sake of seeking alms for a meal."
He immediately opened the door and invited me to enter.
Once I had entered his house, the blind man said:
"I have cooked beans in a basin and cooked vegetables placed in a basket, yet I cannot see them now."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will take as much as he pleases.
The blind man spoke again:
“The donor who provides offerings for the World-Honored One has gone out briefly on another errand.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Great King:
"I shall act according to the custom of Uttarakuru; having taken the food with my own hand, I will finish eating and depart."
After the potter Xi-hu returned home, he saw that someone had taken portions from his beans and vegetables;
he asked his parents, "Who ate these beans and vegetables?"
The blind parents then recounted the events in their proper sequence.
Upon hearing this, Nandipāla was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"I have attained a great benefit; the Buddha Kāśyapa has entered my home and partaken of food at his own pleasure."
Due to this heart of joy, he sat cross-legged for seven days and entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Having arisen from that concentration, because of the power of that absorption, his right mindfulness remained undistracted for fifteen full days without interruption. During those seven days, by the power of the concentration, the domestic vessels and food were always full, providing for his parents without any lack.
The Buddha said to the king:

"At another time, I was staying for the three-month rains retreat in the village of Veṇugrāma. At the beginning of that summer, there was heavy rain; the roof of my dwelling leaked, whereas the workshop of the potter Nandīpāla, which was under construction, had its thatch entirely covered with new grass."
At that time, I said to my attendant bhikṣu:
"You should go together to the potter Nandīpāla’s workshop, tear down the new straw from his shed and roof, and bring it here to cover this house."
When those bhikṣus heard my words, they all followed his instructions and performed the task accordingly.
At that time, Nandagopa had gone elsewhere on business. When Nandagopa’s parents heard the sound of the house being demolished, they immediately asked, "Who is this noble one?"
"Who is this noble one who has come to tear down the newly thatched grass hut? They replied:

"I am the attendant bhikṣu of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Because the dwelling where the Buddha resides is leaking from the rain, I have come to take this fresh grass in order to thatch the roof for the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The potter’s parents said to the Noble One, “Our son is not here; take whatever you require.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus tore down the straw thatch from the workshop and used it to roof my temple.
After returning home, Nandagopa saw that the new straw for his workshop had been torn up;
he then asked his parents, "Who came and tore up my new workshop straw and took it away?"
The parents replied,
"Not long after you had gone out, we heard a workshop being demolished, so we asked,
'Who is this noble one?'"
“Who is this noble one who has torn down my new thatched hut? He then replied:

"We bhikṣus are the attendants of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Because the dwelling where the Buddha resides has been leaking due to rain, we have come to take this fresh grass in order to thatch the roof for the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
He immediately replied, "My son is not here; take him as you please.
When Nandīpāla heard what his parents said, he was greatly delighted and thought to himself:
"I have attained great benefit; the Buddha Kāśyapa has accepted my offerings at home without hindrance.

Having realized this, his heart was filled with joy and exultation. He sat cross-legged for seven days, maintaining continuous and focused mindfulness without ever wavering for a moment. By the power of his celestial merit, even throughout those seven days—
"Even though that roofed house was torn apart, not a single drop leaked despite heavy rains.
The Buddha said to the Great King, "Do not harbor such thoughts;
my refusal of your invitation for the three-month rainy-season retreat and the fourfold offerings is just like Nandapāla’s newly thatched barn."
Then King Kṛkī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Ratnākara has now obtained great benefit; the Buddha Kāśyapa encountered no difficulty in receiving offerings at Ratnākara’s home."
At that time, the king rejoiced and spoke these verses:
“Among all sacrifices, fire is supreme; Among the Vedas, the gods are supreme;
Among those honored in the world, the king is supreme; Of all flowing waters, the ocean is supreme.”
Among all the lunar mansions, the moon is supreme; among all the luminaries, the sun is supreme.
Among those above, below, in the four quarters, and throughout the heavens, making offerings to the World-Honored One is most supreme.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened King Kṛkī with the sublime Dharma, departed immediately.

Then King Kṛkī, having escorted the World-Honored One out of the village with various kinds of offerings, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and returned to his own palace.
He dispatched a messenger with five hundred wagons, each loaded with non-glutinous rice, to deliver it to the potter, saying:
"Inform Nandipāla that this non-glutinous rice, carried on these five hundred wagons, is for the purpose of making offerings to your blind parents and to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa."
At that time, the messenger, having received the King’s command, delivered the rice and proclaimed the King’s decree:
"The non-glutinous rice carried in these five hundred carts is to be used for making offerings to your blind parents, as well as for making offerings from time to time to Kāśyapa Buddha."
Then, when Nandipāla saw that the king’s rice had arrived, he replied to the messenger, saying:
"The king has many affairs of state; I do not dare to accept it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor such thoughts, young brahmin; it was I myself who was that person.
In the past, I slandered Kāśyapa Buddha, saying: 'He cannot attain perfect enlightenment, for he must practice asceticism;
since he does not undergo such hardships, how could he possibly achieve true and equal awakening?'"
"Because of this malicious slander, I must now undergo six years of suffering as karmic retribution.
You bhikṣus should know that the ripening of karma must be experienced by oneself; as explained at length before, you should train yourselves in this manner."
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Scroll Eleven;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Scroll Twelve.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.

When the Buddha was in the city of Śrāvastī, at the very moment that the Bodhisattva had gone beyond the city walls, Yaśodharā became pregnant. During the six years of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices, Yaśodharā also practiced austerities within the royal palace; due to these causes and conditions, the fetus remained hidden within her womb.

At that time, the Bodhisattva realized that his ascetic practices were of no benefit; he then relaxed his breath at will, partook of fine food—eating his fill of rice mixed with various delicacies to nourish his body—and anointed his limbs with oil and bathed in warm water.

Having heard of these matters, Yaśodharā likewise relaxed her body and mind within the palace, conducting herself just as the Bodhisattva had; through this joy, her fetus grew and her abdomen gradually became large.
Upon hearing this, the Śākyas laughed and ridiculed him, saying:

"The Bodhisattva left the household life and practiced asceticism to the utmost; yet you, within the palace, have secretly consorted with other men, causing her to become pregnant and her belly to swell."
Having heard this, Yaśodharā vowed, "I am free from such a fault.
Not long thereafter, she gave birth to a son; at that very moment, Rāhula grasped a bright moon.
He gathered his kinsmen together, prepared a celebratory feast, and invited them to bestow a name upon the child.
The kinsmen consulted one another, saying:
"When this son was first born, Rāhula grasped the moon with his hand; therefore, this child should be named Rāhula."
At that time, the Śākyas deliberated among themselves, saying,
"This is not the son of the Bodhisattva.
When Yaśodharā heard these words, she immediately wept and, embracing Rāhula, made a solemn oath.
He placed Rāhula upon the "Stone for Dispelling Fatigue" where the Bodhisattva used to rest while in the palace, and cast him into the pool where the Bodhisattva bathed, making this vow:
"If this child is truly the offspring of the Bodhisattva, let him float as soon as he enters the water;
if it be otherwise, let him sink."
Having spoken these words, Rāhula floated together with the stone and did not sink beneath.
Yaśodharā spoke to him again, saying:
"You should go from this shore to the other shore, and then return once more."
He arrived as soon as he wished.
When the multitude saw him, they all felt a sense of wonder. The mother, holding her child, thought to herself:

"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, after six years of ascetic practice, attains enlightenment and remains for another six years—totaling twelve years—he shall return here once more, so that I may cause these people to witness with their own eyes whether this is true or false."
At that time, the World-Honored One later returned to the city of Kapilavastu, taking his meal at the royal palace on one day and within the inner palace on another.
Then Yaśodharā thought to herself:
"Is there some skillful means by which I might cause the World-Honored One to follow my wishes?"
At that time, there was a female heterodox practitioner (*tīrthikī*) in this city who was skilled in magical arts and capable of making men fall in love with women.
Yaśodharā entrusted her with five hundred gold coins and sent a messenger with this message:
"Perform a magical rite and send it to me."
She immediately sent one love-inducing medicinal pill to the palace.
Having received it, the mother placed the pill before the palace attendants and put it into Rāhula’s hand, saying:
"Son, take this medicine and give it to your father."

The Buddha, possessing all-encompassing wisdom, had previously understood and foreseen that Yaśodharā’s giving birth to Rāhula would invite worldly slander; he knew that this defamation would be cleared away today.
The World-Honored One, having known this, manifested as five hundred Buddhas, all identical in form.

At that time, Rāhula carried the medicine and went on his rounds; although he passed by many Buddhas, he did not offer it to any of them. Upon arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, he then presented the medicine. After the Buddha had accepted it, he returned it to Rāhula.
At that time, the son received it and immediately consumed it. Knowing he had eaten, the Buddha offered a blessing and departed from his seat.
Rāhula followed after the Buddha, but the palace ladies would not let him leave the inner quarters; Rāhula then wept in sorrowful distress, vowing to go with the Buddha.
After the World-Honored One had departed, he thought to himself:
"I know that Rāhula will not undergo further existence; he shall realize the fruit of holiness and will not remain in the secular world.
Having known this, the World-Honored One then proceeded with him.
At that time, due to the influence of past karmic conditions, Rāhula was able to recognize the World-Honored One among five hundred Buddhas and refused to leave him.

When King Śuddhodana, the palace attendants, the retinue, and the members of the Śākya clan saw this extraordinary event, they revered Yaśodharā; knowing that she had been falsely accused in the past, they now felt joy as her ill repute was extinguished.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had arrived at his original location, he desired to ordain Rāhula.
Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!”
"If you must ordain Rāhula, I beg for one day so that I may extend my offerings.
The World-Honored One granted his request and permitted him to bring forth the offerings.
At that time, King Śuddhodana prepared a grand assembly for Rāhula on a vast scale and arranged a high seat to honor him.
On the second day, he went together with Rāhula to the place where the Buddha was; having paid homage to the World-Honored One, he spoke these words:
"Venerable Sir!
Please allow Rāhula to go forth as a renunciant."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Rāhula! You shall now take him away and grant him the going-forth according to the Dharma."
Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Śāriputra caused Rāhula to go forth into the religious life according to the Dharma.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One:

"By what causes and conditions did the youth Rāhula, while holding medicinal pills in his own hands amidst the great assembly, recognize the World-Honored One in the presence of five hundred Buddhas?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"This Rāhula! It is not only in this present life that he has known me; in the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, amidst the great assemblies, he was already acquainted with me, honoring me with garlands of flowers."
Listen attentively, and I shall speak for you.
Once in the past, there was an elder in a village who took the daughter of a neighboring elder as his wife.
Before long, she became pregnant and gave birth to a son.
He then said to his wife,
"Now that we have this son who shall consume my wealth, he will also be able to repay our debts for us."
"I am now taking various goods to sea for trade; you may remain behind to look after this child and manage the household affairs.
His wife replied to her husband, "I shall follow your instructions exactly."
The elder entered the sea and encountered a storm; his ship was wrecked, and along with all his wealth and goods, he perished in the waters and did not return.

When his wife heard of her husband’s death, she observed the rites of mourning and cultivated merit, while also working as a hired laborer herself. Together with her kinsmen, they supported one another and sustained their son, gradually allowing him to grow to maturity.
Beside his house lived a skilled weaver who supported himself through his craft.
When the elder’s wife saw him, she thought to herself:
"Engaging in maritime trade is not as good as making weaving one's profession."
"Those who enter the sea mostly die and do not return.
As for those who weave nets, they can always remain at home, seeking their livelihood and supporting themselves.
He then thought again:
"Now I shall have this son of mine learn the craft of weaving.
Having reflected thus, he immediately took his son and went to a weaver's house, saying to the master weaver:
"Elder brother!..."
"This nephew has taught me the craft of weaving.
The weaver replied, "Excellent!"
He kept his son to teach him weaving.

The son was intelligent and became proficient in a short time; he would often weave alongside the master weaver at the same loom. Although the profits they earned were brought back to their original home, the goods obtained were insufficient for the family's daily needs.
The weaver’s gains were such that he had more than enough to spare.
His nephew asked his uncle, "I am now engaged in the same craft as you; why is it that your household is always abundant and prosperous, while my own family can never manage to get by?"
The uncle replied to his nephew:
"I perform two types of karma, while you perform but one.
The nephew asked his uncle:
"What is your second occupation? He replied,
"I commit theft at night."
The nephew replied, "I also followed in the theft.
His uncle then said to him:
"You cannot steal," [he said]. He replied,
"I am quite capable of doing it."
The uncle thought to himself,
"I shall first test him.
Having had this thought, they went together to the market, where the uncle bought a rabbit and ordered him to prepare it.
"I shall come immediately after bathing to eat.
After he had finished preparing the meal, before his uncle had returned from his bath, the nephew ate one leg. When the uncle returned from his bath, he asked his nephew, "Is the meal prepared?"
He replied, "I have understood.
His uncle said:
"When the cooking is finished, bring it here for me to see.
The nephew carried the rabbit over and gave it to his uncle; when the uncle saw the rabbit, he noticed that one foot was missing, so he asked the nephew, "Where is the fourth foot of the rabbit now?"
The nephew replied, "This rabbit has originally possessed these three legs; why do you ask me for a fourth?
The uncle then thought to himself:
"I was previously a thief, but now this nephew of mine is a greater thief than I.
He then took the rabbit with him into a tavern; once his nephew-in-law was seated, he called for him to sit and drink together, and immediately ordered the nephew to calculate the price of the wine.
The nephew replied:
"If one drinks wine, they may be made to calculate it; I originally did not drink, so why discuss calculation?
Since you, uncle, are now drinking yourself, you should calculate for yourself."
The uncle thought to himself:
"I was formerly a thief, but now this nephew is a great thief who surpasses me; if he were to join with me as we were originally, he would be fit to be a thief as well."
He then went with his nephew during the middle of the night and bored a hole through another's wall, intending to steal property.
Once the hole was made, the uncle first attempted to thrust his head into it, whereupon the nephew said:
"Uncle, you are unskilled in the art of theft; why do you first insert your own head into the hole?"
"This is unwise; one should first enter the hole with one's feet.
If one enters first with the head, one will have one's head cut off by him, and being recognized by everyone, the calamity will extend to the entire clan. Now, one should first enter with the feet."

Upon hearing this, the uncle thrust his foot inside. The owner of the property, having awakened, immediately cried out, "Thief! Hearing the sound, the people together seized the thief's foot from within the hole.

At that time, the nephew again pulled his uncle out from the hole; however, as he lacked sufficient strength and feared that disaster might befall himself, he immediately severed the uncle's head, took it with him, and fled.
At that time, the ministers reported this matter to the king.
The king told his ministers:

"The one who cut off the head and fled is the greatest thief. You should take that corpse and place it at a crossroads, then observe it closely. Should anyone come along weeping and carry the corpse away, that person is the thief; you must seize him immediately."
The ministers, having received the command, immediately took the corpse and prepared it according to the king’s instructions.
The thief’s nephew then thought to himself:
"I should not now simply embrace my uncle's corpse, for I fear the people will recognize me."
"I should feign madness at the various crossroads, perhaps embracing a man or a woman, or embracing a tree or a stone, or embracing an ox or a horse, or embracing a pig or a dog.
Having formed this thought, he then carried out these actions.

At that time, when the people of the world saw that man embracing objects everywhere, they all knew he was mad; however, when the thief’s nephew first embraced his uncle, he wept with utmost grief and sorrow and then departed immediately.
The ministers reported to the king, all saying:
"As for those who guarded the corpse, there was only one madman who embraced the body, wept in grief, and departed;
there were no others. The king then declared:
"He is a dog-thief; why have you not seized him?
You must capture him now!
At that time, the thief further thought to himself:
"How can I not bury my maternal uncle?
I must certainly bury him.
He then took on the guise of a cart driver, filled his cart with bundles of firewood, and drove it up to the corpse. He quickly unfastened the yoke from the oxen, set the cart ablaze, and fled.
At that time, the fire from the funeral pyre had completely consumed the corpse; the guards then reported to the king, saying:
"The corpse of that thief has now been entirely burned away."
The king asked him,
"Who burned the corpses of the thieves?
The minister related the matter in full.
The king said:
"You all should know that the driver of that carriage is none other than the dog-thief; why did you not seize him?
He must be captured now."
At that time, the thief again thought to himself:
"I must now perform various sacrificial offerings at the place where my uncle’s corpse was buried.

Having thought this, he assumed the guise of a pure-practicing Brahmin and went throughout the city begging for alms. He then placed the food he had received in five locations at the cremation site to secretly sacrifice to his uncle; having finished, he departed.
Then the corpse-keeper reported the matter in full to the king.
The king said, "He is a dog-thief; why was he not seized?"
"This is most unwholesome.
At that time, the thief again thought to himself:
"I must now take my uncle's bones and cast them into the Ganges River."

Having formed this thought, he assumed the form of a skull-wielding outsider (Kāpālika) and went to the place where the bones lay. He took the remaining ashes to smear upon his own body, collected the burnt bones and placed them within a skull, and cast them into the Ganges River; having done so, he departed.
The corpse-warden reported this again to the king, who said:
"That man is a dog-thief; why was he not seized?
This is most unseemly."
"You all should stop; I shall catch it myself.
At that time, the king boarded a large boat and traveled along the Ganges River with attendants in front and behind, stationing men on the riverbanks to guard and intercept him.

The king had a daughter whose countenance was so upright and beautiful that all people delighted in seeing her. While they were playing together in the river, he ordered them to move some distance apart and said to his daughter, "If anyone seizes you, you must cry out loudly."
He further commanded the guards on the bank, saying:
"When my daughter makes a sound, you must immediately draw near.
If you see a man, you may seize him."
At that time, the dog-thief again thought to himself:
"Now the king is sporting with his daughter in the river; I must certainly join her in our amorous play."
Having formed this thought, he immediately stayed upstream and released a single earthen cooking pot to float down with the current.
When the men on the bank saw it, they mistook it for a thief and scrambled to strike it with clubs; the pot broke, and only then did they realize it was not a thief.
The second and third times were likewise repeated, up to ten times.
At that time, the shore-keeper, having repeatedly seen the earthen pot, abandoned it and ceased striking.
Then the dog-thief, carrying a pot upon his head, went down with the current to the place where the princess was and climbed onto her boat.
Holding a sharp blade in his hand, he said to the princess, "Do not make a sound; if you do, I shall kill you.
Terrified, the princess did not dare to utter a word, and so they engaged in dalliance.
Having finished their debauchery, they fled.
Seeing the thieves depart, the woman wailed aloud and spoke these words:
"Those thieves have forcibly violated me; they have now already gone."
The riverbank guards replied to the princess, "While you were playing, you enjoyed yourself in silence;
now that the bandits have already departed, you only begin to weep. Where can we seek out the bandits now?"
The shore guards reported this in full to the king, who said, "How is it that you failed to guard properly and allowed such a thing to happen?
At that time, the king’s daughter had been violated by the dog-thief and subsequently became pregnant; when the ten months were complete, she gave birth to a son.
At that time, when the dog-thief heard that the King’s daughter had given birth to a son, he thought to himself:
"I must now perform a great celebration for my child.
Having formed this thought, he immediately transformed his appearance into that of a servant and emerged from the royal palace, announcing to the people:

"The King has issued a decree: 'My daughter has given birth to a son; you people of this land may tonight indulge yourselves in pleasure as you wish, freely stealing one another's clothes, wealth, and silks according to your desires.'"

At that time, when the ministers and the multitude of people in the kingdom heard these words, they gave rein to their passions and indulged in merriment; the clamor of their voices reached the inner quarters of the king.
The king asked his people, "Why is my countryfolk making such a clamor as this?"
The people of the country replied,
“We were previously commanded by Your Majesty to act in this manner.
Upon hearing this, the king realized that it was the work of the dog-thief, and he thought to himself:
"If I cannot capture this dog-thief, I shall renounce my royal throne.
He then devised a stratagem and constructed a great hall.

Once the hall was finished and his son was six years old, he ordered his ministers to beat the drums and proclaim a decree, summoning every male inhabitant of the kingdom to enter the hall; anyone who did not come would be seized and executed.
At that time, all the people of the country entered the hall, and the dog-thief was also among them.
Then the king took a flower garland and said to his son:
"Take this garland and go into that assembly; if you see your father, give the garland to him."
He further ordered an attendant to follow him, saying:
"When that boy gives you the flower garland, you must seize it.
At that time, the boy took the flower garland and went into the assembly; by the power of his karma, he saw his father and gave him the garland.
At that time, bystanders seized the dog-thief and brought him before the king.
The king assembled his ministers to deliberate on this matter:
"How shall we dispose of such a criminal?"
"He may indeed be killed. The king then reflected:
"This is a wise thief; how can I kill him?"
He addressed his ministers, saying, "This man is both courageous and endowed with wisdom; he may be retained to serve as my guard.
He then gave him his daughter in marriage to be his wife and bestowed half of his kingdom upon him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the dog-thief was none other than myself.
The child at that time was none other than Rāhula."
"Because you were able to recognize me among this assembly in the past, you are now likewise able to recognize me here in this assembly.
Monks, you should know that the power of karma is inconceivable; you must act in accordance with your own karma."
At that time, Yaśodharā thought to herself:
"When Rāhula’s father enters the palace, I must employ various skillful means to serve and provide for him so that he does not leave the palace."

Having formed this thought, Yaśodharā, along with Gopikā, Mṛgajā, and others—sixty thousand beautiful women—each adorned themselves with various ornaments and prepared all manner of exquisite perfumes. Once everything was ready, they waited.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl; surrounded and attended by the bhikṣus, he entered the royal palace for the sake of subduing sentient beings.

At that time, Yaśodharā and her two other wives, accompanied by sixty thousand court ladies, performed various musical pieces and engaged in singing, dancing, and acrobatics; they adjusted their garments with coquettish and seductive allure, standing before the World-Honored One with the intent to provoke desire and attachment.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"The time for the meal is now approaching. If I were to eat first without preaching the Dharma to these women, I fear that the opportunity for their conversion will pass; their lustful desires will become so intense that they will fail to receive the benefit of the principles of the Four Noble Truths."
"I should now, by means of my supernormal powers, bring all those women to subjection.
Having formed this thought, he immediately vanished from the ground and appeared in the sky to the east, moving, standing, sitting, and reclining therein with sovereign mastery over his deportment.

He again entered the Fire-Light Samādhi, emitting from within his body various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white. At times, water issued from his upper body and fire from his lower body; the same occurred in the south, west, and north. He then vanished from mid-air and suddenly appeared upon the lion throne at the head of the bhikṣus.
When the various beautiful women saw this, they all fell prostrate before the Buddha like trees cut down by an axe; they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the dispositions, faculties, intentions, and aspirations of the women, extensively analyzed the principles of the Four Noble Truths for them.

Upon hearing this, the women attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); however, because Yaśodharā’s defiled mind was still heavy, she had not yet attained the fruit. She then formed this thought and spoke these words:
"I possess a flavor that can cause those who taste it to give rise to attachment."
He then prepared various kinds of fragrant and delicious food and drink, holding them with his own hands to offer to the World-Honored One.
Having formed this thought, the bhikṣus all heard of it and reported it to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
In the past, when I had not yet abandoned the three poisons, I felt no attachment even toward various fragrances and flavors;
how much less could they defile me now that the three poisons have been abandoned?
"Even if Yaśodharā were to possess the taste of food, I would have no fear.
At that time, the bhikṣus, all filled with doubt, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Why did Yaśodharā develop a defiled attachment toward the Blessed One because of the *modaka* sweetmeat?
The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣus!"
"This Yaśodharā did not become attached to me because of the *modaka* sweetmeat due to a desire born in this present life; rather, such a thing occurred previously in the past.
Listen attentively!"
In times past, there was a village, not far from which lay a forest hermitage abounding in flowers, fruits, and clear, beautiful springs.

At that time, there was a rishi who ate those fruits and flowers and wore garments of tree bark; having performed such ascetic practices, he realized the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). All the birds and beasts were not afraid of him, but constantly came to draw near him.

Later, on one occasion, he wished to go for a small urination. A female deer followed the seer as he went; when the seer urinated and emitted semen, the deer followed him and immediately consumed it, and further licked his private parts with her tongue. Because the karmic power of sentient beings is inconceivable, she subsequently became pregnant.
When the months were complete, the deer came to that same place and gave birth to a boy; having given birth to this child, she recognized him as human and departed.
When the rishi saw him, he thought to himself, "Whose son is this?
He then reflected further and recognized him as his own child, whereupon he took him in and raised him.
Later, as he gradually grew up and reached the age of twelve, a single horn sprouted from his head; consequently, they gave him the name "The Single-Horned One" (Ekasṛṅga).
His father fell ill, and although Ekasṛṅga employed various medical treatments, he could not cure him. His father’s condition grew increasingly critical, and his life was about to end.
He said to Ekaśṛṅga, "In this place of mine, there are always various mountain sages who come and go; you should welcome them and inquire after their well-being.
If they do come, provide them with flowers and fruit for my sake."
He spoke in verse: "All that is accumulated must disperse; what is lofty will surely fall;
those who meet must part; all who have life return to death."
"Thus it was until the seer passed away; that Unicorn Seer, according to the rites of seers, performed the funeral for his father.
Through the grief, sorrow, and distress caused by mourning his father's death, he then realized the five supernormal powers."

Later, on another occasion, while going to fetch water, he obtained some and was returning along the road when he encountered rain; the ground became slippery with mud, and he fell to the ground, whereupon his water jar was broken.
He scooped up the water from the broken jar and placed it in his palm; then, reciting a mantra with his mouth toward the sky, he scattered it afar, saying:
"Since you have caused my jar to break by raining down, do not rain again for twelve years from this day forward."
Due to the power of this seer’s incantation, the rain ceased to fall; the city of Vārāṇasī suffered a great drought, and the people, stricken by famine, scattered and fled.
At that time, the king summoned the diviners and asked them:
"For what reason does the heavens not send down rain?
The diviners replied:
"Because the rishi is angry, the heavens do not send down rain.
The king asked the diviners:
"What expedient means should be employed so that sweet rain falls throughout the world and the people enjoy abundance and joy?"
The diviner reported, saying:
"If you defeat the seer’s ascetic discipline and his cultivation of the Way, the heavens will send sweet rain.
If you do not defeat the seer and cause him to violate his ascetic discipline, the heavens will never send rain for twelve years."

When the king had heard this, he rested his cheek upon his hand and fell into deep reflection. Seeing the king distressed, the palace ladies, the queen, and the various ministers addressed him, saying:
"For what reason are you so distressed?"
The king replied: "Due to the power of the seer’s incantations, the heavens do not send rain... [and so on,] as explained at length above.
I do not know what stratagem to employ now to cause that seer to fail in his cultivation of the precepts."
"Because of this anxiety and distress, I find no joy.
At that time, the king had an eldest daughter named Śāntā, who addressed the king, saying:
"There is no need for such distress; I shall devise a stratagem to ensure that the rishi's ascetic conduct is inevitably ruined."
The king asked the girl,
"What plan do you have?
The girl replied to the king:

"I have studied the incantations of the Brahmins, as well as other methods with twenty court ladies in one place; I pray that Your Majesty may construct a boat upon the water, secure it with planks, place soil upon it, plant trees, and sow various flowers and fruits, making it exactly like the dwelling place of the rishis."
"We shall board a boat and go to where that seer dwells; we can then cause him to fail in his ascetic practices and bring him here.

Having heard this, the king acted according to the woman's words: he moored the boat, fixed planks, and planted various flowers and fruits as previously described. He then secretly filled the fruits with medicinal wine and likewise placed medicine within all the food and drink.

Thereupon, Śāntā and the other ladies assumed the appearance, forms, and attire of sages; wearing garments of tree bark and letting their hair hang loose behind them, they were no different from true sages.
Descending from the boat, he proceeded at a slow pace toward the seer, reciting Brahmanic incantations as he went until he reached the seer’s dwelling.
Seeing from afar that twenty visiting seers were approaching, the seer’s disciple immediately informed his master, saying:
"There are visiting seers who have now arrived here."
At that time, the one-horned seer thought to himself: "Welcome!
Call him in to enter the room."
At that time, after the various seers had entered the chamber, the Unicorn Seer observed closely and saw that their complexions were unusual; he then spoke this verse:
“Never having undergone hardship, Their gait is moreover composed;
No beard grows upon their faces, And there are elevations and depressions upon their chests.”
“The appearance of this seer has arrived; this matter is truly extraordinary.
Although that Unicorn Seer harbored doubts, he nevertheless prepared a seat for the visiting seer and provided him with fruits.
The Seer Śānta said:
"In the place where you dwell, there are many such bitter and astringent fruits; however, the fruits in my current dwelling are excellent, like nectar. I now invite you to come to my dwelling."
Then the one-horned seer immediately accompanied him, and they boarded a boat to travel upon the water. From a tree on the boat, he took coconuts;
inside these fruits, he had placed aphrodisiac wine, which he offered to the one-horned seer.
Having drunk it, he reported to the false immortal that they would practice unrighteousness together.
Due to this sexual defilement, he subsequently lost his supernatural powers; his observance of the precepts was already impaired, his mantra-power ceased, and dark clouds rose up on all sides.
Upon seeing this, Ekāṅga raised his face and reviled Heaven. Śānta replied:
"Your own body has committed wrongs, yet you do not even realize it; why then do you raise your face and, out of old resentment, blame Heaven?"
Ensnared by lustful passion, he remained silent.
Śānta proceeded directly before the king and addressed his father, saying:
"This man is that very rain-summoning seer."
When the king saw the seer arrive, he was so overcome with joy that clouds gathered across the sky and a sweet rain fell; the people enjoyed abundance and prosperity, and the five grains flourished.

At that time, the father-king married Śāntā to the seer as his wife and bestowed upon him many beautiful women for his service. However, in later times, he abandoned the princess and subsequently engaged in illicit affairs with other women.
Upon seeing Śānta, his mind was filled with jealousy; he immediately engaged in a fierce quarrel with the rishi, kicking him with his foot and striking the rishi’s face with his shoe.
The rishi thought to himself:
"In the past, when the heavens sent forth clouds and thunder, I caused them to cease through my incantations."
"Suddenly, bound by lustful desire, he was humiliated by the woman.

At that time, the rishi, weary of the defilement of desire, abandoned his state of tranquility; through diligent practice of meditative concentration, he immediately realized the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and traveled through the air to return to his original dwelling.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The seer of that time was none other than myself; the princess Śāntā is now Yaśodharā.
Because of her past attachment to flavors and her craving for sensual passion,"
"Now you wish to weary me further with these balls of joy.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha departed from the palace.

Upon seeing that the Buddha knew her thoughts, Yaśodharā’s mind was stilled; she ceased her searching and immediately ascended the seven-storied high tower. Disregarding her own life, she threw herself to the ground, but the Buddha, through his supernormal power, caught her so that she was not harmed.
When the people saw that she had not been injured, they were struck with wonder and astonishment.
When the community of bhikṣus saw this, they asked the Buddha:
"This Yaśodharā, out of her love for the Buddha, did not spare her own life but threw herself from a high tower onto the ground."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Because Yaśodharā loves me, it is not only in this present life that she has not spared her own body or life for my sake; in the past as well, she likewise did not spare her body or life for my sake."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively.
In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who, on one occasion, went out on a hunting expedition and slaughtered many living beings."
As he traveled through the mountain valleys, he saw a kinnara sleeping with his wife guarding him by his side.
The king then drew his bow and shot the kinnara; hitting a vital spot, the kinnara died instantly from a single arrow. Having captured the kinnara’s wife, the king desired to take her as his queen.
Then the Kinnara wife immediately addressed the king, saying:
"I only pray, Great King, that you permit me to perform the funeral rites for my husband; once they are completed, I shall follow you."
The king then thought to himself:
"How could he possibly run?
I shall watch his manner of salutation."
Having formed this thought, he immediately released her.

Then the Kinnara woman piled firewood on all four sides and set it ablaze; out of longing for her husband and disregarding her own life, she threw herself into the flames, and both husband and wife were consumed by the fire.
The devas in the sky spoke these verses:
"Seeking this very thing, one instead encounters its opposite;
Having originally hoped for celestial music, both husband and wife have perished."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The kinnara of former times was none other than myself.
The kinnara wife was none other than Yaśodharā."
"In the past, for the sake of my love, she already threw herself into the fire;
now, out of craving and attachment, she has again leaped from a high building.
The Buddha thought thus:
"If it is for the sake of transforming Yaśodharā, now is precisely the right time; I should cause her to emerge from the ocean of birth and death.
Having formed this thought, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to Yaśodharā.

Having heard this, he used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty peaks of the mountain of self-view, completely destroying them all; he realized the fruit of stream-entry and gave rise to faith.
Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, she applied herself with diligence to her practice and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā stood in the midst of the assembly, her heart filled with shame and remorse.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Among my entire assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā possesses the greatest sense of shame and modesty."
The assembly of bhikṣus was filled with doubt and again questioned the World-Honored One:
"By what karmic retribution did this bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā conceive Rāhula for six years?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, as previously described, and spoke in verse.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the past, there was a village where an old woman had only one daughter. She raised many dairy cows and prepared curds and whey every day; mother and daughter would go together around the village to sell them."
Later, on one occasion, the girl, while carrying the curd, suddenly conceived a deceptive thought and said to her mother:
"I wish to see the wind; I pray that you carry the curd and proceed slowly forward."

The mother then took the curd and departed carrying it on her back. Because the daughter was perverse, negligent, and possessed a deceitful mind, she stayed six *li* away and did not follow after her mother.
Due to this karma, Yaśodharā has now received the retribution of carrying the fetus for six years in this life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The meaning is as explained above," and he spoke these verses.
Then the bhikṣus, having further doubts, questioned the World-Honored One:
"What karma did this Rāhula previously commit?"
"Now he undergoes this retribution by dwelling in the womb for six years.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Rāhula himself committed these evil karmas," as explained above, along with the verse: [Verse omitted per instructions]
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"Not far from this city of Vārāṇasī, there was once a forest abounding in flowers and fruits. In it lived two brothers:
one named Śaṅkha and the other named Likhita. They wore garments of tree bark and constantly subsisted on fruits and various medicinal herbs."
Śaṅkha was the teacher and Likhita was the disciple.
At that time, the King of Vārāṇasī and the people knew that there were two practitioners of the path in this forest:
one named Śaṅkha and the other named Likhita.

Later, at one time, Śaṅkha rose at dawn and went into the mountains to gather fruit, carrying a full water jar. His younger brother, Likhita, rose at the fifth watch of the night and entered the mountains before his elder brother; he did not carry a water jar, yet having gathered flowers and fruit, he arrived first and was parched with thirst, needing water.
When he turned toward his own bottle, there was no water for him to drink; he then took his teacher’s water and drank it.
Having finished drinking, he did not refill his teacher’s bottle.
At that time, Śaṅkha arrived late when the sun was high; being exhausted and thirsty for water, he took his own water-flask to seek water to drink.
Seeing that the flask was empty of water, he immediately became angry and cursed:
"What violent thief has stolen my water?"
Then Rikṣita immediately replied, "I am that thief;
I used the water from the jar. I only pray that my preceptor will punish me for this grave offense."
Śaṅkha replied, "You are my disciple;
you may drink as much water as you wish, and I shall not punish you.
Rikṣa then said to his preceptor (upādhyāya):
"I am a thief; I wish to be given a heavy punishment, for if it is not given, my mind will find no peace.
Upon hearing this, Śaṅkha became greatly incensed and replied:
"I cannot now be angry with you and grant you punishment. If you must have punishment, go to the King's presence and seek a heavy sentence there."
Then Rikṣa proceeded toward the king’s location; on the way, he encountered the king who had gone out hunting, and raising his hands in salutation, he offered this prayer:
"May it be so, Great King!"
"May you live long and be free from illness, always victorious in battle.
He then spoke this verse:
"Great King, I am a thief; I have stealthily stolen and drunk your water."
"I pray that Your Majesty, following the laws for thieves, will grant me the punishment for stealing water. The King then replied,
"Even one who takes water without permission is not a thief."
The king asked again,
"Whose water did you take?
At that time, Likhita reported the matter in detail to the king as described above, and the king then replied:
"Since he is both your elder brother and your upādhyāya, even though he drank water without permission, he is not a thief.
You may now go in peace; it is not fitting to inflict punishment upon him."
Then Rikṣa again addressed the king, saying:
"I am a thief; I pray that you impose upon me a heavy punishment.
If you do not do so, my mind will find no peace."
When the king heard these words, he immediately gave rise to anger and replied:
"Stay right where you are now; do not go east or west."
"Wait for me; when I have returned from my mountain excursion, I shall give you instructions.
The king departed to hunt and returned to the palace by another route, whereupon he forgot to inform the seer whether he might proceed or not, and six days passed.
At that time, the rishi did not dare to move east or west;
the ministers said to the king, "That rishi has followed your instructions for six days and does not dare to move east or west; we only pray that Your Majesty will quickly grant him a resolution."
The king then replied, "We have been punishing the guilty for six days; you are now without fault, so we release you and let you go.
The minister reported this to the seer:
"Six days have now passed since you were punished; by royal decree, you are now free to go wherever you please.
Lekita was delighted and immediately returned home.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The King Brahmadatta of old was none other than this Rāhula. Because he gave rise to a mind of anger in a previous life and did not permit [the child] to go east or west for six days, [this consequence has followed]."
Now, for six years, by the power of karma, he has remained within his mother’s womb. O Bhikṣus!
Whether it be black karma, white karma, or mixed karma, all have their retribution.
“O bhikṣus! You should abandon black karma and mixed karma, and cultivate purely white karma.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what karma did this venerable son of noble family (bhadraputra) perform such deeds that he is now the king among the preeminent Śākyas?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“This venerable son of noble family has himself sown the seeds of meritorious karma,” and so on, until he spoke these verses (gāthā).
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a poor man who traveled through the human world and arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī.

Within that city, there were other poor people who, upon seeing this man arrive, immediately conceived feelings of resentment; they vied with one another to strike and assault him, driving him out beyond the city walls."
In that city, the king possessed a royal park. Having been driven out, the man took refuge within this park and made his dwelling there.

At that time, during the month of spring, when flowers and fruits were in full bloom and beautiful birds gathered in competition, the king went with his palace ladies and court attendants to the park for recreation and sightseeing.
Having arrived at the garden, he wandered here and there with his court ladies, gazing about and engaging in play and amusement.
At that time, the king became weary and fell asleep.
It is the constant nature of women:
Whenever they saw flowers or fruits, they would immediately give rise to craving and attachment.
At that time, having seen the king asleep, they each scattered through the forest to gather flowers and fruits.
Then, the king arose from his sleep and returned to the city; seeing the king return to the city, those palace attendants each hurriedly followed after him.

At that time, a certain palace attendant was in a state of hurried agitation and did not notice that she had left her necklace behind on her person. After the attendant had departed, the poor man saw it and thought to himself:
"If I were to take this, someone might discover it and surely cause me distress."
He immediately took the necklace and hung it upon a tree, thinking to himself:
"If the original owner comes, let him take it as he pleases.
He then watched it from afar.
"If it were not for the master taking it, I would not have intended to give it.
Once those palace women had returned to the palace, they realized the necklace was missing and remembered it being in the garden;
they said to the king, "Because of our haste, we forgot the necklace there in that garden."
At that time, the king immediately addressed his ministers:
"I have left a necklace within the garden; you must search for it quickly so that it is not lost.
The ministers, having received the king's command, led many laborers to search throughout the garden. Finding the necklace tied to a tree, they all deliberated together, saying:
"Who tied this necklace upon this tree?
He immediately ordered his men to search in every direction, until they saw a poor man beneath a thicket.
They asked him, "Did you see anyone tie this necklace here?"
The poor man reported everything as it had happened above.
Thereupon, the king’s ministers took the necklace back to the palace to present to the king and related the preceding events in detail.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately dispatched a messenger to pursue and fetch the poor man.
When the poor man arrived, the king said to him:
"For what reason did you previously obtain my necklace and, instead of taking it with you, tie it to a tree?"
The poor man replied, "Great King, you should know that this is a precious possession of Your Majesty; previously, being impoverished, I was unable to make use of it.
Upon hearing these words, the king was greatly delighted and said to the poor man:
"What wish do you seek?
I shall grant it to you," he said. The poor man replied:
"May the King grant food and drink, as well as clothing, to every poor person within this city, and let me be appointed as their leader.
Upon hearing these words, the king addressed his ministers:
"To all the poor people within my kingdom's cities, provide food and drink as well as clothing, and let this man be made their leader."
The minister, having received the command, beat the drum in the city of Vārāṇasī to proclaim:

"Let all the poor assemble! Once they had assembled, he provided them with food, drink, and various garments, and announced the king’s decree, ordering that the former poor man be appointed as their leader, and that they should all accept his instructions.
When those poor people had obtained food and clothing, they were all filled with joy and honored him as their lord.

Previously, while these poor people had been robbing and stealing food from others in the streets, the owners of that food had harbored resentment and constantly beat and reviled them. Later, having received the King’s favor, their acts of seizing and plundering increased; the people of the country, fearing the King, did not dare to beat or revile them.
At that time, the people of the kingdom went to the king’s presence and reported this matter in detail.
The king then replied, "You yourselves should provide protection; do not beat the poor."
Later, at another time, there was a person in the city who placed various cakes and foods inside a basket; when the aforementioned poor man saw this, he seized it and fled.
The poor people vied with one another to pursue him, seeking to snatch it away by force.

The leader of the poor fled to the riverbank, where he was again pursued; he then placed his basket of cakes upon his head and floated across the river. Having reached the opposite bank, he sat down beneath a tree.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
