"When a Buddha-Tathāgata has not yet appeared in the world, there will be Pratyekabuddhas who appear in the world to benefit all living beings, passing by as they go about their conduct."
Seeing his dignified and composed demeanor, that poor man thought to himself:

"Because in my past lives I did not understand the precepts or the practice of giving, and was unable to make offerings to such a person, I have resulted in this body being so impoverished and destitute."
"If that virtuous person accepts my gift, I shall give it to him.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, perceiving his thought through his supernormal knowledge, approached him with his alms bowl for the sake of benefiting him and begged for the rice cakes.
The poor man, filled with joy, took all the cakes and food and offered them as a gift.
It is the constant law of the pratyekabuddhas that they do not preach the Dharma with their mouths, but benefit others by manifesting supernatural powers with their bodies.
Having received the cakes, he leaped into the air and manifested various supernatural transformations.
When the ordinary worldlings saw these miracles, they swiftly made virtuous vows and prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground like falling trees, making this great aspiration:
"Now that we have made offerings to this holy person, may we in a future life become kings, the foremost among all nations."
"I have now seen a Pratyekabuddha; in a future age, I vow to see a Tathāgata and cross the ocean of birth and death.
Having made this vow, all the poor people crossed the river and went together to seek food and cakes. The leading poor man replied, "I have already finished my giving; you all should rejoice in it."
The poor people asked,
"When you gave us these cakes and food, what vow did you make?
The leader replied:
"May I, in a future age, become a king among all nations and be the foremost leader among them.
Upon hearing this, everyone made a vow:
"Since you have attained the status of sovereign, we vow to be your most eminent ministers and assistants."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The foremost poor man at that time was the Śākya son, the present King Bimbisāra.
The other poor men were the five hundred Śākyas of the present day."

Because that virtuous son formerly made a vow to offer food to a pratyekabuddha, he has now become a king among the Śākyas; furthermore, having seen me leave the household life to study the Path, he has realized the fruit of arhatship.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this:

by performing black karma one obtains the retribution of black karma; by performing mixed karma one obtains the retribution of mixed karma; and by performing white karma one obtains the retribution of white karma."
"You all should abandon black karma, mixed karma, and defiled karma, and cultivate purely white karma.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Kālāma village in the Śeṣavata Forest.

There were many bhikṣus there, and their alms bowls, as well as the World-Honored One’s bowl, were left in the open air. A monkey came down from a śāla tree and took one of the bowls; the bhikṣus then went forward to strike it and drive it away.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not strike it; let it take what it wishes, for I do not fear its damaging [the bowl].

At that time, the monkey went to the side of the bowl and took the Buddha’s bowl, climbed a śāla tree, and in a brief moment returned with the bowl filled to the brim with honey to offer to the Buddha. Because there were bees within the honey, the Tathāgata would not accept it.

At that time, the monkey, knowing the Tathāgata’s mind, took the bowl of honey to a secluded place, removed the bees, and returned to offer it to the Buddha; however, because it was still not pure, the Buddha would not accept it.

The monkey, again perceiving the Buddha’s intention, took the bowl of honey to the edge of a clear stream, drew water to sprinkle over the honey, and returned to offer it; the Buddha then accepted it.

At that time, having seen the Buddha accept his honey, the monkey felt great joy; he joined his palms in prostration and leaped about with such vigor that he failed to heed what was before or behind him, and consequently fell into a well, whereupon he passed away.
He immediately took rebirth in the womb of the wife of a pure Brahmin in the village of Nādika.
Once he had entered the womb, by virtue of his meritorious karma, the heavens sent down a rain of honey throughout the boundaries of the village of Nādika.
At that time, the people asked the diviners, "What is this matter?
The diviners replied,
"It is because of the power of karma that a child has been conceived in the womb of the Brahmin woman."

When the tenth month was complete and the day of the child’s birth arrived, honey-rain fell once more; the kinsmen and relatives assembled together, and for twenty-one days they provided food and offerings.
The kinsmen then asked:
"What name shall we give to the newborn child?"
The family members replied, "When his son was conceived, honey-rain fell; it was likewise when he was born.
His father’s surname is Vasiṣṭha; for this reason, he is named Amitaujas-Vasiṣṭha, which means 'Supreme Honey'."
As the boy gradually grew up, through the power of his past karma, he conceived faith and went to where the Buddha was.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he resolved to leave the household life; he was then ordained according to the Dharma. Having become a monk, he naturally received three bowls of honey every day:
one bowl to offer to the Buddha, one bowl to offer to the Saṃgha, and one bowl to eat with his friends and relatives.
At that time, the entire great assembly was filled with doubt and went together to address the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does this most excellent Bhikṣu Madhumatī possess such honey-like excellence day after day?"

The Buddha said, “This most excellent honey was produced by the bhikṣu himself through his own meritorious deeds; therefore, he experiences this retribution of honey day after day. The full explanation is as above.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Did you see in the past a monkey come down from a śāla tree and offer me a bowl of honey?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
We have seen it in the past."
The Buddha said,
"That monkey was none other than this Bhikṣu Most Excellent Honey (Madhu-vara).
It is due to the causal conditions of his previous act of faith in giving honey that he has obtained this retribution."

Yet for this bhikṣu, what difficulty is there in being able to transform three bowls of honey in a single day? If he were to wish for the four oceans to be entirely turned into honey, it would not be difficult. Why is this so?
"Because the merit from giving honey to the Buddha has increased,
as explained in detail above, one should abandon black karma and defiled karma,
and cultivate purely white karma. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃghabhedavastu*, Fascicle 12.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Scroll 13,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.

While the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu, on the occasion of his ordaining five hundred Śākyas and Upāli, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt. They brought this matter before the Buddha, saying:
"What karma did this Upāli perform in the past to become the king’s barber?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a barber to a king. A Pratyekabuddha came and stood before his door and said to him: 'Good man!'"
"Shave my head, and you shall obtain a wholesome fruit.
That barber had a nephew, to whom his uncle said: "I am on a mission for the King;
after I have gone, you should shave this man according to the proper method, just as one does for the King himself."
At that time, having heard these words from his uncle, the nephew thought to himself:
"If I send him to this man to have his head shaved according to the Dharma, I shall surely gain great merit."
Having formed this thought, he immediately focused his mind with clarity and shaved the head of the pratyekabuddha according to the Dharma.
At that time, the pratyekabuddha reflected:
"This person has shaved my head according to the Dharma; I shall protect and assist him so that he may surely obtain great benefit."

When the Pratyekabuddha had formed this thought, he immediately leaped into the air and manifested various supernatural transformations. Upon seeing this, the man was filled with great wonder; he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and made this vow:
"Since I have now shaved the head of this person, who resembles a king, I pray that in all my future lives I shall always be able to shave the heads of kings, no different from my maternal uncle."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The nephew at that time is now Upāli.
Because he shaved the head of a pratyekabuddha and made a vow in a previous life, he has now become the king’s barber.”
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"Upāli had another vow in a previous life; I shall now speak of it, so listen attentively."
In the past, there was an elder in a village who took a wife and fathered two sons.
At that time, the king had a barber who was a close friend of this elder.
That barber possessed great wealth and treasures, yet he had neither sons nor daughters. He often thought privately to himself:
"I now have abundant property, but no offspring; once I pass away, there will be no one to whom I can entrust it, and the king will surely seize it all."
At that time, seeing the barber dejected and unhappy, the elder immediately asked him,
"Why are you now so sorrowful? The barber then answered as he had done before.
The elder said, "I have two sons;
I shall now give the younger one to you as your son.
Having made this agreement, he took the young boy and adopted him as his own son.
Later, when the elder passed away from illness, the elder’s son was playing with other children; during a quarrel, the children said to him, "You are not of noble lineage."
"Why is this? Your younger brother has been seen as the son of a barber.
At that time, having been addressed with these words, the boy became dejected and unhappy, and he thought to himself:
"If my younger brother had not become the son of a barber, how could he have been so humiliated by others today?
I must now seize him back."
Having formed this thought, he immediately seized his younger brother and brought him back.
At that time, the barber felt deep resentment in his heart and gathered the members of his family who were barbers, addressing the assembly, saying:
"I have raised this boy for many years, yet now he has been taken away by force."
"From this day forward, none of my kinsmen shall serve as barbers for this family.
At that time, because those brothers were unable to have their hair shaved, their hair, body hair, nails, and claws all grew long and unsightly.
The king, seeing this suddenly, asked:
"Why are your hair, body hair, nails, and claws so long and unsightly?
Then the brothers replied to the king:
"The king’s barber has issued a restriction on all his kin, ordering them not to perform hair-cutting services at my house.
The king asked again:
"What is the reason for this?"
Then the brothers related the previous events in detail.
Having heard this, the king immediately declared:
"The father has given his son to another; it is not right for you to take him back."
Having received the king’s command, he immediately took his younger brother and gave him to the other as a son.
Later, the elder brother deliberated, saying:

"Because my younger brother was given to him to be shaved-headed as a son, we have constantly been subjected to insults and humiliation by him. I should now kill my younger brother; then we will surely be spared from such talk."
At that time, someone who heard this went to the barber’s house and said to his younger brother, “Your elder brothers have discussed it;
fearing they will bring disgrace upon the clan, they intend to kill you. You should guard yourself well.”
Having heard these words, the younger brother said to the barber:
"My elder brother now intends to come and kill me; you should release me now so that I may leave the household life and study the path of the sages."
The barber thought to himself:
"If I stubbornly detain this boy and do not allow him to leave the household life, he will surely kill me.
It would be better for me now to release him and let him go forth."
Having reflected thus, the father said to his son:
"I now grant you permission to go forth; once you have attained the methods of the sages, bring them back to teach me.
The son then replied:
"Excellent! I shall obey your command.

Thereupon, the son went at once to the mountain forest where the rishis dwelt; however, though he searched for them, he could not find any of the rishis. He then sat upright, concentrated his mindfulness, and reflected deeply, whereby he immediately realized the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha.
Having realized the fruit, he immediately thought:
"I previously made a vow with my foster father, saying:
'If I attain the wholesome Dharma, I shall return and teach it to you.'"
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to his father’s place; upon arrival, he soared into the air and performed various supernatural transformations.
When his father saw this, his heart was filled with great joy, and with palms joined, he made this vow:
"May I, in every lifetime, always serve as the king's barber."
At that time, the barber later encountered five pratyekabuddhas, all of whom made this vow:
"May I, in life after life, serve as the barber for various kings."
"Furthermore, during four successive births, he encountered Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and likewise made this same vow.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That barber was none other than Upāli here."
"Because he made this vow in a previous life, he has now become a barber for the king.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus again had this doubt:
"What meritorious deeds did Upāli perform to realize arhatship and become foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya?"
The Buddha said:
"Upāli, there is another causal connection for this.
Listen well, and I shall now explain it for you."

In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, appeared in the world, known as Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān.
At that time, the Buddha had a disciple who was an Arhat and the foremost among those who upheld the Vinaya.
Upāli served as that disciple’s attendant; throughout his life he maintained the holy life (brahmacarya) but did not attain the fruits of realization. As death approached, he made this vow:

"By the merit, karma, and roots of goodness from the precepts I have upheld, may I, in a future age when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni appears in the world, become a disciple of that World-Honored One in charge of the Vinaya, no different from my own Upādhyāya."
"That disciple was none other than Upāli; because he made this vow in the past, he has now attained this fruit.
Therefore, monks! Black karma brings black karmic retribution; white karma brings white karmic retribution; and mixed karma brings mixed karmic retribution."
"One should abandon the two types of karma and continue to cultivate white (wholesome) karma," and so forth, as explained extensively before.
At that time, the World-Honored One, beneath the Bodhi tree, subdued thirty-six koṭis of māra armies and realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then Māra went to the city of Kapilavastu and, from the midst of the sky, addressed King Śuddhodana, the members of the royal court, the ministers, and the common people, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has died this very night."

When King Śuddhodana heard this, his heart was filled with anguish; he fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground, and likewise the ladies of the palace, the ministers, and the common people all wept and were overcome with grief.

At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven surveyed the region below and, beholding this event, descended from mid-air and addressed the king and the multitude of people in the city of Kapilavastu, saying:
"Gautama has not died; he is now beneath the Bodhi tree, having realized the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, King Śuddhodana, the palace ladies, and the state ministers, upon suddenly hearing these words, leaped for joy with great delight.
At this very moment, King Amṛtodana gave birth to a son; because this day was one of universal rejoicing, the child was named Ānanda.
Once this child was born, eight wet nurses were appointed to raise him together.
At that time, King Amṛta summoned various physiognomists and sent them to examine the child. The physiognomists reported, saying:
"This child of yours shall personally serve as the attendant to Śākyamuni Buddha."
When King Amṛta heard these words, he thought to himself:
"I must now provide special protection for this son of mine; I must not allow Śākyamuni Buddha to see him."
Later, when the Buddha arrived at the city of Kapilavastu, the king immediately hid this son in the city of Vaiśālī, intending to bring him back once the Buddha had departed.

It is the constant nature of the World-Honored One that toward all sentient beings, there is nothing his mind does not perceive and nothing he does not know; this is explained in the same way as in the section on the precept against false speech and in the account of the eighteen-headed fish. Furthermore, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"This youth Ānanda has reached his final birth; it is fitting that he should go forth within my Dharma to serve as my personal attendant. He will be able to receive all the teachings I preach and retain them without any loss."
"After my parinirvāṇa, I shall attain the fruit of arhatship.
For the sake of delivering Ānanda, I must enter the palace of King Amṛtodana in Kapilavastu, yet I must ensure that neither the people of the palace nor the city do not know I have come."

Having formed this thought, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his supernormal powers and, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus, entered the palace of King Amṛta and sat down according to the Dharma.

When the king heard that the Buddha had arrived at his palace, he immediately hid the youth Ānanda in a room; the Buddha, knowing this, exercised his supernormal power to cause the door of that room to open of its own accord.
Ānanda arrived first at the Buddha’s dwelling and, having prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet, took up a fly-whisk and stood in attendance behind the Buddha, fanning him.

King Amṛta arrived later; after he had prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet and sat down to one side, the Buddha preached various subtle and wondrous dharmas to the king, and then rose from his seat and departed.
Due to the causal conditions of his past karma, the youth Ānanda followed the Buddha anyway.
Although the king, the queen, and their retinue of court ladies attempted to seize and detain the youth Ānanda, they were unable to hold him back.
The Buddha then addressed the king, the queen, and the others:
"This youth Ānanda is in his final existence.
None of you can detain him; you should permit him to depart."
The king then addressed the Buddha:
“If it must be so, World-Honored One, please allow him to return home for now; I shall see to it that he is sent forth in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"Very well, I grant you this.

Thereupon, King Amṛta immediately commanded all his kinsmen, both internal and external, as well as inviting śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to provide food and offerings; he even bestowed wealth, money, clothing, and garments upon the poor, the lowly, and beggars.

The youth Ānanda, having bid farewell to his kinsmen within that assembly, adorned himself with necklaces and mounted an elephant embellished with the seven treasures; escorted by a vast retinue surrounding him before and behind, he proceeded to the Nyagrodha Grove.

Upon reaching the city gate of Kapilavastu, the elephant upon which he was riding saw various exquisite lotus flowers in a pond; the elephant immediately went to the edge of the pond and, using its trunk, gathered up the lotus flowers.
The diviners and physiognomists examined these signs and reported to King Amṛta:
"The youth Ānanda has now gone forth to study; he does not forget what he hears with his ears."
Then Ānanda arrived at the Nyagrodha Grove, descended from his elephant, and approached the Buddha on foot; he prostrated himself in reverence and sat to one side.
The Buddha said to Daśabala Kāśyapa:
"You should deliver this youth Mahānandika according to the Dharma."
Having received the Buddha’s command, Daśabala Kāśyapa immediately ordained him and conferred the full precepts upon him.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Kapilavastu and proceeded to the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, a small sore broke out on the back of Ānanda; the Buddha ordered Jīvaka to treat it, and Jīvaka, following the Buddha’s instruction, attended to Ānanda.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne and extensively expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for the great assembly; the Venerable Ānanda was also present in this gathering to listen to the Dharma.
Jīvaka thought to himself:
"I shall treat Ānanda’s wound; now is precisely the right time.
Why is that? [Because...]"
"Because his mind was so focused on hearing the Dharma, he did not even know the pain as his flesh was being cut.
Having thought this, he took excellent medicine and applied it to the wound.
Once the wound had ripened, he cut it open with a knife to drain out the pus and blood, and again applied a superior ointment; consequently, the man was immediately healed.
However, while this procedure was being performed, Ānanda, because he was listening to the Dharma, remained completely unaware.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, Jīvaka addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"While I was treating Ānanda’s wound in the midst of his seat for the Dharma—cutting, excising, and lancing it with needles—Ānanda, because he was listening to the Dharma, did not perceive any of it."
The Venerable Ānanda replied,
"For the sake of hearing the Buddha's Dharma, even if my body were cut and minced like sesame seeds, I would not feel any pain."
At that time, the King of Physicians, the Great Healer, having witnessed this event, was struck with wonder.
Then all the bhikṣus, being filled with doubt, requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Venerable Ānanda, what karma did he perform in the past such that a carbuncle grew upon his back?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen now to the prior karma of Ānanda; it shall be explained in detail as before," and so on, until he spoke these verses:
“Even if a hundred kalpas should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must experience the retribution oneself.”
"In the distant past, in a bordering kingdom named Kīlaṭa, there was a king who ruled and governed. At that time, no Buddha had appeared; only a Pratyekabuddha had manifested in the world."
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha who, for the sake of alms, came to this city and approached the king’s palace.
Upon seeing him, the king became angry and struck him on the back with a pellet from a slingshot.
At that time, the Venerable One, having subdued his own pride, recognized that the king was not a fit vessel for the Dharma and departed from him. O Bhikṣus!

The king of that former time was none other than this Nanda. Because he struck a Pratyekabuddha with a lute out of a mind of anger, he suffered the retribution of malignant sores upon his back for five hundred lifetimes; such is the remaining karmic residue in this, his final body.
“Bhikṣus! If one performs deeds that are black, white, or mixed, one shall experience their retribution; this has been explained at length as before.
It was the constant custom of the Venerable Ānanda to feel joy:
If one practices in accordance with the true body of the Tathāgata, the mind will always be reverent;
if one practices in accordance with the emanation body of the Tathāgata, the mind will have little reverence.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Tathāgata and the bhikṣus to his home to provide various offerings.

Then, when the time had come, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the bhikṣus preceding and following him, went to the householder’s offering. Having finished the meal, he returned to his original location.
A bhikṣu asked Ānanda: "Today,
as you followed the Tathāgata to the meal offering, did you follow the true Buddha,
or did you follow the emanation Buddha?"
Ānanda replied, "Today I went there together with the Buddha, the World-Honored One; it was not a transformation body. The bhikṣus said:
"How do you know this? Ānanda replied,
"If I were to give [alms] to one who is a true practitioner of the Buddha's path, my heart would naturally feel reverence and inwardly harbor a sense of shame."
"If it were one who walks with a transformation Buddha, it would not be like this.
The bhikṣus said to one another:
"This Ānanda is truly extraordinary; he is able to discern the various characteristics, distinctions, and relative status between the true body and the transformation body."
Thereupon, people from both near and far all came to know that Ānanda was skilled in discerning various signs.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Rājagṛha for Śrāvastī and stayed in the Jeta Grove. The Venerable Ānanda donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for food.
At that time, there was a brahmin who encountered Ānanda on the road and thought to himself:
"I have previously heard that this disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama is skilled in divining signs; I should now test him to see whether he understands or not."
He then asked Ānanda, "In this Śālavana forest by the side of the road, how many leaves are there in total? Ānanda replied:
"There are this many hundreds, this many thousands, this many tens of thousands, and this many koṭis.
Having replied thus, he departed.

Then that brahmin took a handful of leaves from within the grove and counted them; he found there were seven hundred and seventy-seven leaves. He cast them outside the grove and stood there in silence.
Then, after Ānanda had finished his almsround, he returned by the same path; the brahmin asked him, "Noble One!
How many leaves are there in this forest?"
He replied, "Previously there were this many hundreds of thousands of koṭis; now seven hundred and seventy-seven leaves are missing.
When the brahmin heard this report, he marveled at how remarkably rare it was that he so well understood calculation.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What karma did this venerable Ānanda previously plant such that he is so skilled in divining signs and calculating?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“In the past, he planted roots of merit; the details are as extensively explained before, up until the recitation of this verse:
‘Even if a hundred eons should pass, The karma one has created does not perish;’”
"When causes and conditions meet, The fruit of retribution is received by oneself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In a former age, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a brahmin who took a wife and begot a son. When the boy reached twenty-one days of age, he gathered his kinsmen and prepared various foods and drinks; for this reason, he gave the child the name Mahāśveta (Great White)."

As he gradually grew older, he traveled among the people and studied the methods of calculation consisting of sixty thousand verses; he mastered them thoroughly and subsequently taught the methods of calculation to others.
"For this reason, throughout five hundred lifetimes, I have been clearly aware, and I have also taught others;

now, in this final body, I have attained this penetration. On another occasion, the Venerable Ānanda went to the palace of King Prasenajit. Upon seeing him arrive, Jayasena rose with joy, prostrated, and sat to one side. He addressed the Venerable One, saying:

"Since my birth, through the natural ripening of karma, there has always appeared for me a meal consisting of silver *śāli* fragrant rice, two heads of cooked partridge, and a single stalk of sugarcane. At every mealtime, these descend from the sky and enter a silver platter; however, one head of partridge always falls upon the ground instead of into the platter."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard these words, felt great wonder. He returned to the monastery and informed the others.
Then all the bhikṣus went together to inform the Blessed One of this matter. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the past, there was a householder in this city of Vārāṇasī who possessed many precious treasures and many fields and estates. From one of his estates, he sent new non-glutinous rice, as well as dead pheasants, sugarcane, and other such things."
It is the constant law of the world that if a Buddha does not appear in the world, there shall be Pratyekabuddhas who manifest to teach and transform beings.

At that time, a certain Pratyekabuddha was wandering from door to door begging for food and arrived at the house of a householder; entering its gate, the householder saw that his deportment was upright and his speech was gentle, and his heart was filled with joy. He then took fresh non-glutinous rice, two roasted pheasants, and a stalk of sugarcane, and offered them as alms to the Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted it with his bowl; the sugarcane, the rice, and one partridge entered the bowl, while the other partridge fell to the ground.
It was due to this karmic cause that he received such a retribution.
That householder at that time was none other than King Jayasena; for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, he was born in the heavens and experienced various pleasures.
Having exhausted his celestial retribution, he was again born in the human world as a king, experiencing such supreme fortune.
"Therefore, you all! If you wish to provide food as an offering to the Saṅgha, you should diligently bestow it and ensure that it does not fall to the ground.

When King Jayasena heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, recounting this account of the past, his heart was filled with joy; he conceived great faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and sitting alone in one place, he reflected thus:
“Because I made offerings to pratyekabuddhas in my previous lives, I have obtained such a reward as this.
I should extensively provide for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, so that I will surely receive great benefit in future lives.”
Having had this thought, the diviner reported:
"Tomorrow Ānanda shall rightfully receive the rank of the head-wrapping reward and the rank of consecration."
Upon hearing these words, the king remained silent and said nothing.
During that night, a malignant ulcer suddenly broke out on the forehead of the Venerable Ānanda. After one night had passed, the king heard of it and immediately thought:
"To make offerings to those of virtuous merit brings immeasurable blessings; I have personally served him."
Having formed this thought, he immediately commanded all renowned physicians throughout the land to assemble at the palace:
"Ānanda is ill; you shall go to treat him."
The physicians, having received the royal decree, went to Ānanda’s quarters; there they selected a highly skilled practitioner who immediately applied the needle to drain the foul blood.
The King himself held a parasol with a thousand-spoked wheel over Ānanda, and once the bleeding was finished, he applied excellent medicinal ointment.
The King himself wrapped a silk cloth around Ānanda’s head, and on that very day his wound was healed; the King then prostrated, took leave of Ānanda, and departed.
When the assembly of monks witnessed this event, they were all filled with doubt and uncertainty, and they said to the Buddha:
“Venerable World-Honored One!”
“What meritorious deeds did Ānanda perform in the past,
such that he now experiences the King personally attending to him?
The Buddha said:
"This Ānanda planted the roots of merit in the past; the details are as previously explained.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a physician. At that time, a pratyekabuddha fell ill and went to the physician's place."
The physician immediately served him with all his heart and reverence, saying to the Pratyekabuddha:
"Venerable One!
Whatever robes, food, and all necessary medicines you require, I shall provide them all; I will certainly see that your illness is cured."
"Serve him as instructed until his illness is cured.
The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣus!"
The physician at that time was none other than Ānanda.

Because he made offerings to a sick pratyekabuddha in the past, he enjoyed celestial bliss for immeasurable lifetimes and, throughout five hundred births, constantly received superior karmic rewards among humans, being personally honored by all kings, brahmins, ministers, and nobles.
"In this final birth, King Jayasena personally held the parasol for me, and as a sovereign of ten thousand chariots, he humbled himself to serve me, as has been explained at length previously.

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Śrāvastī and traveled by stages toward Vārāṇasī; eventually arriving outside the city, he stayed in a village called Brāhmaṇagrāma, where a great assembly of śrāvakas surrounded him and remained nearby.

They were as follows: the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya; the Venerable Aśvajit; the Venerable Bhadrika; the Bhikṣu Mahānāman; the Bhikṣu Yaśas; the Bhikṣu Pūrṇa; the Bhikṣu Vimala; the Bhikṣu Gavāmpati; the Bhikṣu Subāhu; the Venerable Śāriputra; the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana; the Venerable Mahākāśyapa; the Venerable Kauṣṭhila; the Venerable Kapphiṇa; Aniruddha; Nandika; and Kimpila—all of whom were dwelling at the village of Bālakalpa.
The bhikṣu Miaozhen, Ānanda, and an immeasurable assembly of great śrāvaka bhikṣus came to the Buddha’s dwelling after midday, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down in order.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I am now advanced in years and my physical strength is gradually fading; I lack the power to preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.

While the Buddha was staying among the brahmin villages of Vārāṇasī, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana requested Ānanda to serve as the Buddha’s attendant, and Ānanda followed the venerable ones' instructions exactly.
The Buddha then praised Ānanda.
At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus all conceived doubts and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What meritorious deeds has Ānanda cultivated?"
"Now he has become my paternal uncle's younger brother on the mother's side;
furthermore, he serves as my attendant, being so intelligent and wise that he hears the Buddha's words without ever forgetting them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should all know!
Ānanda himself committed this karma," [the Buddha said], "as explained at length above.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, there was a king in the city of Vārāṇasī named Sūrya. He ruled the kingdom with established laws and rites, causing every person to be abundant, joyful, peaceful, and free from all calamities and hardships."
Later, the king had a son born to his queen. Within twenty-one days, he summoned his ministers and officials, assembled them in court for a banquet, and intended to bestow a name upon the child.
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty’s name is Sūrya; it is fitting that the son be named Mahāsūrya."
As his son gradually grew up, he was appointed as the crown prince.
Later, another son was born to the queen consort; the ministers conferred upon him a name, calling him Sūryamati.
The crown prince constantly contemplated with a joyful heart the thought of leaving the household life.
Whenever he saw his father, the king, either practicing unrighteousness or following the laws of the kingdom, the prince would reflect upon these matters and think:
"If I should later inherit the royal throne and practice such ways as these, I will surely fall into hell from which there shall be no time of escape."
Having formed this thought, he went to the place where the king was, and after performing his prostrations and obeisances, he addressed his father, the king, saying:
"I now wish to leave the household life; I pray that Your Majesty will show me compassion and grant me permission to go."
Then his father, the king, said to his son:

"There are various seers and non-Buddhists who serve fire and worship deities, practicing austerities and observing precepts; they perform such deeds solely seeking to be born in a royal family in a future life as a prince to enjoy all manner of pleasures."
"You now see this body receiving its karmic retribution; why then do you abandon pleasure and wish to perform such arduous tasks?
At that time, the Prince again addressed the King, saying, "Please grant me permission to leave the household life."
The king, knowing that his son’s intention was not to seek worldly pleasures, granted him permission to renounce the household life.

Once the prince had received the king’s release, he immediately entered the mountains to the abode of the rishis to renounce the world and practice the Way. The father-king then installed his younger brother, Divākara, to succeed to the position of crown prince.
At that time, Prince Sūrya, having reached the mountains, applied his mind in contemplation and realized the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha.
Later, when his physical illness had subsided and his strength was restored, he returned to the city of Vārāṇasī.
When the people saw him, they said to the king:
"Prince Sūrya has entered the mountains to practice the path and realized the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; he is now coming into the city.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately went out to welcome Sūrya, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Great Seer! You require food and clothing, while I seek merit; I now invite you, Great Seer, to dwell in my grove, where I shall provide whatever necessities you require at all times."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that he had accepted, the king immediately commanded Prince Divākara to attend upon the Pratyekabuddha, providing for him and supplying all his needs.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Seer, while in meditative concentration, perceived that Prince Sūryajñāna would pass away seven days hence; he addressed the prince, saying:
"Brother, why do you not now seek to leave the household life?"
The younger brother said,
"I wish to go forth.
The Pratyekabuddha told him:
"Please inform the Father King.
Prince Divākara went to his father’s presence and said, "I wish to renounce the household life;
I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission."
Upon hearing these words, the king became enraged and said to the crown prince:
"Your elder brother, Sūrya, has now gone forth into homelessness; after my death, there must be a successor to the lineage. Therefore, I will not permit you to leave."
At that time, having heard that the king would not release his younger brother, the Pratyekabuddha went to the king’s presence and spoke these verses:
“Sūrya, release Divākara, And let him follow me into homelessness;
Homelessness is the most supreme matter, Praised by all the Buddhas.”
The Father King replied:
"Great Seer, you should know!

Since you have already left the household life, my national law requires that there must be a successor. Only Ajātaśatru (Dayi) shall be made aware of the royal position; it is sufficient for him to cultivate merit while remaining at home. What need is there for him to leave the household life?"
Then that Pratyekabuddha spoke again in verse:
"The King’s former thoughts were one thing, but this matter is another;
seven days from now, Divākara will pass away."
The king asked the Pratyekabuddha,
"Will Prince Divākara certainly not survive after seven days? He replied:
"So be it," the king said. "If this is so,
release him and let him go forth into the religious life."
After the Prince had left the household life, he gave rise to a virtuous mind and made offerings to a pratyekabuddha.
That pratyekabuddha suffered from wind-disorder; as he held his alms bowl in his hand, it shook and was unstable.
When the prince saw this, he took a golden bracelet and used it to support the bowl, yet the bowl remained motionless.
Having observed this, the prince rejoiced and made this aspiration:
"May my listening to the Dharma likewise be such that when the Dharma enters my heart, it shall never again waver."

"In the past, when the Pratyekabuddha had not yet attained the realization of the fruit, he constantly preached the perfect, subtle, and supreme Dharma for his younger brother, Divākara; now that he has attained the realization of the fruit, he no longer preaches the Dharma."
Having seen this, Divākara said to the Pratyekabuddha, "While you were not yet ordained, you constantly preached the Dharma; for what reason have you attained the fruit and now remain silent?
The Pratyekabuddha replied:
“I have not, in truth, preached the Dharma.
Ajita asked, “Who, then,
is fit to preach the Dharma?”
The Pratyekabuddha replied,
"When you know that a Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world, you shall preach the various kinds of perfect and sublime Dharma.
Upon hearing this, the Prince made the following aspiration:

"By these roots of goodness, may I in a future age become a younger brother to the Buddha; furthermore, may I leave the household life to personally attend upon and make offerings to him, and by hearing the Dharma and grasping its meaning, may I attain great dhāraṇī."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha said to his younger brother:
"Seven days from now you shall reach the end of your life; always maintain this state of mind and do not let it be forgotten."
When the seven days had passed and he had not yet attained the realization of the fruit, as he was about to depart, he again made this vow:
"May it be as previously wished.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The Pratyekabuddha’s younger brother at that time was none other than Ānanda.
Because he had made offerings to the Pratyekabuddha in a past life, he made this vow:
'In a future age, may I become the Buddha's younger brother, personally receiving his teachings and making offerings to him, possessing great learning and total retention (dhāraṇī).'"
"This is why he is now my brother;
he is foremost in intelligence, like water poured from one vessel into another.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What virtuous deeds did Ānanda perform in the past,
such that he now receives this praise and acclaim from the World-Honored One amidst the great assembly for his incomparable intelligence, his powerful memory, and his flawless retention?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Ānanda cultivated meritorious deeds in the past; the details are as previously explained.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, during this Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of sentient beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Kāśyapa, who resided at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī."
The Buddha had a disciple who was foremost among the learned, possessing vast knowledge that he never forgot and being preeminent in intelligence.

This disciple had a follower who, from the time of his ordination, constantly practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet until the end of his life, he failed to attain the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*).
At the time of death, he made a single-minded vow:
"By these roots of goodness I have cultivated, may I, in a future life, become a close attendant disciple of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, no different from how it is now."
"Among my disciples, he is foremost in intelligence; I pray that Śākyamuni Tathāgata will grant me a prediction [of enlightenment] no different from his. O bhikṣus!
That disciple was none other than Ānanda himself.
Because of the power of the vows he made with a virtuous mind in a previous life, he is now foremost among my disciples in intelligence.

"O Bhikṣus! If one performs actions that are black, white, or mixed, one will each receive their respective retribution. You should abandon mixed and black actions, and constantly cultivate white actions."

The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, surrounded by five hundred bhikṣus who were all arhats, with the sole exception of Devadatta, who had not yet attained the fruit of sainthood.
At that time, the land was suffering from famine, and as the people had no food, it was difficult for them to obtain anything through begging.

Among the assembly was a bhikṣu possessed of supernatural powers who, soaring into the air, descended into the Jambūvana grove to gather fragrant and delicious jambū fruits. Having filled his bowl to capacity, he returned to his original location, where he provided for the fourfold assembly and satisfied himself as well.

Alternatively, he went to the Mīra grove, descended into the Kapittha grove, or descended into the Amṛtavana garden, or descended into the Āmalaka grove to gather fragrant and delicious fruits. Having filled his bowl to capacity, he returned to his original location, where he provided for the fourfold assembly and satisfied himself as well.

There may be a bhikṣu who possesses mastery over supernormal powers (ṛddhi), who ascends into the air and goes to Uttarakuru to take naturally grown, fragrant, and delicious non-glutinous rice, returning to his original location with his bowl full to the brim; he then makes offerings to the fourfold assembly and also satisfies himself.

Or there may be a bhikṣu who possesses mastery over supernormal powers, traveling through the air to other lands to beg for various kinds of exquisite food and drink, until his bowl is full, as described at length above.

Or there may be a bhikṣu who, by means of his supernormal power, goes to the abode of the Four Great Kings, or to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, to take the refined and wondrous food from the celestial kitchen, returning with his bowl full to the brim, as described at length above.
At that time, Devadatta, seeing the bhikṣus possess such supernormal powers as taking various fruits and foods, thought to himself:

"This land is suffering from famine and the people have no food," and so on, as extensively described before, until he took food and drink from the celestial kitchen of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, thereby satisfying the fourfold assembly and himself as well.

"If I possessed supernatural powers, I would immediately ascend into the void and descend into the Jambūvana grove to gather fragrant and delicious jambu fruits, filling my bowl to sufficiency; I would then offer them to the fourfold assembly and satisfy myself as well. As explained at length previously, this would extend even to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where I would take food and drink from the celestial kitchen to satisfy the fourfold assembly and satisfy myself as well."
"Who possesses the power that will enable me to see the Noble Path? Relying on the power of their teaching, may I attain supernatural powers?
Having had this thought, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side.
Devadatta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that you, out of compassion, will teach me the Noble Path so that I may attain supernormal powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Devadatta had conceived a mind of transgression and rebellion, said to Devadatta:

“You should receive the higher training in ethics and practice it with diligent mind; you will then attain supernormal powers. Furthermore, you should receive the higher training in mind and the higher training in wisdom, and practice them diligently within your mind; you will then attain supernormal powers as well as other dharmas.”
When Devadatta heard these words, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One is unwilling to teach me the path of supernatural powers.
Having had this thought, he rose from his seat and went to where the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya was.
Having arrived, he asked Ājñātakauṇḍinya: "Venerable One!
I pray that out of compassion you will teach me the Noble Path so that I may attain supernormal powers."
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya observed the Buddha and knew that Devadatta had conceived a mind of transgression and rebellion. Having observed this, he said to Devadatta:
"You should increase your cultivation within the mind of form; then you will immediately attain supernormal powers as well as other dharmas."
Having heard these words, Devadatta thought to himself:
"Even this Elder is unwilling to teach me the methods of supernatural powers.
He then went to visit Aśvajit, Vāṣpa, Kapphiṇa, Mahānāman, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, Subāhu, and so on, up to the five hundred Elders; having arrived, he asked them:
“Venerable Elder, have compassion!
Teach me the Noble Path so that I may attain supernormal powers.

At that time, the five hundred bhikṣus, including Subāhu, all observed the Buddha’s intention and knew that Devadatta had conceived a mind of transgression and rebellion. Having observed this, they addressed Devadatta, saying:

"You should diligently practice by increasing the mind focused on form; then you will attain supernormal powers as well as other dharmas. This applies even up to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: you should diligently practice by increasing the mind focused on consciousness; then you will attain supernormal powers and all other dharmas."
When Devadatta heard these words, he thought to himself:

"These five hundred elders likewise refuse to teach me the supernatural powers of the Noble Path; it seems these five hundred elders have previously consulted with the World-Honored One and decided not to permit me to receive instruction in the Noble Path."
"Why is this? Now I see that the Buddha and the five hundred elders are unwilling to teach me the path of the noble ones and supernormal powers.
He then thought further:
"In this way, who could teach me the noble path and supernormal powers?
At that time, Daśabala Kāśyapa was in the Sennyaka Cave at Rājagṛha; I went to that place."
"That Elder is upright in heart and free from guile; furthermore, my younger brother Ānanda is his personal teacher. That Elder Daśabala is able to teach me the noble path and supernormal powers."
Having thought this, Devadatta went at once to the place where Daśabala Kāśyapa was, prostrated himself at his feet, stood to one side, and spoke these words:
"Venerable Daśabala Kāśyapa, out of compassion, please teach me the noble path and supernormal powers."

At that time, Daśabala Kāśyapa did not discern the intention of the Buddha nor the intentions of the assembly of five hundred senior elders; furthermore, he was unaware that Devadatta had conceived such a mind of parricide.
Because he did not observe [the truth], he taught Devadatta the supernatural powers of the Noble Path.
At that time, Devadatta dwelt practicing wholesome deeds during both the first and last watches of the night; relying upon the first dhyāna, he attained supernatural power.
By means of supernormal power, he transforms a single body into many bodies and merges many bodies into a single body, appearing or disappearing at will.
Through the power of his wisdom and vision, he is able to manifest in such a manner.
Furthermore, they pass through mountain crags, walls, and barriers without obstruction, as if through empty space;
they emerge from and submerge into the great earth as if it were water;
and they sit cross-legged in mid-air as if upon the ground.
Some leaped into the air like flying birds, while others, standing on the ground, reached out their hands to touch the sun and moon.
Having attained these supernormal powers, Devadatta thought to himself:

"I have attained such supernormal powers; I can also perform various miraculous transformations. Let me go to the Jambū forest, take fragrant and delicious fruits, fill my bowl to capacity, offer them to the fourfold assembly, and satisfy myself as well," as described in detail previously.
He even went as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three to take food from the celestial kitchen, offering it to the fourfold assembly while also satisfying himself.
He then reflected further:
"Who is the most eminent person in this kingdom of Magadha?"
"I shall submit to him;
because of that person, I will cause all people to revere me.
He then reflected further:
“The crown prince of this country, Ajātaśatru, shall become king after his father the monarch passes away; I must subdue him.
If I can bring Prince Ajātaśatru under my control, I will cause all people to revere me.”

Having formed this thought, he went to where Ajātaśatru was; he immediately manifested a supernatural form, transforming himself into a white elephant. He entered through the main gate and exited through a small gate, or entered through a small gate and exited through the main gate. Having done so, he manifested his own body again and entered the main gate, transforming into a swift horse and exiting through a small gate, after which he manifested his own body once more, intending to enter a small gate.

Having emerged from the main gate in the form of a bull king, he immediately manifested his true body; holding his almsbowl according to the Dharma, he went to the place where Ajātaśatru was. He then transformed his body to appear like a small child, wearing golden necklaces, and sat upon the crown prince’s lap, rising and sitting again and again as he moved about restlessly.
The Prince, recognizing these as the signs of Devadatta’s supernatural powers, would either clap him, embrace him, pat him, or kiss him, and then spit into his mouth.
Because Devadatta’s mind was greedy for the benefit of offerings, he immediately swallowed that saliva.
At that time, Ajātaśatru gave rise to a perverted thought and reflected thus:
"This Devadatta possesses supernatural powers superior to those of the Buddha."

At that time, Devadatta manifested his true form; the prince, conceiving a heart of reverence, immediately prostrated himself in worship and offered various gifts, sending five hundred precious chariots as an escort.
When Devadatta departed, Ajātaśatru returned to his own quarters and visited Devadatta twice every day to attend upon him and provide offerings.
At that time, the Prince ordered five hundred large cauldrons to be set up to prepare various foods and drinks, which were sent to Devadatta as an offering.
Then Devadatta took them and ate himself, surrounded by five hundred bhikṣus with whom he shared the meal.
At that time, while a bhikṣu was begging for alms in the city of Rājagṛha at dawn, he heard these words:

"This Devadatta has received various kinds of beneficial offerings from the crown prince, which continue daily at two sessions without interruption; furthermore, he is served and honored with five hundred chariots and precious carriages, provided with food and drink prepared in five hundred cauldrons, and he eats surrounded by five hundred bhikṣus who partake of his own meal."

When the bhikṣus had heard this matter, they returned to their respective quarters after completing their almsround in sequence. Having eaten according to the Dharma and put away their robes and bowls, they washed their feet, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down in order.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
This morning we entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms and heard that Devadatta had received great gains and offerings from Prince Ajātaśatru, as described in detail above."
"Even as many as five hundred bhikṣus sat surrounding him to eat together.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, Devadatta accepted these benefits and offerings, yet through this he brought harm upon himself and harm upon others as well."
For what reason? O Bhikṣus!
It is like the plantain tree, which withers and dies as soon as it bears fruit; in this way, it brings about its own destruction.
Devadatta’s reception of these offerings was likewise so:
just as bamboo or reeds wither and die once they produce flowers or fruit, and just as a mule dies upon conceiving and bearing a foal.
"O bhikṣus! Devadatta’s receiving of these benefits was likewise so. O bhikṣus!"
If Devadatta accepts offerings and gain, he will incur ignorance.
Day and night, Devadatta shall long endure ill repute, suffering, and lack of benefit; such is the retribution he receives.
“Monks, you should understand it thus.
At that time, Devadatta obtained extensive offerings and gains, which gave rise to greed; no longer seeking anything further, he developed a perverted mind and gave rise to a contrary thought:

“The World-Honored One is now old and his strength is weak; he is weary from preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. It would be better for the World-Honored One to entrust the fourfold assembly to me, so that I may instruct them and preach the Dharma for them myself.”
“World-Honored One, you should now sit in tranquil seclusion, cultivate wholesome dharmas, and dwell eternally in peace and bliss.
When Devadatta had formed this thought, he immediately lost his supernormal powers, yet he himself did not realize that he had lost them.

At that time, the bhikṣu Kakudra cultivated the four fearlessnesses and eliminated thoughts of greed; upon his death, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven. There he saw that Devadatta had lost his supernatural powers, though Devadatta himself was unaware of it.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was staying on Mount Gayāśīrṣa in the forest of Terrifying Deer within the kingdom of Kajaṅgala.

Then the Brahmā-son Kakuda, vanishing from that heaven, went to Maudgalyāyana’s location in the time it takes to bend or stretch an arm; he prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and spoke these words:
“Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
Now it can be known that for the sake of gain and offerings, Devadatta gave rise to greed and further desired more; with a perverted mind, he conceived this thought:
"The World-Honored One is now old and his strength is weak; he is weary and exhausted from preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly."
"Blessed One, it would be better if you were to entrust the fourfold assembly to me; I myself shall instruct them and preach the Dharma for them.
The Blessed One should remain in tranquil seclusion, realizing and practicing the wholesome dharmas in constant peace and happiness."
"At that moment, as soon as Devadatta gave rise to this thought, he immediately lost his supernormal powers, yet he himself did not realize that he had lost them.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"

Arising with a heart of compassion, he went to where the Buddha was and related the aforementioned circumstances concerning Devadatta, up until the point that he lost his supernatural powers without even realizing it himself.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana silently accepted the words of the Brahmā-son.
Knowing that Maudgalyāyana had accepted them, the Brahmā-son Kakuṇḍala felt great joy; he prostrated at Maudgalyāyana’s feet and suddenly vanished.

At that time, having seen the Brahmā depart, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered such a state of meditative concentration that he vanished from Mount Śarkarākṣa and reappeared within the Bamboo Grove Monastery at Kalandakanivāpa in Rājagṛha. He approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana reported in full all the words he had received from the devaputra Kāḷodāyin.
Then the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Did you already know of Devadatta’s aforementioned deeds?"
"Or shall I inform you so that you may know for the first time?
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have known him for a long time.
While the World-Honored One was speaking these words with Maudgalyāyana, Devadatta, together with four bhikṣus—
firstly Kālika, secondly Khaṇḍadravya, thirdly Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and fourthly Samudradatta— approached the place where the Buddha was with these four men.
The World-Honored One saw Devadatta and his followers approaching from afar and said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Cease and say no more!
Those ignorant ones, Devadatta and his followers, are coming."
"This ignorant man will now, in my presence, surely speak of these matters as described above and praise himself.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, entered such a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), vanished from the Bamboo Grove, went to Mount Gayāsīsa, reached his original location, and sat down according to the Dharma.
At that time, Devadatta went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you are now advanced in years and your strength is weak; preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly is a wearisome task for you."
"Blessed One, it would be better for you to grant me your assembly; I myself shall instruct them and preach the Dharma to them.
The Blessed One should remain in tranquil seclusion, cultivating wholesome dharmas and dwelling forever in peace and happiness."
The World-Honored One replied:

"Even though Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana—my foremost disciples, who are wise and intelligent, who have practiced the holy life, attained supernormal powers, and realized the fruit of Arhatship—I do not even entrust the community of bhikṣus to them; how much less so to you, a witless fool who eats the spittle of others?"
At that time, having heard these words, Devadatta thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One now praises Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others, while harboring resentment toward me."
He reviled him, saying:
"Are you an unintelligent eater of spittle?
At that time, Devadatta consequently gave rise to the seven kinds of rebellious thoughts toward the World-Honored One.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Scroll Thirteen.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Scroll Fourteen.
At that time, Devadatta let out a cry of distress, nodded his head three times, and then rose and departed. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, Ānanda was standing to the left and right of the Buddha, fanning him.
Then the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"You should now go into this Bamboo Grove Monastery and summon all the bhikṣus to assemble here in the dining hall."
At that time, Ānanda, having received the command, went around summoning everyone to assemble in the dining hall.
Then Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The assembly has now gathered."
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the dining hall, spread out his seat, and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this world, there are five kinds of teachers."
What are these five?

First, there is a teacher who, though not himself endowed with the precepts, claims to be so; his disciple has lived with him for a long time and thus knows that his teacher is not endowed with the precepts.
They said to one another:
"If we were to tell others, and they were to hear it, our teacher would be held in contempt; how then could we continue to live with and serve him?"
"The teacher knows what is good and what is evil; we should protect him and not speak of it to others. Why is this?
This teacher of ours provides us at all times with robes, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and bedding."
At that time, the disciple, coveting these provisions, will shield the teacher and not speak to others to let them know of his broken precepts.
At such a time, that teacher will require the disciple to shield him.
As has been stated above, this is the first teacher in this world.

Furthermore, as for the second teacher: there is a teacher in the world who maintains his life by means of impure things, yet lives himself with what is pure; this, too, is not a fault or transgression.

A disciple of his had lived in one place for a long time; later, he learned that my teacher sustained himself by using impure things, and that even one who uses pure things would likewise incur guilt.
"If my disciples were to speak of these matters concerning their teacher, outsiders would hold them in contempt.
For this reason, if my disciples must live by means of it, let this teacher personally incur all manner of impure offenses; however, it does not concern my disciples."
Furthermore, this teacher constantly thinks:
"We provide him with clothing, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and bedding from time to time.
At that time, the disciples become greedily attached to these provisions and seek to protect the teacher; meanwhile, the teacher constantly dwells on these thoughts:
"This disciple has deceived me.
This is the second teacher in the world.
Furthermore, as for the third teacher: there is another teacher in the world such as this:
The teacher’s wisdom and vision are impure, yet he himself maintains that his wisdom is pure and without fault.
His disciple has resided with him for a long time in one place and thus perceives that the teacher’s wisdom and vision are indeed impure.
"The teacher himself considers his wisdom to be pure and faultless, yet he now speaks of us to outsiders; the teacher treats us with contempt and discourtesy when he goes abroad.

Having obtained such a teacher, how can we possibly survive? This teacher’s impurity of wisdom and vision and his own offenses are matters he should know for himself; they are no concern of ours, his disciples."
Furthermore, this teacher constantly thinks:
"We provide them with food, drink, clothing, medicine, and bedding from time to time.
At that time, the disciples become greedily attached to these provisions and seek to protect their teacher; meanwhile, the teacher constantly reflects:
"May this disciple protect me. This is the third teacher in the world.
Furthermore, as for the fourth teacher: again, there is such a teacher in the world as follows:
He falsely bestows various predictions upon others, yet considers himself not false, thinking: "The predictions I bestow are all entirely true.
His disciples have lived with him for a long time in one place; seeing their teacher falsely bestowing various predictions upon people while considering himself not false, they think:
"The predictions he bestows are all entirely true."
The disciples said:

"If we were to report this to outsiders, our teacher would surely treat us with contempt and discourtesy. Since we have obtained such a teacher as our companion, whatever offense this teacher commits by falsely bestowing prophecies is his own affair; he should know it himself, but it is none of our disciples' business."
This teacher thinks: "I shall provide protection for all of them.
This teacher constantly reflects upon this from time to time.
"We, as your disciples, shall provide you with clothing, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, and bedding.
At that time, the disciples, being greedily attached to these provisions, sought to protect their teacher; the teacher thought to himself:
"I have falsely bestowed a prophecy upon them so that the disciples might protect me, and they will constantly keep this thought in mind toward me."
This is the fourth teacher in this world.
Furthermore, as for the fifth teacher: there is another teacher in the world who constantly teaches what is false and delusive, yet considers himself to be speaking the truth.
A disciple of his had lived with him for a long time and observed that the teacher constantly taught doctrines that were false, yet he took them to be true.

[The disciple thought: "If we disciples speak of this to outsiders, they will surely despise and fail to honor us. Since we have obtained such a teacher as our companion, how can we coexist with him? This teacher’s sin of teaching false doctrines is something the teacher himself must know; it is not the business of us disciples."
The teacher constantly thinks:
"My disciples provide me with clothing, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and bedding.
Those disciples, being greedily attached to these provisions, seek to protect and support the teacher; the teacher, in turn, constantly thinks:
"Although my teaching is false and illusory, I can cause my disciples to protect me.
This is the fifth teacher in this world.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I maintain the purity of my precepts; I personally possess this reality of pure precepts, for I know myself to be free from defilement. Furthermore, because I teach my disciples to practice the pure precepts, I do not need to constantly shield them on account of their conduct. I have no anxiety or fear regarding this. I sustain myself with pure things, for I employ these truly pure things; thus, I do not need to constantly shield my disciples, and I have no anxiety or fear regarding this."

"O Bhikṣus! My wisdom and vision perceive the true nature of reality, and this too shall remain true. I have no anxiety regarding this fear; you should not cause my disciples to protect me for the sake of my wisdom and vision."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"That which I have prophesied is indeed true; because I am mindful of the truth, I have no sorrow regarding this fear. You disciples should not feel the need to protect me for the sake of my prophecy."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“I teach the Dharma according to reality, and because it is likewise based on reality, you need have no anxiety or fear regarding this. You should not cause my disciples, for the sake of the Dharma, to seek to shield or protect me.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know that there are five kinds of false teachers in the world who, because they themselves possess faults, cause their disciples to shield them.
I should not be like this; I should have no anxiety or fear, nor should I rely on the power of you, my disciples. I shall constantly reprove you, bhikṣus."
If there are bhikṣus who can endure my reproaches, they may remain close to my Dharma;
if they cannot endure my reproaches, let them withdraw and disperse of their own accord.
It is like a potter placing unbaked vessels into a fire: those that are well-made manifest their true durability, while those that are defective naturally shatter.
The potter neither gives rise to a mind of attachment nor feels any fear; good and evil reveal themselves, and he should remain as one who acts appropriately.
I am also like this; when you receive and study my Dharma, I constantly reprove and scold you.
Those who are good may practice the truth for themselves, while those who are evil may withdraw and disperse as they please.
Because the Dharma I have taught is pure, you should not feel fear.
"You all should know!
Having said these words, he rose from his seat and entered his own vihāra.
At that time, the bhikṣu Devadatta spoke to four bhikṣus:
The first was named Kokālika, the second Khaṇḍadravya, the third Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and the fourth Samudradatta. They said, "Come, let us be your companions;
while that śramaṇa Gautama still lives in this world, we five, being of one mind, shall break up the Great Assembly and destroy the Wheel of Dharma."
After we have passed away, our names will be renowned in future generations, and such a reputation as this will emerge concerning us:
"The Venerable Devadatta and others, while the Śramaṇa Gautama was still in the world, possessed great supernormal powers and majesty."
"Devadatta and the other five have succeeded in breaking the Wheel of the Dharma of the Saṃgha;
my name shall spread throughout the four quarters. Kokālika then replied to Devadatta:
"We are unable to break the harmony of the Saṃgha of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, nor can we break his Wheel of Dharma. Why is this? "

Devadatta! Furthermore, the World-Honored One’s śrāvaka disciples possess great supernormal powers and majesty, as well as the divine eye; they know my thoughts from afar, and if we were to deliberate on matters together, they would fully understand them all.
"For this reason, we are unable to break their harmonious Saṃgha.
Devadatta replied to Kokālika and the others, saying:
"I have an excellent expedient: let us go to the elder bhikṣus and request that they provide us with offerings."
"Whatever things you require, we shall provide them all so that nothing is lacking.

Furthermore, he went to the young bhikṣus to provide for them: to those without bowls he gave bowls; to those without robes he gave robes. Whatever they required, he provided it fully; to those seeking the Dharma he bestowed the Dharma, and to those seeking instruction he taught them, causing them all to achieve success.
Kokālika and the others replied to Devadatta,
"This expedient will also accomplish the task. Thereupon,
Devadatta, in order to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, went to the elder bhikṣus and explained his intention.
The elder bhikṣus immediately realized that Devadatta intended to break the harmony of the Saṃgha by employing such means.
Having understood this, the elders informed one another, saying:
"Devadatta intends to employ means for the purpose of breaking the unity of the Saṃgha."

Having seen this cause, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and reported that Devadatta intended to split the harmonious Saṃgha and the Wheel of Dharma; they informed the World-Honored One in detail of these circumstances:
"Devadatta has the intent to destroy the Saṃgha and the Wheel."
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should separately admonish Devadatta, as well as anyone else who acts in such a manner."
One should admonish him, saying: "Devadatta!
Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha by persisting in acts of strife and contention."

Devadatta! You should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Great Teacher’s instruction and Dharma may be made radiant and you may dwell in peace and happiness.
“Devadatta! You and your followers should now desist from the act of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

One should dwell in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and a single voice, like water and milk mixed together, so that the teachings of the Great Master may be made radiant and one may abide in peace and happiness.
"Devadatta! You should now desist from this act of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus thus admonished him individually, Devadatta remained obstinate in his position and had no intention of relinquishing it, saying:
"This matter is true; all else is false.
Then the bhikṣus reported this entire incident to the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."

"I have already admonished Devadatta individually; while we were admonishing him individually, Devadatta remained obstinate and refused to relinquish his position, asserting that this matter is true and all else is false."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) against Devadatta to admonish him before the assembly; if there are others of a similar kind, they should be admonished in this same manner."
When it is time to spread the seating mats, the *gaṇḍī* should be struck, and one should first announce: "The Saṃgha is requested to assemble.
Once the Saṃgha has assembled, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Devadatta desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by engaging in contentious matters and dwelling in what is contrary to the Dharma.
When the bhikṣus have already offered him separate admonitions, he remains obstinate during those admonitions and refuses to relinquish his position, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false."

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, the Saṃgha should authorize this: the Saṃgha now performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to admonish Devadatta regarding this matter:
'You, Devadatta, must not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, nor persist in engaging in acts of strife and contention.'"

Devadatta should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and he may dwell in peace and happiness.
"You, Devadatta, should abandon the act of schisming the Saṃgha.
Thus he should announce.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Devadatta desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by taking up and persisting in matters of contention.
Although the bhikṣus have already admonished him individually, during that individual admonition he stubbornly clings to his position and refuses to relinquish it, saying:"
"This matter is true; all else is false.
The Saṃgha now performs the formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to admonish Devadatta regarding this matter:
"Devadatta, do not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, nor persist in engaging in acts of contention and strife."

Devadatta should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Master’s teaching may be made radiant and the community may dwell in peace and happiness.
"You, Devadatta, should relinquish this matter of schism in the Saṃgha.
If the venerable ones consent to perform the formal ritual of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish Devadatta regarding this matter:
"You, Devadatta, must not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by engaging in and persisting in acts of contention."

"You, Devadatta, should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, being of one mind and one voice like water mixed with milk, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and you may dwell in peace and happiness."
"Devadatta, you should renounce such an act of schism in the Saṃgha.
If he remains silent, [it is accepted];
if he does not consent, let him speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this manner.
"The Saṃgha has now completed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish Devadatta; the Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence. Thus do I now uphold it."
When the bhikṣus had thus received the Buddha’s instruction, they immediately exhorted Devadatta by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
