At that time, Devadatta remained obstinate and would not relinquish his position, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false."
At that time, Devadatta had four companions who followed him in harmony as he spoke of matters concerning the schism of the Saṃgha, saying to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not engage in any discussion with that bhikṣu, whether it be good or bad. Why is this?

For that bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks only by relying on the Dharma and the Vinaya, speaking with full knowledge and not without knowledge.
"Whatever they delight in, I too delight in.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One, explaining it at length as above, up until the words, "I too delight in it."
The World-Honored One said:

"O bhikṣus! You should perform a formal admonition against these four companions individually; if there are others of a similar kind, they too should be rebuked and admonished. It should be done in this manner:..."
“O Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta! You know that this bhikṣu intends to cause a schism in the Saṅgha by engaging in contentious matters and persisting in them;
do not act as his accomplices, do not comply with him in speaking of matters that cause a schism in the Saṅgha, and do not speak to the bhikṣus in this way:
‘Venerable sirs!...’”
Do not engage in any speech—whether favorable or unfavorable—with that bhikṣu. Why is this?
Because that bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks whether favorably or unfavorably only in reliance upon the Dharma and the Vinaya.

Why is this? Because that bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks only by relying on the Dharma and the Vinaya. He speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge. What he delights in, I too delight in.
Why is this? Venerable one!

That bhikṣu speaks words that are not in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya; he does not speak based on the Dharma and the Vinaya. He speaks out of ignorance, not from knowledge, and remains obstinately attached to his position.

Do not take pleasure in causing a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead delight in the harmony of the Saṃgha. You ought to live in concord with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, being of one mind and one voice like the blending of water and milk, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and the community may dwell in peace and happiness.
"Venerable ones!
You should now relinquish this conduct that conforms to causing a schism in the Saṃgha and discord.
Then the bhikṣus, having received these instructions, proceeded to admonish those four men with a formal separate admonition, speaking to them as follows:

“You four—Kokālika and the others—know that those bhikṣus desire to break the harmony of the Saṃgha by engaging in contentious disputes and persisting in them; do not associate with them, following what is wrong and opposing what is right.”
"Venerable friends! Do not speak thus to the bhikṣus:
'O Venerable Ones!'"
Do not engage in debate with that bhikṣu regarding what is good or bad. Why is this?

Because that bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma and the Vinaya; he speaks based upon the Dharma and the Vinaya. He speaks knowing [the truth], not speaking out of ignorance. What he delights in, I also delight in.
Why is this? Venerable one!
For that bhikṣu speaks words that are not in accordance with the Dharma or the Vinaya; he speaks without relying on the Vinaya, speaking out of ignorance rather than speaking from knowledge.
Venerable one!

Do not take pleasure in causing a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead delight in the harmony of the Saṃgha. You ought to join with the harmonious Saṃgha in joy and without dispute, being of one mind and one voice like water mixed with milk, so that the Great Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and may abide in peace and happiness.
"Venerable one!
You should now abandon these actions that accord with causing a schism in the Saṃgha and promoting discord.
When the bhikṣus were thus admonishing him individually, those companions refused to accept their words and persisted in their refusal to desist, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir!..."

"I have already given private admonitions to Kokālika and the others; while we were giving them these private admonitions, Kokālika and the others stubbornly clung to their position, having no intention of relinquishing it, and said:
'This matter is true; all else is false.'"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* against Kokālika and the others to admonish them before the assembly.
If there are others of a similar sort, you should likewise assemble the community as before and perform the *jñapti-karman*; it should be done in this manner."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These individuals—Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta—know that this bhikṣu intends to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by engaging in contentious matters and persisting therein; they follow his course regarding these discordant affairs."
When the bhikṣus offer such admonition, [they should say]: "Do not speak to the bhikṣus in this way:
'Venerable sirs!'"
Do not engage in any speech, whether favorable or unfavorable, with that bhikṣu.

Why is this? That bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks in reliance upon the Dharma and the Vinaya. He speaks knowing [the truth], not speaking out of ignorance. What he delights in, I too delight in.
Then the bhikṣus gave him a formal admonition.
During that formal admonition, he remained obstinate regarding that matter and spoke these words:
"This is the truth; all else is false."
"If the Saṃgha deems the time appropriate, let the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now admonish the four individuals, Kokālika and the others, by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*:

'You, Kokālika and the others, know that those bhikṣus desire to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and persist in engaging in acts of strife and contention, and you comply with those acts of discord.'"
When the bhikṣus offer such admonition, [the others] say:
"Venerable sirs, do not speak to the bhikṣus in this manner:
'Venerable ones!'"
Whatever that bhikṣu may say, whether good or bad—why is this?

Because that bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks in reliance upon the Dharma and the Vinaya, speaking with knowledge and not speaking without knowledge. What he delights in, I also delight in.

Why is this? Because that bhikṣu speaks what is not in accordance with the Dharma and speaks what is not in accordance with the Vinaya; that bhikṣu adheres to and dwells in what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya, speaking out of ignorance rather than speaking from knowledge.
Venerable ones!

Do not take pleasure in causing a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead take pleasure in the harmony of the Saṃgha. You should dwell together with the Saṃgha in harmony and joy, free from contention, with one mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Teacher’s dispensation may be made radiant and may abide in peace and happiness.
"Venerable sirs!
You should now relinquish this act of supporting the schism of the Saṃgha and its state of discord.
Thus is the formal announcement.
"Next, perform the *karmavācanā*; it should be done according to the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Once the bhikṣus had received these instructions, they replied: "So be it."
"We shall offer them counsel.
Thereupon, they admonished Kokālika and the others by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
At that time, those four individuals remained obstinate and would not relinquish their position, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha of this matter, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
When we admonished Kokālika and the others through the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, they stubbornly clung to their position and had no intention of relinquishing it, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Devadatta, together with his four companions, follows what is false and opposes what is right.
From this day forward, they shall cause a schism in my harmonious Saṃgha of disciples and break the Wheel of Dharma, possessing great power."
When Devadatta heard these words, he spoke thus:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has given me this prediction, saying to the bhikṣus:
'Devadatta, together with his four companions, follows what is false and opposes what is right.'"
"From this day forward, you shall have the great power to break the harmonious Saṃgha of my disciples and to disrupt the Wheel of Dharma.
He then addressed Kokālika and the others:
"You should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has granted me this prophecy:"
“Devadatta, together with four companions, follows the heterodox and opposes the orthodox.
From this day forward, he shall cause a schism in my harmonious Saṃgha of disciples and break the Wheel of Dharma, possessing great power.”
At that time, Devadatta became even more resolute in his efforts to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it in full to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and spoke at length as previously described, until the Blessed One questioned the bhikṣu Devadatta, saying:
"You truly desire to break the harmonious Saṃgha and persist in creating strife and contention. Devadatta replied,
"Venerable Sir!..."
"It is indeed so.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Devadatta, saying: "You are not a śramaṇa;
you do not follow the path; you are impure; this is improper and should not be done; it is not the conduct of one who has left the household life."
If a bhikṣu employs means with the intent to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta) in every instance.
If, during the process of private admonition, he does not relinquish his position, he incurs an offense of gross transgression (sthūlātyaya) in every instance.
If, when performing the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*—admonishing in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions—one relinquishes [the offense], it is well.
If one does not relinquish it, at the conclusion of the *jñapti*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
When the first motion is completed, one also incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one does not relinquish it when the third formal act (*karmavācanā*) of the ordination procedure is concluded, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

At that time, while remaining on his original seat, the World-Honored One, wishing to establish the training rule concerning those who associate with a schismatic monk for the sake of his śrāvaka disciples, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus, you need not rise yet; the Saṃgha has a minor matter to attend to."
The Blessed One, knowing this, asked them intentionally, as explained in detail previously.
The Blessed One then questioned the four individuals, including Kokālika, saying:

"Do you truly know that Devadatta intends to split the harmonious Saṅgha, employs means to break the Saṅgha, and persists in inciting disputes while remaining obstinate; and that you have become his companions, following what is false and opposing what is right?"
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones!

If you engage in discussion with that bhikṣu regarding anything, whether good or bad," and so forth, up to "that which is not to be done by one who has left the household life," as explained at length previously.

At that time, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa was teaching the methods for supernatural powers to Devadatta. Then, the bhikṣus said to Daśabala-Kāśyapa, "Why does the Elder teach the methods for supernatural powers to the wicked man Devadatta?"
Daśabala Kāśyapa replied: "Venerable one!

I would not have known this person to be of evil conduct; had I known this man was of evil conduct, I would not have taught him even the syllables of the *ṛṣi*, let alone the methods for attaining the Way."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus said to Devadatta:
"The benefits and offerings you have received are entirely due to the merit of the Elder Daśabala-Kāśyapa."
"Since you have attained such [realization], you should go to make offerings to Daśabala Kāśyapa.

The great assembly spoke these words as a skillful means, intending to send Devadatta to Daśabala Kāśyapa so that he might be instructed to abandon this evil mind and be led to practice virtue; it was for the purpose of explaining this matter to him.
At that time, Devadatta said to the bhikṣus:
"What power does Daśabala Kāśyapa have over me?

I myself have constantly sought diligence and ascetic practice day and night, thereby attaining the foremost power of meditative concentration; this was achieved through my own seeking and has nothing to do with Daśabala Kāśyapa."
When Devadatta uttered these ungrateful words, all his supernormal powers completely vanished.
At that time, the bhikṣus knew that because Devadatta was ungrateful, his supernormal powers had vanished.
At that time, the bhikṣus had doubts; they went to the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, and said to the World-Honored One:
"Because Devadatta was ungrateful toward Daśabala Kāśyapa, all of his supernormal powers have completely vanished."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Devadatta was not only ungrateful at this present time, whereby he lost his supernatural powers; it was also due to his words of ingratitude in the past that he lost his supernatural powers, and all the dharmas he had studied completely fell away."
"Listen attentively!
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this city of Vārāṇasī, there was once a king named Brahmadatta."

At that time, there was a caṇḍāla in that city who was well-versed in the dhāraṇī-mantras and prohibitions of the Gandharvas. Relying on the power of those mantras, he flew through the air to Mount Gandhamādana, where he gathered extraordinary and wondrous flowers and fruits out of season, and brought them back to the city to present to the king.
Seeing his respectful conduct, the king felt great joy and immediately rewarded the caṇḍāla with a village.
At that time, there was a young brahmin (māṇava) from South India who, in order to study incantations, went to the city of Vārāṇasī and asked the people:
"Who is skilled in the methods of incantation?"
When the people were thus questioned, they replied to the māṇava:
"In this kingdom there is a caṇḍāla who is skilled in the treatment of spells.
Having heard this, the māṇava went to the caṇḍāla’s dwelling, joined his palms, and said:
"I have now come here to serve my preceptor.
The Caṇḍāla asked, "For what purpose do you seek this, that you speak of making offerings?"
He replied, "It is for the purpose of studying incantations.
Thereupon, the Caṇḍāla spoke this verse:
“‘One does not bestow the vidyā-mantra upon others; it is given only in exchange for a mantra, or perhaps through the performance of service, or by obtaining precious wealth.
If it is not thus, one will not transmit it even at the cost of death.’”
Then the young brahmin replied to his preceptor, saying:
"I have no precious objects; I can only offer service and support. After how long will I be able to obtain this mantra?"
The Caṇḍāla said, "Do you know whether you have served and made offerings to me for twelve years?
Because the young brahmin was studying incantations, he served and made offerings with single-minded devotion until gradually a year had passed.
At that time, the Caṇḍāla, having become intoxicated from drinking liquor for the sake of a family gathering, arrived at his home at night. Seeing this, the disciple, a Māṇava, thought to himself:
"Now that my teacher is drunk, I should attend upon him with even greater devotion and service tonight."
He immediately prepared a bed and mat for him, and laid his preceptor upon it so that he might rest in comfort.
At that moment, as the preceptor shifted on the bed, a crossbeam suddenly broke.
Hearing the sound of the bed’s frame breaking, the Māṇava rose of his own accord and thought to himself:
"The teacher's bed frame has snapped; he will not sleep in comfort."
"I shall place a support beneath the bed frame under the bed so that it does not fall to the ground.
Having formed this thought, he immediately placed a support under the bed frame and secured it so that it would not fall.
According to the common nature of those intoxicated, one who possesses physical strength usually regains consciousness during the second watch;
however, his preceptor had drunk so much that he did not wake until the first watch of the night, vomiting repeatedly upon the body of the Māṇava.
When the Māṇava saw that his own body was covered in vomit and filth, he thought to himself:
"If I were to speak out regarding this transformation, my preceptor would be unable to sleep upon hearing it."
Having formed this thought, he remained beneath the beam, silent and still.
Then, at midnight, his preceptor awoke and saw the young brahmin (māṇava) beneath the bed; his body was soiled and disheveled with vomit. The preceptor immediately asked, "Who is under the bed?"
The disciple replied, “I am a māṇava. The preceptor asked:
"How is it that he is beneath the bed?
The disciple then related everything as previously described.
Upon hearing these words, the preceptor was filled with great joy and called out to the young brahmin:
“I am greatly delighted with you; rise from your bed, bathe yourself for purification, and come, and I shall bestow the Dharma upon you.
Then the young brahmin immediately washed his clothes and arrived at dawn. Upon seeing him, the Preceptor bestowed the incantation-dharma upon him.
At that time, after the disciple had learned the mantra according to the ritual, he thought to himself out of a sense of urgency:
"Now that I have obtained this mantra, I should perform the ritual within the city to test my supernatural powers."

Having thought this, he immediately ascended into the air, went to Mount Gandhamādana to fetch out-of-season flowers and fruits, and returned to Vārāṇasī to present them to the ministers of the kingdom.
Having received them, the minister presented them back to the king.
The king asked the minister, "From where did you obtain these excellent flowers out of season? The minister replied:
"A young Brahmin (maṇava) from the kingdom of South India brought [this] to me and I immediately presented it to Your Majesty.
That young Brahmin is extremely proficient in the methods of incantation and his lineage is also noble; I only pray that Your Majesty will retain this young Brahmin as a master of spells.
Do not employ this Caṇḍāla; this Caṇḍāla practices impure conduct, so I pray you expel him immediately and transfer all the villages to the young Brahmin."
Having spoken thus, the king then followed the minister’s request, drove away the caṇḍāla, installed the māṇava, and likewise returned to the village.
The caṇḍāla replied to the king, saying, "This young brahmin is my disciple; could his mantra-technique surpass mine?
Then the king questioned the young brahmin.
"Is this incantation method of yours not the teaching of a caṇḍāla?
At that time, the māṇava replied to the Great King:
"I practiced asceticism for one year, day and night without ceasing, to seek this dharma; the caṇḍāla gave it to me for nothing."
“At that time, because the māṇava showed no gratitude toward his preceptor, he immediately lost the efficacy of his incantations, and all the rites he subsequently performed failed to succeed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“That māṇava had mastered divine spells, but because he lacked gratitude, the power of his incantations dissipated; he is none other than Devadatta in this life, whose supernormal powers have dissipated due to his ingratitude.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know:
it is not fitting for a preceptor with whom one has studied the Dharma to be ungrateful. From this day forward, whoever is ungrateful shall incur an offense against the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Rājagṛha for Gayāśīrṣa Mountain, while Devadatta traveled among the people accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus.
King Ajātaśatru, being fond of Devadatta, provided him with five hundred cartloads of grain as provisions for his journey; while on the road, he encountered various bhikṣus.
The bhikṣu asked the man driving the cart, "Whose cart is this? The man replied:
"This was given by King Ajātaśatru to Devadatta.
Having heard these words, the bhikṣus went immediately to the Buddha's presence and reported what they had been told:
"At that time, the ignorant King Ajātaśatru took five hundred carts of grain and gave them to Devadatta as an offering, rather than giving them to the World-Honored One."
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This King Ajātaśatru is not the only one who, lacking wisdom in this present life, has made offerings to those who lack wisdom; in previous lives as well, he was just the same."
Listen attentively!

In the distant past, there was a village in Eastern India; not far from that village was a forest, where various kinds of flowers and fruits flourished, and where flowing springs and bathing pools abounded.

There were five hundred sages dwelling in that forest; they constantly ate fruits that had fallen of their own accord, taking the roots of trees as their food and drink, and also using tree bark as their clothing.
At that time, there was an āmalaka tree whose branches and fruit hung down to the ground, nearly ripe in abundance.

When those five hundred rishis reached the side of the tree and begged for fruit according to their needs, the tree deity, out of greed and stinginess regarding the fruit, prevented it from falling to the ground.

At that time, seeing that the fruit had not fallen, the assembly of sages left one sage behind to watch the place where they were staying, while the others went to other trees to seek fruit once more.

After the assembly of immortals had departed, five hundred bandits came to the forest; arriving at the foot of that tree, they saw the abundance of fruit and consulted one another, saying, "By what means can we eat the fruit of this tree?"
The Venerable One said, "Take axes and cut down this tree so that the fruit falls to the ground; you may eat until you are satisfied.
When the tree deity heard these words of the Venerable One, sorrow and fear arose within her heart, and she felt deep attachment toward the tree.
At that time, the tree deity shook its body, causing all the fruits to fall to the ground; the bandits then gathered together and ate the fruits.
Once they had finished eating, the rishi arrived and saw that the tree was bent and all the fruits had fallen away.
The assembly of seers then asked that forest-guarding seer:
"By whom have these tree fruits been eaten up?
The forest-guarding seer then answered the seers in detail regarding the aforementioned matter.
At that time, the sages rebuked the tree deity:
"It is you who are ignorant, hating the virtuous and loving the wicked, by not granting fruit to the good man while granting it to the evil man."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The tree deity who was then without wisdom is now King Ajātaśatru.
The leader among the thieves is now Devadatta."

In the past, this King Ajātaśatru, lacking wisdom, gave fruit to wicked people and failed to make offerings to virtuous ones; now, lacking wisdom, he gives goods to Devadatta and fails to make offerings to pure bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled from Magadha to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, where he dwelt surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus standing before and behind him.
At that time, Devadatta was in Rājagṛha, constantly practicing unrighteous and unwholesome deeds among the people.
Then, all the people within the city went to inform the Buddha:
"Devadatta is currently committing various evil and unwholesome acts."
When the Blessed One heard these words, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Take a single bhikṣu with you as an attendant and enter the streets and alleys of Rājagṛha. Whenever you see brahmins, elders, or householders in the world, speak these words to them:
'As for Devadatta and his companions, even if they are unrighteous, evil-doing persons, you need not slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.'"
Why is this? Because such a person is not one who practices the Buddha-dharma.
If someone says that Devadatta possesses supernatural powers and majestic virtue, you should reply to them:
“Devadatta previously possessed supernatural powers, but now they have all degenerated and been lost; not a single miraculous sign remains.

At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately entered the city of Rājagṛha and spoke the aforementioned words. He added: “If Devadatta later commits further unwholesome and evil deeds, do not come before the Buddha again to shamefully proclaim his faults.”
At that time, out of compassion, the World-Honored One manifested physical illness.
Then the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, prepared a medicinal decoction of clarified butter for the Buddha; the medicine was named Nārāca.
The Buddha asked the King of Physicians,
“This medicine is inconceivable.
The King of Physicians replied to the World-Honored One:
"It is truly inconceivable.
The Buddha again addressed the King of Physicians:
"It is utterly inconceivable."
He replied, “It is truly and utterly inconceivable.
The World-Honored One questioned the King of Physicians once more:
“Do you understand? He replied, “I understand.”
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, again addressed the King of Physicians:
"You truly do not know. He replied:
"I truly do not know.
The Buddha spoke again to the King of Physicians:
"What is it that is inconceivable?"
He replied, "Cows that eat water and grass can produce nectar; this ghee, when boiled together with these ingredients, becomes this wondrous Nārāyaṇa medicine.
The Buddha again questioned the King of Physicians:
"What is most inconceivable? He replied:
"That a Buddha appears in the world and is able to preach the sublime Dharma, and is able to cause the Saṃgha to act in accordance with the teachings—this is the most inconceivable."
The Buddha again asked the King of Physicians,
"Which of these things can you know? He replied:
"All must return to death; none can escape it except for the Buddha.
The Buddha again asked the King of Physicians:
"What is it that you truly do not know?"
He replied, "I know that a person perishes, but I do not know where they go.
At that time, having heard these words, the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and asked one another:
"This attendant Śivaka well understands the Buddha’s intention.
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately asked the World-Honored One,
"Does this attendant Śivaka truly know the Buddha’s intention?"
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Jīvaka did not merely come to understand my intentions well in this present life; he also understood my intentions well in past lives."
"Listen attentively! The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, in a certain village, there was an elder named Śobhana. His family was extremely wealthy. Later, he took a wife, who became pregnant and after ten months gave birth to a daughter. On the twenty-first day, he gathered his kinsmen and requested that they choose a name for her; the kinsmen then gave this infant girl the name Śubhakāriṇī."
Eventually, he fathered another son. He gathered his kinsmen and requested that they choose a name for him; the kinsmen gave him the name Śīlavat.
The elder thought to himself:
"Now that I have a son, I shall take my wealth and treasures to go forth and engage in business."
He further reflected: "If I engage in business, I shall leave behind much wealth in the future; I fear my wife might spend it all.

Having had this thought, he left only a small amount of property. He filled a golden jar with his remaining precious treasures, sealed the mouth of the jar with a necklace of pearls, and taking it to the Cool Grove beneath the Horse-Ear Tree, he dug a pit and buried it.
Setting aside his capital, he went forth to engage in trade; upon reaching another country, he gained manifold profit, whereupon he took a wife and eventually fathered many children.
As his stepson gradually grew up, he asked his mother,
"Where is my father? His mother said:
"I have heard that your father is currently in such-and-such a city, possessing abundant wealth and living in great peace.
You should go there; if your father sees you, he will surely provide for your needs."
Upon hearing these words, the son went to his father’s place; they met within the marketplace,
and as soon as the father saw his son’s face, he recognized him and called out,
“Where have you come from?”
"Where do you wish to go?
The son recounted the aforementioned matters in detail. Knowing that his son was about to return to his own dwelling, the father told him:
"You must truly not tell others that he is your son."

When he reached his dwelling, a feeling of affection arose in his heart; he washed the clothes and felt a renewed sense of attachment toward them. His other wives and children then asked him, "Who is this person?"
The father said,
"This is the son of my friend.
When the other sons saw their father show him such affection, they thought to themselves:
"This must be our son, coming to seize our wealth.
The father then thought:
"I should now give him the principal capital and let him return to his own dwelling."
"If it were not so, his other sons would certainly harbor jealousy and harm him.
The father further reflected:
"If I give him wealth, for the sake of that property, these relatives here might fear and kill him."
He then composed a verse in a letter and gave it to his son; having finished the letter and verse, he sent him back.
As the son was on the road, his relatives seized him and asked, "What did your father give you?"
He replied, "I gave him only a single letter. The people said:
"By all means, use skillful means to cause him to return.
He was released according to his wish and reached his own country, where he saw his mother and prostrated before her. His mother asked:
"What did you receive from your father?
He replied, "I received nothing else; he gave me only this letter."
The mother said, "Your father has deceived and slighted you; you have gained nothing but hardship. The son said:
"My father was truly wise; he did not slight me at all.
He then read the verse and contemplated its meaning, providing an explanation.
Having fully understood it, he went to the place where the jar was located, dug it up, and brought it home, thereby becoming immensely wealthy and noble.
The Buddha said:
"Monks! He who was the father in the past was none other than myself."
That son of his is now Jīvaka;
I instructed him through skillful means, and he immediately understood my intention;
it is just the same now.
At that time, Jīvaka thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata possesses a body of great adamantine substance; how could a small amount of medicinal ghee suffice?
Two *liǎng* should be used."
Having formed this thought, he immediately measured out two *liǎng* of refined ghee and placed it in the Buddha’s bowl.
After the World-Honored One had eaten, he left a small remainder and gave it to the bhikṣus, who paid their respects and expressed their gratitude to the World-Honored One.
At that time, having seen this event, Devadatta thought to himself,
"I should eat ghee," and he asked Jīvaka:
“How much does the śramaṇa Gautama eat? Jīvaka replied,
“Only two *kārṣāpaṇas* worth.”
He said, "I also wish to eat two *liǎng*. Jīvaka replied:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses a great adamantine body; the amount of ghee he consumes can be digested by him, but it is not within your power.
Devadatta said, "I too now possess a great adamantine body; why should I not be able to digest it?"
He immediately took two *liǎnjīn* (two pounds) and ate them.
When morning dawned, the ghee consumed by the Buddha had been completely digested; Jīvaka brought rice porridge to offer to the World-Honored One, and the Tathāgata ate it at once.
Devadatta still had the butter in his stomach when he also ate the gruel; his abdomen immediately began to ache violently, and he rolled about, crying out, restless day and night.
Ānanda, feeling affection for his own kinsman, was moved by compassion upon hearing of his suffering. He went to the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Devadatta, having eaten much butter that has not yet been digested, consumed some gruel as well; his belly aches and he is ill at ease."

At that time, the Tathāgata extended his hand—adorned with the merit of a hundred blessings, marked by the thousand-spoked wheels, and possessing the palms of fearlessness—and, penetrating through the mountain wall, placed it upon Devadatta’s head. He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In my mind, I regard Devadatta and Rāhula with equal impartiality; there is no difference between them."
"Devadatta’s intense sufferings shall all be completely extinguished.
When he had spoken these words, Devadatta’s manifold pains were instantly removed; he revived from death and, upon examining his hand, realized it was the Buddha’s arm.
He then thought: "This is the arm of the śramaṇa Gautama."

Because Devadatta had harbored malice for immeasurable kalpas, even though he knew that [the others] had escaped their intense suffering by relying on the Buddha’s majestic power, he spoke these words:
"That Siddhārtha has skillfully mastered such medical arts; it is by means of this dharma that he is able to save himself and others."
At that time, a great voice resounded from the four quarters:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, by means of his words of truth, has rescued Devadatta from his intense suffering and affliction."
When Devadatta’s followers and the people heard these words, there was none who did not rejoice; they all praised together, saying:
"The supernatural power of the World-Honored One is inconceivable and most extraordinary."
Then the bhikṣus went to Devadatta’s place and said to him,
“If the Buddha does not save you, you will surely die. Devadatta replied:
"The Buddha knows skillful means; he intends for all people to follow him, and therefore he has performed this rite.
The bhikṣus said, "Devadatta, do not speak such words! You should quickly remain silent and observe within your own mind: Is it not the Buddha who saves us?"
Devadatta said, "What does his ability to save me have to do with it?
Once the butter inside my belly has been digested, the pain will naturally cease."
At that time, having heard these words and knowing that there was no gratitude or recompense, the bhikṣus went to the World-Honored One and said to the Buddha:
"We pray only that the Tathāgata will deign to hear us regarding Devadatta."
"The World-Honored One possesses great compassion for him, yet he now shows neither gratitude nor recompense.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃghabhedavastu*, Fascicle 14. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃghabhedavastu*.
Fascicle Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Devadatta has not been ungrateful and unrequiting only in the present; he has likewise been ungrateful and unrequiting since ancient times.
Listen well, and I shall explain it for you.”
The summary verse says:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, in this city of Vārāṇasī, there was a large village. Not far from the village was a great forest, lush with flowers and fruits, and abounding in flowing springs and bathing pools."
There was a rishi named Kauśika who dwelt in that forest; he subsisted on fallen fruits and wore garments of tree bark.
Possessing great compassion in his heart, all manner of birds and beasts relied upon him for refuge.

There was a female elephant in that forest who, at the time of her delivery, heard the roar of a lion; her heart was greatly terrified, she lost control of her bowels and bladder, and abandoning her calf, she fled out from the forest.

At that time, a rishi was gathering fruit when he saw a young elephant cub and realized it had lost its mother. The rishi gave rise to a heart of compassion and felt pity for the cub; he searched for its mother but could not find her. He then took the cub back to his own dwelling and raised it, no differently than if it were his own son.
As he gradually grew up, he began to destroy the flowers, fruits, and trees in the hermitage.
When the seer saw this, he immediately rebuked him with anger; knowing the seer was angry, the elephant no longer damaged the forest.
The elephant grew larger and its mind became increasingly fierce; later, it again damaged the grove, and although the seer rebuked it once more, the elephant felt no fear.
The seer intensified his harsh anger, and the elephant gave rise to a malicious intent, wishing to trample the seer.
The seer fled into his cell; the elephant, using its trunk and tusks, destroyed half of the seer’s hut and then immediately ran away.
At that time, the deity of the forest spoke this verse.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The seer of the past is my very self today.
The elephant of the past is Devadatta today.
Just as he was ungrateful in the past, so too is he now; there is no good retribution for him. You all should know this!"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Devadatta further possesses a nature of ingratitude and a lack of requital.
Listen attentively!
In the past, in this city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Mahendraśakra. The kingdom was abundant and its people were all happy.
The king had a queen named Candraprabhā, whose dreams were always realized as reality.
Within that kingdom, there was a bodhisattva who served as the king of deer; his form was golden in color, exceptionally sublime and handsome, such that no one who beheld him could ever be satiated.
Knowing himself to be handsome, his mind was constantly filled with fear; he was perpetually terrified of hunters and always kept himself hidden.

At that time, the various birds and beasts could understand one another's speech. Then, a certain crow went to where the deer king was and, conceiving a feeling of affection, spoke these words: "Uncle!..."
"What do you mean by 'eating grass with fear'?
The golden deer king then replied, "Because I am handsome, whenever any hunter sees me, they fear they might kill me; for this reason, as I eat grass, my heart is constantly filled with fear."
The crow then replied:
"I too am afraid of owls during the night; from this day forward, we and our uncle shall protect one another."
"If during the day I remain in this high tree to observe all that is good and evil, I shall report any matters to the King.
When night falls, Your Majesty should keep watch, and I shall report any matters to you."
In that country, by the side of a great river within the forest, two men who had previously been enemies suddenly encountered one another.
One man, being superior in strength, bound his enemy and threw him into the river. As the current was swift and the man was drifting and drowning, he spoke these words:
"Whoever can save me, I shall become their slave."

At that time, the deer king, together with his retinue of five hundred, went to the river to drink water; having heard this sound, he gave rise to a heart of compassion and entered the water, intending to rescue the drowning man.
At that time, an old crow came to where the king was and said:
"This black-headed creature is utterly devoid of gratitude and righteousness; you need not rescue him, for once he escapes this peril, he will surely harm the deer king."
At that time, out of compassion, the deer king did not heed the crow’s words; he went to the place where the man was drowning, took him upon his back, and carried him out.
Once they reached the shore, the deer untied the rope with its mouth and waited until the man had recovered. Then it spoke to him:
"Son, you must know that this is the way home; you should go safely."
Then the drowning man knelt on his right knee with palms joined and replied to the Deer King:
"I have regained my life through Your Majesty; I pray that I may always serve as your slave to repay your kindness."
Then the deer king spoke in verse:
"I do not need you as a slave, nor do I require your service;
only do not speak of having seen me, for I fear they will take my skin."
"I now seek one further matter from you: if you comply with my wish and do not speak of having seen me, that shall be your repayment of my kindness.
Why is this? My body is upright and majestic, endowed with perfect physical marks; I fear that person might learn of it, kill me, and take my skin. Therefore, do not say that you have seen me here."
That man replied, "I respectfully comply with Your Majesty's wish; I shall certainly not speak.
He then rose, joined his palms, circumambulated [the king] three times to the right, paid his respects, and departed.

"At that time, Lady Candraprabhā, exhausted from indulging in the pleasures of the five senses, fell asleep. During the latter part of the night, she saw in a dream a king of deer with golden-colored skin, exquisite and majestic, seated upon a lion throne, preaching the most profound Dharma to various kings and the assembled multitude."
While dreaming, he thought to himself:
"This dream I have had must certainly be true.
He awoke with joy and immediately went to tell the king what he had seen in his dream.
Having heard this, the king believed his dream and felt a sense of wonder and alarm, thinking:
"How could there be a deer upon the lion throne preaching the Dharma to the assembly?
At that time, Queen Candraprabhā spoke pleasing words to the king; the king was greatly delighted and immediately earnestly requested her to seek out the golden deer for him.
The King issued a decree to his ministers, commanding that all hunters within the kingdom be summoned and assembled.
The ministers, obeying the command, called for the hunters and led them to the King’s presence.
The King questioned the hunters:
"I have heard that there is a golden deer within our kingdom; have you all seen it?
If any of you have seen it, bind it with a soft cord so as not to injure it, and bring it here to see me."
Then the hunters said to the Great King:
"We have hunted for many years, yet we have neither seen nor heard of such a deer.
Since Your Majesty has heard of it, where is this deer?"
"Please seize him for the King.
The King commanded his ministers to beat the drums and proclaim:
"Whoever has seen him, come and report it to me; I shall immediately reward them with five hundred villages."
The ministers received the command, beat the drum to assemble the multitude, and proclaimed the king’s reward for the search.
At that time, the drowning man, hearing of the king’s heavy bounty, immediately thought to himself:
"I am currently impoverished; shall I now seek the king’s heavy reward out of greed?"
"Should he not speak of the deer in order to repay his debt of gratitude?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is the constant law of the world that all sentient beings, bound by the five desires, will do nothing that is not evil."
At that time, the drowning man’s mind was greedy for the five desires, and he immediately thought back to the time when he had been seized and bound by his enemy.
He further thought:
"I shall now turn my back on gratitude and seek to repay that enmity; I have no fear of future suffering as before, and I must avenge myself."
Having formed this thought, he went to the gate of the royal palace. Seeing the various adornments according to the king’s righteous dharma, he had the gatekeeper inform the Great King.
Once the King had heard this, he immediately summoned him to enter. The man reported to the King:
"In the mountain forests, there are all manner of flowers and fruits."
"There is a king of deer, his body and hide golden in color, surrounded by a thousand deer; he is of the most exquisite beauty.
I know his location and will lead the King to see him.

Upon hearing these words, the King was filled with great joy; he summoned his ministers and led forth his troops. When those from foreign lands who were paying court saw the King’s grand procession, they also followed in his wake.
The man led them forward to where the deer king was and deployed his troops to surround him.
At that time, a crow who was a close friend of the deer king was perched high in a tree; from afar, he saw the host of soldiers gradually approaching the forest.

The crow immediately descended from the tree and reported to the deer king, saying, "The man who was previously rescued from drowning is an ungrateful person; Your Majesty need not save him, for he did not heed my words.
The deer king asked:
"Why is that? the crow replied to the deer king:
"Previously, the man who was drowning led a host of soldiers here to hunt you, O deer king."
At that time, hearing the sound of the troops, those thousand deer fled in terror and scattered.
Then the Deer King thought to himself:
"If I flee now, the troops will search for me and likewise kill the thousand deer."
"I would rather die myself so that those thousand deer may live.

Having formed this thought, the Deer King went to where the king was. At that time, the man who had previously been rescued from drowning saw the Deer King from afar; he immediately raised both hands and pointed toward him, saying to the king, "The one coming there is the Golden Deer King."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If sentient beings commit extremely evil deeds, they may experience the retribution even in this very life, without waiting for a future birth.
Because that man who was drowning did not recognize his debt of gratitude and committed an evil deed by pointing at the deer, his hand immediately fell to the ground."
When the king saw this, he marveled and asked,
"Why have your two hands suddenly fallen off?
At that time, the drowning man, weeping in agony, immediately addressed the king with a verse in reply:
"One who breaks through walls to steal goods is not called a thief;
one who receives kindness and fails to repay it—that is called a great thief."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately asked that person:
"What is the meaning of this verse?
I do not understand it now."
Then the drowning man immediately related the previous events to the king in detail.
Having heard this, the king spoke these verses in response to the ungrateful drowning man:
"O ungrateful drowning man, why does your body not sink into the earth?"
Why was your tongue not split into a hundred pieces?
Why did the Vajra-wielders, grasping their swords and staves, not slay you?
"All the ghosts and spirits, why do they not strike you?
You are utterly ungrateful; for what reason have you given so little in return?
The king, knowing that the deer was a great bodhisattva of immense majestic power, addressed his ministers, saying:

"You must provide a grand offering for the Deer King. Return quickly to sweep and sprinkle the roads, hang silken banners and canopies, and burn various famous incenses; I shall enter the city together with the Deer King."
Upon hearing the command, the ministers fully complied with the King’s instructions.

At that time, the King ordered the golden-colored deer to lead the way, while the King and his ministers followed behind the Deer King into the city of Vārāṇasī. They prepared a lion throne at the palace gate, adorned it with various ornaments, and invited the Deer King to be seated.
The king, Lady Moonlight, the ladies of the inner palace, the princes, and the common people sat surrounding him.

At that time, the deer king was preaching the sublime Dharma; once the king, the lady, and the entire assembly had heard the teaching, they immediately requested the deer king to receive the five precepts, and all sentient beings vowed to take refuge in Bodhi.
Having seen this, the king was filled with great joy and said to the deer king:
"The mountains, forests, and wildernesses where you roam shall all be granted to you, O deer king.
From this day forward, I shall forever renounce the taking of life, and I shall also prohibit my subjects from hunting. May all sentient beings be free from fear in whatever places they dwell."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The deer king at that time was none other than my own self.
The ungrateful man who fell into the water then was Devadatta."
"In the past he was ungrateful, and now he is likewise.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Devadatta further possesses the conduct of one who is ungrateful and fails to repay kindness."
Listen attentively!

Long ago, in a village on the borders of Vārāṇasī, there lived a florist. Beside that village flowed a river, and the florist would regularly cross the water to go back and forth in order to gather flowers.

Later, on one occasion, wishing to cross a river, he obtained an out-of-season mango fruit in that river; carrying it to the royal city, he gave it to the gatekeeper, and the gatekeeper passed it on to the chamberlain.
The attendant, seizing the opportunity, presented it to the king; the king, having received the fruit, gave it to the queen, and the queen, having received the fruit, immediately ate it.
Because the fruit was fragrant and delicious, she requested more from the king, who then asked the attendant:
"Where did you obtain this fruit?"
The usher replied, "I obtained it from the gatekeeper.
The king immediately sent for the gatekeeper and questioned him.
"From where did you obtain this fruit?
The gatekeeper replied,
"I obtained this fruit from a garland-maker."
The king again sent for the flower-garland maker and asked,
"Where did you obtain these fruits?
The flower-garland maker replied:
"It was found in the river.
The king said to the flower-garland maker,
"Go to the river and seek this fruit once more."

Having received the imperial decree, the flower-garland maker took provisions with him and went once more to the riverbank; following the course of the water, he traveled until he reached a mountain, where from atop a high cliff he saw fruit trees in the distance.
The cliffs were so precipitous that not a single monkey could climb them, let alone a human being.
The garland-maker had searched for many days without finding a way up, and his provisions were exhausted. He thought to himself:
"I received the King's command to find these fruits; now that I have failed to obtain them, how can I return?"

Having formed this thought, he disregarded his own body and life; grasping with his hands at the precipitous cliff, he climbed upward little by little, but before reaching the location of the fruit, he suddenly fell, plunging into a deep abyss below.
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva who had become a king of monkeys wandering through the mountains and valleys. He saw a garland-maker fallen into a deep pit, suffering from hunger.

The Bodhisattva resolved to save all sentient beings; employing skillful means, the monkey king devised a plan: he took a large rock equal in weight to a human being, trained himself to carry it on his back, and once he knew he could reach the edge of the pit, he carried the garland-maker out gradually.
From this, he became utterly exhausted and his body was weary.
At that time, all the birds and beasts were able to understand human speech.
Then the monkey king asked the flower-garland maker:
"For what reason have you fallen into this deep pit?
At that time, the garland-maker explained at length as previously described.
Then the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"This fruit-gatherer will surely suffer punishment for failing to obtain his fruit;
I should now take some *āmra* fruits for him.
Although the Bodhisattva was exhausted, he nevertheless climbed a high cliff, plucked the fruits, and threw them down to the garland-maker.
Having obtained them, the man ate his fill and placed the remaining fruits in his robe-pouch.
The monkey descended from the tree and said to the garland-maker, "I am now weary and wish to sleep for a short while; you must remain vigilant and guard me."
The Flower-Garland replied,
"Very well! I shall remain vigilant."
The monkey then fell asleep.
At that time, the flower-garland maker thought to himself:
"My provisions for the road are exhausted; if I eat these fruits, with what shall I serve the king?"
"You should kill this monkey, dry it out to make jerky, and take it as provisions for the journey; only then can you reach your destination.

At that time, because that wicked man was ungrateful, he gave rise to an evil thought; he seized a large stone and struck the monkey on the head, shattering both its marrow and skull, whereby the monkey met its death.
At that time, a deva in the sky, having witnessed this event, spoke these verses:
"Attending upon and honoring him as if he were a virtuous friend—
how can there be such a person who does not know how to repay kindness?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should know this:
the monkey king of the past was none other than myself."
That wicked man Puṣpamāla was none other than Devadatta;
not only did he fail to recognize gratitude in the past, but he is likewise so now.
Monks, you should know this.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Devadatta further possesses the conduct of being ungrateful and unrepaying.
Listen attentively!
In the past, there was a mountain forest abounding in various flowers and fruits.
At that time, there was a bird named Woodpecker; on one side of that forest lived a lion king, who habitually killed and ate deer.

Later, he killed a deer and proceeded to eat it; however, a bone became stuck across his throat and could not be dislodged. Suffering for a long time, he was unable to eat, becoming emaciated, weak, and famished.
While playing, that bird saw the lion king and immediately asked him,
"Uncle! Why are you so emaciated?"
The lion replied, "I am in pain. Then the bird asked:
"Why are you suffering?
The lion king replied at length as previously described.
The bird then answered again:
"I am treating your suffering; you are the king of all beasts—can you repay my kindness?
Give me food every day. The Lion King replied:
"I shall always provide whatever you require.
The bird then thought to itself:
"I must devise a plan to remove its bones; once they have been removed, I will let him know."
"Only when the lion is asleep may I remove the bone.
Having formed this thought, he went briefly to wander among the trees in search of food.
At that time, the lion king, encountering a cool breeze, fell into a deep and pleasant sleep.
Once the bird saw that [the lion] was asleep, it placed a piece of wood in his mouth and examined him closely; it then entered his mouth, bit a bone, and emerged.
Perching upon a tree, it waited for the Lion King to wake from his sleep and showed him the bone.
At that time, the lion king awoke from his brief sleep and suddenly realized that the bone in his throat had vanished and he was free from pain;
he crouched down and let out a yawn. Seeing this, the bird was filled with joy; it flew down from the tree, showed him the bone, and said to the lion, "Uncle!..."
"All this suffering arises from these bones.
The lion, filled with joy, replied to the bird: "Nephew!..."
"I have long suffered in pain, which has now been cured. I wish to provide offerings and serve you for the rest of my life.
I only pray, nephew, that you will come here every day."
Upon hearing these words, the bird departed with joy.

Later, while the Lion King was in the midst of eating the deer, the woodpecker was pursued by a hawk; terrified and driven by hunger, he flew to the lion for refuge and recounted the circumstances of being chased by the hawk and his desperate hunger, saying, "I pray you, Uncle, grant me a single meal."
Then the Lion King replied in verse:
"I shall practice slaughter; my nature is evil and my deeds are evil.
My fangs are sharp; once you have entered my mouth, you shall not escape."
"You should rejoice within yourself; what more could you possibly seek now?
Hearing these words, the bird also replied in verse:
"Things fallen into the sea are lost; What gained in a dream is lost upon waking."
"To serve wicked people is a loss;
to rescue those who show no gratitude is an even greater loss. What do I seek from you?
Having spoken this verse, the bird immediately flew away.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The woodpecker king of that time was none other than myself.
That ungrateful lion king was none other than Devadatta."
"Previously you did not recognize kindness nor repay it; now it is the same.
You all should know this!
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Devadatta further possesses conduct that is ungrateful and unrequited.
Listen attentively!
Long ago, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a poor man who constantly gathered firewood to sell in order to sustain his life.”
On another occasion, that man took up a rope and an axe and went toward the edge of a forest, intending to cut firewood.

He encountered an untimely, great storm of wind and rain that did not cease for seven days. To avoid the wind and rain, he traveled by stages until he reached the side of a mountain, where he saw a stone cave and intended to enter it.
As he approached the entrance of the cave, he saw the bear inside; terrified, he turned back and fled.
Seeing him fleeing in fear, the bear called out to him, saying:
"O son of good family, come here!"
"Do not be afraid of me.
Although the man heard the bear call out to him, he remained gripped by terror; he stood there hesitating, neither advancing nor retreating.

Seeing that he had stopped, the bear immediately took him into its cave, ensuring he was not frightened, and provided him with various delicious fruits and edible tree roots, nourishing him for seven days until the eighth.
The bear went outside to observe the wind and rain; seeing that they had subsided, he immediately gave him fine fruits and sent him on his way.
The man knelt down long and with palms joined, saying:
"I have received your sustenance and my life has been preserved. From this day forward, how shall I repay your kindness?"
The bear immediately replied,
"If you simply do not speak to outsiders that I am living here, that shall suffice as repayment for my kindness.
The man then circumambulated the bear once, walking a path around it, and addressed the bear, saying:
"I shall never dare to let anyone else know," he said, and having spoken these words, he departed immediately.
As the man was traveling toward the city gate of Vārāṇasī, he saw a hunter who intended to go hunting; they had been acquainted with one another previously.
The hunter asked:
"You have not returned home for many days; your wife, children, and kinsmen are all filled with anxiety and distress, saying:
'Have you been swept away by wind and rain, or devoured by tigers and wolves?'"
"I was about to die.
Since the great rains have passed and many birds and beasts have perished, how have you managed to survive?
At that time, the woodcutter recounted how the bear had cared for him, as described in detail above.
The hunter asked,
"In which mountain and which cave does that bear dwell now?
I pray that you will show it to me."
Then the wood-gatherer replied to the hunter,
"Even if I were to die now, I could never return to the mountain forest.
The hunter replied with many clever words, exhorting and persuading him in various ways:
"If I can kill it, I will give you the greater portion and take one part for myself.
The man immediately gave rise to greed and turned back; he went toward the bear's location until he reached the edge of the cave, where he pointed at the bear from afar and watched it.
At that time, the hunter piled up a great deal of firewood at the entrance of the cave and smoked it with fire.
Then the bear, oppressed by the smoke and fire, suffering and on the verge of death, spoke this verse:
"I dwell in these mountains, And do not harm a single person."
Eating fruits and tree roots, I constantly gave rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion.
Now that my life is coming to an end, what plan should I make?
Reflecting upon my past karma, I see that good and evil deeds now receive their retribution.
When the bear had spoken this verse, he immediately passed away.
Knowing that the bear was dead, the hunter entered the cave, took the bear, flayed its skin, and divided the meat into three portions. He said to the woodcutter:
"Take two portions of the meat; I shall take one."
At that time, the woodcutter reached out his hands to take the meat; as he was taking it, both his hands fell off. Seeing this, the hunter cried out:
"How marvelous!"
"How marvelous!
The hunter, without taking even his own flesh with him, returned to the city and reported this extraordinary event to the king, recounting it to the people of the land.

Having heard this, the King went in person to see it; he took the bear skin and proceeded to the monastery, where he struck the bell to assemble the community and placed the bear skin before the monks.

After the King had paid his respects to the monks, he related the aforementioned events to the monastic community. The presiding elder (sthavira) of the monastery, who was an Arhat, replied to the King in verse:
"Great King, you should now know: This is not truly the body of a bear;
He is a supreme Bodhisattva, Who shall attain the unsurpassed fruit."
"He should be honored with offerings throughout the three periods of time; Great King, you must erect a stūpa for him.

When the king heard this, he commanded his ministers to fetch various kinds of fragrant wood and go to the bear's cave to cremate the body. He then erected a stūpa, arranged various flowers and incense, hung silk banners and canopies, and performed offerings by sprinkling water and sweeping the grounds.
The king, his ministers, and all the people together established a covenant that they would assemble annually to make offerings.
Having made this covenant, they paid homage to the stūpa and departed.
"Should any person come to pay homage to that stūpa or make offerings to it, they shall all be reborn in heaven.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The bear of former times was my own self."
The man who was the woodcutter in the past is none other than Devadatta today.
In the past he was already devoid of gratitude and lacked the sense of recompense; now, once again, he is without gratitude and without shame.
"You all should know this.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Devadatta further possesses conduct that is ungrateful and fails to repay kindness."
"Listen attentively!
Long ago, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a poor man who sustained his life by constantly gathering firewood to sell.

On one occasion, he took his rope and axe and went into the forest; having reached a tree, he intended to gather some wood, but upon encountering a tiger, he became terrified and fled, climbing up a large tree."
Unaware that there was a bear on the tree, he became terrified upon seeing it and did not dare climb back up.
Seeing his fear, the bear gradually descended and said to him,
"You need not be afraid!"
"Simply rely on me.
Having heard this, the woodcutter did not dare to approach.
Seeing him, the bear felt compassion and came forward to take hold of him; she chose a secure spot in the tree, and the bear sat there embracing him.
At that time, the tiger beneath the tree replied to the bear, saying:
"This creature is ungrateful; later it will bring calamity and harm upon you, so why must you protect it?
You should simply cast it down beneath the tree, for I must eat it."
"If I do not obtain food, I shall never depart.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"According to the ways of the world, even those who merely seek refuge are protected; how much more so should a Bodhisattva protect those who come to him for refuge?"
Then the bear replied to the tiger, saying, "This man has sought refuge with me; I shall never violate my word.
Hearing these words, the tiger, though tormented by hunger, also refused to leave.
The bear said to the woodcutter, "I shall now hold you while I rest briefly from my fatigue; in a short while, you must wake yourself and guard me.
Then, with his head resting upon the woodcutter, he began to reflect:
"I shall sleep for a moment; when I have rested, I will preach the Dharma in ten verses to you, woodcutter.
Having formed this thought, the bear immediately fell asleep.
Seeing that the bear was sleeping, the insect said to the woodcutter:
"How long can you remain perched upon this tree?
You should throw the bear down to the ground so that I may eat it and depart; thus you will avoid harm and be able to return home."
When the woodcutter heard these words, he immediately conceived an evil thought:
"This insect speaks so pleasantly; how much longer can I remain in this place?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately cast the bear down from the tree, pushing it off; as soon as the bear realized it was falling, before it had yet reached the ground, the man uttered ten words, and having spoken them, it reached the earth.
Once the insect had obtained the bear, it ate its fill and departed.
Having heard the bear explain the secret method of the ten characters, the woodcutter immediately reflected:
"The bear possesses an excellent dharma; he should surely speak it to me."
Thereupon, greed arose and affliction was born; because he had lost the Dharma, his mind became deluded and he ran about wildly.
He uttered ten words, saying:
"At that time, the woodcutter’s relatives, seeing him thus crazed, brought him back home; he spoke no other words, only these ten."
When his relatives saw that he had become insane, they sought out physicians and those skilled in incantations; though they treated him with various medical prescriptions, they could not cure him.
Not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a forest abounding in fruit, where flocks of birds gathered and produced exquisite sounds.

At that time, there was a seer in that forest who possessed the five supernormal powers. The relatives of the madman led him to see the seer; they knelt down in prostration and immediately said to him:
"This member of our family is insane and his mind is deranged; he speaks no other words but proclaims these ten syllables. We do not understand them—how may he be treated and cured?"
The seer replied: "This man committed evil and was utterly ungrateful.

He killed a great bodhisattva and cast him beneath a tree; before the body had even reached the ground, he uttered ten characters. Having recited these ten characters—which correspond to ten verses—he fell to the earth and died, whereupon he was devoured by a tiger. At that time, the woodcutter immediately went mad."
Then all the kinsmen and the disciples of the seer addressed the seer, saying:
"What are these ten verses?
Furthermore, what is their meaning?"
At that time, the seer explained it in succession and spoke these verses.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!"
The bear of the past is my present self;
the woodcutter who was ungrateful at that time is now Devadatta.
Just as he was ungrateful in the past, so too is he now.
"You all should know this.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Devadatta further possesses conduct that is ungrateful and unrequiting."
Listen attentively!
In the past there was a city named Śānta, and therein was a king also named Śānta.
The land was abundant and the people lived in peace and happiness; there were no thieves or robbers, and they did not wage war against one another.

The king was compassionate by nature, regarding all sentient beings with pity as if they were his only son. His heart delighted in giving and he constantly took pleasure in hearing the Dharma; free from stinginess and greed, he made offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor and sick, never feeling weary or satisfied.
It was the king’s established custom to first attend upon his parents every morning at dawn, and afterwards to visit the sick before attending to the affairs of state.

At that time, there was a poor man suffering from a grave illness who was extremely distressed; the physicians and caregivers were unwilling to give him medicine, all declaring that he was certain to die.
Having heard this, the sick man was filled with distress and, weeping bitterly, wandered on until he reached the city of Śānti.

At that time, King Vāsava, together with his ministers, queens, and retinue, wished to go out for a stroll in the park; as they were proceeding to the city gate, the sick man, leaning on a staff and weeping, knelt before the king and said to him:
"I pray only that Your Majesty will save me, save me from such suffering of illness, and grant that my life be preserved."
Having seen this, the king gave rise to great compassion; he turned his carriage back toward the palace and commanded his ministers, saying, "Summon all the physicians within my realm.
The ministers received the king’s command and immediately assembled all the physicians, who were then brought before the king.
The king summoned the sick man and personally inspected him, saying:
"You physicians must certainly cure him.
Upon seeing him, the physicians said to the great king:
"Observing this person's illness, the medicine is extremely difficult to obtain.
The king then asked, "For what reason is it so difficult to obtain?"
The physician replied to the king:
"It is necessary to obtain the blood of a person who has never known anger throughout their entire life; by boiling it into porridge for treatment, you may then be cured."
"If the illness is not cured, it will not be eliminated.
Having heard this, the king thought to himself:
"Since I cannot save even one person's life, what is the use of this royal throne or my own life?"
He then reflected within himself, "Throughout my entire life, there has never been a cause for anger.
Having formed this thought, he commanded his nurse and immediately asked her,
"When I was young, did I not have anger?"
The wet nurse replied, "Since my birth, I have never felt anger even while holding the Prince; how much less so toward his person!
Yet, not yet considering this to be certain, she questioned the biological mother again:
"Has the child ever shown anger since he was born?
The mother replied, "Even while I was carrying the Prince in my womb, I had no anger; how much less so now that he is the Prince himself!"
Having heard this, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking to himself:
"Have I now obtained the medicine?
He then addressed the physicians:
"Apply needles to five places on my body and draw out the blood.
The physicians replied to the king:
"The patient is of low station while Your Majesty is noble and exalted; we do not dare to rashly apply needles to Your Majesty's person."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All bodhisattvas are skillfully adept in the various worldly affairs.

At that time, the king gave rise to a heart of compassion; he immediately pierced five places on his own body with needles to draw blood until the vessels were full, then entrusted it to the physician, who was ordered to prepare gruel for the sick man to eat."

At that time, when the people of the kingdom saw that the king had been so compassionate and kind in nurturing his subjects, the prince, ministers, queens, court ladies, and all the citizens wept together and said to one another:
"The king has pity for but a single person and does not spare even his own life; he abandons us, and now we are left without a protector."
Having heard this, the king replied to the people, saying, "Do not be distressed; this is no evil matter.
At that time, the great king bled himself daily for six months to provide for the sick man; consequently, the king gradually became emaciated and his body grew weak.
When the pure devas witnessed these events concerning the king, they thought to themselves:

"This is the body of a Bodhisattva of the Bhadrakalpa; it would not be a good thing if he were to suffer decline or death. We shall, through the skillful means of our celestial power, cause nectar to enter every one of his pores."
Having thought this, he immediately bestowed his majestic power upon them; the king was restored to life and the patient recovered.
Through the empowerment of the devas, the king regained his health and the patient likewise recovered.
The King then further granted five excellent villages to the sick man.
At that time, within the city of Śānti, the sick man became of equal status with the king’s ministers, officials, and nobles, and his fame spread throughout the eight directions.
After six months had passed, he was cured only by being fed the blood of the patient; furthermore, five excellent villages were bestowed as a reward.
When this report reached the eight directions, everyone was filled with wonder and came to that city to ask the patient:
"Did the king truly bleed himself for six months to provide offerings for you?"
That wicked man, being ungrateful and unthankful, immediately said to the people:
"What benefit has this king provided me?
Since my body possessed foul blood that ought to have been discarded, what is so strange about his giving it to someone else?"

However, as soon as that wicked person had uttered these words, fire burst forth from the earth, burning this man's house until everything was utterly consumed, while that sick person instead contracted a wasting disease.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of that country was none other than my own self in this present life.
The sick man of that time, who showed neither gratitude nor recompense, was Devadatta."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Devadatta further possesses conduct that is ungrateful and fails to repay kindness.
Listen attentively!

In the distant past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king whose story is as extensively told before; eventually, the queen gave birth to a prince whose countenance was upright and majestic, his complexion ruddy-white, and his head and face perfectly rounded like a parasol.
His arms hung down like the trunks of elephants; his two eyebrows met, his forehead was broad, and his nose was straight; all his limbs and joints were perfectly formed.
At the time of his birth, all auspicious signs appeared before him. Twenty-one days having passed since his birth, all his kinsmen gathered together and celebrated with various joys.
At that time, the ministers addressed one another, saying:
"When the prince was born, hundreds of thousands of auspicious signs appeared before us; therefore, we shall establish his name as 'Sucarita' (Good Conduct)."
The details are as explained above, up until he gradually grew up.

At that time, that Sudatta (Good Conduct) was of a nature of great compassion; he gave rise to a heart of pity for all sentient beings, always delighting in giving, and provided for śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor, including travelers from afar.
At that time, the father-king spoke to Sudāna, saying:
"From this day forward, you should not constantly practice such giving; the treasuries of my kingdom cannot provide for it sufficiently."
At that time, the queen gave birth to another son; at the moment of his birth, hundreds of thousands of calamities and inauspicious omens all manifested, and thus he was given the name Duṣkṛta.
"He has grown up there.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is a constant law of the world:"
The one who practices giving is beloved by all people, and his fame is heard everywhere.

A certain king, hearing of his virtuous conduct and his fondness for practicing generosity, desired to give his daughter in marriage to Sudatta as his wife; he sent many precious jewels, chariots, and servants, along with a letter, dispatching an envoy.
He went to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to inform the king; upon hearing this, the king was delighted and consented to the marriage.
At that time, Sudhana came forward and said to his father, the king:
"I do not wish to deplete the royal treasury; I shall now go to sea to seek treasures for myself, and having obtained them, I will take a wife."
The king immediately granted his permission.
Having received permission, Sudhana joyfully prepared his gear and provisions, intending to depart.
When Duṣkṛta saw this, he thought to himself:

"Now this elder brother of mine is loved and respected by both our own people and those of other nations. If he returns from the sea having gathered treasures, the King, his ministers, and all the people will redouble their respect for him. My father will surely appoint him as the sovereign of the kingdom, leaving me with no share of the realm."
I should now employ a skillful means to follow him into the sea and seek to kill him, so that I may return home.
Whether he likes it or not, my father will surely appoint me as the crown prince.
Having formed this thought, he also went to his father's presence and said to the King, his father:
"I wish to follow my elder brother into the sea to seek jewels.
Upon hearing this, the King granted him permission; Duṣkṛta rejoiced and likewise prepared his equipment.
At that time, Kalyāṇakārin beat the drums and rang the bells within the city, proclaiming to all the people:

"I intend to go to sea. Anyone who is able to go should prepare provisions and pack their belongings to follow me. I shall serve as the caravan leader; whether by water or land, I can protect you from all obstacles and hardships. I will protect you all so that you have no fear, nor shall you have to pay any taxes."
Having spoken these words, five hundred men came to the Prince’s presence and said to him,
“We beg to follow the Prince. Then,
selecting an auspicious day, they departed together.
The details are as previously described, up until they entered the sea, where he suddenly told his younger brother:
"If this ship should suddenly meet with disaster and break apart in the midst of the ocean, you should seize hold of me; do not be afraid."
The one of evil conduct replied,
"As my elder brother has instructed.
The ship encountered a favorable wind and eventually reached the place of treasures.
At that time, the ship’s captain addressed the prince and the multitude, saying:
"In the past, you have heard of an island of precious jewels; this place is it.
There are all kinds of treasures here; take as many as you wish."

Upon hearing this, the multitude was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they immediately disembarked from the ship and gathered various treasures until the vessel was filled like a field of hemp or wheat.
Prince Sudhana took the wish-fulfilling jewel, fastened it at his waist, turned the ship around, and returned.
Desiring to reach the other shore, they encountered a makara fish that shattered their boat.
At that moment, Duṣkṛta seized his elder brother, and all the ship's treasures were lost to the waves.
Only through the power of his elder brother did Duṣkara reach this shore.
