Having emerged from the sea by exerting his own strength, Sukara was utterly exhausted and fell asleep; Duṣkara remained guarding his brother and subsequently saw the precious jewel at his brother’s waist.
He then thought to himself:
"My brother has obtained fine jewels while I have lost what I acquired. I should now blind my brother's eyes and take the jewels back alone.
Having formed this thought, he first stole the treasures and then blinded his brother's eyes with thorns, abandoning him and departing.
Because he had practiced virtue, the blind man did not know the way back. Later, a cowherd saw him and asked, "Where have you come from?
At that time, the blind man related everything as it had happened above.
The cowherd, recognizing him, immediately gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness and took him back to his home.
Since Sudhana was naturally exceptionally skilled at playing the lute, he played the lute while staying in that house.
The cowherd’s wife conceived a feeling of affection and, giving rise to lustful desire, said to the blind man,
"Commit adultery with me.
Upon hearing this, the blind man covered both his ears with his hands and said:
"Do not utter such words; I do not wish to hear them.
You are my sister; why do you speak such words?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is the constant law of the world:
all sentient beings have minds that crave form; if their desires are not fulfilled, they each give rise to anger.
At that time, seeing her wishes unfulfilled, the woman immediately conceived hatred and gave rise to a mind of slanderous defilement, saying to her husband:"
"That blind man wishes to defile me with lust; how can we keep such an evil person within our home?
The Buddha further addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is a constant law of the world:"
All sentient beings give rise to anger and vexation when their beloved wives are defiled by others; compared to all other enemies, this enemy is the most grievous.
For this reason, having heard his wife’s words, the cowherd conceived a profound resentment toward the blind man and further thought:
"This man has committed a grave offense; seeing him now blind is his retribution, so there is no need to kill him—simply drive him out."
Having formed this thought, he immediately drove him out.
The blind man, carrying his lute, departed and wandered through cities and towns begging for his livelihood.

Later, after the father king had passed away, the younger brother, Duṣkṛta, succeeded to the throne. The blind man, continuing his gradual begging, eventually arrived at the capital city of his wife’s kingdom.
His wife was advanced in years, and the princes of various kingdoms all vied with one another to seek her hand. Her father, the king, said to his daughter:
"When you were first given in marriage, Prince Śubhakārin went out to sea and perished when his ship sank."
"Now there are princes and others who are vying with one another to come and solicit you; if I do not give you in marriage, I fear they will harbor resentment in their hearts.
Therefore, I have now consulted with you: what is your own inclination?"
The woman said to the king:

"I only pray that my father, the King, will issue a decree to the people within the realm to thoroughly cleanse the city and assemble all the citizens of the country, so that I may personally select [a husband] from among them."
The father-king granted his daughter’s request and subsequently issued an edict throughout his realm and to all foreign lands:
"I have a daughter whom I now wish to marry; let all the people of the nations assemble so that she may choose her own son-in-law."
He then immediately adorned the city walls and moats like the Garden of Joy (Nandana-vana) and ordered the beating of drums to proclaim:

"All people currently within the city, as well as those arriving from afar, listen! The King’s daughter seeks a husband; choose according to your own inclination. You all must adorn yourselves according to your means and assemble here."

When the clear dawn arrived, the princess was finely adorned and went forth accompanied by her handmaidens; like the Goddess Śrī amidst the wondrous flower groves in the Nandana Garden, she proceeded through the city amidst a great multitude numbering in the hundreds of thousands, traveling in order to seek a husband for herself.
At that time, Kalyāṇakārin stood to one side playing the lute. Through the convergence of the karmic forces and conditions of sentient beings, they encountered one another.
Hearing the sound of his lute, she felt a sense of longing and affection; she then cast a flower garland from afar onto him and declared, "This man shall be my husband."
At that time, the great assembly was each filled with grief and distress, and together they uttered words of reproach:

"In this assembly there are many from noble clans, as well as princes and high ministers from all quarters of exquisite youth and beauty, along with the handsome men within this city; how can she abandon these and choose a blind man to be her husband?"
At that time, the king’s close attendants, having witnessed this event, were filled with anxiety and distress; they entered and addressed the king:
"Your Majesty has yielded to your daughter's wishes and sought out a husband for her."
The king asked, "How so? They replied:
"Blind! Hearing this, the king was distressed with grief; he summoned his daughter and asked, "Young woman, what is your meaning?"

In this city now there are many worthy men, eminent figures, ministers, and great officials, as well as numerous men who have come from the four quarters; for what reason do you not choose one of them, but instead take a blind man?
The daughter replied to her father, "I love this.
The king said:
"If that is so, you ought to go to him.
Why do you remain here?
The woman then went to him and said:
"Kind sir, you are my husband.
He replied, "You have acted improperly; why do you entertain such thoughts as to consort with other men?"
The woman said,
"Virtuous one, I have no such intention to do this. He asked:
"How can this be known?
The woman then spoke with sincere earnestness and words of true faith:
"May you now verify that my heart is as I have thought."
“If Prince Kalyāṇakārin and you feel a desire for one another and have no other thoughts, may your eye be restored to its former state.
When this young woman uttered these words of truth, the blind man’s eye immediately opened and became clear.
He said, “Noble lady!”
"I am Sukṛta, and my younger brother Duṣkṛta has done me harm.
The woman asked,
"How do you know that you are Sukṛta?"
He immediately uttered words of truth, saying:
"When I was struck in the eye by one of evil conduct, my heart harbored not the slightest resentment toward him.
If these words are true, let my other eye be restored to its former state."
When he spoke these words of truth, his two eyes shone with clarity.
Thereupon, the princess led Sudhana to her father the king and said,
"This is my husband."
The king did not believe her, so the woman then recounted the previous events in detail to him.

The king was greatly amazed and immediately ordered a grand ceremony to formalize their marriage. He then mobilized a large force of soldiers and horses, sent Sudhana back to his original city, expelled Duṣkṛta, and installed Sudhana as the successor to his father’s throne.
"O bhikṣus, what do you think? Was Prince Sudhana anyone else?
He was none other than myself."
As for that man of evil conduct, he is none other than Devadatta.
It was not only in the present time that he lacked gratitude; it was likewise so in the past.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda: The Matter of the Schism in the Saṃgha, Fascicle Fifteen;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda: The Matter of the Schism in the Saṃgha, Fascicle Sixteen.
The Buddha said: "Furthermore, listen to how Devadatta, in times past, failed to repay kindness. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
In the distant past, there was a royal capital where the population was flourishing and the people lived in peace, security, abundance, and joy.
The king had four sons:
the first was named Mahāśākha, the second Upaśākha, the third Anuśākha, and the fourth Cūlaśākha.

As the four princes grew older, they each took a daughter of a neighboring king as their wife. Together, they conceived a rebellious intent toward their father. Once the father became aware of this, he banished them from the kingdom.

Each took his wife and traveled until they reached a wilderness where their provisions were exhausted. They established a cruel rule among themselves: they would kill one wife at a time, taking her flesh for food to sustain their lives so they might complete their journey.
At that time, Little Branch thought to himself:
"It would be better for me to die than to take another's life.
Since there is no other recourse, I should secretly flee with my wife to another country."
Having formed this thought, he fled with his wife.
Pressed by hunger and thirst, the wife became exhausted and unable to proceed further, and she said to her husband:
"Noble son!..."
"My life is about to end, and I have no means to travel the road.
Little Branch thought to herself:
"I have preserved this person's life from my evil Rākṣasa companions; for him to perish here would be deeply tragic and lamentable."
He immediately cut flesh from his thigh to give her to eat and pierced his arm to provide blood for her to drink.
After his wife had consumed the flesh and blood, they gradually made their way on foot to a mountain valley, where he gathered roots and fruits to sustain their lives.

In the midst of that mountain range there was a great river. At that time, a certain man, having been robbed by hostile bandits who severed his hands and feet, was cast into the river and carried away with the current, crying out in agony.

Xiaozhi heard the sound of piteous cries emerging from within; moved by compassion, he followed the sound to search for its source. He then saw a man being carried down by the current, so he entered the river, carried him on his back out, and set him upon the riverbank.
Seeing that both his hands and feet were missing, his heart was pierced with intense grief, and he asked:
"O son of good family!
For what reason have you encountered such bitter suffering?"
The man related the matter in full.
Little Branch replied,
"Though you suffer now, do not give way to grief or fear."
He gave him roots and fruits to eat and said to his wife, "You must look upon this man with compassion and care for him.

Having received such kind treatment, the man’s suffering from the wound gradually subsided; the wife then conceived a sense of affection for him and frequently approached him to engage in conversation.
The Bodhisattva was by nature one who practiced few sensual desires; even when gathering with others at times, he harbored no lustful intent.

However, all the roots and fruits in this mountain, through the Bodhisattva’s majestic power, became exceptionally exquisite; once the women had eaten them, their depraved minds were further inflamed, and they went to the man's place seeking to engage in unrighteous acts.
She refused him, replying:

"I nearly lost my life, yet by good fortune I have been saved by you. To engage in an evil deed together would be to cast aside such kindness; if your husband were to find out, he would surely cut me limb from limb."

The wife repeatedly sought him out and, being tormented by affliction, eventually engaged in sexual intercourse with him; she became deeply attached to him and did not wish to be parted from him even for a moment, feeling no affection or pleasure for her original husband.
Although she sent him away, he did not see her following him, and he thought to himself:
"This woman is now infatuated with me; her illicit affair with another's wife is a great enmity, and I shall surely suffer."
They then consulted together and said to his wife:
"If our husband were to discover that we have committed this unlawful act, he would surely take our lives; of this there is no doubt."
When the woman heard these words, she agreed with them and devised another stratagem.
Possessing the clever wit that comes naturally without study, she immediately wrapped her head in her garment, used a stone as a pillow, and lay down.
When the youth returned to her side after gathering fruit from the small branches, he noticed an unusual appearance and asked:
"O noble lady! What is troubling you?"
He replied, "Noble son! My head is in great pain."
The younger branch replied,
"What do you wish to do? The woman,
secretly harboring a scheme and conceiving this evil intent, said to her husband:
"I previously had a headache; the physician gave me stone-amber to apply to my head, and it was immediately cured.
Xiaozhi replied, "Where could one obtain such a thing?"
"I went there to seek it.
The woman said,
"At the foot of that cliff, by the side of the mountain stream, I saw this medicine."
"Since it is so high and precipitous, you must descend by feeling your way down while I hold you from above.
That man was a great being of upright nature, free from deceit or hypocrisy, and he replied, "So be it."
Tying a rope around his waist, he descended the precipice intending to gather the medicinal herbs; however, his wife let go of the rope, causing him to fall over the cliff and into the water.
Because that sentient being was destined for a long life and was fated to inherit the royal throne, he did not die from the fall but drifted with the current until he reached the capital city.
When the king of that country died without an heir, the ministers and the citizens deliberated together:
"The king has died without a son; whom among us shall we establish to succeed to his position?"
He summoned the physiognomists and ordered them to seek out a person fit to be a king.
At that time, the physiognomists searched in all four directions, as it is said in a verse:
"Even if one passes through a hundred kalpas, The karma one has created does not perish;..."
"When causes and conditions meet, one must personally experience the resulting retribution.
At that time, because his karma had matured and he was destined to receive the royal throne, Little Branch emerged from the water and sat upon the edge of the cliff.
However, due to the Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue, the place where he dwelt was exceptionally radiant.

At that time, several physiognomists happened to travel there and, seeing that this Great Being possessed the auspicious marks of a king, were all filled with joy. They went to inform the ministers, saying:
"We have found a Great Being who possesses the auspicious marks of a king and is fit to be the sovereign of the nation."

Upon hearing this, the ministers immediately ordered the people of the kingdom to adorn the city walls and prepare for the great ceremony; they selected an auspicious day and together enthroned him as king.

However, as there was yet no queen, the ministers issued a proclamation to the noble families of all nations, commanding that if there were any beautiful and virtuous maidens, each should adorn her and bring her to the royal capital; whoever met with the king's favor was to be taken as his queen.
The king, having encountered great suffering and distress on account of a woman, felt profound revulsion and had no thought of looking back upon her.
The ministers addressed him, saying:
"Great King, you should know!"
‘If the Queen were to die, it would sever the royal lineage; therefore, let beautiful women from all quarters gather here, so that one may be consecrated as Queen and others as court ladies.
The King did not grant permission, for he spoke of the faults and perils of women.”
Wherever beings possessing merit reside, their flowers, fruits, food, and drink are all sweet and delicious, and they possess great vitality;
however, after the Bodhisattva had fallen from the cliff, none of the flowers, fruits, roots, or stalks grew in that mountain, and even those that did grow were bitter, astringent, and flavorless.
Because those two evil men lacked strength due to the lack of vigor in their sense organs and fruits, they gradually became so weak that they could no longer survive.
At that time, the evil woman took up the man who was without hands or feet on her back and emerged from the mountain; she entered various villages, wandering about to beg for alms.
If others see him and ask, "Who is this person?
he should reply:
"This is my husband. Although she described him in this manner, she had no other intention.
Nevertheless, according to the laws of the land, if there is a woman who is chaste and diligent toward her husband, many people hold her in high esteem and provide her with offerings.
Wherever this woman went, there was an abundance of food and drink; thus she traveled on until she gradually reached the royal capital.
Upon hearing of her arrival, all the people sighed in admiration, and some, filled with joy, went outside to gaze at her from afar.
When the people within the city witnessed this event, they raised criticisms together, saying:

"The King says that women have many faults and afflictions; yet do you not see this chaste and prudent woman, who, with no hands or feet, carries her husband upon her shoulders and begs from door to door to provide for him?"
At that time, the gatekeeper, having witnessed the events described above, reported them in full to the king.
Upon hearing these words, the king issued an order for her to be summoned inside. Once the woman had entered, the king, upon seeing her, smiled and spoke this verse:
“Having eaten the flesh of my thigh to satisfy hunger, And drunk my blood to quench thirst;”
Carrying a lump of flesh upon my shoulders as I walk, where is there any integrity or prudence?
With evil intent he sought a stone slab, hoping that I would fall from the cliff and perish;
carrying a lump of flesh upon my shoulders as I walk, where is there any integrity or prudence?
When the woman heard this verse from the king, she felt ashamed and immediately lowered her head.
The ministers, hearing the verse but not knowing its cause, said to him:
"Great King!..."
"What is the meaning and purpose of the verse you have spoken?
The king then explained it in detail and in sequence for his ministers.
The people of the city detested this woman; they cried out together that she was wicked and banished her from the country.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think?
Who else could that person who was the 'Little Branch' in times past have been?"
I am that very person. As for that woman, she is now Devadatta.
It is not only in the present time that he has failed to repay kindness; it was likewise so in past ages.
“O bhikṣus, listen again with careful attention. Devadatta was ungrateful and failed to repay his kindness.

Long ago, in times past, there was a royal capital ruled by a king named Svāmimitra. The populace was flourishing, peaceful, secure, and prosperous; he governed according to the True Dharma and held the virtuous and worthy in high esteem. He constantly cherished great compassion for the benefit of both himself and others, always seeking the Sublime Dharma, and felt deep affection for all his subjects.”

Later, at another time, the queen gave birth to a son whose physical form was upright and exceptionally beautiful to behold; his complexion was radiant like a bar of pure gold, he had a crown-like topknot on his head, long and slender arms, a broad and level forehead, joined eyebrows, a high and straight nose, and all his sense faculties were complete.

His kinsmen bestowed upon him the name Svayambhū. He was entrusted to eight nurses, and as he gradually grew older, they sent him to school. There, he became thoroughly proficient in calculation, strategy, seals, scripts, and secret characters; he attained complete mastery in all arts and crafts, including the skillful management of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, as well as archery and the use of weapons, leaving nothing unmastered.

That youth Īśvara was respectful and faithful toward the virtuous, his heart filled with benevolence and courtesy; benefiting himself and others was his fundamental practice. He was constantly compassionate and universally loved the common people, abandoning stinginess and greed to cultivate the practice of giving.

He was without even a single thought of stinginess regarding all his wealth; throughout the entire kingdom, everyone heard of this and came to admire him with total devotion. From the four quarters, those who were solitary or impoverished, extending for more than a hundred *yojanas*, all flocked to him; he ensured that none lacked anything and caused them all to give rise to joyous hearts.

Once, on one occasion, the Bodhisattva went out for a pleasure excursion to a fragrant garden riding in a carriage. That carriage was adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, and the celestial blue jewel (*indranīla*); its poles and yokes were made of exquisite sandalwood. The carriage was further embellished with the skins of lions, tigers, and leopards and decorated with various precious pendants, such that all who saw it felt love and joy. Drawn by four horses as swift as the wind, it proceeded toward the garden.
At that time, there was a learned and wise great Brahmin who came and said to the youth:
"You should know that all people in the world have heard of your practice of giving;
though this precious chariot is dear and important to you, you ought to give it to the Brahmin."
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva immediately and swiftly descended from his chariot with a heart of joy. He then pointed to the vehicle and said to the brahmin:
"I now renounce this precious chariot, Joyfully bestowing it upon you, O brahmin;
May I likewise renounce the three realms of existence And proceed toward unsurpassed bodhi."
At that time, the brahmin, having obtained the chariot and horses, mounted them and departed.

On another occasion, the Bodhisattva mounted a great white elephant named Rajavardhana, whose color was as white as crystal, snow, or silver flowers; its seven limbs were perfectly formed, it was endowed with all auspicious marks, and it stood with perfect composure, like Śakra’s Airāvaṇa, moving with such dignified gait that all who saw it were delighted.
Surrounded by his retinue and all his attendants, he was like the full moon shining amidst the stars and the Milky Way.

Furthermore, it was during the season of spring; various flowers were in full bloom, the springs and ponds were crystal clear, and flocks of birds sang in harmony. At that time, the Bodhisattva desired to go to the fragrant garden for a brief excursion.
At that time, an enemy from another country informed a brahmin, instructing him to beg a great white elephant from the Bodhisattva.
The brahmin then raised his hand and begged from the Bodhisattva, reciting this verse:
"All those among the hosts of devas and humans Are alike renowned for their love of giving;”
"The great white elephant upon which I ride should be taken away by you.
When the Bodhisattva heard these words, he immediately and swiftly dismounted from the elephant with a heart full of joy, and pointing toward it, he said to the brahmin:
"I now relinquish this white elephant; I joyfully bestow it as a gift upon you, O brahmin."
"May I emerge from the stream of the three realms of existence and swiftly reach the shore of Bodhi.
At that time, various ministers reported to the father-king:
"Prince Īśvara has now given the great elephant Candana as a gift to a Brahmin who is an enemy of our kingdom."
Upon hearing these words, the king was seized with great rage and immediately commanded his messenger to summon Prince Īśvara.
When the prince arrived, the king addressed him, saying:
"You should no longer reside within my kingdom."
Having heard these words, the Prince thought to himself:
"My father now abandons me; I shall now don the armor of wisdom and give up this great elephant, seeking unsurpassed bodhi for the benefit of all beings."
He further thought to himself:

"If I remain at home now, I will certainly be unable to practice giving according to my heart's desire; it would be better for me to go to the mountain forests and strictly maintain the observance of the precepts."
"Therefore, I shall now abandon my domestic ties and dwell alone in the forest thickets; should anyone come to beg, I vow not to refuse them.
Having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva returned to his palace and informed his consort in detail.
Having heard this, the consort, fearing separation from her husband, was filled with grief and sorrow; she immediately joined her palms and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying: "Noble Son!
If it must be so, I too shall follow you to the mountain forests. I can never bear to be parted from you for even a moment; were we to be separated, my life would not endure."
Then he spoke a verse to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"The sky without the moon has no radiance; The great earth without seedlings produces no fruit.
The lotus pond with its waters dried up— A woman without a husband is just like this."
The Bodhisattva said:

"It is a constant law of the world that there must be separation. You were born and raised in the royal palace, where you had sufficient fine food, clothing, and bedding; because of such nourishment, your body and flesh are soft and delicate.
If you stay among the mountain forests, you will spread grass upon the ground and sleep upon it, take fruit as your food, and walk through thorns while gathering flowers and fruit."

Constantly maintaining the practice of the precepts, you shall see that the minds of others are also firm and steadfast; when those who come offer support, you should resolutely give whatever they desire, and at the time of giving, do not give rise to anxiety or distress.
The Bodhisattva spoke again to his consort, saying,
"You should deliberate upon this for yourself.
The consort replied:
"I shall follow the will of the Noble Son.
The Bodhisattva further told him:
"If it be so, you must constantly keep this in mind and make a vow, saying:"
Having made this vow, the Bodhisattva went to his father the King, prostrated himself, and said:
"I pray that my father will forgive my transgression, for I have given away the great elephant to a Brahmin who is an enemy of another kingdom."
"Because of these faults, I shall go to the mountain forests; may the King’s treasury always remain abundant and never suffer from lack.
Having heard these words, the king parted from his son, his heart filled with desolation, sorrow, grief, and distress, and he said to his son:
"You should remain here; do not go to the mountain forests, but give as you please in charity."
The Bodhisattva replied to his father, the King, in verse:
"The mountains and forests of the great earth might yet be made to turn back;
But my resolve to give to those who beg shall never waver."
“When the Bodhisattva had spoken these verses, he took his leave of his father and departed.
At that time, the Crown Prince’s consort, their son and daughter, along with thousands of attendants, all wept bitterly as they went out together from this city.”
At that time, there was a man who, hearing this great assembly weeping and wailing in grief, asked:
"For what reason is this great assembly weeping so sorrowfully? They replied:
“Have you not heard? he replied with a verse:
“In the city there is a prince, who personally gives away his precious elephant as a gift.”
"The King has sentenced him to exile and banishment; for this reason, the multitude weeps.
At that time, having already departed the city, the Prince addressed his attendants:
"All of you, turn back."

You should now know that all meetings with those one holds dear must inevitably end in separation; the gathering of kinsmen is by nature not long-lasting, just like travelers who rest together in the shade of a tree for a brief moment before they must inevitably part ways.
He then spoke in verse:
"All people in this world, though they meet, must inevitably part.
When the Bodhisattva had finished speaking these words, he traveled for thirty *li* and saw a Brahmin approaching him, who addressed him, saying:

"Kṣatriya youth! I have heard of your reputation from afar, having traveled thirty *yojanas* to come here for the sake of seeking a four-horse chariot; I pray that you will grant me this four-horse chariot."
At that time, when the Prince’s consort saw the brahmin coming to beg, she gave rise to feelings of contempt and addressed the brahmin with harsh words, speaking in verse:
"O you of most wretched disposition! You speak thus to the brahmin:
While staying amidst the forest trees, You have come to beg for a chariot drawn by four horses."
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to his consort:
"Do not speak harsh words to this brahmin.
He then spoke in verse:
"If there were no beggars, to whom would my gifts be given?
For the sake of attaining enlightenment, I shall give everything away and cast off the mind of stinginess."
"The excellence of the merit of the six perfections Is called the conduct of a bodhisattva;
To realize awakening, One fully cultivates all-knowledge.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva felt joy in his heart and spoke further in verse:
"I shall now remove this stain of stinginess and greed, and bestow this precious chariot upon the brāhmaṇa;
the great sages of antiquity all practiced this together, and they all attained the state of untainted bodhi."
At that time, having made this vow, the Bodhisattva felt great joy in his heart and presented the precious chariot as a gift to the Brahmin.
Then the Bodhisattva himself took his son upon his shoulder, and the Queen likewise placed their daughter upon her shoulder; they proceeded on their way, gradually reaching the mountain forest.
Having arrived at the forest, his mind gave rise to few desires, and he dwelt there relying upon the practice of the precepts.
Later, on another occasion, a brahmin came to the forest and approached the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in search of a son and a daughter.
At that time, Mṛgī was away gathering fruit; the brahmin raised his hand in praise and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying, "Kṣatriya youth!..."
"May you attain supreme victory.
Then, he addressed the Bodhisattva with these verses:
"I currently have no attendant; I have sought one for my wife in many places."
"I pray that you will grant these two children of yours to me as a gift.
When the Bodhisattva heard these words, he reflected for a moment on parting from his beloved children. At that time, the brahmin spoke again to the Bodhisattva:
"O Kṣatriya youth!"
"I have heard that you are able to give everything; why then must you hesitate now as I beg from you?
He then addressed the Bodhisattva in verse:
"Your fame now pervades all directions, For you are able to give all things through compassion."
"As you have heard in the past, one should be able to practice giving; O Benevolent One, you should now accordingly carry out this practice.
When the Bodhisattva had heard these words, he addressed the Brahmin in verse:
"I shall now certainly sacrifice my body and life, For my original vow shall not give rise to any other thought."
"Even if I were to give my children to others, I would never turn back from this resolve.
He further addressed the brahmin, saying:
"I now abandon these two children, husband and wife, to dwell in the forest thicket."
Women are by nature compassionate and affectionate; how could she remain so?
Let no one say of me later that, lacking compassion, I abandoned my own child;
for I could not bear to give away my son while withholding my own body.
At that time, the brahmin said to the Bodhisattva:
"Kṣatriya youth, you should not act in this way.

You were born and raised within a royal lineage, a fact known and heard throughout this great earth; your fame extends to the ten directions and accords with all beings. You have conceived great compassion for all sentient beings, bestowing various gifts and offering respectful worship like a fragrant elephant."

He was able to support and provide offerings for all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, teachers, elders, the poor, and the widowed or orphaned; according to their various requests and aspirations, he fulfilled them all in accordance with their original intentions.
Those who see you are drawn to you and never leave empty-handed; whatever they encounter you, you bestow as alms, so that their merit is never in vain.

Having traveled from afar and endured every hardship, I have come with hopes for what I seek; may my aspirations be fulfilled. The horse of the mind is difficult to tame and has no means of remaining still; it turns over in an instant and cannot be made constant. I fear that my original resolve might falter and I be unable to practice giving, causing me to return home weary and disappointed. You, O Benevolent One, should now fulfill my original wish and send me on my way.
He then praised the Bodhisattva with a verse, saying:
"Your fame pervades the ten directions, And you are able to bestow upon all;
I pray that you will deign to show compassion, So that my hopes may be fulfilled."
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva, because he was separated from his beloved sons, felt grief and sorrow in his heart, and thought to himself:
"If I now give up these two boys to this brahmin, I and Mandāravī will suffer great and intense pain due to our separation from our beloved children."
"If I do not relinquish it, my holy life (*brahmacarya*) will be greatly compromised.

Furthermore, the Brahmin will depart with his hopes dashed and his words rendered empty. Now, I shall certainly undergo the great suffering of grief and sorrow at being separated from my beloved son, which will cause me to wither away in this place; yet, in the end, I cannot violate my original vow or compromise my holy life."
Her mind became firm in her resolve to abandon her son, and she made this vow, speaking in verse:
"I now renounce this son, May I obtain great fruit and benefit;
By means of this supreme merit, May I deliver sentient beings from the ocean of suffering."

At that moment, as soon as the Bodhisattva had given away the boy and girl, this great earth shook in six ways. The various sages dwelling on the nearby mountains, seeing the earth tremble, were all struck with alarm and said to one another:
"By whose power of merit, and by what cause and condition, does this great earth suddenly shake?"
"Now we should carefully observe whose power it is that has brought about this auspicious omen.

Among the assembly of sages was one who was the most venerable in years, well-versed in the art of divination and physiognomy, and also proficient in celestial phenomena; he then addressed the other sages with a verse:
"This is a Bodhisattva who delights in mountain forests, Sustaining his life by eating fruit and drinking water; He has come here to seek the Dharma, And will surely attain supreme enlightenment."
"The lovely children have now been abandoned; for this reason, the great earth manifests these omens.
At that time, the two boys, knowing their father’s resolve to abandon them, wailed and wept piteously. They prostrated at their father’s feet, joined their palms, and said:
"We pray that our father will look upon us with compassion and not forsake us. Now that we are without a father, upon what shall we rely?"
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with despondency and his eyes overflowed with tears. He then addressed the beloved children in verse:
“Children, you should know this: It is not that I lack love or compassion;
It is for the sake of relieving the suffering of sentient beings That I have abandoned my own children.”
"By this most excellent merit, may we deliver sentient beings from the ocean of suffering;
may they emerge from the ford of delusion and together attain the fruit of Bodhi.

At that time, having heard their father’s words, the two youths knew that their father was determined to renounce them for the sake of giving. Weeping with piteous cries and tears, they prostrated themselves, joined their palms, and spoke with choked voices, addressing their father in verse:
“Father now bestows me upon me with final resolve; I leave this parting word to entrust myself to my mother.
Whatever faults or transgressions I have previously committed, I pray that my mother will look upon me with compassion and grant me forgiveness.”
Due to my youth and ignorance, I failed to follow and respect the words of my parents' instruction;
now that I am unable to repay their compassionate kindness, I pray that you will forgive such a transgression.
When the sons had finished reciting these verses, they prostrated at their father’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed from their father with eyes brimming with tears.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, mindful of the boys’ piteous words and feeling a heart filled with sorrow and suffering, gave rise to the bodhicitta and entered the grass hut.
As soon as those two sons had left the grass hut, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas in the void spoke these words:
"Alas, how marvelous! How extraordinary!"
With one voice and in unison, they spoke this verse:
"How extraordinary is this great virtue of his giving! The Bodhisattva’s resolve is thus determined;
Though two young sons were born from his own body, He gave them away entirely, his heart feeling no regret."

At that time, the boy’s mother, Mandīrā, having gathered fruits and wishing to return to her grass hut, saw this great earth shake in six ways; her heart was struck with alarm, and she hurried swiftly toward the hut.

At that time, there was a son of heaven who transformed himself into a lioness and stood blocking the path. Seeing that the Bodhisattva, desiring to liberate all sentient beings, was now about to abandon his two children, he feared that Mandāravī would create obstacles to his mind regarding the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
When Mandīravī saw the lion blocking the road, she addressed her mother, the lioness, with this verse:
“O Lioness, you are the wife of the King of Beasts; For what reason do you block this path of mine?”
"Now that we both serve the same husband, you should quickly depart and go elsewhere as circumstances require.
You are the wife of the Lion, King of Beasts; I am the consort of a human sovereign, a king.
Since we are united by righteousness, let us be sisters; you must make way so that I may pass."
At that time, having heard these words, the celestial lion turned aside from the path and departed.

Then, as Mandāravī traveled along the road, she beheld various ominous portents: namely, she heard the sound of lamentation in the sky, and she further heard all the sentient beings dwelling in the mountains and forests weeping with tears and heaving long sighs.
In an instant, she thought to herself: "I have seen such portents; there must certainly be some misfortune at that grass hut."
And he spoke in verse:
"My two eyes are now blurred, As all the birds together cry out in sorrow;
My heart is pierced with grief, For I am certain to be parted from my son."
"Thus the great earth shakes, and both body and mind tremble;
my entire frame is now ill at ease, so I know for certain that a parting is at hand.
When Mandāravī had spoken these verses, she contemplated a thousand kinds of calamities and then went to the grass hut.
Having entered the hermitage and searched everywhere, he did not see his two sons; filled with grief and distress, he thought to himself:
"Have my two children gone to play with the young deer, or have they been playing at building castles out of sand?"
She immediately went to search for him; when she could not find him after searching, she further thought:
"He must have entered the hut and fallen asleep because he did not see me.

With this reflection, her heart was filled with fear as she longed to see her son. She cast aside the flowers and fruits she had gathered, her eyes brimming with tears, and prostrating at her husband's feet, she asked:
"Where are my two young children now?
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"The Brahmin who has come here Is one who transcends begging."
"I have given those two children as alms; you should rejoice in this.

When Mandāravī heard these words, she was like a doe struck by a poisoned arrow, fainting and collapsing to the ground; again, she was like a fish out of water writhing upon the earth; like a quail that has lost its chicks, she was filled with piercing grief; and like a mother cow that has lost her calf, she uttered mournful cries.
At that time, Mandāravī uttered these verses of lamentation:
"My two sons have faces like flowers, Their hands and feet as soft as lotus petals;
To undergo such suffering together at once— How can they leave me alone and depart?"

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that the Bodhisattva and Lady Māndhātṛī were together engaged in a resolute and most rare difficult practice, descended from the void surrounded by the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens. Radiating brilliant light, he arrived at the mountain forest hermitage where the Bodhisattva resided.
Remaining in the air, he addressed the Bodhisattva with these verses. [There are verses here.
At that time, having composed these verses, Śakra caused the Bodhisattva’s mind to become firm, steadfast, and courageous, and he reflected:
"Now the Bodhisattva has only Lady Māndhārī as his attendant; if someone should beg from him and he were to give her away, there would then be no one left to serve the Bodhisattva."
"I should now go and beg for Lady Māndhātṛ and bring her back.
Having thus temporarily entrusted her to the Bodhisattva’s care, she suddenly vanished.
Not long thereafter, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested in the form of a brahmin, went to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling, and spoke this verse:
"This woman’s appearance and demeanor are most exquisite; she alone devotes her heart exclusively to one husband.
Such a noble and beautiful lady—by all means, I pray you, grant her to me so that she may serve me."
When Queen Mandāravī heard these words, her heart was filled with grief and distress; she grew angry at the beggar and spoke thus:
"You are a shameless one driven by greed, the most wicked person in all the world!
If you knew the Dharma and understood the dignity of a noble lady, how could you have forcibly begged me from my husband?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva, his heart filled with sorrow, turned back to look at his wife. His wife addressed him in verse, saying:
"I am not grieved now, nor do I worry about my own physical suffering;
I only worry that you dwell alone—how will you be able to survive?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied to the lady in verse:
"I have no need for you to worry here; I seek the firm and indestructible path.
You need only follow me with reverence; I shall die like a wild beast in the forest."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with supreme joy, and he spoke again in verse:
“This is my final gift upon this mountain; now that the lady has departed, I have no sorrow.”
Having spoken half of the verse, the Bodhisattva then took Mandāravā with one hand and held the water vessel with the other, and addressed the Brahmin in verse:
"This man is pure and free from defilement; His speech is eloquent and his service skillful.
I now offer this wife, whom I hold dear, To you, O Benevolent One; may you protect her."
At that time, having given away his wife, the Bodhisattva made this aspiration:
"By the merit of this gift, may I quickly attain Buddhahood.
As he spoke these words, the great earth shook in six ways.
Then the Brahmin led his wife away, not far from that place. At that time, Mandarika, her heart filled with grief and emotion, spoke these words:
"I have now parted from my revered husband and my beloved, most excellent children; I know not what karmic offenses I committed in past lives."
Thus she wandered and lamented in this wilderness, like a mother cow who has lost her calf.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw this sight, he resumed his true form and addressed Mandāravī with these verses:
“O exquisite lady, I am not a brahmin, Nor am I a human; I am Śakra, the Lord of Devas.”
"You who were able to defeat the great celestial kings of the asuras—now I cherish you with my profound heart.
'What wish do you require? I shall grant it all to you.'"
Having heard these words, his heart was filled with joy; he immediately paid homage with profound reverence and spoke in verse:
"The Lord of a Thousand Eyes has saved my son, Causing him to leave this lowly body and attain liberation;
May he always rejoice in meeting his father— O King Śakra, this is my prayer."
Having spoken these words, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, returned with that exquisite maiden to the Bodhisattva. Taking Mandāravā’s hand in his right hand, he said to the Bodhisattva:
“I entrust this woman to you, Noble One, so that she may constantly provide offerings and attend to you; should anyone come seeking her, you must not give her to them.”
"This is a deposit; if you were to transfer it to another, people of the world would find it shameful.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, went to the place where the Brahmin was with the child, causing him to become bewildered and disoriented, not knowing what to do, and to fall into a state of frantic panic. He then returned to his own city, intending to sell the child.
Having seen this, the minister reported to the sovereign:

"There is someone who has brought two grandsons of the King—the elder named Manoharā and the younger named Kṛṣṇaka—and, lacking any heart of compassion, is crying out for them to be sold in the marketplace."
Upon hearing these words, the king was deeply moved by grief and astonishment; he immediately dispatched a messenger with the command:
"Go and bring that man back.
Do not let my son fall into the hands of his enemies."
Upon hearing this, the palace attendants were filled with grief and distress, and the entire city was overcome with sorrowful lamentation.
The messenger quickly led him to the king’s presence.

When the king saw his grandson, he commanded him to draw near; seeing his son clad in tattered rags, emaciated by hunger, frail and weak, and covered in grime and filth, his heart was immediately overwhelmed with confusion and anguish. He then cast himself from his lion throne onto the ground, falling into a swoon before regaining consciousness after a long time.
The people within the city, the ministers and high officials, and the palace ladies all wailed at once, their cries shaking the city walls as they collapsed from their seats to the ground.

The various ministers, officials, and women of the inner court likewise wailed with such unceasing and piercing grief that it took a long while before they regained consciousness; they then addressed the ministers, saying:
"Though my son remains in those mountain forests, he does not cease his practice of giving alms. I shall now dispatch an envoy to go and quickly welcome him back."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra again came to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling; once his business was concluded, he took leave of the Bodhisattva and withdrew.
Not long thereafter, the father king passed away, and the ministers deliberated together:
"Now that the Great King has departed from this world, we should all go to welcome the Crown Prince."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went forth to welcome the prince and consecrated him as king.

Once he had ascended the throne, he held a great assembly of giving, not begrudging anything internal or external; he bestowed gifts extensively upon all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as upon the poor and beggars.
To those who had come from afar, as well as the king’s retinue, friends, and relatives, he bestowed all manner of merits and gifts, universally satisfying them all. He then spoke these verses:
“For the sake of seeking enlightenment, I give with a joyful heart To kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, śūdras, and the rest.”
Whether toward a candāla or those of evil nature, or toward one who maintains pure precepts;
regarding gold, silver, precious necklaces, or even one's wife, children, and family— giving all these with a heart of renunciation.
One immediately attains a pure body in this life and in future lives.
Just as a king who saves his grandson, or a brahmin who receives precious jewels,
rejoices together with his kinsmen, so too does one attain peace and security.
All this is due to that prince, who claims, "I am the most supreme;
I am a field of merit for people, and thus deserve to receive offerings.
It is because of this that he has acquired wealth and treasures.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus! You should know this:"
"What event was this?
At that time, the king who gave away his son was I myself.
The brahmin at that time was Devadatta; this brahmin acted without gratitude or righteousness."
"O bhikṣus! You should not be satisfied with such meager offerings; you must cultivate a profound sense of respect, all the more so when the gifts are abundant.
O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way."

At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a householder named Ratnaka in the city of Campā who possessed abundant wealth and enjoyed great prosperity. Not long after he had taken a wife, she became pregnant; her husband then provided her with ample service and attendants, as described in detail elsewhere.

Later, the householder went to Rājagṛha; when the months were complete, another son was born to him under the constellation Tiṣya. His appearance was so handsome and dignified that it was rarely seen by others, and beneath his feet grew hair four finger-widths long, the color of which was like pure gold.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to Rājagṛha to inform the elder, saying:
"A son has been born. The elder asked:
"What news? the messenger replied,
"The elder has fathered a son."
To such questions, they all replied,
"The householder has fathered a son.
Then the messenger said:
"What need is there for further questions?
He did not speak a word in reply.
The elder said:
"Why do you not speak these words a hundred times?
I shall now give you a mouthful of gold for every hundred repetitions; since you spoke them three times, I will give you three mouthfuls of gold."
He sent a messenger back to inform the keeper of the treasury:
"Give twenty koṭis of wealth and provide daily food for the boy.
The elder then went to the king's presence and addressed the Great King, saying:
"I have given birth to a son.
At that time, the king replied:
"I shall give you my city of Campā, along with a magnificent elephant adorned with seven heads and exquisite jewels, to your son."

After the elder Ratnaśrī had thus addressed the king, he returned to his native city. When twenty-one days had passed and his kinsmen had assembled, as the child was born under the constellation Puṣya, they gave him the name Puṣya.
He entrusted him to eight nurses:

two to provide milk, two to constantly carry him, two to wash his clothes, and two to play with him; he was nourished with various kinds of food and drink, gradually growing up like a lotus in the water.

When the boy had thus grown to maturity, his father sent him to school; he became thoroughly proficient in mathematics, the appraisal of precious gems, and all other arts and skills, such that people vied with one another to bring their daughters to seek his hand in marriage.

His father provided him with three types of private chambers and gardens for the three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—and established for his use three grades of women, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
That man constantly amused himself with pleasure in the upper palace, consuming five hundred taels of gold daily for his meals, which he provided for the men to eat.
At that time, Devadatta wickedly admonished King Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Your father’s hair has turned white and yellow, yet he does not tire of female diversions and various foods and drinks."
"Now that you have grown up, I shall not grant you the throne; the day for this is yet uncertain.
King Ajātaśatru asked, "What do you intend to do now?"
Devadatta replied, “One must attend to the affairs of others;
there is no kind of request that I would not fulfill. You should have the Tathāgata consume ghee.”

The King-Father, carrying the porridge, was on his way to the Bamboo Grove to visit the Tathāgata when King Ajātaśatru, from the middle of the road, hurled a spear and pierced King Bimbisāra, breaking the porridge pot; the king then turned back and returned home.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having foreknown everything with his knowledge of others' minds, addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Devadatta has incited Ajātaśatru to fall into hell; furthermore, when I sought rice gruel from Bimbisāra to eat, my cauldron was struck and broken."
"You should go for my sake to the city of Campā and beg for some gruel from the son of the householder Ratnaka, bringing it back here.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat upright and entered meditative concentration; he vanished from Rājagṛha and appeared in Campā.
That elder’s son worshipped the sun deity at every occasion; when he was performing his worship at dawn, Mahāmaudgalyāyana descended from within the solar orb.
Upon seeing Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the elder’s son was struck with extreme wonder and spoke this verse:
"Now I behold the body of the Sun Deity, Descending from the sun before me."
Who has caused this body to appear?
Answer quickly: who is this person?
Could it be the sun?
Is this a deity of great learning? Or is it the moon?
Or perhaps the body of Śakra?
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having scrutinized and understood the intention of the elder’s son, spoke these words:
“I am not the thousand-rayed sun; I am not the god of great learning (Bṛhaspati).
Nor am I the body of Śakra; I am a son of the Muni.”
"Extremely endowed with majestic radiance, you have come here to beg for gruel in order to make an offering to the Buddha’s body.
The son of the elder asked:
"How does he compare to the Buddha?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied in verse:
"A mustard seed cannot be compared to Mount Sumeru; A tiny firefly cannot be compared to the sun."
"The water in a cow's footprint is not comparable to the ocean; likewise, the various non-Buddhists are not comparable to the Buddha.
At that time, having heard these words, the son of the elder asked:
"What is it that you require for the purpose of your coming here?"
He replied, "I have come to beg for gruel for the Tathāgata. He asked:
“What is the clan of the Tathāgata? Maudgalyāyana replied, “There is a śramaṇa Gautama of the Śākya clan;

having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma-robes, he practices with a mind that is upright and true, has left the household life to cultivate the Way, and has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—he is the Buddha.”

The son of the elder had never before heard of a Buddha; upon hearing the name of the Buddha, his heart was filled with great joy and the hairs on his body stood on end. He took all five hundred gold coins he had used to procure food and drink, and at once offered them, placing them into the bowl.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately entered into meditative concentration, vanished from the city of Campā, and appeared in Rājagṛha; he went out into the Bamboo Grove to present [the food] to the World-Honored One.
Bimbisāra, meanwhile, was bringing the rice gruel to the Buddha’s location when he smelled the pervasive fragrance of the food and thought:
"It must be that the devas and Śakra, Lord of Devas, have come to make offerings to the Buddha; the gruel I have prepared is not fit for use at all."
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and various other devas have come to make offerings to the Buddha; this bamboo grove is exceedingly fragrant and beautiful."

The Buddha said, “Within the king’s realm there is a great city named Campā. There is a son of a householder who daily spends five hundred gold coins to prepare food; it was from him that the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana went to beg and receive it. Such is the power of that householder’s merit.”
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and wished to send a messenger to summon him.
The Buddha, knowing the king's intention, spoke to him, saying:
"Do not treat him lightly by sending a messenger to call him."
He further addressed the Great King:
"Would you be able to eat the remnants of food remaining in my alms bowl?
The Great King replied:
"I am a descendant of the royal lineage of King Jñānagupta, consecrated by the touching of his crown; it is not fitting for me to eat the leftovers of others.
However, since the Buddha is my Dharma King and has commanded me to eat, I shall do so."
The Buddha asked the king,
"Since you were born, have you ever been able to eat such food as you please? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I was born in a royal palace and was raised in a royal palace; having been a king with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), I have never before eaten such excellent and delicious food.
The Buddha said:
"Great King, you should know that this son of a householder is a person of great merit; he constantly partakes of such superior-flavored food and drink.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having prostrated at the Buddha's feet, withdrew and returned to his palace, where he immediately issued an edict to his ministers:
"Let the fourfold army be fully prepared and sent to the city of Campā.
The ministers asked the king,
"For what reason are you going there?"
The king said,
"I wish to go and see the son of Ratnavatī.
The ministers replied:
"What is the reason for going to see him within the borders of the kingdom?
Send someone to summon him.
Thus spoke the king.
"That man possesses great merit; he must not be summoned.
The ministers replied to the king:
"We shall employ skillful means so that the man will come of his own accord without being called by Your Majesty."
The king said, "So be it;
it shall be as you intend. The ministers immediately wrote a letter and dispatched a messenger to deliver it.
"Cleanse and sprinkle the city; the Great King wishes to come.
Upon hearing this, the son of the elder was filled with joy.
The minister reported further:
"The prince is also coming.
At that time, the son of the elder, having heard that the prince’s character and conduct were fierce and coarse, feared there might be some loss or damage.
The various ministers then sent another letter to inform him:
“Since neither the King nor the Prince will come, you must devise a plan to block the Gaṅgā so that the water flows backward, ensuring not even a single drop passes downstream.”
Upon hearing this, the elder was filled with extreme anxiety and fear, thinking:
"One must know that the King intends to punish us; he has sent this letter.
The people of Campā city gathered together and collectively drafted a letter which they dispatched to inform the Prime Minister:
"The King has repeatedly sent letters with the command:
'The King shall come.
He has further said:"
"Come, my son," he said,
"and cause the Gaṅgā to be dammed up so that its flow is reversed.
Having read this letter, he further received a reply stating:
"The King and the Prince have both not yet arrived; the King wishes to see the son of Ratnaka, so you must quickly dispatch him—this is the essential matter.
At that time, a man from Campā secretly sent one person to Rājagṛha to investigate the truth of the matter. That person then learned that everything was exactly as stated in the letter.
At that time, the people of the city and town went together to the house of the elder and addressed Ratnaśrī, saying:

"The Great King wishes to see your son; the words of the kingdom’s ministers and counselors are true and not false. We have secretly dispatched men to go and investigate, and it is exactly as stated in the letter: we must see the elder’s son, Ratnaśrī."
He replied, "Even if you were to block the Ganges River with gold, my son could never be sent away.
The people spoke again:
“The householder is one of great wealth and status; he even knows how to block the Ganges with gold.
We are poor people and have no means to obtain it; you must show us compassion.”
The elder replied,
"If each family within the city sends forth one son to follow my son, I shall release him.
At that time, the multitude all complied with the elder's words.
The elder then went to his son’s location and spoke secretly to him, saying:
“The people of the city have all come together to inform me that King Bimbisāra wishes to see you.”
The son said to his father,
"I shall depart this very moment.
The father said:
"You must certainly have golden hair beneath your feet if you wish to be seen; do not lift your feet to show them to the Great King.
Take a precious jewel and go to that king's presence; place it upon the king's foot, and after prostrating before him, sit cross-legged, and the golden hair will appear naturally."
At that time, Ratnaśrī thought to himself:
"Now that I am sending my son away, shall I have him go by elephant,
or rather by horse or by chariot?"
"Is it to send someone by boat?
He further reflected to himself:
"It would not be as secure as traveling by boat."

He immediately ordered a ship to be built; within the ship, he further constructed various gardens and groves where many beautiful birds sang diverse melodies. Then, having adorned themselves, the court ladies set out for Rājagṛha.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Scroll Sixteen;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Scroll Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree:

At that time, King Bimbisāra heard that the son of a householder was coming by boat; he had a canal dug from the Gaṅgā River straight to the great city of Rājagṛha, filling the area within five *li* with sesame seeds.

When the ship reached the city, he issued an edict to sweep and sprinkle the ground, removing all tiles and stones, sprinkling it with scented water, and scattering various famous flowers until it resembled a celestial palace; having prepared excellent offerings, he welcomed the son of the elder into the city of Rājagṛha.
When the son saw the king, he prostrated with his head at the king's feet, placed a precious jewel upon them, and withdrew to one side to sit cross-legged.
At that time, when the king saw the golden hairs beneath his feet, he was struck with amazement and exclaimed:
"You are a person of great merit and power of fortune; have you ever seen a Buddha?"
He replied, "I have not seen it. The king said:
"You may accompany me to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
He asked the king,
"Upon what does the Buddha ride?"
The king said,
"Those who have left the household life do not use vehicles.
The son of the elder replied:
"I shall also walk there.
At that time, the multitude all stripped their clothes and spread them upon the ground for the elder’s son to step upon, asking:
"Does that Buddha, the World-Honored One, walk by treading upon these clothes?"
He replied, “I did not step on it.
The king then ordered his clothes to be removed.
When the elder’s son stepped upon the ground with his feet, the devas removed their garments and spread them over the earth.
He asked, "I did not tell you to put on these clothes; for what reason are there garments upon the ground?"
The bystanders replied,
"This is a celestial robe, not a robe of ours.
They also ordered it removed, and the deity departed once the robe had been taken away.
When the son of the householder set foot upon the ground, at that moment the great earth shook in six ways.
Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ninety-one kalpas past, this son of the householder has always walked with his feet covered by clothing; he has never stepped upon the ground with bare feet."
"Now, because this son of a householder values the Dharma so highly, he has pressed the earth with his foot, and for this reason the earth trembles.
At that time, the son of the householder approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to them according to their respective faculties and dispositions. Having heard the Dharma, they rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and requested ordination to receive and uphold the precepts.
The Buddha said,
"It is not so! Son of a householder, if your parents do not give their permission, you cannot leave the household life and receive the precepts."
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I am the sovereign of this kingdom; regarding the storehouses and assets of that elder, all matters depend upon me. Since Your Majesty has granted permission, I only pray that the Tathāgata will allow him to go forth."
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu! Instantly he went forth;
clad in the saṃghāṭī robe and holding his water jar and alms bowl, his dignified deportment was like that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing.
At that time, the six bhikṣus mocked him together, saying:
"O son of a householder, you are like fresh butter; what capability do you have?
What benefit is there now in your diligent cultivation of the holy life?"
At that time, the six bhikṣus saw him and mocked him, saying to one another:
"This man’s appearance is like a lump of fresh butter; what could he possibly achieve by practicing with such vigor within the Buddha’s true teaching?"
Having heard these words, he went immediately to the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: "Venerable One!
How does a bhikṣu practice with determination so as to quickly achieve accomplishment and attain right concentration?"
He replied, "As the Buddha has taught:
by practicing the samādhi of diligent walking meditation, one will swiftly attain right concentration."

Having heard this, he immediately went to the charnel ground and practiced walking meditation while established in samādhi; though he focused his mind on the factors of enlightenment and contemplated wholesome dharmas, he was ultimately unable to realize them.
Again, he gave rise to a thought:
"I have now exerted myself with diligence surpassing that of all the śrāvakas, yet I have not attained the realization of the fruits.
I still possess my own home, family, and wealth; it would be better for me to return to lay life and personally practice giving and cultivate various meritorious deeds."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, addressed a bhikṣu, saying:
"You should go to the cemetery and inform the son of the elder, saying: 'You may come here.'"
When that bhikṣu had received the Buddha’s command, he went into the forest and announced:
“The World-Honored One summons you.
Having heard this, they went together to the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side.
The Buddha said to that son of a householder:
"You should not dwell alone in a secluded forest, sitting in meditation and engaging in such irrational reflections as these:
'Whatever ascetic practices the śrāvakas diligently cultivate, I shall surpass them all; by not severing the outflows, I shall attain liberation of mind.'"

"My kinsmen possess great resources and enjoy abundant wealth; you should return home to experience various sensual pleasures, practice extensive giving, and cultivate all manner of meritorious deeds."
When the son of the elder had heard what the Buddha said, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One now knows the thoughts in my mind.
Immediately, struck with amazement, fear, and distress, the hair on his body stood on end, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha again addressed the son of the householder:
"I now ask you; answer according to my intention.
What work did you regularly perform when you formerly lived at home? He replied:
“You are skilled at playing the lute.
He asked again, “If, when tuning the strings, the strings are tuned too tightly, will the sound be harmonious, elegant, and pleasing to the mind, such that it is fit for use?”
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
He asked: "If the strings of a lute are too loose, will its sound be harmonious and elegant, pleasing to the mind, capable of producing a fine tone for use? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
"If the strings of a lute are neither too loose nor too tight, but the tuning is balanced and correct, would its sound be beautiful?"
He replied: "So it is, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told the son of a householder:
"If there is someone who exerts extreme diligence and their mind becomes agitated, or if they are overly lax and their mind becomes indolent, you should therefore cultivate the Middle Way."
If it is so, before long you shall sever all outflows, attain liberation of mind, and attain liberation through wisdom; you shall see the Dharma and realize the fruit:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the son of the elder rejoiced and accepted it with faith; he contemplated it with focused attention, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.

Having heard the World-Honored Buddha’s instruction through the skillful means of the lute parable, the son of the elder dwelt alone in a quiet and secluded place, practicing without negligence and single-mindedly cultivating right mindfulness.

“Good son! You have set your mind upon the aspiration for renunciation, shaving off your hair and beard and donning the saṃghāṭī robe; with right faith you have gone forth to train for the unsurpassed fruit.”
The holy life has been established; having attained the ultimate realization of all phenomena, he has personally realized and achieved the fruit of enlightenment, knowing:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"You should know that you have realized the fruit.

At that time, the Venerable One personally realized the fruit of Arhatship; having attained excellent liberation and achieved the fruit, he experienced with single-mindedness the joy and bliss of liberation, and thought:
"Now is the very time for me to go to the Buddha’s presence to offer worship and respect."
Having formed this thought, he rose from his meditation in the late afternoon and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit at one side.
Then the Venerable One addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Whenever there is a bhikṣu who has attained the fruit of arhatship, whose outflows are exhausted, who has accomplished what was to be done, who is no longer subject to further existence, and who has laid down the heavy burden and realized his own benefit—"
Having exhausted all fetters of existence, being well-liberated through wisdom, and having attained mastery over the mind, one attains six kinds of supreme liberation, namely:

first, the supreme liberation of renouncing worldly life; second, the supreme liberation of benefiting others; third, the supreme liberation of tranquility; fourth, the supreme liberation of the exhaustion of craving; fifth, the supreme liberation of the exhaustion of all [defilements]; and sixth, the supreme liberation of not losing right mindfulness.
He said: "Virtuous One!
Suppose there is another person who, having conceived even a small amount of faith, seeks liberation."
Do not hold such a view [that one attains liberation from greed, hatred, and delusion and escapes birth and death].
Venerable sir!
If there were another person who, by generating even a small amount of ethical discipline (*śīla*), seeks to escape birth and death and attain liberation free from illness, affliction, and sorrow.
Do not hold such a view: that by exhausting greed, hatred, and delusion, one becomes free from illness and affliction and attains liberation.
Venerable Sir!
If there is another person who, for the sake of seeking fame and profit or for the sake of reputation, practices the conduct of tranquility while seeking liberation.
"Do not hold such a view; one attains the exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion, becomes free from craving and grasping, and achieves liberation without losing right mindfulness.
Venerable sir!

If there is a bhikṣu who has attained arhatship, whose outflows are exhausted, who has accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, achieved his own benefit, and forever severed all states of existence, his mind is well-liberated and his wisdom is well-liberated."
These Arhats have attained these six kinds of superior liberation.
Venerable Sir!

If a bhikṣu has attained the training rules and seeks the excellent path of unsurpassed nirvāṇa, he does not cling to form; at that time, those training rules constitute pure śīla. Having accomplished the training rules and tamed the sense faculties, he subsequently attains the destruction of the outflows.
He attains liberation through the untainted mind and achieves liberation by wisdom;
regarding the phenomena present before him, he realizes them through his own direct knowledge and attains fulfillment, knowing:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"At that time, that Arhat was accomplished in the precepts (*śīla*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and had perfected the faculties (*indriya*) of one beyond training.
Venerable sir!

It is like a young child whose mind is lazy and who delights in sleep; when he reaches full youth, his precepts and faculties are all fully accomplished; later, when he is old and his faculties have withered, his precepts remain accomplished."
Venerable sir!
It is the same for a bhikṣu.

If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in the precepts and has attained mastery over the mind, he seeks the excellent path to unsurpassed nirvāṇa; he does not cling to form, abides in śīla, and his faculties are well-subdued.
At a later time, having exhausted all out-flows (*āsrava*), he attains untainted wisdom within the untainted mind and achieves the life of liberation;
having personally realized the dharma before him, he attains perfection.
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence; thus, the morality of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-śīla) is fully accomplished.
Having realized the fruit, one perceives all forms such that the mind does not grasp at them, nor is it deluded."
His mind is in right concentration and free from inversion; through skillful cultivation, his mind neither increases nor decreases.

Even when confronted with confusing and distracting matters, he cannot lose his right mindfulness. Whether the ear perceives sounds, the nose perceives odors, the tongue perceives tastes, the body perceives tangibles, or the mind perceives mental phenomena, these dharmas such as form cannot confuse or distract him, and he does not lose his right mindfulness.
Stable and undistracted, with a mind free from inversion, he is well-liberated and well-cultivated, perceiving the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
"Furthermore, it is like a city or a village, not far from which stands a great mountain of rock, without fissures and without interstices, consisting entirely of a single stone;

even if a great wind should arise from the east, that mountain would not move, would not shake, nor would it lean toward the west; winds from the south, west, or north would likewise cause it neither to move nor to shake."

Just as past forms and other objects appear before one like a great tempest, so too the mental consciousnesses of the eye and other faculties remain free from inversion; they are neither moved nor shaken, for the mind is settled and free from distraction.
If one attains liberation and has cultivated the wholesome, one perceives the phenomena of arising and ceasing.

Furthermore, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which can cognize sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth—these six types [of sense objects] delude the body and mind; yet, one who attains the fruit does not lose right mindfulness, and the internal mental states do not lose right mindfulness, remaining free from distraction and inversion.
"Having attained liberation well and cultivated what is wholesome, one perceives the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
After the Venerable Bhikṣu had spoken these words, he further recited a verse:
"The one who has gone forth and attained liberation Has no illness, affliction, or sorrow in the mind."
Abiding in the ground of tranquility, he delights in the exhaustion of craving and desire.
One who proceeds toward liberation and its cessation, whose mind does not lose mindfulness,
and who thoroughly understands that phenomena are mind-born— such a one attains liberation of the mind.
When the mind attains liberation, it dwells in tranquility, having seen the Truth;
having completed what was to be done, one need not do it again.
Like that great mountain of rock, even a violent wind cannot move it.
"Forms and sounds are likewise; they cannot cause harm.
One whose mind has attained concentration perceives the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
When these verses were spoken, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt. Since the World-Honored One is able to sever all doubts and perplexities, they immediately addressed him, asking:
"Venerable Bhikṣu, what kind of karma did you plant?

By the power of that karma, you were born into a wealthy and noble family; beneath your feet there are golden hairs; every day you consume food of five hundred flavors; and for ninety-one kalpas, your feet have not touched the ground."

As soon as he was born, he received twenty koṭis of gold coins; later, he went forth into homelessness within the teaching of the World-Honored One to practice and study, severing all afflictions and realizing the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The venerable one has accumulated virtuous karma whose ripening of fruit is such that it must necessarily be experienced by him alone, like a violent torrent."
"O bhikṣus, you should know that what one does oneself, one must experience oneself; as has been explained at length elsewhere.
He then spoke these verses:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, The karma one has created does not perish."
"When causes and conditions meet, the retribution of the fruit is received by oneself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles."
That Buddha was surrounded by sixty-two thousand bhikṣus as he traveled through the human world and gradually arrived at a royal city named Priyaṃkara.
