At that time, there were sons of householders in the city who heard that Vipaśyin, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, accompanied by sixty-two thousand bhikṣus surrounding him in front and behind, was traveling through the human world and had arrived there.
Having heard this, they all went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the essential Dharma for the youths, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, and then remained silent.
At that time, the assembly of youths rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will permit us to provide the four requisites as offerings for three months during the summer retreat for the Buddha and the community of monks."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had consented, the youths prostrated at his feet, took their leave, and departed.
Once those youths had reached the city, they gathered in the council hall and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"How shall we make offerings to the World-Honored One?
Shall we prepare a single meal together as an offering,
or shall each person prepare a separate meal as an offering?"
Among them, some said, "If we all work together to prepare food for offerings, it will cause us to neglect our livelihoods, such as farming and other tasks.
Then the assembly deliberated together:
"Each person shall take turns preparing food for the offering on one day at a time.
They then prepared the offerings according to their respective means.
Among them was a youth from a poor family who consulted with his mother:
"My family is poor; how can we prepare food in the proper sequence?
Then his mother replied, "My beloved son!"
"One may offer the final oblation on the last day; however, from now until that day arrives, one should prepare everything according to one's means so that it is fully provided.

When the day arrived, he spread out a bear skin, and as the Tathāgata stepped upon it and proceeded to his seat, he prepared food and drink of five hundred flavors to make an offering to the Tathāgata.

Prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground, he made this great vow: "May I always be born into a wealthy and noble family wherever I am reborn. Furthermore, may my feet never touch the ground, just as beneath the feet of the Tathāgata there are four-finger-widths of golden hair; may my conduct and vows be like those of the Buddha."
"I vow that whenever a Buddha appears in future ages, I shall offer him worship.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The poor boy at that time was none other than the son of the elder Ratnakaṇṭha."

Due to the maturation of the karmic fruit of the vow he made in the presence of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, he attained great wealth and nobility; there was hair beneath his feet that was golden in color, and for ninety-one kalpas, he has never once set foot upon the ground.
On the day he was born, twenty koṭis of gold coins sprang forth from the earth each and every day.
He immediately went forth into homelessness within the Buddha’s teaching to practice and study, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If one performs black karma, one shall receive a black retribution; if one performs white karma, one shall likewise receive a white retribution; and for all mixed karmas, it is likewise so."
"O Bhikṣus! Just as you should not perform mixed or black deeds, you should instead perform white deeds.

For instance, because of his evil friend Devadatta, Ajātaśatru committed a great act of parricide against his father, King Bimbisāra; he hurled a spear that struck the king’s finger, causing all the people of the kingdom to join in mocking and discussing it."
"How could one have failed to kill such an evil person while he was still in the womb as King Ajātaśatru?
At other times, some people would discuss:
"This was not the fault of King Ajātaśatru."
"It is due to the fault of that evil friend Devadatta. Or some might say:
"Because the Buddha ordained Devadatta, he did not carry out an act of banishment to send him to another region where he could dwell in peace."
Some may criticize and say:
"The Buddha is indeed without fault, for that community of bhikṣus does not abide by or uphold the teachings of the Saṃgha.
When the King, our father, heard these various discussions, no ill intent arose in his heart, and he said:
"Because of my own karma from previous lives," some say; others further state:
"This is the fault of the Buddha and the Sangha."
"Because of these words, my heart is filled with sorrow and distress.
At that time, the bhikṣus each gave rise to doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what reason do those people commit transgressions while causing this person to suffer the calamity?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that such an event as this occurred; in the distant past, it happened then as well.
Listen attentively!
I shall now explain it for you.
Long ago in the distant past, there was a king named Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī; the people were peaceful, secure, wealthy, and enjoyed abundant prosperity.
At that time, there were two dogs in that city:
One was black and one was white; they fed on the leather of saddles, bridles, and reins.
At a later time, when the king wished to go forth to battle, he addressed his ministers, saying:
"Your Excellencies, quickly prepare the weapons!"
The minister immediately inspected it and saw that it had been bitten by a dog and was no longer fit for use; he then informed the king.
Upon hearing this, the king became enraged and ordered all dogs to be killed. Once the dogs in the city had been slaughtered, they fled the country.
At that time, a dog from another country came in from outside; seeing the local dogs fleeing in terror, he asked, "For what reason is it so?
The dogs of the city answered him in detail regarding the matter.
He asked, "For what reason did you not inform the Great King?
The city dog replied:
"Who dares to inform the King?
the outer dog replied, "Remain at ease;
this very night I shall go before the King and inform him."
He then went before the king with dignified and composed bearing and spoke this verse:
"Within the Great King’s palace there are two dogs:
one white and one black, endowed with both color and strength. You ought to execute them rather than let me perish; it is not right that you should execute one and not the other."
At that time, having heard these verses, the king said to his ministers:
"You should seek out the one who recited this gāthā and bring him before me."
The ministers investigated:
"Who recited this verse for the King in the middle of the night?
And someone spoke up, saying:
"A dog from another country has come and recited a verse for the King.
The King said, "Examine this thoroughly: is it truly these two dogs in the palace who ate [the food]?"
"Or was it eaten by another dog?
The ministers gathered for consultation:
"The King has now ordered an investigation; how shall we conduct a thorough examination?"
Among them, some said: "Why bother with elaborate arguments?
Simply take a lock of hair and place it in the dog's mouth; if it eats the skin, it will naturally vomit it up."
Once the hair had been settled, the two dogs of the royal palace vomited up the hide.
They reported this matter to the king, who said:
"It is fitting that these two dogs be punished, while the other dogs are without fault.
O bhikṣus, what do you think? Were those two dogs of old anyone else? [They were none other than yourselves.]
Devadatta and King Ajātaśatru are those very individuals; because of their past transgressions, they caused others to suffer.
Now it is likewise: they have committed offenses, and the Buddha and the Saṅgha have incurred blame on their account.
"Listen further, all of you, to the account of Devadatta’s ingratitude.
Long ago, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled and transformed the people."
At that time, there was a man who entered the mountains to gather wood; encountering a lion on the path, he fled and fell into a well.
The lion pursued him but did not see the well, and consequently fell upon it.

There was also a venomous snake chasing a rat, which in turn was trying to claw at an owl; these three simultaneously fell into the well together, each giving rise to a malicious intent to devour the others.
The lion said:

"Now that I possess power within this well, I am able to devour you all; however, since we are together in a place of calamity, you should cease your evil intentions and refrain from harming one another."

By a coincidence of causes and conditions, there was a hunter who, while pursuing a deer, arrived at this place and looked down into the well; the man within the well then raised his voice and cried out: "O Noble Sir!"
"I pray that you will rescue me.
At that time, the hunter first pulled the lion out of the well; the lion immediately prostrated at the hunter's feet and said, "I now recognize your profound kindness and shall surely repay it."
"As for that black-headed creature within the well, it is ignorant of kindness and righteousness; you must certainly not rescue it.
The lion then departed.
Subsequently, the hunter rescued all those in the well—the snake, the insects, the birds, and others—in succession, until they were all saved.

Later, the lion captured a deer; the hunter happened to come upon that place while traveling and rescued it. Upon seeing him arrive, the lion immediately handed over the deer to the hunter and departed after prostrating himself in worship.
Later, on one occasion, King Brahmadatta and his court ladies went out of the city for recreation to a park, where they indulged themselves in pleasure until they eventually fell fast asleep.

When the palace women saw that the king was asleep, they felt no fear; some paced back and forth, some stood, some sat, some slept, some went far away, some removed their clothes to dry them, and some took off their necklaces and lay down beside them to sleep. A crow, perched by a well, seized one of these necklaces and flew far away, presenting it to the hunter who had previously saved its life as a token of gratitude for his kindness.
At that time, King Brahmadatta awoke from his sleep and, together with his retinue of ministers and attendants, quickly returned to the city.
Meanwhile, the palace lady who had lost the necklace searched everywhere for its location but could not find it; she then went to the king and said, "Great King!..."
"The necklace has been lost within the pleasure groves.
At that time, the king addressed his ministers, saying, "The necklace has already been lost in the various pleasure groves; you must investigate and seek it out—who has stolen it?"
When the ministers and attendants had received the king’s command, they immediately began their search.

From time to time, the "black-headed" creatures (the monkeys) went to the hunter's place, seeking an opportunity to examine the necklace; having seen it, they knew that this was the king’s necklace and that it was now located there.
That black-headed creature then cast aside all sense of gratitude and righteousness, and went to the king’s presence, saying: "Great King!
I now know for certain that the lost necklace is in the hands of the hunter."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately became enraged and ordered a messenger to go and seize the hunter.
When the king’s messenger arrived at the hunter's location, he said to him:
"You have stolen a necklace belonging to the king's consort from within the royal park."
The hunter, filled with fear, replied:
"We truly did not steal the King's necklace.
He then explained in detail to the messenger how he had come by it and returned the necklace to him.
Having received them, the messenger led them to the king’s presence, and the hunter was immediately bound and imprisoned at that very spot.
Upon seeing this, the mouse hurried to inform the snake, saying to him:
"That black-headed creature, a man of evil deeds who recognizes neither kindness nor virtue, has caused my good friend to be seen and now imprisoned by the king's messengers."
Having heard these words, the snake replied:
"Tell the hunter: 'Today, for your sake, I shall bite the king within the royal palace.
You must recite your incantations, and I shall withdraw my venom.'"
"The King will surely rejoice and release you, and he shall also grant you a reward.
Having received these words, the mouse reported them in full to the hunter. The hunter said, "Excellent!"
"You should act in this way.
The serpent immediately bit the king's body; at that time, the king suffered from the venom which spread throughout his entire frame, and he summoned physicians extensively, saying:
"Who is able to cure me?"
At that time, none of the physicians were able to treat him.
After the king had made his proclamation everywhere, a hunter heard it and sent the man he was currently holding, saying:
"You should report to the king on my behalf that I am capable of curing him."
The official in charge reported the matter in detail to the king, who said, "Order him to be released immediately and brought here.
Once he arrived at the king's presence, the hunter treated him; the ailment was cured instantly, and he was then released.
The king was greatly delighted and bestowed further rewards upon him.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“What do you think?”
Could this have been anyone else?
The hunter at that time was my own self.
That ungrateful creature with the black head was Devadatta.

"In the past, he was without gratitude and lacked righteousness, failing to recognize kindness and virtue; now, likewise, he does not know the meaning of gratitude or righteousness, nor does he recognize kindness and virtue.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this way, Devadatta does not know the meaning of gratitude or righteousness, nor does he recognize kindness and virtue."
Listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you.
In the distant past, there was an untimely season when it rained heavily for seven days without ceasing; a mongoose entered its burrow, and a mouse likewise entered that same burrow.
Later, there was a venomous snake that, seeking a place to avoid the rain, also entered that same hole.
However, as the mongoose intended to harm the mouse, the venomous snake said to the mongoose:
"You and we have all encountered great hardship and peril; do not harbor thoughts of mutual injury, but each remain at peace."
Each of those venomous snakes established its own name: the venomous snake was named Priyaka, the mongoose was named Nandika, and the rat was named Gaṅgāpāla.
Then Priyaka, Nandika, and the others said to Gaṅgāpāla:
"You are diligent and capable; you should go to another place on our behalf to seek out food and drink and bring it back."
That mouse was by nature upright and honest, and his mind was virtuous and kind; he diligently sought food for both the snake and the mongoose.
Before he had yet returned, the mongoose said to the snake, "If he fails to find food and returns empty-handed, I shall eat him."
Upon hearing these words, the snake thought to himself:
"This mongoose is now beset by such hardship because he intended to harm that mouse; I fear that if he fails to find food and returns empty-handed, he will certainly be eaten."
"I must now inform that mouse in advance.
Having formed this thought, he immediately sent a message to inform the mouse, saying:
"That mongoose has spoken thus:"
"If you come empty-handed like a rat without food, you will certainly be eaten by me.
The rat, having failed to obtain food or drink despite its piteous pleas, thought to itself:
"Since I cannot find food now, if I go back empty-handed, he will surely eat me."
The mouse again sent a message to the snake, replying in verse:
"If a person is stingy and lacks compassion, Driven by the fire of hunger, they become frantic;
You have shown me great kindness for speaking these words, But I shall no longer come to visit you."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"As for that mouse, could it have been anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
That mongoose was Devadatta; in former times he likewise lacked kindness and righteousness, and even now he remains ignorant of gratitude and virtue.
Then King Ajātaśatru threw his sword before his father, and the king asked:
"My beloved son!
For what reason have you thrown a sword before me?"
He replied to the king:
"I have anger. My father has enjoyments, whereas I have none."
Upon hearing these words, the king said to his son, "If that is so, I shall grant you the city of Campā for your enjoyment.
Having received the city for his use, the son was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he then went to Devadatta and spoke as follows:
“Venerable One!
I have now obtained the city of Campā and shall enjoy it to my heart’s content.
Then Devadatta replied to the prince:
"You have now exerted effort, and through the power of the manifest fruition of that karma,
you shall both receive and enjoy [its results]. The Prince replied, "Noble One!"
"I have now seen it.
He spoke again:
"You should employ even greater effort; you will surely attain further excellence."

At that time, the Crown Prince dispatched [officials] to the city of Campā to collect taxes and impose heavy labor services upon the common people. Being oppressed and coerced by these measures, the people dispersed and fled in all directions; some went to Rājagṛha, others to various other kingdoms. Among them, some sent envoys to report to the King, saying:
"The Crown Prince is oppressing us so severely that the people of Campā have scattered and fled to foreign lands."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will suppress this unlawful conduct.
At that time, the father-king immediately summoned the crown prince and said to him:
"For what reason do you now oppress the common people?"
The Crown Prince replied,
"It is because the soldiers are unable to provide for their own livelihood.
The Father King said:
"If it be so, then with the exception of Rājagṛha, let the people of the kingdom of Magadha enjoy [the land] as their own.
Having received this, the Prince went to Devadatta and reported, "Noble One!"
"Except for the single city of Rājagṛha, all else is mine to obtain.
Devadatta replied, "One who exerts effort now obtains such a reward; you should likewise exert further effort."
At that time, the Prince immediately dispatched messengers to inflict harsh labor and cause damage to the cities and towns of the people of Magadha.
When the people had been thus oppressed and tormented, the multitude of citizens petitioned King Śreṇika, saying:
"The Prince is now inflicting harm upon the people and cities of Magadha; we pray that Your Majesty will restrain him and not permit such actions."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately summoned the crown prince. When the prince had arrived, the father-king addressed him, saying:
"For what reason have you again caused harm to the cities, towns, and people of the kingdom of Magadha?"
The Prince replied,
"My soldiers are so numerous that I cannot provide for their sustenance.
The King said:
"If it be so, I shall now leave you with all the wealth of the royal palace, with the exception of one single treasury; as for Rājagṛha itself, it is yours to enjoy.
Having received this, the Prince went to Devadatta and said:
"I have now further obtained Rājagṛha; with the exception of one single treasury of wealth, everything else has been acquired by me."
Devadatta replied, "This is the ripening of the fruits of my diligent efforts.
He spoke again:
"Insofar as a king relies on his treasury as his power, if he possesses a treasury, he is truly a king; for the sake of that treasury, he must exert effort."
At that time, the prince again sent people to inflict harm upon the inhabitants of Rājagṛha.
Then the multitude of people in Rājagṛha, as well as the multitudes from Campā and Magadha, each harboring fear, secretly reported the matter in detail to the King, saying:

"We have been subjected to urgent suffering and injury by the prince. Your Majesty has hitherto nurtured the common people like your own infants; now that we are being harmed by the prince, many of us have fled and scattered to various countries, and we ourselves now wish to do the same."

King Bimbisāra was deeply devoted in his faith and, out of compassion for sentient beings, remained steadfast in upholding the True Dharma. Upon hearing these words, he immediately summoned the crown prince.
When the prince had arrived, the king spoke with reasoned words that accorded with the prince’s own inclinations; stroking the prince’s head with his hand, he said:
"I now entrust all my cities and subjects to you. For what reason, then, do you now distress and trouble the people?"
"You ought now to provide for his upbringing.
The prince replied,
"It is because I have no storehouses that it is so."
The Great King replied, "If it is so, with the exception of my own palace attendants, all other treasuries are at your disposal.

However, the Crown Prince was by nature violent and wicked; even having obtained the treasuries, he remained unsatisfied and continued to harass and disturb the people of the kingdom, refusing to desist.
Then the multitude of people returned to the king’s presence and reported the matter in detail to him. Having heard their words, the king said to the crown prince:
"I have now given you the people and the treasuries; why do you continue to harass and disturb the common folk, refusing to desist?"
Having heard these words, the Prince became exceedingly enraged and addressed his ministers and attendants, saying:
"You should know this: if there were someone who reviled and abused a Kṣatriya king who has been consecrated, what punishment and retribution would be appropriate for such a person?"
The ministers replied,
"He deserves the ultimate punishment.
[The king said,] "The one who has now reviled me is my father."
"What is this harm?
For now, let him be confined in the inner palace.
Thereupon, the ministers and attendants immediately imprisoned him.

When the Great King was imprisoned, the palace ladies, ministers, officials, and the multitude of citizens within the city all became distressed upon hearing that the King had been incarcerated; they all recollected the Great King’s past kindness and affection.

The king was imprisoned. When the crown prince ascended the throne, he became violent, cruel, and murderous; he was fierce and savage, such that none of his ministers or attendants dared to remonstrate with him.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having been imprisoned, thought to himself:
"This has come about through the causal conditions of my past karma."
"According to the time, the Queen Mother of the state, Vaidehī, regularly provided him with food.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru asked the gatekeeper:
'In what way is the old king currently sustaining himself?'"
Then the gatekeeper addressed the king, saying,
"The Queen Mother regularly sends food herself to provide for the Old King.
Upon hearing these words, King Ajātaśatru said to the gatekeeper:

"You must ensure that no more food, drink, or water is allowed to enter; inform all the palace attendants not to send any food either, for anyone who does so shall be subject to the ultimate punishment."
At that time, seeing that the instructions were so severe, no one dared to bring food to the old king’s location; thus, for many days, no one was able to reach the king.

At that time, the King’s consort, Vaidehī, could not bear her thoughts of the King’s affection; she mixed ghee and honey with parched grain flour to smear upon her body, and used the hollows of her anklets to hold water, which she then brought to the King to prolong his life for a few more days.

At that time, the mind of the officer on duty was immediately filled with suspicion; although he had momentarily become aware of it, out of consideration for the King’s favor, he did not report it even before Ajātaśatru had asked.
Later, at another time, King Ajātaśatru asked the gatekeeper:
"In what condition does the old king currently exist?
The gatekeeper then related the situation in full:
"Queen Vaidehī has mixed ghee with parched grain flour and smeared it upon her body; she offers water from within the hollows of her anklets to the King, by which he now remains alive.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru commanded his attendants:
"From this day forward, do not allow the Queen to enter and see the Old King again."

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking up and down on Vulture Peak, directly in line with the king’s window. The king saw the Buddha’s shadow from afar; because of seeing the Buddha, his heart gave rise to joy, and by virtue of this root of goodness, his life was sustained.
Then King Ajātaśatru further questioned the palace attendants on duty:
"I have already cut off the supply of food; how does the old king survive now?
The gatekeepers replied:

“From within his window, the king saw the World-Honored One from afar; the World-Honored One, out of compassion, took him under his protection, and by the power of this merit, the King was able to survive.
The king then ordered the windows to be sealed shut and had the king’s feet pierced so that he could no longer stand.
Then the official in charge immediately followed the king’s command, closing the windows and piercing the soles of his feet.
At that time, the old king suffered from intense pain and distress; choking with sobs and weeping, his tears flowed incessantly as he thought to himself:
"Now I am in such suffering and affliction; why does the World-Honored One not take pity on me and look upon me?"
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has nothing he does not know or see.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
with great compassion, they gather in and sustain sentient beings, providing certain protection while abiding in right contemplation.

If one can subdue these three matters, transcend the four violent torrents, and settle in the four bases of psychic power; if one is fully endowed with the five factors, transcends the five paths, abides in the seven factors of enlightenment, and demonstrates the eightfold path; if one is skillful in means and enters the nine meditative absorptions accordingly, possessing the ten powers, and one’s fame fills the worlds of the ten directions—surpassing even a thousand-fold sovereign wheel-turning king—because one surveys all sentient beings with the Buddha-eye throughout the three periods of day and night.
In the wisdom that functions in accordance [with reality], what diminishes?
What increases?
What is oppressed?
Who is being oppressed?
Who has descended into the evil destinies?
Who is heading toward the evil destinies?
Who is it that proceeds resolutely toward [the lower realms]?
Who is it that bears this heavy burden?
By what skillful means can I now rescue them from these evil destinies, establish them in the realms of humans and devas, and further enable them to attain liberation?

They cause those who have not yet cultivated roots of goodness to cultivate them; they cause those who have already cultivated roots of goodness but have not yet brought them to maturity to achieve fulfillment; and they cause those who have already achieved fulfillment to attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Go to King Bimbisāra and convey my words to him:
'May the King be free from illness.'"
He spoke these words:
"The Buddha told the Great King:
'As for what a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) ought to do, I have already done it.'"
"I shall now rescue you and deliver you from the three evil realms.
I will cause you to always dwell among gods and humans, transcending the realm of birth and death.
Upon hearing what the Buddha said, he immediately entered samādhi; he vanished from Vulture Peak and appeared before the king in the royal prison of Rājagṛha, where he addressed the king, saying:
"Great King! The Buddha said to the Great King:
'May you be free from illness and affliction.'"
At that time, the King paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the King:
"The Buddha told the Great King:

'As for a virtuous friend, I have performed my duty toward you, the King, by causing you to leave behind the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, and establishing you in the states of humans and devas, exactly as previously described.'"

"By reason of karmic causes and conditions, Great King, you should know that it is due to karma that he is thus confined, his feet have been pierced, and he is deprived of food, his body being subjected to suffering and harm."
The King asked Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
"Where can one find excellent food and drink?
At that time, Maudgalyāyana replied:
"There is excellent food and drink in the realm of the Four Great Kings.
Having thus informed the king, he immediately transformed his body and departed for Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru was suffering from an abscess on his finger and went to the King’s presence. The King took him into his arms, stroked him with his hands, and sucked upon the sore.
At that moment, the prince wept incessantly; as the King sucked the abscess, it burst open, and pus and blood entered his mouth. He spat the pus onto the ground.
When the prince saw the pus on the ground, he wept incessantly.
At that time, Queen Mother Vaidehī, having witnessed this event, sighed and lamented deeply.
When King Ajātaśatru saw his mother sighing and lamenting, he asked her:
"Why do you sigh? He replied:

"Since the time of my great-grandfather, our lineage has never suffered from this affliction of rashes. You too once had this affliction; your grandfather sucked at your sores, drinking the pus and blood as it came out without spitting it on the ground. Fearing that if he saw the pus you would weep again, for this reason your grandfather consumed your pus and blood."
He asked, "Do you truly have such affection for me?
His mother replied:
"I cherish you in this way.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru’s heart of anger ceased and a heart of affection arose, and he said to his ministers and counselors:
"Suppose there were a person who said:..."
"To him who says, 'The old king lives,' half the kingdom shall be granted.
Because all the people felt compassion and affection for the old king, upon hearing these words of the king, they rushed and vied with one another to go see him.
The old king, hearing from afar the sound of a great multitude rushing toward him, was struck with fear while in prison and thought to himself:
"They must surely be calling for me to undergo various forms of painful torture."

Sighing deeply and gasping for breath, he fainted upon the ground and immediately passed away, being reborn by sudden transformation upon the lap of the Northern Heavenly King in his celestial palace.
Then the deva Vaiśravaṇa asked, "Who are you? He replied:
“My name is Jyotīrasa. “Why are you named Jyotīrasa?
“There was a deity whose food and drink were always present before me, appearing according to my thoughts; for this reason, I am long called by the name Jyotīrasa.”
At that time, the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; as only the Buddha could resolve it, they addressed him together, saying:
“By what karma did King Bimbisāra bring its fruit to maturity such that he was born into the royal palace, possessing great wealth, nobility, and abundant resources?”

"Furthermore, he was able to see the Buddha and understand the principles of the Noble Truths; yet later, his feet were pierced and he was imprisoned, suffering the torments of hunger and thirst until he died of starvation.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If one performs black karma, one experiences black maturation; if one performs white karma, one experiences white maturation; if one performs mixed karma, one experiences mixed maturation."
Therefore, bhikṣus! One creates one's own karma and must experience its results oneself.
As it is said in a verse:
“Even if a hundred eons should pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When the causes and conditions converge, One must experience the retribution oneself.”
"Therefore, bhikṣus! You should abandon mixed karma and black karma; you should cultivate pure, white, and clean karma. All you bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way."
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Volume Seventeen;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda,
Volume Eighteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!

In times long past, when no Buddha had appeared in the world, there were only pratyekabuddhas who occasionally took pity on the poor and destitute, yet they themselves possessed few bedding materials, food, or drink.
At that time, there were only pratyekabuddhas in the world. During this period, a pratyekabuddha was wandering on his travels when he arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī.
He stayed at the potter’s wheel-shed, where several other merchants were also resting together.
Among them was one person who, while in his room at night, inadvertently discharged excrement that defiled the floor; he then departed immediately.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, had they not investigated, would not have known of this matter beforehand.
The Pratyekabuddha stayed overnight there, intending to beg for food at dawn the following day.
When the host entered the room, he saw that it was defiled and filthy with excrement.
However, an ordinary person of deluded nature, ignorant of good and evil, conceived an evil thought and replied to the Pratyekabuddha:
"You are a renunciant; why did you not go outside the room to defecate instead of voiding your excrement here inside the room?"
Then the host locked the door with a bolt and said,
"You may now starve to death in this room.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"Thinking, 'I fear this host will later suffer a painful retribution; yet if I were to open the door and leave on my own, I also fear his anger and resentment,' he remained there in silence.
When it was time for the midday meal, the host’s anger subsided, and he addressed the Pratyekabuddha, saying:"
"Come and eat," [he said].
[The other] replied, "My time has already passed; I shall not eat anymore."
"If it be so, you shall stay for another night this evening, and partake of the midday meal tomorrow morning.
Because the Pratyekabuddha was moved by compassion and sought to sustain him, he remained there immediately.
When morning came, he prepared pure and exquisite food to offer as an oblation to the pratyekabuddha.

At that time, for the sake of benefiting his host, the pratyekabuddha manifested various transformations to preach the Dharma; he displayed supernormal powers, emitting fire from the upper part of his body or water from the lower part of his body, manifesting all manner of miraculous transformations.

At that time, the host, seeing this divine transformation, felt a profound sense of repentance; it was as if a swift wind had blown through a great tree, uprooting it entirely so that it snapped and fell. In the same way, he threw himself down in prostration and cried out:
"O Great Sage!"
"Please descend for a moment; I have now fallen into the defilement of sensual desire, so I pray that you will compassionately pull me out.
The Buddha descended further, and the man prostrated at his feet and made this vow:
"I harbored evil intentions toward the Noble One; may I suffer no karmic retribution for this."

Furthermore, may the merit and roots of goodness from these offerings cause us all to attain vast wealth and mastery in future lives, and to constantly make offerings to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas with hearts free from weariness or detachment.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think?
The potter's son at that time was none other than King Bimbisāra."

At that time, because he harbored malicious intent toward a pratyekabuddha and uttered coarse words, through the ripening of that karma, his feet are now being pierced by knives, and he lies confined within a room, dying of hunger and thirst.

Due to the power of his remorse and the force of his aspiration, that karma matured, and he was born into a royal palace with great wealth and prosperity. In the presence of the World-Honored One, he shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of satkāyadṛṣṭi (the view of a self-identity), piercing through them with wisdom, and realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:

"Those who perform black deeds obtain black retribution; those who perform white deeds shall mature the fruits of white deeds; and those who perform mixed black-and-white deeds shall obtain mixed black-and-white karmic retribution."
"O bhikṣus! You should abandon black karma and mixed black-and-white karma, and devote yourselves exclusively to the practice of white karma; you should train yourselves thus.
At that time, the ministers and assistants came and addressed the Great King:
"The body of that old king has now perished.

Upon hearing these words, he fell to the ground in a faint; then, water was sprinkled on his face and he regained consciousness. He immediately entered the chamber to don the mourning garments for his father, and no one could offer counsel to make him abandon his grief.
At that time, the ministers deliberated together:
"By what skillful means might the King be freed from sorrow?
At that moment, a musician from the kingdom of South India arrived and was brought before the King to perform various musical entertainments.

The king’s heart was devoid of joy; he remained silent without responding and did not offer a kind word. When the performers had all departed, he wandered on until he reached the place where the World-Honored One was, and addressed him, saying:
“Excellent, O Great Being!”
With hearts filled with joy, they immediately beat drums and performed music.

At that time, the World-Honored One himself emitted light and smiled; various rays of light issued forth like sparks from a fire, some ascending and others descending. These rays descended as far as the Avīci Hell.
Wherever the light reached, those suffering from cold were warmed, and those suffering from heat attained coolness.
All who were undergoing suffering found relief and thought to themselves:
"I have been reborn in another place."
The Buddha manifested a person within the hell and addressed them, saying:
"You have not been reborn elsewhere; it is because another person has emitted light that your suffering has come to an end."

When those sinners saw that emanated being, joy arose in their hearts and their sins were extinguished; they all attained rebirth in the realms of humans and devas, becoming fit to receive and hear the noble Dharma of the Four Truths.

That light ascended as far as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; within the light, verses on the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and emptiness were proclaimed. The light shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm and then returned to follow behind the Buddha.
If the Blessed One intends to speak of past events, even those concerning the matter of unsurpassed enlightenment, the light rays enter through his back.
If he intends to speak of future events, the light rays enter through his front.
If he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light enters through the soles of his feet.
If he intends to speak of matters concerning the animal realm, the light enters through the back of his heels.
If he intends to speak of matters concerning the hungry ghosts, the light enters through the spaces between his toes.
If he speaks of rebirth among human beings, the light enters through his shins.
If he speaks of a wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*), the light vanishes into his left hand.
If he speaks of a great wheel-turning king, the light comes to his right hand and vanishes there.
If he speaks of matters concerning the heavens, the light vanishes into his navel.
If he speaks of the matters of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the light vanishes from his arms.
If he speaks of the Dharma of Pratyekabuddhas, the light enters between his eyebrows.
If it is to be prophesied that they shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the light enters through the crown of the head; the details are as extensively described before.
At that time, these rays of light reached the Buddha, circled him three times, and entered between his eyebrows.
At that time, Ānanda joined his palms and praised the Buddha by reciting verses, as described in detail previously.
He praised the Buddha with these verses:
"A thousand wondrous and diverse colors issue forth from a single path of the mouth;
Illuminating the ten directions, like the sun first rising;
Speaking verses without a self, those who hear them cast off pride;
All create the causes and conditions for Buddhahood; Without a [specific] cause, I do not emit light.
"Subduing all enemies and the like.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see that musician who, out of joy for me, beats the drum and performs music?"
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, “I have seen it.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"This actor shall attain the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha and be named Ya-ho-yin (Melodious Voice).
At that time, Devadatta said to King Ajātaśatru:
"I have instructed you so that you have now obtained the royal throne; you must now establish me so that I may become a Buddha."
Then the king said to Devadatta,
"The Buddha’s body is golden in color, while your body is not golden.
Would you establish yourself as a Buddha?"
He further addressed the king, saying,
"It is also possible for my body to become golden in color.
Thereupon, Devadatta summoned a goldsmith and commanded him:
"Make my body golden. The goldsmith replied, "Noble One!"
"If you can endure the pain,
you may do it. He replied,
"I can endure the pain."
The goldsmith then immediately smeared his body with hot oil and, undergoing various hardships,
applied thin gold leaf over his skin. Separately, another bhikṣu asked the bhikṣu Kokālika, "Where is Devadatta now?"
He replied, "I am not here because I have gone to dye my body golden.
When that bhikṣu heard this, he immediately went to see Devadatta; there he saw him undergoing various hardships and crying out as he sought to make his body golden.
The bhikṣu immediately came and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Devadatta is undergoing great suffering because he desires to make his body golden in color.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"At that time, Devadatta did not merely undergo the hardship of his body becoming golden in the present; in the past, he underwent the hardship of wearing a golden cap until death."
In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a woman whose husband had gone away on a long journey and was not at home.
A crow came before this woman and uttered sweet, melodious sounds.
The woman said, "If my husband arrives safely and early with a voice as beautiful as yours, I shall give you a golden cap.
Before long, her husband arrived home safely; then the crow again produced a beautiful sound before that woman.
Then that woman immediately threw the golden cap to the crow; having received it, the crow flew away toward the east.
Separately, there was an owl who, for the sake of that golden cap, struck the crow’s head so that it fell to the ground and died.
The Buddha said,
"The crow at that time was none other than Devadatta.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
This Devadatta still possesses such habitual tendencies from the past, that for the sake of a golden cap, he now undergoes such hardship for the sake of a thin layer of gold."
Furthermore, Devadatta said to King Ajātaśatru:
"I established you so that you have now attained the royal throne; you must likewise establish me as a Buddha.
The king replied:
“The Tathāgata has the mark of the wondrous wheel upon his feet; by establishing this, he is entitled to be called a Buddha.
Devadatta spoke again to the king, saying, “I am able to create the mark of the wheel on the soles of my feet.”
At that time, Devadatta summoned a skilled craftsman and asked him,
"Are you capable of creating the mark of a wheel upon my two feet? The man replied:
"Noble One! If you wish to be able to endure this pain, I shall perform it for you. Devadatta said:
"I can endure the pain.
At that time, the artisan thought to himself, "This man possesses great physical strength; if he were to stamp his heel upon me while making the impression, I would surely die because of it."
He then said to Devadatta, "Step out into the room with your foot, and I shall place my seal upon it.
He replied to the craftsman:
"Very well.
At that time, the artisan immediately heated a wheel-shaped iron until it was the color of fire and branded it upon the soles of his feet;
at that moment, he experienced extreme suffering. Then, a bhikṣu came and asked Kokālika:
“Where is Devadatta now? He replied, “He is currently at a certain place fashioning the mark of a wheel on his feet.”
Then that bhikṣu went to the monk’s quarters to see Devadatta.
Upon arriving there, he saw Devadatta having the wheel-marks made on his feet; as his feet were being burned, he was undergoing great suffering and crying out in pain.
At that time, that bhikṣu, his mind filled with doubt and wonder, went to the place where the Tathāgata was; for only the Buddha can sever doubts and delusions, he addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I saw Devadatta having the wheel-marks made upon his feet, and he is undergoing great suffering and pain."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, he also suffered for his feet; his habitual tendencies remain.
For instance, in the past, there was a great elephant in the Snowy Mountains who went down the mountain to drink water."
A jackal was following behind the elephant and, seeing the elephant's footprints, measured them for himself, thinking, "I shall pass away from here and be reborn in the heavens.
Because of this, he leaped up, only to be suddenly struck by a withered tree that crushed his body, leading to his death.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? At that time, that jackal was none other than Devadatta."
"At that time, while measuring the footprints, you forgot to maintain the intention for contemplation; now, because of those wheel-marks on your feet, you undergo great suffering.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling in the deep and remote palace of the Yakṣa on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha. Then Devadatta said to King Ajātaśatru:
"I now establish you as king; you may in turn establish me as the Buddha."
"However, I now wish to kill the śramaṇa Gautama; Your Majesty should devise various stratagems with me.
I do not yet know with what object to strike him, nor where first to strike so as to bring about his death."
At that time, there was a skilled craftsman capable of constructing catapults who came from the kingdom of South India to the city.
Having heard this, Devadatta immediately summoned the craftsman and said to him,
"Are you able to construct a catapult that can be drawn by five hundred men?"
He replied, "I am now well-versed in the construction of this catapult.

Thereupon, Devadatta took a necklace worth a thousand pieces of gold and gave it to the master craftsman, ordering him to build the vehicle; he also provided a thousand men for his service and said to the craftsman:

“The Buddha is at Vulture Peak Mountain; you should now station five hundred men with catapults near the place where the Buddha sits on that mountain, and station another two hundred and fifty men with catapults in other locations.”
Furthermore, he ordered another two hundred and fifty men to be stationed elsewhere with catapults.
He addressed those men, saying:
"You should know that whenever the śramaṇa Gautama comes or goes on his travels, you must strike him with a catapult and take his life."
Then those men, having received Devadatta’s instructions, went immediately to Vulture Peak Mountain and finished constructing five hundred catapults. At that time,
the five hundred men deliberated among themselves, saying,
"We have built these great catapults with the intent of harming the World-Honored One."
They all spoke these words:
"You should know that we would rather each give up our own lives than harm the body of the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, who is revered by both gods and humans."
Having spoken these words, he immediately abandoned the catapult and sought a secluded path down from the mountain peak, fearing that Devadatta might see him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the people, manifested a flight of stairs. When the multitude saw this, they discussed it among themselves, saying:
"This steep, high mountain previously had no stairs; you should know that this is the majestic power of the World-Honored One."
At that time, those people conceived great pure faith toward the Buddha, the Tathāgata, and descended the stairs to the place where the World-Honored One was.

Then, for the sake of subduing them, the World-Honored One was walking up and down on Vulture Peak Mountain. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their faculties, dispositions, and latent tendencies, taught them the Four Noble Truths to bring about their awakening.

Having heard this, they were able to shatter the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) with the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom and realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Having realized the Truths, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!

It is through the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that I have attained the fruit of liberation; this was not something that could be accomplished by my parents, kings, devas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, or kinsmen."

Because I encountered the World-Honored One as my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he rescued me from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts and established me in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas. I shall now bring an end to birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Having transcended mountains of bones and dried up oceans of blood, I have shattered with the vajra-pestle of wisdom the twentyfold view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) accumulated since beginningless time, and have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and receive the five precepts: from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall refrain from taking life, and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will bear witness that I am an upāsaka.
At that moment, the artisan, believing that he had harmed the Buddha, took the necklace from his throat and fled in secret.

At that time, Devadatta repeatedly gazed from afar, thinking that the head of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already fallen to the ground; yet he saw that the Buddha remained serene and entirely unhurt.

Seeing five hundred people listening to the Dharma at the Buddha’s side, he gave rise to resentment and took another path up the mountain. There he saw a craftsman carrying a pearl and fleeing in secret; because of this, he himself led five hundred men to set off a catapult.
The Buddha had this thought:
"This is the ripening of the karmic retribution accumulated through my past deeds that has now arrived; the violent torrent of the waters of desire cannot be stopped or turned back.
One reaps what one sows; it is impossible for another to experience the results of one's own actions."
The Buddha, having understood their karma, addressed the five hundred men, saying:
"Virtuous ones, you should know!
Devadatta is of very evil intent and wishes to lead your bodies up Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. This is my own karma that must certainly be experienced; we may proceed together."
At that time, the devas looked down toward the lower realms, whereupon the Vajrapāṇi yakṣa thought to himself:
"This Devadatta has raised up evil and rebellious intent, desiring to harm the Tathāgata."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the palace of the yakṣa Kumbhīra and informed the yakṣa, saying:
"Devadatta has constructed a great catapult on the summit of Vulture Peak Mountain and is flying large stones to attempt to harm the Buddha’s body."
Once the World-Honored One is dwelling securely in your palace, when Devadatta hurls the rock, I shall shatter it in mid-air with my vajra; you should assist me.
Fearing that flying fragments might strike the Buddha’s body, you should shield and protect him.
Kimbila said: "Excellent! It is so."
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and was about to enter a deep mountain cave.
Then Devadatta, together with five hundred men, released a stone by means of a mechanical device, aiming it directly at the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi deity struck the rock in mid-air with his vajra, shattering it into pieces. One fragment of the rock was about to fall upon the Buddha’s body.
Then the yakṣa Kumbhīra caught the stone but could not hold it; it struck him himself and, flying off from him, damaged the World-Honored One’s foot.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Not in the midst of empty space, Not in the ocean nor in mountain caves;
There is no place on earth Where one can escape the retribution of karma."
At that time, the yakṣa Kumbhīra, his body struck by the stone and knowing for certain that he would die, gave rise to a virtuous thought:
"After my life ends, may I be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
It is the constant law of the devas that, having been born in heaven, they give rise to three thoughts:
first, "Where am I now? and second, "By what cause was I born here?"
Third, by what karma did they come to be born here? Having carefully observed and recognized that this is a celestial realm, they further realize that in their previous lives they were yakṣas;
having conceived a pure intention toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they have attained birth in the vast and supreme Heaven of the Thirty-three.
He further thought to himself:

"Now that I have been born in heaven, I ought not to remain for a night enjoying this sublime pleasure before seeing the Buddha; it is fitting that I go at once to pay my respects to the World-Honored One."

Having formed this thought, his body and hands were immediately adorned all over with exceptionally exquisite and wonderful necklaces; he also held four kinds of subtle and wondrous lotuses, such as the *māndārava*. His celestial hair was soft, fragrant, pure, and curled to the right in a deep blue-black hue. His physical form was so dignified and majestic that it could not be compared to anything else. With a composed and orderly gait, he descended from Vulture Peak Mountain, the celestial power of his majesty and radiance brilliantly illuminating the mountains and valleys.
Having approached the Buddha’s presence, he scattered flowers as an offering and withdrew to sit at one side for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his faculties, inclinations, and latent tendencies, preached to him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, causing him to attain awakening.
Having heard the Dharma, he shattered the mountain of the twenty-fold view of self-existence with the vajra-pestle of wisdom and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, he declared three times:
"O Virtuous One!..."
It is by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that I have attained the fruit of liberation.
This was not something that could be accomplished by my parents, kings of men, hosts of devas, śramaṇas, brahmins, friends, or kinsmen.

Because I encountered the World-Honored One as my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he rescued me from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts and established me in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas. I shall now bring an end to birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Having transcended mountains of bones and dried up oceans of blood, I have used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) accumulated since beginningless time, and have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and receive the five precepts: from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall refrain from taking life, and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will bear witness that I am an upāsaka.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
“The power of the World-Honored One is vast and far-reaching; He has closed and secured the gates to the evil realms.”
He revealed the sublime and virtuous path to rebirth in heaven.
Having now attained the unconditioned fruit, I have personally received the great compassion of all Buddhas; all evils are eliminated, and I have obtained the divine eye.

At that time, the yakṣa deva from his former life—like a merchant gaining profit, like a farmer reaping a harvest, like a warrior achieving victory, and like one whose illness has been cured—departed after paying homage to the Buddha with his customary deportment.

At that time, from the first watch of the night until the last, the bhikṣus were each engaged in meditative reflection; suddenly seeing a light shining everywhere before the Buddha, they were all filled with doubt and uncertainty, and approached the Buddha to inquire:
"By what causes and conditions has this occurred?"
"The Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devas, along with the hosts of the Four Great Kings, have come here to pay their respects.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"It was not Brahmā, nor was it Śakra or the hosts of the Four Great Kings who came here to visit me. It was because Devadatta had constructed a great catapult on Vulture Peak Mountain to hurl stones at me; the Vajrapāṇi deity struck and shattered them in mid-air with his vajra. At that time, the yakṣa Kumbhīra could not catch them as they fell, and so he struck himself."
Because he gave rise to a virtuous mind at the time of his death, he was reborn in the vast and superior Heaven of the Thirty-three. For this reason, he has come to pay homage to me.
I have preached the Dharma for him, and having attained the vision of the Truths, he has returned to his celestial realm.

Therefore, monks! If one performs black karma, one obtains black fruit; if one performs purely white karma, one obtains purely white fruit; and if one performs mixed karma, one will necessarily experience mixed fruit.
"You should abandon black and mixed karma and accumulate only white karma; you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and said to the Buddha:
"The yakṣa Kumbhīra lost his own life for the sake of protecting the Buddha."
The Buddha said, "It is not only today that he has lost his life for my sake; in past lives as well, he sacrificed his own body and life for my sake.
You should listen attentively!"
In the distant past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who governed the realm according to the True Dharma, free from all injustice and corruption.
At that time, the world was pure and free from calamities; the five grains were abundant, and the myriad people lived in peace and happiness.
At that time, not far from the city, there was a separate village with many gardens and groves of exquisite flowers and fruits, where various kinds of birds sang together in a lovely harmony.

At that time, there was a rishi dwelling within this forest who practiced asceticism by abstaining from grain and subsisting solely on roots and fruits, wearing garments of tree bark to ward off the cold and heat.
In this very place, there was also a hunter who regularly carried a bow and arrows, killing various birds and beasts to sustain himself.

Then this hunter went from the forest to the place where the seer was; seeing him arrive weary from his journey during the cold season, the seer felt compassion in his heart and gave him roots and fruits to eat. Thereupon, they formed a bond of affection and treated one another as father and son.
At that time, the hunter served the rishi with reverence, addressing him as "Father," and the rishi likewise felt compassion for him and loved him like a son.

Later, on another occasion, King Brahmadatta went out at dawn to observe the sights and entered a deer park. There, a wild deer, struck with terror and crying out piteously, rushed toward the rishi; however, the king immediately shot and killed the deer.
Having witnessed his death, the seer was filled with indignation and said to the king:
"Your wicked nature is utterly contrary to reason; that deer sought refuge with me, yet you have immediately subjected it to slaughter."
When the king heard this, he became extremely incensed and addressed his ministers, saying:
"If there were a person in this world who addressed harsh and evil words to a consecrated Cakravartin king, what punishment would be appropriate for such a crime?"
The ministers said to the king,
"An unrighteous and evil man such as this deserves the death penalty.
The king said:
"However, this seer has insulted and disparaged me.
At that time, the ministers wished to harm the seer, but when the hunter saw them from nearby, he thought to himself:
"As long as I am alive, how could they dare to harm such a great seer?"
At that time, the hunter immediately engaged him in battle, and the rishi fled.
Then, as the king possessed great majesty and power at that moment, the hunter was slain by the king.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus! What do you think?"
The rishi at that time was my own self;
the hunter was none other than the yakṣa deva of my previous life.
At that very moment, he already lost his life for my sake.
"Now he has come back for me and has brought about my death; the stone struck my foot, and the blood flows like this without ceasing.

The World-Honored One endured the pain. At that time, Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, came to the Buddha’s dwelling three times every day. The people of Rājagṛha, as well as merchants from various countries—whether poor or wealthy, noble or humble—who possessed faith and right view, all went with the King of Physicians to the Buddha’s dwelling.
Then the multitude addressed the King of Physicians, saying,
"What medical prescription shall we prepare?
The King of Physicians replied:
"I understand this prescription, but its medicinal ingredients are difficult to obtain.
Then Ānanda asked the King of Physicians,
"What are these medicinal herbs that are so difficult to find?"

He replied, "In this region, they use ox-head sandalwood incense; I have already searched for it in many places without success. Even if merchants possessed some, they would not dare to sell it out of fear of King Ajātaśatru’s violent nature."
If the king requires it, only then will they bring it forth to present to him.
On the day the king requires the incense, if there is nothing to give him, he will certainly be put to death. Why is this?
"Because he has previously sold sandalwood incense, it is known that he possesses its fragrance.
At that time, a perfume merchant was among the assembly; hearing what Sīvaka said—that sandalwood was required to treat the World-Honored One’s illness—he thought to himself:
"King Ajātaśatru is close with Devadatta and harbors envy toward the World-Honored One."
"If the World-Honored One hears that I gave him the ox-head sandalwood incense, he will surely punish me.

He further thought: "The World-Honored One is one to whom gods and humans should offer sustenance; for his sake, even if my own life must be forfeited, I must still present this ox-head sandalwood incense to the Tathāgata."
He immediately went to fetch the incense and returned to make offerings to the Buddha. Kneeling on his right knee, he said:
"World-Honored One!
I have obtained sandalwood incense; out of your compassion, World-Honored One, you should please accept it."
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"Receive this sandalwood incense from this Great Being.
Following these instructions, he received it.
The merchant was filled with great joy; he prostrated himself before the Buddha with his head at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and five-colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—emanated from his mouth and eventually entered between his eyebrows.
As explained in detail above,
at that time Ānanda praised the Buddha with verses, as previously described at length.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Did you see that merchant give rise to a joyful heart and offer me *gośīrṣa-candana* incense?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, “I saw it.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Just like that merchant, who with immeasurable roots of goodness and reverent faith gave as a gift the ox-head sandalwood incense, he shall in a future age realize the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha, named Candana.”
"Because they have conceived great joy toward me, they shall receive this retribution.
At that time, although the World-Honored One had obtained this sandalwood to anoint his feet, the bleeding still did not cease.
Jīvaka again addressed the Buddha, saying, "One should apply the breast milk of a young girl to the wound.
At that time, the bhikṣus were puzzled and did not know what was meant by "the breast milk of a young girl. Then the Venerable Ānanda asked Jīvaka:
"What is meant by 'the milk of a maiden'?
He replied, "If a woman gives birth for the first time after conceiving a child, that is called the milk of a maiden."

At that time, the fourfold assembly went to various places to seek the milk of young girls; throughout the city of Rājagṛha, with the exception of Devadatta and his close associates, they sought this milk from all other members of the fourfold assembly.
Devadatta and his evil associates proclaimed:
"Do not give them milk! Desiring to perform rites of malevolent sorcery and illusion, they themselves lacked the resolve to break through the mental obstructions of others.

At that time, there was only one woman in the city of Rājagṛha who was herself thin and small; her newborn child was likewise thin and small, and even though the mother’s breast milk could not satisfy him, how much less would she have given it to another?
At that time, when the woman heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, required the milk of a young girl, she thought to herself:
"If I were to offer my own milk to the Tathāgata, I would be emaciated and weak, and many calamities would arise:
first, my son would surely die; second, Devadatta is close to the King and has long-standing friends who, upon hearing that I have given him my milk, will certainly kill me."
She further thought to herself:

"Even if my own life were to end and my son were to perish, for one who is worthy of offerings from gods and humans, I shall offer my breast milk to the Tathāgata, mindful of his affliction with pain in his toes."

Then that woman drew forth her milk and placed it in a bronze vessel; taking it with her, she went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated herself at his feet, knelt on her right knee to offer it to the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I have brought the milk of this girl; having heard that the Buddha requires the milk of a young maiden, I have now brought it here. May the Buddha please accept this milk.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This woman’s heart harbors right faith; you should accept this milk."
Then Ānanda, following these instructions, received [the gift], and the woman, having prostrated her head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled and emitted light of five colors, which filled the three thousandfold world system, as described in detail above.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Did you see that woman who brought milk to offer to me?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I have seen it.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"This person has offered me milk with a heart of joy; by means of these immeasurable roots of goodness, they shall realize the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha in a future life."

At that time, as the World-Honored Buddha applied milk to his wound, the flow of blood did not cease. Monks from various directions, as well as brahmins and others, hearing that the Buddha was afflicted with a wound, all came to where the Buddha was. Some applied scented ointments and powdered incense to the wound; though they employed every kind of medical treatment, they were ultimately unable to cure it.
At that time, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa made a great vow with words of truth:
"If it is true and not false that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, regards all sentient beings as his own children, then may this bleeding cease and the wound be healed."
Having made this vow, the blood immediately ceased and the wound was instantly healed.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as all the monastics and laypeople of Rājagṛha, were filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for gladness.
Only Devadatta, King Ajātaśatru, and the evil bhikṣu Kokālika and their like were not pleased in their hearts, and they said:
"It is truly well that he has recovered from his illness; for by this, he will be able to cultivate various roots of goodness."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and uncertainty; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, could sever them.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What was the cause and condition?
After Daśabala-Kāśyapa had made his vow, the flow of blood ceased and the wound was healed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that such a cause and condition exists; it also occurred in a past life.
You should listen attentively!
Long ago in the past, I was afflicted with a poisonous ulcer, and he cured it by uttering a word of truth."
In the distant past, there was a large village in a mountain wilderness. Not far from the village was a great forest, abundant with roots and fruits.
Various kinds of birds dwelt and roamed there, producing harmonious and elegant sounds that were most delightful.

There dwelt a rishi therein who subsisted solely on roots and fruits, drank only clear mountain streams, wore garments of tree bark, and was devoted to the recitation of divine mantras. In this village there was an elder who, within his own clan, took a woman as his wife; they lived together in joy, and before long the wife became pregnant.
When his years were complete, he gave birth to a son; when the twenty-first day had passed, a gathering was held to establish the child’s name, and he was named Nandika.
Once grown, whether walking, sitting, or lying down, he constantly contemplated virtuous matters and always practiced wholesome deeds.
At that time, the villagers saw that he was joyful and named him Dharmakāma (Love of Dharma), because he sought what is wholesome.

From time to time, they went to the place of the seer to serve and make offerings to him. Seeing that he delighted in the seer and diligently practiced ascetic exercises, the people further named him Yogācāra (Practitioner of Yoga).

At a later time, that son of a householder suffered from a poisonous ulcer; though he was treated with various medicines and incantations, it would not heal. Thereupon his parents took their son together to the place of a seer and said to him: "O Seer!..."
"The attendant is now suffering from a severe wound and is extremely distressed; may he be healed.
At that time, the seer immediately made a vow with words of truth:
"Now this son of a householder has given rise to equanimity toward both friend and foe, harboring no discriminatory thoughts."
"If these words are true, may my poison be cured.
Having made this vow, the poisonous ulcer was immediately healed at that very moment.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? The son of the elder at that time was none other than my own self.
The rishi at that time was none other than the body of Mahākāśyapa of the Ten Powers. Because he made a true vow at that time, his illness was cured."
"The present time is likewise so.
At that moment, Devadatta felt remorse and thought:
"I struck the Śramaṇa Gautama with a stone, yet it could not harm him; it was useless, and everyone knows I have gained nothing but an evil reputation."
Devadatta then sat cross-legged beneath that tree and reflected deeply within himself.
When the bhikṣus saw Devadatta, they each deliberated and discussed among themselves:
"Devadatta harbors such hatred toward the Tathāgata that he has struck the Tathāgata with stones."
At that time, the bhikṣu Kokālika, a friend of Devadatta, addressed the bhikṣus:

"O venerable ones, you have failed to reflect carefully before speaking what is untrue. Do you not see that Devadatta is currently staying in the fourth dhyāna beneath that tree? Such a great being would not commit an evil deed."
At that time, the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and uncertainty; for only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can sever such doubts.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, speaking as previously described.
At that time, Devadatta’s friends, the bhikṣus Kokālika and others, having seen [this] and reported it to the Buddha, rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:
"You yourselves have no sense of shame, yet you say that we, Devadatta and I, have committed evil deeds."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, Kokālika also spoke words devoid of shame.
Listen attentively!
In times past, there was a king in the city of Rājagṛha who first established a decree ordering his attendants to set up two cemeteries:
one for men and one for women.
In the charnel ground for men, women were placed; in the charnel ground for women, men were placed.

At that time, a eunuch later died and was being taken to the *śmaśāna*; the guardian of the charnel ground for men would not allow him to be placed there, and the guardian of the charnel ground for women likewise did not permit it. Thus, he had no place in either.
Not far from the city of Rājagṛha, there was a grove where the flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees were lush and lovely, and various birds emitted harmonious and elegant sounds.
A certain seer dwelt therein, subsisting on roots and fruits, drinking clear spring water, and wearing garments of tree bark.
Near that place where the fields were tilled, there was a *pien-ma* tree; the man placed this corpse beneath that *pien-ma* tree.
At that time, there was a jackal who, smelling the stench of a corpse, followed the scent and came to devour the dead man.
An old crow, perched in concealment upon a *pien-ma* tree, thought to himself:
"I shall now offer praise to this jackal; he will surely give me a small portion of food."
The old crow praised him with a verse:
"Your chest is like that of a lion, and your waist is like that of a bull-king;
I pay homage to the lord of beasts, who provides me with food."
At that time, having observed everything thoroughly, the jackal replied in verse:
“Who dwells upon this tree in the thicket, The most excellent among those born later?
Your body’s color illuminates all places, Like a single mass of precious gems.”
The old crow again praised him in verse, saying:
"I possess many useful implements, And so I have come to see you;
Now that I pay homage to the King of Beasts, Give me some of your leftover food."
The wild jackal replied with a verse:
“Your neck is like that of a peacock; the black birds are most lovely.
Your cry is supreme and wondrous; come and take your meal as you please.”
Then the crow descended from the tree and ate the dead man together with that jackal.
Seeing this, the seer returned to verse, saying:
"I have observed you for a long time, You who are joined together in shamelessness; I see you now, O crow and jackal, Eating the flesh of a human corpse."
"Among trees, you have the most excellent voice; yet among those who eat, you are the lowest of men.
Having heard these words, the old crow replied in verse:
"The lion and the peacock feed upon that which is eaten by all; they share in the highest food."
"A bald man has come here; what business of yours is it?
At that time, the seer, having become angry, replied with a verse:
"An old crow is the lowest among birds; a wild jackal is the meanest among beasts."
“Bian-ma wood is unfit for timber; a eunuch is the lowest among men.
A triangle in the ground is an ugliness; look at this and you will not know shame!

At that time, the old crow gave rise to a heart of great anger and went immediately to the seer’s fire altar. Looking all around the four sides, he found no spot where he could cause damage, so he defiled the center of the altar with dung, overturned the water pitcher, broke it, and then fled.
When the seer returned, he saw that the sacrificial fire altar was defiled with filth and impurity, and the water jar had been knocked over and broken.
Upon investigation, the seer realized it was the crow’s excrement that had defiled the area and its hand that had broken the jar; he then spoke this verse:
"Just like that fierce and wicked creature, Shameless and full of anger;..."
"He destroys my fire altar and breaks my water jar;
whether he be of our kind or not, do not speak with him at all.
If one must speak, let it be but little; silence is the greatest bliss."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? The seer at that time was none other than myself."
The old crow was Devadatta.
His companions were the wicked bhikṣus Kokālika and others; at that time, they spoke what was not true and spoke without shame.
At that time, the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and said:
"We pray that the World-Honored One will explain the causes and conditions in detail: for what reason has there been enmity between the World-Honored One and Devadatta since their past lives?"
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
In times past, near this seashore, there lived a saṃjīvaka bird with a single body and two heads."
There were two birds, one named Dharma and the other named Adharma.

At that time, the bird Adharma was fast asleep while the bird Dharma was awake. Seeing a sweet fruit floating down the current, it followed the stream and picked it up with its beak, thinking to itself:
"Since he is asleep, shall I now wake him so that we may eat together?"
"Or shall I eat it myself? He further thought:
"Since we share the same body, if I eat it, he too will be satisfied."
He then ate it. Later, when he had awakened from an unrighteous sleep, he perceived that phenomena were different and again smelled a fragrance; wondering at this, he asked:
"What is this fragrance?"
He replied, "I ate sweet fruit.
He asked again:
"Where is the fruit now? He replied,
"It is not right!"
"I have already finished eating while you were asleep.
He replied, "What you have done is not right; I know my own time."
