Later, while the Dharma-bird was asleep, the Adharma-bird saw a poisonous fruit floating down the current on the water; it extended its beak to pick it up and eat it, whereupon both became dazed and their minds grew frantic and confused.
At that time, Adharma immediately made this vow:
"In all future places of birth, throughout every lifetime, I shall harm you and always remain your enemy."
Then Dharma replied, "May I,
in birth after birth and life after life, always be your virtuous friend.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"What do you think? At that time, the Dharma-bird was none other than myself; the non-Dharma one was Devadatta. From that time onward, a knot of enmity first arose between us: I always maintained a mind intent on benefiting others, while Devadatta constantly harbored intentions to cause harm."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, in Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Śrīkhaṇḍa who ruled over that land. His kingdom was abundant and its people were numerous and flourishing, all attaining peace and happiness."
Near the borders of that kingdom lived the daughter of a king; he took her as his wife, and they dwelt here in joy, sporting and enjoying themselves.
Later, she became pregnant and gave birth to a daughter, who gradually grew up.
She became pregnant once more, and when the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was so dignified and handsome that all who saw him were delighted.
The kinsmen gathered together and consulted with the ministers regarding the child; because he had been born at the time of the sun’s first rising, they named him Āditya (The First).

He entrusted the child to eight nurses for his care and upbringing, as described in detail previously; thus nourished with various milks, curds, fresh butter, clarified butter (*sarpis*), and the essence of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the boy grew rapidly like a lotus in water.

Later, he was sent to school to be taught writing, calendrical calculations, and arithmetic; he became thoroughly proficient in all manner of arts and crafts, the art of riding elephants, the methods of archery with bows and arrows, and the principles of statecraft.
At a later time, the old king established him as the crown prince.
Previously, the old king had a senior consort named Dharmā, and he also had a minister named Go-vadhaka, whom the old king deeply cherished and upon whom he relied.

At that time, the king sported with his chief consort; later, she became pregnant. An astrologer divined her condition and declared that she would certainly give birth to a son who would surely kill the king and seize the throne for himself.
Later, when the king fell ill, he was treated with various medicinal herbs—roots, sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits—but the disease could not be cured.
The Great King then thought to himself:
"I must now establish the crown prince and settle him upon the royal throne; for after my death, the prince will surely kill those in my inner palace."
He further thought to himself: "What plan shall I devise?

He immediately summoned his chief minister and counselor, bestowed upon him many articles of enjoyment, provisions, and wealth, and entrusted Dharma to the minister's care, charging him with his protection, saying:
“You are my intimate minister, and Queen Dharmā is my intimate consort.

I now know for certain that I shall die; after my death, when the Crown Prince ascends to the throne, you must regard her with compassion and protect her, ensuring that Queen Dharmā is not put to death.”
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"I shall act in such a way that Queen Dharmā will certainly not be put to death.
The king then spoke this verse:
"All accumulations end in dispersal; All that is lofty must fall;
All meetings end in separation; All life ends in death."
Having spoken these verses, he immediately passed away.
After the king had been interred with various banners, flowers, and jeweled stupas, the crown prince was then established as the Great King.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Scroll 18.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Scroll 19.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree:
"At that time, having ascended the throne, the Crown Prince addressed his ministers, saying:
'You must put Dharma to death.'"
Then the minister in charge of cattle addressed the Great King, saying:
"Without conducting an investigation, for what reason do you kill Dharma when there is no cause?
She is currently pregnant; it is not yet known whether she will give birth to a boy or a girl. Only when a boy is born may she be put to death."
Then the king replied to the minister, saying, "It may be done so; you should look after it yourself.

After the month of Dharmā had passed, a son was born. At that same time and on that same day, the wife of a fisherman gave birth to a daughter. The minister took money and goods from the fisherman and exchanged the boy for the girl, and he then addressed the king, saying:
“Dharma has given birth to a daughter.
The King said, “Excellent!”
"I have attained liberation.

Later, when the fisherman had raised his son until he gradually grew up, he sent him to school to study; the boy was able to compose texts and skillfully craft literary works, so they gave him the name "Skilled in Composing Texts" (Kauśalya-lekhaka).
The minister came privately to inform Dharmā, saying,
"Your son is now highly skilled in composing literary works.
Dharmā then replied to the minister, saying:
"Now I wish to see his physical form; please use skillful means to bring him here.
The minister replied, "What further need is there to see him?"
"There is no need to look at him.

At that time, the minister, seeing that she was so deeply attached to her son, devised a stratagem: he had the son hold a fish and take on the appearance of a fish-seller, then sent him to his mother's location. His mother saw him from afar.
The physiognomist’s divination stated:
"This fisherman shall surely kill my king and take the royal throne for himself.
This report was passed from one person to another until it eventually reached the king.
Upon hearing these words, the king commanded his ministers:
"Go at once and seize the fisherman’s son; let him not escape.
When the fisherman’s son heard this news spreading from one to another, he fled toward the east to hide himself, eventually entering the house of an old woman.

When the old woman saw this, she hid herself in a secluded place, smeared her body with turmeric so that her complexion appeared like that of a corpse, and was carried by men to the deep *śmaśāna* (charnel ground). Once she was placed within the forest, she immediately rose up and fled.

Recently, there was a man gathering flowers and fruits in a forest who saw from afar this person suddenly rise from among the dead and run away; the fruit-gatherer pursued him immediately and stopped not far behind.
The king’s messenger arrived shortly thereafter and asked the fruit-gatherer:
"Have you seen a person of such appearance? The man replied:
"As soon as you see him go by this path," he said, "pursue and seize him immediately.

The fisherman’s son, frantic with fear, entered a laundryman's house. The laundryman wrapped him in heavy clothes and loaded him onto a donkey; they traveled far from inhabited areas and released him by the riverbank.
The fisherman’s son rose and surveyed the four directions; seeing no one in the distance, he immediately fled at great speed.
On the road he encountered a man who saw him running away and reported it to the king, who sent messengers back to the village to search for his whereabouts. Those who had seen him reported:
"He has run past from this direction."

At that time, pursued with great urgency by the pursuers, he again sought refuge at a tannery where boots were made; there, the members of that household each related his situation in detail, saying, "We are being coerced by the king and he intends to kill us now."
As explained in detail above, he further addressed the family members, saying:
"Out of compassion for me, please make a pair of shoes for me with the heels facing forward and the toes facing backward."
"If one follows my tracks, no one will know where I have gone.
The cobbler replied, "I have never before made such shoes."
He then spoke in verse:
"I have seen various shapes of boots, And have fashioned them according to their patterns;
Yet never before have I made boots and shoes With the heel in front and the nose at the back."
Then the cobbler did exactly as he was told.
Having put on his shoes and run out, and finding no way over the high village wall, he emerged through a drainage pipe.
At that time, the king’s messengers followed his footprints and discovered him at the shoemaker’s house.
The fisherman’s son, overcome with fear, threw himself into the water; the Dragon King, seeing him, took him into his palace.
At that time, the Great King heard word after word that the fisherman’s son had cast himself into the water and was within the dragon palace.
The King commanded his ministers:
"Summon all those in my kingdom who maintain mantras and bring them here."
When the various mantra-masters heard this, they all came to the king's presence. The king then addressed them, saying:
"Go to that dragon palace and, by means of mantras, bring the dragon here."
Having heard this, they all departed.

In another wilderness there was a yakṣa named Piṅgala, who constantly fed on fish and meat; even the trees at this yakṣa’s dwelling were withered, let alone any person remaining alive upon seeing him.

Once the Nāga King had been bound by the spells of the incantation masters, he was unable to rescue them despite his efforts; instead, using his supernatural power, he wrapped the fisherman’s son along with the incantation masters into a single bundle and carried them away to the wilderness where the yakṣas dwell, leaving them there.
The Dragon King said to the incantation masters:
"What you have done is not a good deed; that fisherman's son has been harmed by a yakṣa, and we too have been injured."
The mantra-master asked,
"What plan have you devised?
The dragon king replied:
"Because you have troubled me with these useless matters, I have been driven to desperation and have placed the fisherman's son in the wilderness, so that he may be harmed by the yakṣa."
"You will gain nothing from this either.
Then the sorcerers gradually made their way back to their own country and said to the Great King:
"We harassed and oppressed the Dragon King until he was utterly exhausted; consequently, we sent the fisherman's son into the vast wilderness to be devoured by the yakṣa Piṅgala."
Then the king said: "You are truly excellent!
Furthermore, I permit you to search for him; perhaps he has not yet died?"

At that time, while the fisherman’s son was wandering back and forth in the wilderness, the yakṣa Piṅgala was in a certain place gathered together with various fierce dogs. Seeing these dogs from afar, the fisherman’s son thought to himself:
"I am now certainly going to die."
When the dog saw that man from afar, it again commanded another dog to go after and seize him.
Upon seeing this, the man fled far away and climbed up a tree; the dog remained at the foot of the tree, and the yakṣa soon arrived following behind.
The yakṣa said: "Has he not heard that the yakṣa Piṅgala, who has the form of a human, dwells in this wilderness?
Anyone who comes and stays here shall be harmed; the time for you to descend has now arrived."
The man replied, "I have dedicated my entire life to remaining here.
Then the yakṣa stayed, wrapping his garments around the *sīna* tree, binding himself to it, and remained there.
At that time, the man wished to devise a means of escape; he immediately went beneath a tree and ran toward one direction, while the yakṣa and the dog ran together in pursuit.
As his situation became desperate, he stripped off his own clothes and threw them onto the yakṣa’s body, completely covering its form.
The pack of dogs, thinking he was that man, all seized him together to devour him, but the man managed to escape.
He then thought to himself:
"I have a maternal uncle who has gone forth as a renunciant under a seer; I should go to him now."
The place where that seer dwelt was lush and flourishing with gardens of flowers and fruits, and various birds there emitted harmonious and elegant sounds.
At that time, the fisherman’s son traveled from place to place inquiring his way until he arrived at the seer’s abode.

At that time, the great king sent messengers to search everywhere; they arrived at that very place and captured the fisherman’s son there. He immediately threw himself down into the valley, but they caught him by his topknot as he was in mid-air; his hair remained in the hands of the men while his body fell to the bottom of the valley.
At that time, the king’s messenger thought to himself,
"This man is certainly dead.
Seizing his hair, he brought it to the king's presence and reported:
"Great King! I have now finished executing the fisherman's son.
The king was greatly delighted and bestowed rewards upon the messenger.
At that time, the deity who protects the hermit came and addressed the hermit, saying:
"Your nephew is now being tormented by suffering; why do you not observe him?
The hermit replied:
"If I do not protect him, he will certainly die.
That seer was able to maintain such a vidyā-mantra, which could turn a man into a woman and a woman into a man.
The seer immediately took his nephew under his protection by means of a spell, saying: "Do not be afraid.

Having received the seer's protection, the nephew then transformed himself into a beautiful woman, whose appearance was exceptionally lovely and far surpassed that of ordinary women; he then went to Vārāṇasī and resided in the king’s garden.
When the park keeper saw the beautiful woman, a sense of wonder arose in his heart; he went quickly to the king’s presence and said to the Great King:
"There is currently a young woman of perfected beauty within the park."
Having heard these words, the king replied,
"Bring him here at once.
He was then immediately ushered into the royal palace with a grand retinue and great ceremonial dignity.

At that time, the king developed a deep attachment for that beautiful woman. Having become attached, he saw that the king was momentarily away, whereupon she transformed her female body into that of a man. He immediately donned the royal crown and commanded the minister Ananda, saying:
"Enthrone me as king."
At that time, the ministers and officials, following the grand rites, enthroned him as king.
Then the devas spoke these verses:
"If one's head is not severed, one is not harmed; Rising again, one can still perform such deeds."
"To diminish another as appropriate is not called 'harming,' such as in the case of those who harmed Prince Śvetasikha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "What do you think?"
The prince Śvetaketu who was called the First King was Devadatta; at that time, the son of the fisherman was myself.
"It was from the time of that king that this enmity began.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
In the past, there was a large village in a wilderness where two clever men lived who were experts in appraising precious gems.
Each of them sat at his own stall for trade, and they were not permitted to encroach upon one another's business.
At another time, there was a poor man who knew the value of jewels; he brought a precious vessel to where [the merchant] resided and stayed for three or five days holding this vessel.
A person from one of the shops wished to purchase the jewel, but offered an extremely low price.

At that time, the poor man was unwilling to sell it; he took it instead to another appraiser of jewels. When the latter offered a fair price, the man felt great joy and replied, "You may purchase it."
The shopkeeper replied,
"I do not have such a sum of money to buy it. He answered:
"Give me whatever you have obtained according to the day's earnings.
Having heard this, the man immediately accepted it.
Those who had received a small price then came forward and disputed with him, saying:
"I previously saw that this person was a vessel of jewels; for what reason have you now seized my merchandise?
From that point on, they became enemies.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"He who paid the lesser price was Devadatta;
he who paid the greater price at that time was my own self.
Even until the present day, such enmity and ill will have not ceased."
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, there lived a householder in a village in the wilderness. He married a woman from a family of the same clan, and they lived together in happiness. His wife became pregnant, and after the months were full, she gave birth to a son; immediately thereafter, the mother passed away."
The elder then thought to himself:
"I shall take another wife with whom I may enjoy pleasure.
Not long after he had taken a wife, a son was born, and the mother also passed away.
The elder then thought to himself:
"I too shall marry a wife, but she will die before long; therefore, I shall seek out a daughter for my eldest son.
He immediately married a girl, and they lived together in pleasure, producing many sons and grandsons.
His wife questioned her husband,
saying, "Who is this youth who follows? Her husband replied:
"This is my younger brother.
His wife then asked her husband again,
"Have you already divided the money and goods for me?"
The husband said,
"In worldly affairs, it is customary for brothers to have their shares divided.
His wife replied to her husband:
"If it should be so, you now have many children; once the property has been divided, you must kill your younger brother.

Upon hearing this, the husband—since ordinary people will commit no sin for the sake of wealth—immediately devised a plan and said to his brother, "Come now, let us go together into the mountains to gather flowers and fruits."
When they reached the mountain, the elder brother took a large stone and smashed his younger brother’s head, whereupon the latter immediately passed away.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The elder brother was none other than Devadatta."
"The younger brother was none other than my own self;
at that time, he gave rise to enmity and malice.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall further explain the causal origin of Devadatta’s enmity toward me.
In the past, there was a large village in a wilderness.
A householder took a wife from a family of the same clan, and they lived together in joy and play."
Later, she became pregnant with a child; when the months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter whose appearance was so upright and beautiful that all people loved her.
The householder said, "Should anyone come to me first to beg for her, I shall give this daughter to them."
At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa came to beg, saying,
"I am free from illness.
The householder replied:
"I have a daughter whom I shall bestow upon you as a gift.
At that time, the brahmin said, "I have calculated the seasons, days, and stars, and it is not an auspicious moment; I will not accept her now."
"I shall wait until a later time when the sun and stars are favorable, and then I will come to take it.
Having said these words, he immediately departed.
At another time, there was yet another brahmin who, for the sake of begging, returned to that house and said:
"May you be free from illness; beg for something from me.
He replied, "I have a daughter whom I shall bestow upon you as a reward."
He replied, "Previously,
when a certain brāhmaṇa came to beg, why did you not give him your daughter?
The householder answered:
"Because the constellations were unfavorable for him, he said aloud:
'I shall come to take this girl when the constellations are auspicious.
At that time, the Brahmin said:
"I accept this girl.
He asked, "Why did you not wait to examine the stars and signs for an auspicious moment before accepting her?"
Then the brahmin immediately composed a verse and accepted the girl; having received her, he returned home at once.
When those who had previously come to beg heard that someone else had arrived and taken the girl away, they went to the brahmin’s place and said to him:
"This girl was first accepted by you; why have you brought our daughter back with you?"
He replied: "You consulted the stars and found it not auspicious, so you did not take this girl;
I did not consult the constellations for auspiciousness, yet I have taken her."
At that time, that brahmin gave rise to resentment, malice, and anger; from this, he immediately conceived a heart of enmity and harm.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The brahmin who later came seeking alms and obtained the girl was none other than myself.”
"The Brahmin who previously came to observe the constellations for an auspicious moment was none other than Devadatta.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru had a great elephant named Dhanapāla, who was extremely fierce and of a violent disposition, constantly intoxicated, and daily injuring people; all the people were terrified and dared not go out their doors.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha all came to inform the king:
"The elephant Dhanapāla is extremely fierce and malicious; every day he leaves his stall and goes into the marketplace, causing harm to the multitude at the four-way crossroads."
The King should issue instructions to the elephant keepers not to allow the elephant to go out of its house every day; it must be allowed out only on alternate days.
When it is time for it to go out, bells and drums must be struck in advance to cause people to hide away.
The king replied,
"Very well," and immediately commanded his ministers to summon the elephant keeper.
He sent someone to summon him according to his command and said to him:
"The people of Rājagṛha have come to inform me that the great elephant Dhanapāla is fierce and harmful to the populace; you must stay away on alternate days."
"When it is time for them to emerge, strike the bells and drums in advance to announce that the elephants are coming out.
At that time, the elephant trainers prostrated themselves before the Great King and departed immediately according to his command.
Now, within the city of Rājagṛha, there was an elder who possessed great wealth and many enjoyments; he conceived the aspiration to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.

At that time, Devadatta heard that the elder had invited the Buddha and the assembly for a meal the following day. He immediately took hundreds of thousands of precious gems and gave them to the elephant trainer, saying:

"An elder has invited the śramaṇa Gautama and his community of śrāvakas for tomorrow. You must take the wicked elephant Dhanapāla and release him right before their faces to trample the śramaṇa Gautama."
He replied: "Noble One! It shall be done according to your command."
"Furthermore, you must ensure that the King knows we are acting according to his command.
At that time, Devadatta went to King Ajātaśatru and said: "You could not establish me as a Buddha;
rather, you have obtained this royal throne by killing your father. Now, I shall kill the Buddha and establish myself as the Omniscient One. Great King, you may have the elephant Dhanapāla released."
Then King Ajātaśatru said to Devadatta, "Have you not heard that the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, are able to tame those who are untamed? Having said this,
he departed immediately and spoke to the elephant trainer, saying:
"I have already informed the King; you may bring out the elephant tomorrow.
At that time, the elephant trainer rang a bell and made a proclamation to the people of the city:
"Tomorrow the elephant Dhanapāla will be released; you yourselves must guard against him."
When the householder heard these words, his heart was filled with grief and he lamented to himself:

"I am a man of meager merit; now that I have invited the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus to my home to provide offerings, such a thing has arisen—the release of a fierce elephant. How can I prepare the feast?"
He further thought to himself:
"I must now prepare food and drink; once they are cooked, I shall take them to the Buddha's dwelling.
That very night he prepared the food and drink, and at dawn he went to the World-Honored One’s place and said to the Buddha:
"A bell has been struck in the city of Rājagṛha to inform the people that the wicked elephant Dhanapāla is to be released;
each of you must take precautions. Let the World-Honored One not enter the city now, for the food and drink we have prepared is about to be served."
The Buddha told the householder:
"You may prepare; I am not afraid of the evil elephant Dhanapāla. I shall enter the city of Rājagṛha together with my assembly of śrāvakas."
Having heard this, the elder departed with joy; upon arriving home, he prepared the food and arranged the seats, then gazed afar toward the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha together with the assembly of bhikṣus.
The people of that time immediately released the elephant Dhanapāla.
Upon seeing the Buddha and his assembly of followers, the elephant became enraged and rushed swiftly toward the Tathāgata.
Devadatta, together with King Ajātaśatru, ascended to the top of a high tower and gazed from afar at the wicked elephant, intending for it to trample the śramaṇa Gautama.
Devadatta was filled with great joy and immediately spoke this verse:
"I see the One of Ten Powers Trampled by the might of an elephant;
The Śrāvaka, the son of the Śākyas— Today he shall be utterly extinguished."

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested five lions with his right hand. Upon seeing the lions, the elephant was immediately seized with panic and fear, losing its excrement as it fled in haste.
The World-Honored One again emitted a great fire such that all directions were blazing with heat; yet, beneath the feet where the Buddha sat, it was cool and refreshing.
As the wicked elephant Dhanapāla wandered here and there, he encountered only the scorching fire everywhere, while the place where the World-Honored One stayed remained pure, cool, and refreshing.
When they saw the wicked elephant, all the śrāvakas scattered and fled far away; only Ānanda alone did not leave the Buddha’s side.

As the elephant’s intoxication subsided and it became weak, it approached the place where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One then used his fearless hand—adorned with the hundred jewels and marked by the thousand-spoked wheel—to stroke the elephant’s head and bestow the gift of fearlessness, immediately reciting this verse:
“Do not take pleasure in the state of an elephant; The realm of elephants is an evil destination.”
Do not harm others, and you shall attain the path of the noble ones.
Because of the karmic actions of your previous lives, you were born in the evil realms;
you took pleasure in harming sentient beings.
After dying from this life, where will you be reborn?
And in what realm will you dwell?
O Bhadrapāla, listen well!
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas are without self;
tranquility is nirvāṇa"—in this, faith has arisen in my mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the house of the elder and sat upon the prepared seat; the elephant Dhanapāla followed behind the Buddha.
The Buddha was staying at the house of an elder, and his elephant stood outside the gate. Because it could not see the Buddha, it sought to push through the door, which caused the house to collapse.
The Buddha, by means of his supernatural power, transformed the residence into crystal, so that the interior and exterior reflected one another, allowing the elephant to see the Buddha from afar.

When the World-Honored One had finished his meal and recited the verses on giving, he rose from his seat and departed; the elephant followed behind the Buddha, and the minister of that kingdom reported all that had occurred to the Great King as previously described.
When the King heard of this matter, he informed Devadatta:
"You have caused me great harm.
Once that elephant has departed, the kings of neighboring realms who hear of it will surely rise up as enemies; you have acted most improperly."
When Devadatta had been thus rebuked, he remained silent.
The King commanded his ministers, saying:
"Once the Buddha has departed, you must immediately close the city gates; do not allow the elephant to go outside the city, nor let it follow after the Buddha."
The minister, following the royal decree, informed the gatekeepers of the city and spoke to the elephant trainers:
"Bind and seize the elephant; do not allow it to follow behind the Buddha."
Following these instructions, he was about to seize the elephant.

When the elephant saw the Buddha leaving the city and could not see the World-Honored One before him, it kicked its own trunk with its foot; its breath was cut off, and it died in a state of fainting, to be reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
According to the laws of heaven, those who are about to be born in the heavens give rise to three kinds of thoughts:
"From where did I pass away?
Where have I been born?"
What is the karmic retribution for this?
One should observe oneself: having died from among elephants, one has been born here among the pure Four Great Kings.
In a previous life, one gave rise to a heart of joy toward the Buddha.
"It would be most improper for me to remain here in pleasure and not go to the presence of the Tathāgata.
I must first go to the presence of the Tathāgata, surrounded by all these devas."
That elephant was reborn in heaven, his body adorned with a hundred jewels, its pure form translucent both within and without.
That very night, he filled a robe-sack with various wonderful flowers and went to the Bamboo Grove where the Tathāgata resided; his radiance shone everywhere, surpassing that of the sun by day.

At that time, they scattered various precious flowers over the Buddha’s body and sat before him to listen to his teaching of the Dharma; the World-Honored One, observing them, taught the Dharma according to what each desired to hear.

Having heard this, that deity used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the mountain of twenty kinds of afflictions consisting of views of self, and immediately realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Having realized the fruit, his heart was filled with great joy, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Neither father nor mother can perform such a deed; neither king nor deity can do it; neither kinsman nor friend can do it; nor can past spirits, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas dry up the oceans of blood.

“Only the Buddha can sever the ocean of my suffering and affliction, transcend the mountains of defilement, close the gates to the evil realms, and establish me in the supreme and wondrous state of humans and devas.
He then spoke in verse:
“Because the Buddha has closed the gates to the evil realms, The three miserable paths are filled with much harm;”
Now, having been granted the opening of the path for humans and devas, I have further realized the subtle and wondrous city of nirvāṇa.
Because the Buddha has severed all evil karma, my eyes, afflicted by cataracts, have attained purity;
being able to realize the noble path of quiescent extinction, I have transcended the realm of manifold sufferings within the flow of existence.
Worthy of offerings from all gods and humans, Able to eliminate the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
Not encountered throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, The fruit of this merit is now seen as you behold the Buddha.
I pay homage to the Great Master, offering him jeweled necklaces;
prostrating at the Buddha’s feet with a joyful heart, I circumambulate him three times to the right and, wishing to return, I leap upward to the celestial palace.

At that time, those devas—like merchants who have gained profit, like farmers who have obtained a bountiful harvest, like warriors who have emerged victorious in battle, or like patients who have recovered from illness—having presented their offerings to him, returned with him to the heavens.

At that time, there were bhikṣus in the grove who, during the first watch of the night, were reciting scriptures and walking in meditation. Seeing a great radiance illuminating the forest and wilds, they were struck with wonder and astonishment; they approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"What was the cause and condition that led Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas to come to the World-Honored One’s presence during the latter part of last night?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It was not Śakra, Brahmā, or the various devas who came to my place."
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!
Have you ever seen the great elephant Dhanapāla?
He was so fierce and unruly that he rushed toward me, intending to kill me.
At that time, the bhikṣus all said to the Buddha,
“We have all seen it. The Buddha said:
"I have already instructed him; because he conceived right faith in me and gave rise to joy, he immediately passed away and was reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings."
That night he came to where I was, and for his sake I preached the Dharma until he attained the realization of the Truths; he then returned to his own palace.
The bhikṣus were filled with doubt, and since only the Buddha could resolve it, they said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One! [What was the cause of this?]”
What karmic deeds did that elephant Dhanapāla commit to fall into the realm of animals?
Furthermore, what deeds did he perform to be reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings and to realize the Truths?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That elephant Dhanapāla now carries upon himself the karmic retribution he previously accumulated; like a violent torrent, it must inevitably be experienced."
"This wealth-protector has created this karma for himself and shall experience its results himself; it is not experienced by another.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

"The karma one creates is not received by earth, water, fire, or wind; nor is it received by the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), or elements (dhātus), whether they be wholesome or unwholesome deeds."
And he spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution is received by oneself."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In a past age, during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Kāśyapa, who was endowed with the ten titles, and he resided at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī."

At that time, this elephant left the household life within that Dharma; although his observance of the precepts was not firm, nor did he hold them in high esteem, and there were deficiencies therein, he constantly provided the four requisites to the Sangha and cultivated roots of goodness, so that in every place where he was born, food and drink were abundant.
Upon seeing my True Dharma, his heart was filled with joy; he then passed away and was reborn in the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings.

Furthermore, because he had previously gone forth as a monk during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha and recited the teachings on the Four Noble Truths, Dependent Origination, the Aggregates, the Bases, and so forth, he accumulated roots of goodness through those three types of action and has now attained birth in the heavens. Moreover, having encountered me, he has realized the True Reality.
"In this way, monks!
If one cultivates white karma and so forth, it is as explained at length elsewhere.
At that time, the monks were filled with doubt; since the Buddha is able to sever doubts, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When that intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla was about to come and harm the Buddha, why did all the śrāvaka assembly flee far away, while Ānanda alone did not leave the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said: "Listen attentively! It was not only now;
in the distant past, by the banks of the Anavatapta River, there was a king of geese named Dhṛtarāṣṭra who had two sons."
One was named Pūrṇa and the other was named Pūrṇamukha; Pūrṇa was the elder son and Pūrṇamukha was the younger son.
As for the one named Pūrṇa, his nature and conduct were extremely fierce and cruel; he constantly practiced deception and violence, tormenting and disturbing all the other geese in various ways.
At that time, the geese and others would come regularly to inform the goose king:
"Your son pecks and strikes me.
The goose king then thought to himself:

"Since he is coarse, wicked, and of a fierce nature, if he is established in the position of crown prince, he will surely harm and kill all the geese after my death; I must now employ a skillful means."
He then summoned his two sons, Pūrṇa and Pūrṇamukha, and said to them:
"If you can go to the various ponds where the geese are and investigate, whoever returns first shall be granted the royal throne by me."
At that time, the two goose princes, vying with one another, each led five hundred geese to travel in various directions, wandering east and west to survey the waters of the ponds.
As the geese gradually made their way to Vārāṇasī, there lived at that time a king named Brahmadatta who was duly established on the throne; his kingdom was prosperous, peaceful, and abundant.

Not far from the city was a most excellent pond of exquisite flowers with clear, flowing water, its surface covered by lotuses of various colors; on all four sides of the pond were a thousand flowering fruit trees, and various kinds of birds gathered there, soaring and perching.

At that time, the goose prince named Pūrṇa, together with a flock of five hundred geese, descended into that pond; free from fear, they played and rejoiced, while Pūrṇa remained in the midst of the five hundred geese in the sky.
At that time, one goose said to Pūrṇamukha,
"Shall we descend into this pond? He replied:
"I shall first go to Lake Anavatapta to succeed to the royal throne, and only thereafter may I come here to sport.
He then immediately went swiftly to Lake Anavatapta and succeeded to the royal throne, returning to the lake at Vārāṇasī to sport.
At that time, the people by the pond, seeing the swan playing with such upright dignity and fearlessness, were all struck with wonder and astonishment, saying:
"From where has this king of swans, whom all people delight to behold, come to this pond?"
"The body is adorned, and the various birds of that pond have no equal; all people love them, and they dwell and sport in the pond without fear.
When the people of Vārāṇasī heard this, they all came together and went to the edge of the pond to gaze upon and observe them as they stood there.
The ministers and counselors of that kingdom said to the Great King:

"We do not know from what direction this king of geese of exquisite color has come, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of geese, staying in that pond with a body of such upright beauty that it surpasses all other birds; people can never look upon him enough, and he dwells there without fear."
Then the king said to his ministers, "If it must be so, summon the hunters.
Following the command, the ministers immediately summoned them and assembled them; the king spoke:
"I have heard that an exceptionally wondrous king of geese has arrived in my pond, one whom people delight to behold; I do not know from which direction he came.
You should employ skillful means to surround him on all four sides and bind him, bringing him here without causing injury to his body or its limbs and joints, so that he may be presented to me."
The hunter followed these instructions and departed. Having skillfully employed various means to slowly bind them, the king of the geese, knowing they could not escape, addressed the flock:
"All of you, go quickly to Lake Anavatapta."
The flock of five hundred geese all fled and dispersed, leaving only a single goose remaining, standing there with tears streaming down its face.
When the hunter saw that this one goose was not bound and was staying by the side of the goose king weeping, he was struck with wonder and astonishment. He said to it:
"I feared the King’s command and bound your body; do not weep, for I shall not kill you."

He then took this king of geese to the presence of the King of Vārāṇasī; although one of the geese by his side was not bound, out of mutual affection he also followed after him until they arrived before the king.
The king asked the hunter,
"Since the goose was not tied, by what means did it come here?
The hunter replied to the Great King:
"I am not bound; they have come here of their own accord.
The king, struck with wonder and astonishment, said to the hunters:
"As for those who followed after, it is certain that they are a husband and wife who love one another and will not be parted."
"Release this king of geese and go with him; do not allow anyone to harm him.
The hunter addressed the Great King, saying:
"I fear that others might harm the king of geese. May Your Majesty issue a decree to the ministers and inform all the people that they must not harm this king of geese."
At that time, the king immediately summoned his ministers and said:
"You should now go to the city walls of Vārāṇasī, beat the drums, and proclaim this edict:
'From this day forward, no person within the kingdom shall harm or injure any bird.'"
The minister immediately issued a general proclamation as commanded.
"O Bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts:
the king whose face was full at that time was none other than myself."
He who followed the goose was none other than Ānanda.
Those five hundred flocks of geese were the five hundred bhikṣus of the present time.
At that time among the geese, they all fled and dispersed, yet only Ānanda did not abandon him.
"At this time as well, it was just the same: while the assembly all fled and dispersed, Ānanda did not abandon me.
Then the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall relate to you once more the matter of how the five hundred bhikṣus fled and dispersed, while Ānanda did not abandon me."
Listen attentively!
In the distant past, there was a king named Aṭa who reigned over Vārāṇasī. His kingdom was prosperous, abundant, and peaceful;
it possessed five hundred ministers whose majesty and virtue were such that the kings of neighboring realms all came to pay him homage.
At that time, there was a man coming from South India named Daṇḍīghaṭa; this single man could match a thousand men in combat.
He arrived at the residence of the ministers, who immediately escorted him to see the king and addressed the Great King, saying:
"We have heard of Your Majesty’s majestic virtue. This one man, having already fought, can match a thousand; Your Majesty should accept him."
At that time, the king immediately bestowed upon him wealth and goods for his use.

Later, there was a king in a neighboring territory whose army and cavalry gradually increased in number and became powerful and valiant; he then assembled the fourfold forces of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and came to press upon Aṭa to engage in battle with him.

King Aṭṭha also set out with his fourfold army to engage in battle; the king of the foreign realm was defeated in the fray, scattered, and fled, each returning to their own place before gathering together once more.
He secretly dispatched one man to consult with the five hundred ministers, saying:
"I shall engage in battle once more; you must not fight as my adversaries.
When I obtain the throne, I will bestow upon you all wealth and treasures ten thousand times greater than those given to Aṭha."
The five hundred ministers all changed their minds and became secretly aligned with the king of the foreign realm.

Then the king again came forth with his fourfold army to engage in battle, and Aṭa likewise led his four kinds of troops to confront the enemy; however, those five hundred ministers, being sympathetic with the foreign king, did not fight.
The one who had come from South India, together with King Aṭṭha, was deeply distressed in heart; that man then spoke in verse:
"All friends have been abandoned, Having attended upon you for a long time;
Only this man with the water-jar and staff Does not leave the Great King's side."
"Then that valiant man killed those five hundred ministers.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!
The King Aṭha of that time was none other than myself.
That valiant warrior who could oppose a thousand men was Ānanda.
Those five hundred ministers were these very same five hundred bhikṣus of the present time.
"Those five hundred bhikṣus have all fled and dispersed, leaving me; only Ānanda has not abandoned me.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
Ānanda, you have not abandoned my cause.
Long ago in the past, there was a bodhisattva dwelling among those of indeterminate destiny who, in a certain mountain region, took birth in the body of a lion, the king of beasts.
At that time, there were five hundred jackals who constantly followed him to seek out leftover scraps of food, dwelling together with him in the mountains.
Whenever the lion killed an insect or beast, he would eat the finest portions of its flesh and blood before departing.
Those who remained were scavenged by jackals, who stayed there for a long time.

Later, while that lion king was searching for prey at night, he fell into a dry well in the darkness without realizing it. Among those five hundred jackals, one jackal saw the lion fallen into the well and, remaining by the well's edge, contemplated a means, thinking:
"What plan can I devise to rescue the lion and enable him to emerge from the well?"
The other jackals, seeing the herd of five hundred deer, followed after them.

One of those jackals was wandering east and west near the well when he saw a mound of earth; he pushed the earth with his foot and cast it into the well until the well was gradually filled and the lion was able to escape.
At that time, the devas in the midst of the sky spoke these verses:
"One must act as a friend to all, Whether they be weak or strong;
I saw a jackal Rescue a lion from a well."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The lion at that time was myself; the jackal was Ānanda."
The four hundred and ninety-nine jackals of former times were none other than these four hundred and ninety-nine bhikṣus;
those four hundred and ninety-nine bhikṣus abandoned me, while Ānanda alone did not abandon me but remained.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
In times past, there was a bodhisattva in the state of indeterminate destiny who, at that time and in that place, was the king of five hundred deer."
There was a hunter who, wishing to harm a herd of deer, set snares, enclosures, nets, and ropes by the riverbank, calculating his means of capture.
At that time, the deer approached that place with hearts free from fear; however, as the leader of the deer went before them, he was subsequently bound.
Once they saw him bound, all the deer fled and scattered.
There was one doe, however, who remained by the king’s side and would not abandon him.
At that time, the deer king wished to sever his tether but could not break it. Seeing that the deer king was unable to cut the rope, the doe then spoke this verse:
“O Great and Majestic Deer King, you should quickly and earnestly untie yourself;
those who set the snares and traps—the hunters—are now about to arrive.”
At that time, the Deer King replied with a verse in gāthā:
"What plan can I devise now?
There is no one who can sever this cord; the snare-cord is exceedingly firm and strong, binding my feet so it pierces to the bone."

At that time, the hunter, holding a bow and arrow and wearing a *kāṣāya* robe, arrived at the place where the deer were. When the mother deer saw the hunter intending to harm the king of the deer, she [acted].
Then the doe approached the deer king and spoke in verse:
“O deer king of great majesty, You should quickly and earnestly release me;
The hunter who set this snare Is now about to arrive.”
At that time, the deer king replied in verse:
"What plan can I devise now?
There is none who can sever this cord; the snare is exceedingly firm and strong, binding my feet so that it pierces to the bone."
At that time, the doe, her heart filled with trepidation, approached the hunter and spoke this verse:
"You are a great hunter; You ought to set aside your bow and arrows.
Take your knife and kill me first, And only then kill the king of deer."
At that time, having heard these words, the hunter was greatly astonished and asked the mother deer,
"To what relative of yours does this deer belong?"
The doe replied, "He is my husband.
Having heard these words, the hunter spoke this verse in response to her:
"I shall not harm you now, nor shall I kill the deer king;
I will cause you both to love one another deeply once more, so that husband and wife may be reunited."
At that time, the doe spoke in verse:
"Just as I have shared joy with my husband, And shall see my beloved lord again with deep affection;
So may you, together with all your kinsmen, Always cherish one another and share in constant joy."
At that time, having heard these words, the hunter was greatly astonished and marveled at their rarity; he then released the deer king, who departed together with the doe.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Was that king of the deer anyone other than [myself]?"
I am that very person. Her mother, the doe, was Ānanda.
The four hundred and ninety-nine deer were these four hundred and ninety-nine bhikṣus.
"Those four hundred and ninety-nine bhikṣus abandoned me and departed; only Ānanda did not forsake me but remained.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt, and only the World-Honored One could sever their uncertainties:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
"You should observe Devadatta: for the sake of gain and offerings, he has brought defilement upon himself and harmed his own body.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only in this present life that Devadatta has harmed his own body because of his greed for foul and evil gains and offerings."
Listen attentively!

In the distant past, there was a great lotus pond on a mountain. At that time, a large elephant lived by the side of the pond, while on another side of the pond lived a wild jackal whose body was foul-smelling and filthy.
At that time, the elephant emerged from the pond after drinking water, and a jackal wished to go to the edge of the pond to drink as well.
The jackal said to the elephant:
"Your Honor, you should yield the path; if you do not, we shall fight each other."
The elephant thought to himself:

"This pitiable creature is supremely foul and filthy. If I were to harm it by treading on it with my feet, or with my trunk, or with my tusks, all such actions would be defiled and loathsome. I shall now first defile this filthy object myself before I may harm it."
And he spoke in verse:
"It is not enough to trample you, nor shall I use my snout or tusks;
I shall kill you with a foul substance—for one should slay the foul with the foul."
Then the elephant thought again:
"If I walk toward one side, he will surely follow after me.
He then quickly went toward one side.
The jackal then thought to himself:
"I have intimidated him with my words, and he has retreated in fear.

He immediately pursued the elephant from behind; when the elephant saw that the jackal was close at hand, it exerted its utmost effort to discharge excrement, which struck the jackal, and he died instantly.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do not harbor other thoughts!
At that time, that jackal was none other than Devadatta.”
"Just as one was harmed by impure substances in the past, so too is one harmed now by impure and evil gains.
At that time, the bhikṣus were all filled with doubt; since only the Buddha could sever it, they came before him and said:
"If one can rely upon the Buddha's teachings, all shall cross over the hardships and sufferings of birth and death."
"If one follows the teachings of Devadatta, one will fall into suffering.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 19. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃghabheda-vastu*.
Fascicle Twenty.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“In the past, those who relied upon my teaching all managed to escape great suffering and hardship;
those who relied upon Devadatta all remained amidst suffering and hardship.”
Listen attentively!

Long ago, in a wilderness, there was a village nearby. The trees, flowers, and fruits of that village were lush and abundant. Nearby lived two groups of monkeys, each consisting of five hundred members, and each had its own monkey king.
One of those kings dreamed that five hundred monkeys threw these two kings into a cauldron of boiling oil.
Within this dream, he was struck with great terror, the hair on his body stood on end, and he immediately awoke from the dream.
He summoned the troop of monkeys and immediately recounted this dream, saying:
"Is this dream that I have just seen not an ill omen?
We must abandon this dwelling place where we reside and move elsewhere."
The troop of monkeys replied, "As the Great King has said, we must flee and leave this place.
The Bodhisattva possesses great majesty and virtue; if he sees such a dream, it will surely come true."
The king immediately summoned the second king and said to him:
"I have just had such a dream that we must go to dwell in another place.
The king found this difficult to believe and said:
"Can one immediately place trust in whatever is seen in a dream?
If you wish to go, go as you please.
As for me, I have attained liberation within this realm; I shall never depart."
The king, knowing that this would be difficult for them to believe, led his own retinue of five hundred monkeys and immediately moved elsewhere.
Later, in that village, there was a lowly maidservant parching barley when a sheep came to her side, wishing to eat the grain.
The maidservant immediately set fire to wood and beat the sheep; once the fire caught on its body and it was in urgent distress from the burning, it ran into the royal elephant stable.

Inside the stable there was much fodder and straw; as the sheep shook its body, the fire fell onto the grass, setting the vegetation ablaze and burning the elephants. The elephant keepers then informed the king.
Then the king immediately summoned the physician and said, "The elephants have been burned; what medical treatment should you urgently apply?
At that time, the physician thought to himself:
"Yesterday, a troop of monkeys ravaged my fields; now that I have gained the opportunity, I must avenge this grievance.
He said to the Great King, "This elephant has been burned; it can only be cured by applying monkey fat to its body."
At that time, the Great King commanded his ministers:
"You must quickly seek out monkey fat.
Following these orders, the ministers immediately summoned the hunters.
"You all must quickly seek out a monkey and bring it here.
Following these orders, the hunters went in all directions to capture monkeys.
That King of Monkeys, who was difficult to deceive, along with his troop of five hundred monkeys, were all bound and brought before the king.
Because that physician harbored long-standing resentment, he threw those monkeys alive into a cauldron of boiling oil.
At that moment, the devas spoke these verses from the sky:
"One should not dwell near an enemy, Whether in a city, a village, or the wilderness; Even if one has no other recourse, One must avoid such a person."
"The maidservant was angry that the sheep ate the barley, and the monkeys and others were melted away.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Do not harbor other thoughts!
[They were yourselves in those lives]."
The one who saw the dream of the monkey king at that time was none other than myself.
The monkey king who was difficult to believe was Devadatta.
As for the remaining monkeys who followed my words, they were spared from this fear of fire.
Those who followed the words of Devadatta all encountered extreme suffering;
whereas those who follow my words at this time shall all attain liberation from the great terrors of birth and death.
Those who accepted Devadatta’s instructions all encountered suffering and hardship.
Furthermore, all those who acted in accordance with my own wishes attained peace and were far removed from suffering and hardship.
Those who follow the will of Devadatta shall all encounter suffering and hardship.
"Listen attentively, you bhikṣus!
In times long past, in a certain distant land, there were two monkey kings, each with a retinue of five hundred."
Among them was a monkey king who, together with his retinue of five hundred, was traveling through the human world when he arrived at a certain village.
In that village there was a *kapi-kacchu* tree, its fruits flourishing and abundant.
At that time, the troop of monkeys saw this fruit tree and said to the monkey king:
"The fruit on this tree is so abundant that its branches are about to break.
We have come from afar and are exhausted; let us take and eat its fruit."
At that time, having seen this tree, the monkey king spoke a verse:
"This tree is near a village; The boys do not eat its fruit.
You should know this: This fruit is not fit for eating."
Having spoken these verses, the monkeys immediately departed.
The second monkey king, also accompanied by five hundred followers, was wandering through the human world and gradually arrived at this village.
These monkeys also entered the village, where fruits grew in great abundance;
they then said to the monkey king, "We are exhausted from traveling the road; we wish to eat these fruits and depart in safety."
The monkey king said,
"Excellent! Thereupon,
the five hundred monkeys immediately ate the fruit.
At that time, all the fruits eaten by the monkeys caused them to die.
O bhikṣus, do not entertain other thoughts!
That monkey king who did not eat the fruit was none other than myself.
The second monkey king was Devadatta. Those who followed my will reached safety and were delivered from suffering and hardship;
those who followed Devadatta’s will all encountered suffering and hardship.
At this time, those sentient beings who follow my words shall attain liberation from within saṃsāra;
whereas those who accept the instructions of Devadatta will all encounter suffering and hardship.
At that time, Devadatta attempted to strike the World-Honored One with a stone.
Thereupon, all the brahmins and householders, harboring intense anger, cried out:
"We shall kill Devadatta right now!"
Among them was one who was a friend of Devadatta; he immediately informed Devadatta.
Upon hearing this, Devadatta went to dwell in meditative concentration beneath a tree in a secluded grove.
At that time, the brahmins, householders, and others, seeing Devadatta dwelling in meditative concentration beneath a tree, said to one another:
"You should know that this Devadatta possesses great majestic power; how could we possibly kill him?"
"How is it that I have now brought about such an evil matter?
We should quickly depart from one another.
At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that Devadatta remained in such a posture of dignified demeanor, the brahmins and householders, though momentarily provoked to anger, did not kill him.
All these bhikṣus were filled with doubt; since only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, could sever their uncertainty, they informed the Buddha of the circumstances:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
Please observe how Devadatta commits unrighteous acts while presenting himself to the multitude as one who practices wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It was not only in this life that Devadatta committed such unrighteous acts while appearing to manifest the True Dharma, deceiving mice and causing them to lose their lives."
Listen attentively!
I shall speak for you.
In times past, in a certain region, there was a king of mice who had five hundred mice as his retinue.
There was a kitten named Jvālana. When this cat was young, it killed every mouse it encountered.
Later, as it grew old and decrepit, it thought to itself:
"In my youth, my physical strength was robust; I would seize mice with my power and eat them."
"I am now old and decrepit; my strength and vigor are so slight that I cannot catch them. What skillful means can I employ to capture these mice?

Having had this thought, he surveyed the ground and saw a mouse king with five hundred mice as his retinue dwelling in that place. He then went to the mouse hole and feigned the practice of seated meditation.
At that time, a group of mice emerged from their burrows and wandered about, where they saw an old cat sitting peacefully in meditation.
One of the mice asked, "Uncle!
What are you doing now?"
The old cat replied, "In my youth, when my strength was at its peak, I committed immeasurable sins; now I wish to cultivate merit to eliminate those past transgressions.
Upon hearing these words, the assembly of mice all gave rise to wholesome thoughts.
"This old cat is now practicing wholesome dharmas.
Having said this, they and the other mice circumambulated the old cat three times to the right and then entered their burrows.
The old cat took the very last one each time to eat; before long, the number of mice gradually diminished.
Having seen this, the mouse king thought to himself:
"The number of us mice is gradually diminishing, while that old cat’s strength and vigor are flourishing; there must surely be a reason for this."
The rat king immediately observed and saw mouse fur and bones within the old cat's excrement.
He then knew in his heart:
"The old cat has eaten my rats and others; I shall now closely observe the moment she catches a rat."
Having formed this thought, he immediately looked at the old cat within the cave and saw that the old cat was seizing and eating the very last mouse.
Upon seeing this, the Mouse King stood back at a distance and spoke this verse:
"The old cat’s body grows increasingly fat, While the multitude of mice gradually diminishes."
You eat the stalks, the grain, the roots, and the leaves; dung, hair, and bones are not for you.
That you now practice meditation is not called "good"; for the sake of profit, you falsely pose as one who practices virtue.
May you dwell in health and safety; meanwhile, my entire colony of mice has been devoured by you.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!
That old cat with the flaming tail at that time was Devadatta; having committed unrighteous deeds, he manifested the practice of virtue before the multitude."
All these bhikṣus were filled with doubt, for only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can sever such doubts:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!
Please examine this with careful reflection: those who follow the instructions of the World-Honored One will safely attain liberation from birth and death."
"Those who comply with Devadatta’s instructions will encounter great suffering and hardship.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know that it is not only in this present life that those who follow my instructions attain liberation from birth and death; it was also thus in the past."
"Listen attentively, you bhikṣus!
Listen attentively!
I shall speak for your sake."

In the distant past, there were two guides, each leading five hundred caravans through a desert. Some obtained water and grass, while others did not; after several days had passed, the oxen and calves suffered extreme hardship.
Later, they saw a certain place where the grass was lush and green and many springs welled up.
At that time, the merchants led their oxen and calves to the water and grass; then the merchants entered the water to bathe and gave drink to the oxen and calves.
Having drunk the water, they rested and stayed there.
Among the herd of five hundred cows was a bull king who addressed the other cattle, saying:
"The green grass in this region is lush and abundant, and there are excellent bathing springs; let us stay here and feed and drink as we please."
"If there is a merchant who has prepared his carriage for me, I must lie on the ground and no longer accept his service.
The second bull king said to the herd of oxen, "You all should know!"

These merchants possess great strength and are capable of taming even the most difficult creatures; it would be appropriate to proceed as before, transporting goods by means of carriages in accordance with human custom, lest there be further harm later on.
Upon hearing these words, the great bull king immediately grew angry with the second bull king and said:
"What you have said is based on your former acceptance of being driven by others; this matter is contrary to the Dharma."
"How can there be a human being who can see his own back?
He further addressed the herd of oxen, saying:
"You should all follow my instructions; you need not go apart."
At that time, the merchants wished to yoke the oxen; when those oxen saw the merchants intending to seize them, they immediately became enraged, pawing the ground and tearing at it with their hooves.
Upon seeing this, the merchants each took up clubs and struck them until their hides were pierced and bleeding, then forced them to pull the carts.
The other oxen that were pulling the cart departed without being beaten at all.
At that time, the devas in the sky spoke these verses:
“Now observe this wicked bull-king, Who speaks falsehoods and performs evil deeds;”
Due to this, the cattle suffer; their bodies bleed from hunger and thirst.
Yet, observing the noble Bull-King, who issues pure and harmonious instruction, the various classes of cattle thereby cross the perilous path with bodies plump and full.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor any other thoughts; that most excellent bull-king who brought forth the true teaching was none other than myself."
At that time, the bull king who issued wicked commands, causing those cattle in the herd to encounter suffering and hardship, was Devadatta.
In the past, all those who were able to receive my instructions attained peace and security, and were able to cross over dangerous, painful, and perilous places.
All those who were able to accept the teachings of Devadatta encountered such hardships and calamities.

This was not only in the past; even now, all those who can follow my right view and receive my instruction shall attain peace and security, crossing over the great ocean of birth, death, and afflictions.
"If one follows the wrong views and evil conduct of Devadatta, one will constantly encounter such great hardships and calamities as these.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt.
Only the Buddha can sever it; therefore, he informed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will observe this Devadatta, who is himself ignorant and whose followers are likewise ignorant."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Devadatta was not only foolish in this present life; he was so in the past as well.
Listen attentively!"
I shall explain this for you.
In the distant past, there was a secluded forest glade where a troop of monkeys lived and roamed.
Once, as the monkeys were wandering about, they gradually came upon a well; looking down into the bottom of the well, they beheld the reflection of the moon.
Having seen the moon, they went to the place where the monkey king was and said:
"Great King, you should know!
The moon has been seen fallen into a well; we should now go quickly to pull it out and restore it to its former position."
All the monkeys praised him, saying,
"Excellent! and then they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"How can we employ a skillful means to pull out the moon?
Some among them said, "There is no need for further schemes; let us join our arms together to form a rope and pull it out."

At that time, one monkey was perched on a branch of a tree above the well; the others followed one after another, joining hands in succession. As the monkeys became numerous, the branch of the tree bent low, on the verge of breaking.

Then, the one who was lowest down and nearest the water stirred the water to search for the moon; because the water became turbid, the moon no longer appeared, his tree branch broke, and he fell into the water all at once, drowning to his death.
At that time, various devas spoke in verse, saying:
"These foolish monkeys, Following their deluded leader, Have all fallen into the well;
In their attempt to rescue the moon, they have drowned."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The monkey king of the past was none other than Devadatta.
Because he was deluded by his own ignorance in the past, he took those who were ignorant as his retinue; even now, he has ignorant ones as his retinue."

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha. Because there was a famine in the world and almsfood was difficult to obtain, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I wish to remain in secluded retreat for three months; no one at all shall come to see me, except for those who bring food and on the days of the *poṣadha* ceremony."
"The great assembly should also collectively establish clear regulations.
At that time, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were observing the three-month rains retreat within the Southern Mountains.
At that time, Devadatta also provided food, drink, and various services for three months during the summer retreat.
When the three months were complete, Devadatta extensively expounded the sublime Dharma to the great assembly, saying:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
When the śramaṇa Gautama frequently teaches the Dharma, he praises those who dwell in mountain solitude, free from all afflictions, as attaining liberation most swiftly and most rapidly:

first, those who beg for food; second, those who wear rag-robes; third, those who possess only the three robes; and fourth, those who sit in the open air—it is these four types of persons who remove all dust and defilement and realize liberation.
"If there are those who do not delight in these four kinds of cultivation of the path, nor delight in liberation, they ought to receive a tally and depart from the assembly.
Having spoken these words, at that time the great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus each received a tally and followed Devadatta out of the assembly, proceeding as far as the entrance of the gate.
When Rāhula saw this, he said to the five hundred bhikṣus,
"Why have you abandoned the Tathāgata and followed after this evil faction?
The bhikṣus replied to Rāhula:
“During our three-month rains retreat, we were afflicted by hunger.
We relied upon Devadatta for our food and other necessities;
had he not provided for us, we would all have perished.”

When Devadatta caused a schism in the Saṃgha, the great earth shook violently; meteors flashed and fires blazed in the four directions. All the devas beat their drums with a thunderous roar and cried out in a loud voice: "From this day forward, the path to Nirvāṇa shall cease;

there will be no one who attains the fruits of the Path, no one whose outflows (āsravas) are exhausted, and no one who recites the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma. Minds shall no longer be attached to the forest hermitages (araṇya), nor shall there be any who cultivate the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor any who cultivate Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Humans and devas alike shall fall into chaos."
"In this trichiliocosm, the Wheel of Dharma does not turn; sentient beings follow the person rather than the Dharma.

When Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw this marvel, they composed their minds and entered meditative concentration. There, they beheld Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha and said to one another, "We ought to go and extinguish these disputes and seek to bring about harmony."

When the three months had passed and his three robes were complete, he went to where the World-Honored One was. Traveling by stages, he arrived at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha; having set down his three robes and washed his feet, he proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
Seeing Rāhula standing outside the gate, he said to Śāriputra:
"Upādhyāya, do you know? Devadatta has already caused a schism in the Saṃgha."
Śāriputra said, "I have already understood this, which is why I have come; do not grieve, for I shall bring about reconciliation.
He then entered the assembly, prostrated himself before the World-Honored One, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that the wicked Devadatta has already caused a schism in the Saṃgha, and I wish to bring about reconciliation.
I wonder, World-Honored One, will you graciously grant me your permission?
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately uttered this praise:
“Excellent, excellent!
If one can bring about such harmony within the Saṃgha, the merit obtained shall be immeasurable.
At that time, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having reported this matter and taken their leave of the World-Honored One, went to the Southern Mountains to visit Devadatta.
At that time, Devadatta assumed the majestic demeanor of a Buddha and preached the Dharma to the assembly; Kokālika sat on his right side, and Khaṇḍadravya sat on his left.
At that time, Devadatta saw from afar that the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were approaching, and he thought to himself:
"I have already attained the state of an omniscient one, yet these venerable ones enter into my assembly."
He immediately dispatched his attendants to have them rise, and had Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana sit on either side.
At that time, Kokālika and Khaṇḍadravya, having been forcibly moved from their seats, felt resentment in their hearts and reflected to themselves:
"We have committed a great transgression by assisting in the schism of the Saṅgha; if we do not rise, we fear being struck in anger."
He then immediately moved his seat and had Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra sit on either side of him.
Devadatta said to Śāriputra, "I now have a backache;
you shall expound the sublime Dharma for the great assembly."
At that time, Śāriputra accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Having spoken these words, Devadatta folded his saṃghāṭī robe, placed his head upon it, and lay down on his right side.
Then Śāriputra, by means of his supernormal powers, caused [the Buddha] to lie on his back without being aware of it, and addressed the great assembly:
"Your Great Teacher sleeps like an infant."
Then Śāriputra said to Maudgalyāyana, "For the sake of the great assembly, you should quickly manifest supernatural powers to turn their minds toward the Buddha.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately leaped into the air and displayed the four dignified postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. He entered the fire-light samādhi and emitted various radiances of blue, yellow, red, and white; sometimes water flowed from his upper body while fire issued from his lower body, and at other times fire issued from his upper body while water flowed from his lower body. In the east, west, south, and north, he fully manifested these four kinds of supernatural powers.
Having manifested these supernatural powers, he descended from the air and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the great assembly, seeing Mahāmaudgalyāyana endowed with such supernatural powers, felt sorrow and distress in their hearts, thinking:
"If we had served the Buddha, we too should have attained such supernatural powers and spiritual virtue."
Śāriputra addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O Bhikṣus! If you possess sincere devotion toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, you may follow me."
Having heard these words, they immediately followed after Śāriputra to the place where the Buddha was.
After the monastic community had departed, the bhikṣu Kokālika called Devadatta up and ordered him to pursue Śāriputra.

At that time, Śāriputra, fearing that Devadatta would surely die of grief and vomit blood upon not seeing our assembly, proceeded to walk very slowly and gradually so that Devadatta might catch sight of us.
At that time, Devadatta arose from his sleep, rubbed his eyes, and pursued them.

By means of his supernormal powers, Śāriputra created a large, deep pit across the path; Devadatta, Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, and the other four, unaware of it, fell into the pit, becoming bewildered and unable to find the way out.
He further reflected to himself:
"Now that I have lost my followers, I do not know where to seek them; I shall return to my original place.

At that time, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the assembly of monks gradually approached the Buddha’s location. Upon reaching the edge of the Laṇḍaka Bamboo Grove, they wished to see the World-Honored One; yet, overcome with extreme shame and remorse, they were unable to lift their eyes, each reflecting within themselves:
"How could we have committed such an unrighteous act, devoid of shame and remorse?
they asked, as they gradually approached the Buddha and stood before him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, comforted them with a gentle voice:
“O bhikṣus! You have come to me after enduring great exhaustion.

Now, having attained that which is difficult to attain—a human body—you have heard that which is difficult to hear—the Buddha’s Dharma; you have acquired that which is difficult to acquire—the full complement of the six sense faculties; and you have come to fully understand the nature of both good and evil.”

I have already attained the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān. I constantly proclaim the quiescent Nirvāṇa and ultimate Bodhi; I teach that ignorance conditions volitional formations, volitional formations condition consciousness, consciousness conditions name-and-form, name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, the six sense bases condition contact, contact conditions feeling, feeling conditions craving, craving conditions clinging, clinging conditions existence, existence conditions birth, and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; if volitional formations cease, then consciousness ceases; if consciousness ceases, then name-and-form cease; if name-and-form cease, then the six sense bases cease; if the six sense bases cease, then contact ceases; if contact ceases, then feeling ceases; if feeling ceases, then craving ceases; if craving ceases, then clinging ceases; if clinging ceases, then existence ceases; if existence ceases, then birth ceases; if birth ceases, then old age and death cease; and with the cessation of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
"O bhikṣus! You should constantly contemplate and practice the methods for benefiting yourself and others.
These are the dharmas for self-benefit and the benefit of others:"
