If a dharma is unwholesome, without benefit, without happiness, and ultimately unwholesome; and regarding matters pertaining to oneself—such as the food, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites obtained from the four classes of followers—that which is unwholesome and should not be done, one must not do it.
However, one should always practice and train in that which is beneficial for both oneself and others.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the bhikṣus felt joy in their hearts; their nets of doubt were entirely removed, and they became pure both internally and externally.
There were other bhikṣus who, with doubts arising in their minds, asked:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and karma has he now been used to break the harmony of the Saṃgha?
The Buddha then recounted his past karma for the bhikṣus:
"I myself accumulated and performed these actions, and now I myself experience their results; they are not experienced by another."
"O Bhikṣus, you should know that the karma created by sentient beings is experienced by sentient beings, and not experienced by non-sentient things.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution will surely be experienced by oneself.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, in a pure mountain forest, there was a great rishi who had five hundred junior rishis as his retinue, and they all practiced the Way together.
At that time, a visiting rishi came to their abode, but the host did not provide him with proper hospitality or attend to his needs according to the Dharma."
The visiting seer became distressed and resentful; he then broke apart the harmonious assembly of seers and enticed those junior seers, saying:
"I am skilled in various arts of the Way and the five supernormal powers; I shall instruct you, and you should follow me."
Later, when the Great Seer learned of this matter, he exhorted the visiting seer:
"Do not cause a schism in my assembly; it is not the way of a seer.

He spoke skillful and kind words to inspire joy in him. Although he received such words intended to extinguish the dispute, [the visitor] did not cease his exhortations and instead employed further expedients.

At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha in the world who possessed great compassion; having few desires and being content, he was a supreme field of merit who traveled through the world until he gradually arrived at the place where the seer resided.
Seeing that the Pratyekabuddha was so dignified and sublime, the Great Seer felt great joy; he made offerings and paid him respect, then made this aspiration:
"By the merit of these offerings to the Buddha, may I, in the future, attain the power of great wisdom and supernormal faculties."
"Although the guest seer has attained omniscience, may I be able to cause him to split his harmonious assembly.
To summarize the past and present: at that time, the guest seer was none other than my own self.
Among the five hundred rishis was a great lord of rishis; he was Devadatta in person. This was due to that cause and condition.
Dark karma has dark karmic retribution; white karma has white karmic retribution; and karma that is neither dark nor white has karmic retribution that is neither dark nor white.
“O bhikṣus, you should know!
You ought to abandon all unwholesome karma, cultivate and accumulate wholesome karma, and should train yourselves accordingly.
At that time, because they still had doubts, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does that Devadatta act inwardly as if outwardly, and outwardly as if inwardly?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This Devadatta did not cause what was internal to become external, nor what was external to become internal; in the past, he likewise committed such evil deeds. O Bhikṣus!"
Listen attentively as I speak.

Long ago, there was a jackal of gluttonous nature who wandered through villages seeking food in every place. One day, he came to a dyer’s house and, without realizing it, fell into a basin of indigo dye. When the dyer saw him, he dragged him out and threw him onto the ground.

At that time, the jackal rolled about in the ashes and dust; seeing that his body was filthy, foul, and impure, he immediately entered the river to bathe and departed, his fur becoming lustrous and appearing like the color of blue.
At that time, the many jackals, seeing that his fur and color were different from the ordinary, felt great wonder and asked him together: "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am a messenger of Śakra,
King of the Devas, sent to appoint you as the king among birds and beasts.
At that time, the jackal reflected thus:
"The body is that of a jackal, yet its color is not that of its own kind.

Then the pack of jackals collectively informed the lion, who in turn reported it to the Great Lion King. The Lion King immediately dispatched a messenger to investigate whether the matter was true or false.
When the messenger arrived, he saw that blue jackal riding upon a great white elephant, surrounded on all sides by various birds and beasts as if attending upon a king of beasts.
Having seen this, the messenger returned to the king’s presence and related everything in detail, just as before.

Having heard these words, the Great Lion King went with his host to where that assembly was. There he saw the Wild Fox King riding upon a great white elephant, surrounded by various beasts; tigers, leopards, and other powerful creatures served as his immediate attendants, while the lesser wild foxes remained at a distance, keeping their retreat.
Feeling vexed in his heart, he devised a stratagem: among the jackals, he dispatched one to summon the mother of the king.
The mother asked, "What kind of companions does my son have?"
The jackal replied, "There are lions, tigers, and elephants within; I dwell in the outer courtyard.
His mother said:
"You have gone to surely kill my son," he said, and spoke this verse:
"I dwelt in the mountain valleys with joy, Drinking clear, cool water as the seasons turned; Now I am left alone and destitute, My life is at its end."
"If you do not howl like a wild jackal, you shall dwell upon the elephant's back in peace and happiness.
The messenger returned and reported to his kindred, saying, "He is a wild jackal, not of royal lineage; I personally saw his mother in the mountains."
The companions replied,
"We shall try to see for ourselves," and immediately went to that place.
However, it is the nature of wild jackals that if one cries out while the others do not, their body hair falls off.
When the others then cry out as well, the king of the wild jackals thinks to himself:

"If I do not cry out, my hair will fall to the ground; yet if I descend from the elephant and make a sound, I will surely be killed by him. It would be better for me to make a sound while still atop the elephant.
He then let out a cry.
The elephant immediately recognized that this was a wild jackal; he pulled it down with his trunk and trampled it to death with both feet.
A deva in the sky saw this and spoke a verse:
"To dwell inside yet live outside, To be fit for the outside yet occupy the center."
"All these are improper to do, like a wild jackal riding an elephant.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know this:"
In the past, he who reversed those within to be outside and placed those outside in the middle, thereby destroying his own body as the king of wild jackals, was Devadatta.
Due to that perverted karma of the past, even now he likewise breaks the harmony of the Saṃgha, reversing those within to be outside and placing those outside in the middle.
At that time, Devadatta, having failed to catch up with Śāriputra and the others, returned to his own place. Filled with great rage, he beat his followers, Kokālika and the rest, and said to them:
"It is entirely because of you that I have lost my disciples."
At that time, the bhikṣus, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha:
"For what reason did Devadatta, when Śāriputra and others led away his followers, not become angry though he ought to have been;
and why did he suddenly strike them at random, even though they were innocent and had done him no wrong?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“It is not only in this present life that he has engaged in wrongful deeds; in the past as well, he once seduced another man’s wife and wrongfully killed him.”
In the distant past, there was a pair of elephants, husband and wife, who lived in the mountains and marshes.

The female elephant was licentious and consorted with another male; having been seduced, she desired to follow him away, yet she feared her husband would discover their misconduct and cause a conflict.
While her husband was entering the river to bathe, she said to him,
"Who can submerge in the water and remain there for a long time without emerging?
Her husband called out:
"I can," he replied,
and they both dived into the water together.
While he was still submerged, the other two took the opportunity to flee in secret.
Her husband, the elephant, remained submerged in the water for a long time; he emerged once to look, but seeing neither of the two elephants, he dived back in again.
After doing this two or three times until he was utterly exhausted, he finally emerged from the water.
Not finding his wife, he searched for her everywhere within the waters; because of this, he trampled countless sentient beings to death.
At that time, the devas in the sky spoke these verses:
"Though the elephant’s body is vast, His wisdom is exceedingly shallow."
"The good wife was carried off by him, And all sentient beings were slain in vain.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The husband-elephant at that time was none other than Devadatta."
"Now it is likewise: one person performs the deed, while another person suffers the calamity.
At that time, all the bhikṣus had doubts and questioned the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, you possess all-encompassing wisdom. How was it that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were able to employ such skillful means to exhort, transform, guide, and lead these five hundred bhikṣus, causing them to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, coming thus to the place of the Buddha?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It was not only in the present that Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others deceived and delivered them; in past lives as well, they had previously used such stratagems to entice them."
In the distant past, there was a man who lived constantly in the mountains; he was highly skilled in archery and various other arts.
Later, he fathered a daughter, whom he raised until she grew up.
The man thought to himself:
"I must not marry off this daughter of mine hastily.
Only if there is a man whose skill with the bow and sword is similar to my own shall I give her to him in marriage."
Not long after, two men came to practice the arts:
one mastered all five types of arts, while the other mastered only one, failing to acquire the remaining four.
The man then gave his daughter in marriage to the one whose craft was perfected.
The one whose art had not been perfected became resentful and angry; he abandoned them and departed, joining forces with highway robbers as their companion.
Taking a sword with which he intended to kill her husband, he waited for him at a critical crossing.
Not long after, his kinsmen were passing by in a carriage when they encountered a large caravan of merchants about to cross;
he then asked them, "Why do you all not cross?"
He replied, "There are bandits on the road.
The man reported this, saying:
"We shall simply pass through; there is no need for toil or fear.
The people replied, "If you have no fear, please go on ahead first; we shall follow behind you."
Having heard these words, he drove his chariot away at once.
The bandits climbed trees to look from afar; seeing the chariot approaching, they reported to their leader, "A chariot is coming now!"
The bandit sent one man back with these words:
"You should turn back now; there is no need to come past. I have many mighty warriors here. The man replied:
"Though you are exceedingly strong, I am also very strong.
At that time, the bandit leader dispatched five men to engage him in combat, and they all died.
Furthermore, another twenty-one men were dispatched, and they too were all slaughtered.
Later, when the entire multitude came to fight, they were likewise all killed.
Only one former classmate survived; finally, two men engaged in combat.
However, as the husband released his arrows, they were all severed by the bandits with their swords so that he could not harm them; moreover, five hundred arrows had been completely exhausted.
Only one arrow remained, and he lingered there hesitating. His wife asked him, "Why do you not shoot?"
He replied, "Now, the lives of you and I, two people, are both dependent upon this arrow.
This is because I have kept this arrow for my own protection; if I were to release it now, when the enemy comes, they will kill me and you as well."

Upon seeing this, the woman immediately began to dance; while she was moving about, the thief watched her performance with delight and forgot to guard himself. Her husband, watching for his opportunity, then loosed an arrow, and he died instantly upon being struck.
As his life was coming to an end, he spoke this verse:
"This was not that chariot-owner who could kill me;
It was because I gave rise to a defiled mind That I observed another and caused them to lose their life."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know this: was that owner of the carriage anyone else?
He is none other than Śāriputra here."
The wife at that time was none other than Maudgalyāyana today.
The leader of the bandits was Devadatta today.
Just as the caravan leader and his wife both gained the advantage over the bandits in the past, so too do Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana skillfully gain the advantage over Devadatta now.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Rājagṛha at the Amrapālī Grove, attended by Prince Jīvaka.

Then, on the fifteenth day of the fifth month, as King Ajātaśatru was about to enter the rains retreat, the bright moon shone clearly across the sky with a magnificent and beautiful radiance. Together with his ministers, courtiers, queens, and concubines, he stood upon a high terrace and addressed those present, saying:
"Now that the night moon is clear, leisurely, full, and lovely, what do you and I wish to do?"
"It would be fitting for each of you to express your sentiments and request that the matter be addressed.
At that moment, a courtesan replied at once: "Great King!"
"In human life, one must not let the pursuit of pleasure go to waste; this auspicious night is fit for diversion, and to indulge freely in the pleasures of the five senses is the duty of a king.
Another woman spoke again:
"Great King!..."
"I now intend for all the monastics and laypeople of this city of Rājagṛha to gather together in a joyful assembly and enjoy sensual pleasures;
this is the business of the King. Then the Crown Prince Udāyin said, "Great King!..."

"Tonight, under the clear moonlight, the Great King personally leads the fourfold army to punish the rebellious state; that the frontier wastes shall be pacified and the King returns victorious is the King's own business.
Furthermore, there was a great minister who was a follower of the non-Buddhist paths, who said:
"Great King!..."

On this bright moonlit night, when all that meets the eye is serene and tranquil, as the fifteenth day approaches—the time for entering the rains retreat—there are six great teachers, such as the Venerable Pūraṇa, who are honored and followed by others as preeminent leaders among beings; each has a following of five hundred naked disciples who constantly attend upon them.

"Currently, the city of Rājagṛha is about to enter the rainy season retreat and will be able to receive offerings and benefits; it would be appropriate for us to go there to serve and make offerings at your feet, for this is our duty as kings."
Furthermore, the prince Śivaka was seated among the assembly, and the king said to him:
"Śivaka! Why do you remain silent and say nothing at all?"
Sivaka addressed him, saying: "Great King!
On this auspicious occasion, when the bright moon is clear and pure and all people hold it dear, the time for the summer retreat is approaching."

However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great majestic virtue; he has noble disciples whose compassion universally covers all, and as the Teacher of the World and the supreme field of merit, he is currently observing the rains retreat within my grove. It is the duty of a king to personally provide offerings to him.

When King Ajātaśatru heard these words, he immediately arrayed his majestic retinue and mounted a great fragrant elephant. Accompanied by five hundred palace ladies riding five hundred elephants, each holding a bright torch, he went to the Āmrapālī Garden together with his kinsmen.
On the way, the king’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; he then thought to himself:
"Is this Śivaka not in league with the frontier rebels, coming to lure me in and take my life?"
He then asked Jīvaka,
"With how many people does the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, dwell while seated in the garden?
Jīvaka replied:
“Together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The king asked again,
“If you have no ulterior motives, why do I not hear the sound of coughing or clearing of throats from such a large multitude?”
Upatiṣya replied: "That Blessed One’s three karmas are tranquil and his mind is constantly in meditative concentration; his disciples are likewise so. For this reason, there is no sound of clamor."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s mind became resolute, and he was no longer troubled by doubt or difficulty.

He proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling and, having dismounted from his elephant and horse, beheld the World-Honored One together with the great assembly, their faculties serene and tranquil like the ocean. He then prostrated himself on the ground, touching it with his five limbs, and bowed at the Buddha’s feet. Joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, your great compassion and the three karmas are perfectly still; I pray only that you will skillfully guide and instruct my son, so that he may become like the Buddha, forever free from clamor and distraction.”
At that time, the Tathāgata, with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, consoled the king, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!
You should take your seat; whatever doubts or difficulties you may have, feel free to ask."
Once they were seated, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

In this world there are various types of occupations: there are those who bind flower garlands, those who work with bamboo, some who slaughter animals, some who engage in trade, those who train elephants and horses, some who converse, some who practice archery, some who beg for alms, those who fight with valor, serve kings, shave heads, dye, wash, or sew clothes. Those of such diverse classes each seek their livelihood through their own respective occupations, cultivating merit according to their inclinations and indulging in the pleasures of the five desires."
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps any such class of sentient beings who, within this present life, attain the fruits of śrāmaṇya?
At that time, the Buddha turned and asked the king:
“Great King! Regarding this matter, have you ever questioned others about it?
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding this matter, I have already questioned the non-Buddhist teachers such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others.
Those masters replied:”
"In my sutras, I have taught such a doctrine:
there is no good or evil karma, nor is there retribution for good or evil deeds;
there is no giving or sacrifice, nor is there the karmic fruit of giving or sacrificing."
There are no parents, nor the kindness of parents;

there is neither this world nor another world; there is no one who cultivates the path to attain the fruits of holiness, nor are there any holy ones or those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship; once the four great elements have dispersed, there is nothing left upon which to rely.

If anyone should say, "The causes of karma and the fruits of karma in this life and the future life truly exist," all such words are false speech; whether spoken by the wise or uttered by the foolish, both are equally empty.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have heard the various teachings on the true meaning from the six masters, yet they all answered falsely."
It is like a person who, when asked about *āmra* fruits, answers with pears;
or when asked about pears, answers with *āmra* fruits.
The six heretical teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others, answer falsely when questioned correctly.

Although these non-Buddhists and others offered such various heterodox explanations and various heterodox answers, none of them accorded with my intention; nor did I approve of them, but rather departed, having abandoned them.
He further questioned the other six teachers of external paths, such as Maskarī Gośālīputra and others:

"In this world today, among all sentient beings who perform various karmas, engage in various practices, and cultivate various arts and crafts—such as those who serve and support their parents, make offerings to the Triple Gem, and provide for the field of compassion—is there, within these classes of sentient beings, anyone who, by relying on and depending upon these types of karma, has attained the Way or the fruits of sainthood?"
He replied: "In my scriptures it is stated thus: there is no cause and no effect, no good and no evil;

there are no afflictions and no one who abandons them; there is no nirvana and no one who attains it; all causes and effects within the three periods of time are entirely empty and non-existent; everything is simply spontaneous."
The wise are naturally wise; the foolish are naturally foolish.
There is no one who practices, nor is there anyone who attains; there is no self-benefit, nor is there benefit for others. All sentient beings arise without cause and perish without cause.
"In this way, these teachers and others all make such false assertions; they are not well-spoken and are not reasoned.
I ask one thing and they answer another.
Although I heard these various heterodox teachings, they did not enter my mind; I neither rejoiced in them nor accepted them, but took my leave and withdrew."
He went again to where Saṃjayin was and, as before, raised various questions and doubts:

"Sentient beings perform various karmas and various crafts, engaging in the karma of birth and death. Among these karmas, is there any sentient being who, by means of such karma, can exhaust all afflictions and realize the fruit of sainthood?"
He replied: "Great King, you should know! That which I have spoken is the constant teaching for sentient beings:

to kill oneself and to incite others to slaughter; to hack oneself and to cause others to hack; to roast oneself and to cause others to roast; to commit theft oneself and to incite others to steal; to engage in sexual misconduct oneself and to incite others to do so; to speak falsehoods oneself and to incite others to lie; to drink alcohol oneself and to incite others to drink; to plunder oneself and to incite others to plunder; to destroy families and destroy nations; to kill every sentient being encountered—whether walking on the earth or moving through the air—and if one kills immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, or if one constantly kills boundless beings on this side of the Ganges, one commits boundless evil."

On the other shore of the Ganges, they make offerings to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings and perform immeasurable and boundless meritorious deeds; yet these two types of practice are both without cause and without effect, without gain and without loss, and without increase and without decrease.
"World-Honored One!

When I asked about the correct principle, he made various such false statements; when I asked one thing, he answered with another. Having heard this, I was neither pleased nor did I rejoice, so I left him and departed."
Again, I went to another place where Ajita Kesakambalin was staying. When I questioned him as I had previously, he likewise answered as before, saying:
"There are seven things in total; these seven kinds of entities are natural and were not made by another."
It is not born through transformation, nor does it arise from transformation.
It neither aggregates nor disperses; it is eternally spontaneous.
What are the seven?
Earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and life—these seven things cannot be created by anyone, nor do they obstruct one another.

Regarding these seven matters—virtue and non-virtue, as well as suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—whether they are performed or not performed, they are both indeterminate in their manifestation and lack karmic retribution. There is no one who dies, nor is there anyone who kills. Among the fourteen thousand kinds of pleasures, there are further sixty thousand; and as for the evils of threefold, twofold, single, or even half-fold karma—if one can fully commit such various evils, one will immediately attain liberation from the hardships of birth and death.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Twenty.
